notes.content: In most French words, the final consonant is silent. For example, vous sounds like [voo]. And comment is generally pronounced [kohmaeh']- as in line 5. But if the following word starts with a vowel, then the normally silent final consonant of the first word is pronounced and"linked"to the second word: comment‿allez [kohmaeh'-talay]. This link is called a liaison. Listen to the difference in the pronunciation of comment in sentences and 5. We indicate the liaison with an underline ‿between the two words.
bonjour literally means good (bon) day (jour). It can be used as the equivalent of good morning but also as aformal way of saying hello throughout the day until around pm.

allez comes from the irregular verb aller, to go, the verb used to enquire about someone'shealth or well-being (instead of to be in English: How are you?). Allez is the form used with the formal address for you (vous) when speaking to people other than close friends or family.
va is the third-person singular (he/she/it) of aller.
presenter means to present but, in this context, to introduce. Je vous pré sente is the equivalent of May Iintroduce / Iwould like to introduce, etc.

Comment ç a va ? How are you doing? is equivalent to Comment allez-vous ?, but slightly more familiar. Here, Jeanne (the female equivalent of the masculine forename Jean) is talking to her friend's daughter, so she uses aless formal phrase.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: French has two forms of address: formal and familiar. We'll start by learning the honorific, or formal, mode, marked by the pronoun vous, because this is the one you are most likely to encounter when visiting France and interacting with people you don't know. (In other French-speaking countries, such as Canada, the informal address, marked by tu, is used more frequently.) Which form to use in which circumstances is amuch debated issue, but we've adopted the rule of thumb that tu is strictly for family and friends.

extras.title: Smile!
extras.content: Congratulations! In ashort space of time, and without too much effort, you've learned some important - and useful - words and phrases. Remember that the best way to make progress is to learn alittle every day. That'sthe secret of the Assimil method!

un café is both abeverage (a coffee) and the place where you drink it (a café). If you order un café in France, you will get ashot of espresso without milk, also called un expresso or un express.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: France is ahuge country - the largest in western Europe-with an incredibly varied landscape ranging from the rugged granite cliffs of Bretagne, Brittany, to the lush olive groves of southern France. We will learn more about the French regions as we progress: today we've met a Breton and awoman from the area known as le Midi, another word for the south of France. (If you arrive by train in the Belgian capital, Brussels, one of the two main stations is Bruxelles-Midi, so-called because it is in the south of the city.)

notes.content: Le final - zof avez and savez is silent. The same rule applies to rendez in the next sentence.
In line 2, dix is pronounced [dees] because it comes at the end of the sentence. But in 5, it is followed by another word, so the final xis silent [dee meenewt].
Remember that the final - sis (almost) never pronounced.
L'heure (it's feminine) literally means the hour, but we also use the word when asking the time. Avez-vous l'heure ?, Do you have (i.e. can you tell me) the time?
Another very common way of asking aquestion is to put est-ce que (literally,"is it that") before the verb. So Avez-vous l'heure ? and Est-ce que vous avez l'heure ? have the same meaning.
To form the negative, you need two words: ne (or n' before avowel or an h) directly before the verb, and pas directly after it: Je n'ai pas l'heure, I don'thave the time.
French does not have aneutral pronoun such at it. You have to use either il or elle, depending on the gender of the noun. In neutral contexts, such as when you are telling the time, always use il.
We saw in the last lesson that le Midi is the south of France. The word also means noon ("midday").
Here, the article le means it or that. Notice that it is placed before the verb, not afterwards, as in English.

notes.content: French does not have aseparate verb form to express apresent continuous action (e.g. Iam looking). Instead, you use the simple form (I look), which makes life much easier!

le Metropolitain, known universally as le mé tro, is the underground railway system (subway) of major cities such as Paris, Marseille or Lyon. The word is also used to refer to aspecific station: le mé tro Châ telet, the Châ telet metro station, as well as to the train itself. (You can also ask for une station de mé tro, ametro station.)

As we will see throughout this course, asubstantial portion of English vocabulary is derived from French, and, in many cases, the imported words or expressions are quite formal. For instance, while desole is the root of desolate and desolation, it is an ordinary, everyday word equivalent to the Germanic-origin sorry: je suis desole, I'm sorry.

You will notice that French people use madame and monsieur alot when addressing strangers. This is not as formal as it might sound in English, which lacks a convenient, polite way of catching someone's attention.
une ville, acity or a town. French makes no difference between the two.

voilà is the companion word to voici (lesson line 2). In principle, we use voici to designate something or someone located close to us (like here is/are) and voilà for something farther away (there is/are). But in practice, we use voilà in both instances. For instance, Voilà le mé tro, Here'sthe metro station / train. We can also use it at the beginning of asentence to present something or provide information. We'll see voilà and voici again in different contexts in the coming weeks.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: When you start learning a language, you often get the feeling that people are speaking at breakneck speed! In many cases, this is because several words are run together to form asingle sound. In French, this is often due to the liaison, which can make four words such as nous avons une chambre sound like two - or even one: [nooz-ahvoh'zewn sheeh'bruh]. Remember that we do exactly the same thing in English (Iwant to be astar - > [eyewonabeeva-star]). You'll soon get used to listening out for phrases rather than individual words.

notes.content: Gender: This is possibly the biggest difficulty facing English speakers when they start learning French. Every noun is either masculine or feminine. Masculine nouns take the articles le, the, and un, a, an, feminine nouns take la and une. There is no neuter pronoun, like it in English. There are some basic rules for determining the right gender: the words for woman, wife, grandmother, etc. are feminine (we already know une femme and une fille), while those for man, boy, etc. are masculine. So far, so logical. But why is coffee (le café) masculine and aslice of bread (une tartine) feminine? The simple answer is: because! In fact there are some patterns, which you will learn to recognise. But basically you will have to rely on your memory. We suggest you start by writing down every noun you learn, together with both articles (definite and indefinite), under one of two columns. Here's ashort list to help you get started: Masculine nouns: un/le boulevard, un/le café, un/le croissant, un/l'hô tel, un/le lit, un/le mé tro, un/le plan. Feminine nouns: une/la chambre, une/la tartine, une/la fille, une/la fontaine, une/l'heure, une/la minute, une/la montre, une/la nuit, une/la salle de bains. One of the reasons why it is so important to remember genders is that adjectives 'agree' with the noun they describe, and therefore have both amasculine and afeminine form (we saw this briefly in lesson 6: un grand lit / une grande chambre). We'll learn more about agreements very soon.

Verbs: French verbs are divided into three groups, depending on the ending of the infinitive. (Unlike English infinitives, which are formed with to, French infinitives consist of asingle word). By far the largest group comprises verbs ending in - er. We have already seen quite afew of them, including appeler, to call, chercher, to look for, dé sirer, to want, penser, to think, pré senter, to introduce, tourner, to turn, and traverser, to cross. As in English, French verb endings change depending on the 'person' doing the action (think, but she thinks). Let'ssee what we have learned already: je pense, I think, vous pensez, you [formal] think, and nous pensons, we think. As you can see, there are more forms than in English, which generally has just two in the present tense, but you will soon get the hang of them. Remember, too, that there are no continuous verb forms in French, so je cherche means both Ilook for and Iam looking for. We have also seen some parts of akey verb, ê tre, to be, which is irregular. Remember: je suis, I am, il/elle est, he/she/it is, and vous ê tes, you are. This verb is very important because it is used as an auxiliary, as we will see later on. Another major irregular verb is aller, to go: je vais, I go, il/elle va, he/she goes, nous allons, we go, vous allez, you go, ils/elles vont, they go. Both ê tre and aller are used as auxiliaries. Lastly, remember that you need two words, ne (n' before a vowel) and pas, on either side of averb to form a negative: Je n'ai pas l'heure, I don'thave the time; Il n'est pas breton, He'snot Breton. That'senough for the time being. But just think what you're already capable of saying in French after just six lessons!

The Alphabet: As in English, each letter of the French alphabet has a name, which we use when spelling words aloud. Here is atable to help you pronounce the letter names. a[ah] j[zhee] b[bay] k[kah] c[say] l[el] d[day] m[em] e[uh] n[en] f[ef] o[oh] g[zhay] p[pay] h[ash] qbetween [koo] and [kew] i[ee] r[er] s[ess] w[doobluh-vay] t[lay] x[eeks] u[ew] y[ee grek] v[vay] z[zed]. Acouple of the letters are unusual. For instance, yis igrec or Greek i (which is what the Romans used to call it) and wis double vinstead of double u' (wis rarely used in French). When spelling aword or name with adouble letter, for example, Bailly, you can either repeat the letter (l, l) or say double I' (as in English). Lastly, remember that the pronoun je, I, does not take acapital letter unless it is at the beginning of a sentence.

Vocabulary: French is a Romance language, and most of its vocabulary comes from Latin, which can make it sound rather formal or 'starchy' to an English speaker. But this is not the case. It'ssimply that there are very few Anglo-Saxon words in French. Whereas English often has pairs of words, such as kingly and regal, that have similar meanings but slight nuances, French has only one. You'll soon get past the impression of formality. French and English share some of the same roots, so many words are identical. But beware of what we call false friends' - words that look the same in both languages but have different meanings. For example, we saw the word retard, which means late. (Although our word retard has the same etymology, the meaning is certainly not the same!) However, you may recognise retard as the root of our word tardy, so there are definite links. Lastly, in these early stages, be very careful of French words that look the same as their English counterparts but that are pronounced differently. Aclassic example is Jean, which is pronounced [zəehr] and is a man's name. It may be useful to underline these tricky words or note them down, just to remind yourself.

extras.title: Review dialogue
extras.content: 1 - Hello Chloe, how are you? 2 - Very well, thanks. 3 And you? 4 - Very well. Do you have the time? 5 - Sorry, I don'thave a watch. 6 But Ithink it's noon. 7 - How do you know? 8 - Because Ihave ameeting with my daughter 9and she'salways late. 10 - Thanks very much for your help. Don't worry: after only acouple of weeks of regular practice all these new things - pronunciations, word orders, genders and so on - will be almost second nature!

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: The three major cities in France (Paris, Lyon, Marseille) are divided into districts called arrondissements (from the adjective rond, round). Paris has 20 arrondissements numbered from the first, le premier, to the twentieth, le vingtième. In everyday conversation, it is usual to omit the word arrondissement after the figure. Elle habite dans le septième, She lives in the seventh [district]. In Belgium, un arrondissement is asubdivision of one of the country'sten provinces. And in Switzerland, the word refers to an administrative area in the canton of Bern.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: La mairie (from the personal noun un maire, a mayor) is the equivalent of atown hall. (In major cities, each arrondissement has its own mairie, and the principal administrative centre is called l'hôtel de ville). La mairie plays avital part in community life: citizens register births, marriages and deaths there, and they also renew acarte nationale d'identité, or national identity card, (see next lesson), which has to be produced for official purposes (voting, identity checks, etc.) and, sometimes, when picking up aregistered letter or parcel, etc.

notes.content: d'accord is used to express agreement or consent (it'salso the origin of the English word accord). In everyday speech, however, many French speakers simply use the universally understood OK (or even OK, d'accord!)

Unlike English, the possessive adjective in French agrees with the gender of the object possessed, not the owner. In the previous lesson, we learned son bureau. Why son? Because le bureau is masculine. Here, we have son passeport and sa photo (une photo), both of which"belong"to the young boy. But what matters, as far as the possessive adjective is concerned, is the gender of the noun. We'll go into greater detail in Lesson 14.
mê me has several meanings: here it means even. Followed by que it means the same as. For the time being, simply remember this usage. Other forms will crop up later.

Notice how the present simple tense in French can express an immediate future (je vous fais, I'mdoing = Iwill do) as well as the auxiliary can (je ne trouve pas, I don'tfind = I can't find). Don'tworry about the rule for the time being; just remember these two examples.
regler is aformal way of saying to pay (similar to our settle up). Une caisse is acash desk, checkout, etc.
Zut! I a mild, inoffensive expletive to express annoyance, similar to our damn, heck, etc.

avoir besoin de, to need. Note that in very formal English, we use exactly the same construction: to have need of.

quelque, some / a few. It takes an 's' in the plural. Quelques champignons, afew mushrooms. Quelqu'un, somebody; quelque chose, something. Quelque part, somewhere.

notes.content: des in this context is an indefinite article. It is often translated by some in English: Je veux des fraises, Iwant some strawberries, but, depending on the context, it can also be omitted (Iwant strawberries). We now know all three indefinite articles: un (masculine), une (feminine) and des (plural for both genders).

Allez-yis auseful expression whenever you want someone to go ahead and do something, try something out, walk in front of you, etc. It is translated by Go on / Go ahead, etc. It can also be used in the first person plural: Allons-y, Let'sgo and with the familiar form of you, which we will learn in due course.
bio is an shortened form of biologique (literally"biological"). It means organic. Because the adjective is idiomatic, it does not agree with the noun.

combien (de), how much / how many? Combien de kilos ?, How many kilos? Combien de beurre ?, How much butter? The phrase Ils / Elles sont à combien ? is a common, idiomatic way of asking the price of something.

As we have seen, cher - like all adjectives - agrees in number and gender with its noun. Masculine adjectives ending in"er"are changed to feminine by putting agrave accent over the"e"and adding a final, silent"e": le beurre n'est pas cher, la livre de fraises est cher; the butter isn't expensive; the pound of strawberries is expensive. When used as an adverb, cher always takes the masculine form: C'est trè s cher, it'svery expensive. As we progress, we'll learn more about how the masculine gender takes precedence over the feminine.
tout is used as an indefinite pronoun, meaning everything. See lesson note 3.

notes.content: Qu'est-ce means What is thislthat. But in everyday French, we usually add... que c'est (literally... that it is), sa we say qu'est-ce que c'est... ?. There is no difference in meaning, and the answer starts with C'est...

We know that adjectives usually come after the nouns they qualify: un té lé phone portable, amobile phone. But some are placed before the noun. That is the case with nouveau (feminine: nouvelle), new. We will learn more about these exceptions later on. (Incidentally, the French word for aphone with computer functions is... un smartphone).

pouvez and peux are respectively the second person plural and the second person singular of the verb pouvoir, can / to be able to. The first person plural is pouvons. Notice that the verb which follows pouvoir is in the infinitive: vous pouvez essayer mon té lé phone, you can try my phone.

Some English verbs that are followed by apreposition (pay for, listen to, look at, etc.) are expressed with asingle verb in French: é couter la musique, listen to music; payer un repas, to pay for a meal. There are no hard-and-fast rules on adding these prepositions, so the best way to remember any differences between French and English is to write them down.

marcher mea nsto walk (it'sthe origin of our word march), but the verb is used colloquially in the sense of to function, to work. Cette montre ne marche pas, This watch isn't working. The expression Ca marche ! is used idiomatically to indicate that the person being addressed understands or agrees. - Deux cafes s'il vous plait. - Ca marche ! - Two coffees please. - Coming up!

There are two ways of saying Iknow in French. We say je sais when referring to afact or some other abstract thing, and je connais for aperson or a place. Je connais sa mè re, Iknow his/her mother. Nous ne connaissons pas cette ville, We don'tknow this town. Isait beaucoup de choses, He knows many things. Both verbs are irregular, and the infinitives are savoir and connaî tre. We'll see them again later on.

notes.content: Possessive adjectives: Look at these examples: my father, mon pè re; my mother, ma mè re; my brother, mon frè re; my sister, ma sœur. The possession word (adjective) changes if the singular noun is masculine or feminine. For the plural, the word is mes [may] irrespective of the gender: mes parents, mes enfants. For your, our and their, we have one singular form and one plural form, irrespective of gender: votre carte, your card; votre pè re; vos parents; notre bureau; nos amis; leur adresse; leur maison; leurs photos. (The plural sis silent unless the noun begins with a vowel; leurs amis.) Be careful: the rule for his and her (its) is slightly different from English, where we say his if the possessor is masculine and her if feminine. In French however, the words for his/her/its are adjectives and must therefore agree with the noun they qualify. So son bureau can mean: his or her office; we use son because bureau is masculine. In the same way sa mè re can be his or her mother. The plural is ses: ses enfants, his or her children. There is one exception to these rules of agreement: if the qualified noun begins with a vowel, we use the masculine adjective to make pronunciation easier. e.g. *sa amie would be difficult to pronounce (rather like"a apple"); so we say son‿amie and mon‿amie, allowing the context to show whether the friend is male or female.

Verbs ending in -er: In the last set of lessons we have seen many different verbs with infinitives ending in -er. This is the largest category of French verbs, with literally thousands of"members:"Let'slook at an example: aimer; to like Ito love: j'aime, il/elle aime, nous aimons, vous aimez, ils/elles aiment (the final -ent is silent). As we mentioned in the first lesson, there is also an informal mode of address, tu, which we'll see later on. This is the pattern for all -er verbs. Do you remember these? acheter to buy, commander to order, demander to ask, é couter to listen to, envoyer to send, essayer to try, habiter to live, marcher to walk, to function (idiomatic), parler to speak, payer to pay (for), regarder to look at, rentrer to return, té lé phoner to phone. Note that the past participle, seen briefly in lesson 9, is formed simply by dropping the final rof the infinitive and putting an accent on the final e: trouver → trouvé; aimer → aimé, payer → payé, etc. The pronunciation does not change.

faire and pouvoir: Now that you know aller and ê tre, here are two more important irregular verbs: - Faire translates two English verbs: to do and to make: je fais, il/elle fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils/elles font Qu'est que nous pouvons faire pour vous ?, What can we do for you? Je fais quelque chose à manger, I'mmaking something to eat. - Pouvoir also has more than one meaning, though all of them are connected to the idea of ability or possibility: can, to be able, may, etc. je peux, il/elle peut, nous pouvons, vous pouvez, ils/elles peuvent: Est-ce que vous pouvez prendre des cerises au marché s'il vous plaî t ?, Can you get some cherries at the market please? Vous ne pouvez pas faire ç a, You're not allowed to do that. (The noun le pouvoir means power.)

C'est: It is: We have seen two ways of saying it is: c'est and il est (or elle est with afeminine noun). There is adifference between the two. We use c'est to explain what athing (or who a person) is: Qu'est-ce que c'est ? - C'est une photo de famille. What is it? - It's afamily photo. Regardez, c'est mon cadeau, Look, that'smy present. or to say: It'sme - C'est moi; It'syou - C'est vous; or if the noun is qualified by an adjective: C'est un bon ami, He's agood friend. The plural is ce sont. Ce sont mes bons amis, They are my good friends. Il / elle est is used to refer to anoun just mentioned: Où est le beurre ? - Il est sur la table. Where is the butter? - It'son the table. Où est votre femme ? - Elle est au marché Where is your wife? - She'sat the market. We also use il est if we are talking about the weather: Il pleut, It's raining. Il fait beau, It's fine. or telling the time: Il est huit heures et demie, It'shalf past eight.

Adjectives: 5.1 Masculine and feminine forms: As a rule, we form the feminine singular of an adjective by adding an eto the masculine: petit (small) ⇒ petite; blond (blond / fair-haired) ⇒ blonde; fort (strong) ⇒ forte. It'simportant to remember that some masculine adjectives end in -eand do not therefore change when used with afeminine noun: un placard vide, an empty cupboard; un té lé phone (portable), amobile phone. But if the masculine ending is -e, we do add an e: occupé (busy) → occupé e; fatigué (tired) → fatigué e. Masculine adjectives ending in -er form their feminine by replacing the ending with -è re: dernier (last) → derniè re; premier (first) → premiè re. Another group of masculine adjectives ending in -eux replace the xby -se in the feminine: heureux (happy) → heureuse; dé licieux (delicious) → dé licieuse. There are acouple more rules and afew irregular forms, which we will learn later on. 5.2 Before or after? We know that adjectives are generally placed after the noun they qualify but that some are placed before it. These are the words that describe beauty, age, goodness and size. Think BAGS: Beauty: beau (beautiful), joli (pretty); Age: vieux (old), jeune (young), nouveau (new); Goodness: bon (good), mauvais (bad), gentil (kind / nice), vrai (true); Size: grand (big), petit (small), haut (high / tall), gros (fat). Some of these adjectives are new to you but don't worry: we'll see them all again in the near future. There are few more that do not fall into these categories; we will point them out as we go along.

extras.title: Smile!
extras.content: So much for the rules. In time you will"feel"the correct usage, so don'ttry to do too much at once. But from now on, when you memorize the gender of a noun, try adding asimple adjective (grand or petit, for instance) and making it agree: this will help you to acquire the right reflexes very quickly.

notes.content: We know that possessive adjectives have singular, plural, masculine and feminine forms (lesson 7). So, when used in acompound word - monsieur (mon sieur), madame (ma dame), mademoiselle (ma demoiselle), respectively"my sire," "my lady," "my damsel" - they follow the usual agreement rule: monsieur → messieurs, etc. Acasual way of greeting a mixed-sex group of people - often heard in café s and bistros - is Messieurs-dames, bonjour, Good morning ladies and gentlemen. The phrase should be recognised but not used.
Anumber of French words are identical or very similar to English words but have different meanings. Actual means current, and the adverbial form actualement means currently NOT actually.
Remember that any verb which follows pouvoir, to be able to, is always in the infinitive.

Learning the gender of French nouns is vital, especially since some have two genders, each with adifferent meaning. Here'san example: le tour (masculine) is atour whereas la tour means atower (monument, tower block, etc.) Another example is la livre (see lesson note 4), apound (sterling, weight), and un livre, a book. Only ahandful of these dual-gender nouns are used in everyday conversation, but they have to be learned! We'll look at them in greater detail at the end of the course.

We have already seen two ways to attract attention when asking a question: Pardon (lesson 4) and Excusez-moi (lesson 5). You can also use s'il vous plaî t, please, in exactly the same way: S'il vous plaî t, où est le mé tro ? Please can you tell me where the metro is?
Some nouns are singular in English but plural in French, or vice versa. Agood example is les toilettes, the toilet. We'll learn more of these words as we progress.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: La place (or Place) de la Concorde is alarge public square at the bottom of les Champs-Elysées (literally"Elysian Fields"), one of the main thoroughfares in Paris. It is close to le musée du Louvre (Louvre museum), one of the world'sgreatest art galleries that houses treasures such as La Joconde (the Mona Lisa), la Vénus de Milo (Venus of Milo) and La liberté guidant le people, ("Liberty Guiding the People,"the painting by Eugène Delacroix that symbolises the French republic).

notes.content: When the masculine adjective grand is followed by aword beginning with a vowel, for example architecte, the final -dis pronounced as a twhen making the liaison: [groeh'tarsheetekt].

on is the third person singular impersonal pronoun. It has the same meaning as one in English but is much less formal. In practical use, it can replace either nous (we) - On est en retard, We're late-or the passive voice: On appelle Paris"la Ville lumiè re", Paris is called the City of Light. We'll see this quirky pronoun in greater detail later on.

The adjective grand, big, can be used to mean great, eminent, etc. Like all adjectives, it agrees in gender and number with its noun: un grand architecte (agreat architect), une grande ville (abig OR great city), ses grands magasins (its big stores), ses grandes avenues (its major avenues). See Culture Note below. Also, the adjective vieille is the irregular feminine form of vieux (old).
The second person (singular and plural) is used without apronoun as an imperative: Regardez ! Look! The negative form is regular: Ne traversez pas ! Don't cross!

Just because an adjective ends in edoes not necessarily mean that it'sin the feminine form. Adjectives such as superbe, superb, facile, easy, malade, ill, and moderne, modern, are both masculine and feminine. See lesson 21.

Likewise, not all nouns ending in - eare feminine. This is particularly true with words relating to professions, such as un architecte, an architect. However, the feminine form can be formed simply by changing the article: une architecte. This is arecent development in the French language, which we'll discuss later in the course.

Some masculine adjectives ending in aconsonant are changed to the feminine by doubling the last letter and adding an e: bon → bonne (good), ancien → ancienne (ancient, old). To make the plural, simply add an - sto either form. See lesson 14.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Literally, un grand magasin means abig shop, but the term usually refers to adepartment store. In Paris, several such stores can be found along les Grands Boulevards near the Opera. Another famous landmark in that neighbourhood is le Cafe de la Paix, which opened in the mid-19th century and was frequented by famous composers, writers and intellectuals during La Belle Epoque, the period of peace and prosperity that preceded the first world war. Lutèce (Lutetia in Latin) is the name of the Gallo-Roman city that eventually became Paris. Today the toponym can be found in the names of cafes, restaurants, hotels and other business all over France.

notes.content: The interrogative adjective quel is the equivalent of what or which. Quel est votre nom ? What is your name. Like all adjectives, it agrees in number and gender with the associated noun (qu'elle heure, quelles choses). See lesson 21.
Several English words ending in - ect come from French (via Latin). To find a French equivalent, simply remove the c. Thus aproject → un projet, asubject → un sujet, an object → un objet.

il y a (literally"it there has") is an invariable construction that basically means there is or there are: Il y aune exposition, There is an exhibition; Il y adeux choses, There are two things. (Be careful: when used with an expression of time, il y ait means ago: Il y atrois jours, Three days ago. We'll see this again when we learn the past tense).

avoir envie de (the root of our word envy) means to want to, to feel like: J'ai envie de voir mes cadeaux, Iwant to see my presents. Envie is invariable but the verb avoir has to be conjugated (see lesson 21). The construction is similar in form to avoir besoin de (see lesson note 3).

devoir means both must and to have to (French makes no distinction between the two notions). The verb is irregular: je dois, tu dois, il/elle doit (all three pronounced [dwa]), nous devons ([duhvo"]), vous devez ([duhway]), ils doivent ([dwa]). Any verb immediately following devoir is in the infinitive: il doit aller..., he must/has to go to...
The 24-hour clock is used not only in official or formal settings; it is frequently found in ordinary conversation, too. See lesson 21.

Many words, especially long ones, are abbreviated in everyday usage (the process is known as apocope). Rather than une exposition or le petit-dé jeuner, for example, it'scommon to hear une expo and le petit-dé j. Although you should avoid using such familiar terms, it'simportant to recognise and understand them.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Contrary to what many visitors to France may think (along with many Parisians), Paris is not the only city with cultural treasures aplenty. Of course, the likes of Marseille, Lyon and Toulouse have many spectacular museums and monuments, but so do smaller towns like Lens, which houses an outpost of the Louvre, and Metz, home to part of the Paris-based Pompidou Arts Centre. One of the more original attractions can be found in the former textile capital of Roubaix: La Piscine is an art museum housed in what was once an Art Deco swimming bath, hence the name. Anyone spending time in France should wander off the beaten track to discover its rich and diverse cultural heritage, or le patrimoine culturel.

notes.content: The -ille termination is pronounced [-eevy], more or less as in the English word tea. For example, the old Parisian fortress La Bastille is pronounced [lah basteeyy].

la journé e, the day, refers to the period between dawn and dusk: toute la journé e means the whole day (or daytime) rather than aspecific day or moment in that day, for which we use le jour: le jour de mon mariage, the day of my wedding. A common, and useful, leave-taking expression is Bonne journé e, Have agood day.

By now you are familiar with the partitive articles de, de la and des, reviewed in lesson 21. But de also means from (for example II est de Nimes, lesson 3). When talking about aperiod of time (from... to/till), we say de... à (de neuf heures à dix heures, from until o'clock) but if the following noun is preceded by le, la or les, the partitive becomes du, de la or des, respectively. For example, le lundi et le jeudi → du lundi au jeudi.
regretter, to regret, can be used in conversation when refusing something politely: Je regrette mais je ne peux pas venir demain, I'msorry but I can'tcome tomorrow.

charge, the adjective and past participle of charger, to load, is one of les faux-amis, or false friends, discussed in lesson 7. Used in connection with atimetable or programme, it means to have aheavy schedule or to be very busy (i.e."laden"with work).

un voyage has abroader scope than its English cognate, referring to travel in general (rather than just asea voyage). It basically means ajourney or atrip - Le voyage en bus est trè s long. The journey by bus is very long - but can also refer to travel in general: une agence de voyages, atravel agency. Be careful not to confuse une journé e (see note 1) with a journey.

Other examples of faux-amis (see note 4) include un stage, acourse or an internship, and la formation, training or continuing education; and un agenda (line 13), a schedule. It'simportant to remember these false cognates because they can have very different meanings from one language to the other.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: One of the pleasures of learning alanguage is discovering how common words or terms are used in culture-specific ways. Take, for example, le pont, meaning abridge (le pont de la Concorde, for example). The word also refers to the French custom of taking an extra day off work if apublic holiday falls, say, on a Tuesday or Thursday, in order to make along weekend. The expression in this case is faire le pont ("to make the bridge"). Another culture-specific term is la rentrée, which comes from the verb rentrer, to go back in, and generally refers to the start of the new academic year (called officially la rentrée scolaire), when students go back to school. But the term is used more broadly to means any post-holiday"return,"such as la rentrée politique, when parliamentarians return after the summer recess, or la rentrée littéraire, the period in September/October when new books are published ahead of the literary award season.

notes.content: The adjective beau has several meanings: handsome, beautiful, lovely, great, etc. It is also irregular: the feminine form is belle and the masculine plural is beaux. But because French does not permit ahiatus (abreak between the terminal vowel sound of one word and the initial vowel of the following word), for example un"beau endroit, there is another masculine form: bel: un bel endroit. The same rule applies to nouveau/nouvelle (new): nouvel an (new year). Three other adjectives have this additional masculine form. (We have seen asimilar construction with ce/cette: ce matin, cette femme, but cet aprè s-midi). Note that une belle-famille (with a hyphen) has nothing to do with beauty: it means a family-in-law, usually consisting of une belle-mè re (mother-in-law) and un beau-pè re (father-in-law).

combien is auseful word (lesson note 4). Remember that it translates both how much and how many. One useful phrase is Ç a coû te combien ? or Combien est-ce que ç a coû te ? How much does it cost? (from the verb coû ter, to cost).

The termination - aine can be added to acardinal number, generally amultiple of ten or five (dix, quinze, vingt, etc.), to indicate an approximation (une dizaine, about 10, une quinzaine, about 15, une vingtaine, about 20). Note that une douzaine can mean about twelve OR, when buying eggs, adozen (une douzaine d'œufs).

The difference between the two words for the evening, le soir et la soiré e, is the same as for le matin and la matiné e. But une soiré e can also mean an event held in the evening, such as une soiré e dansante, adinner dance.

The adjective free has two translations: the first, seen in the previous lesson, is libre (i.e. no commitments or engagements: J'ai une soiré e libre, Ihave afree evening); the second is gratuit (absence of cost: Le bus est gratuit ce soir, The bus is free this evening) Moreover, gratuit is the root of the English word a gratuity, something given freely as a gift.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: La Basilique du Sacré Cœur (Basilica of the Sacred Heart) is afamous late nineteenth-century church located atop la Butte Montmartre, the hill overlooking Paris. Built of white stone with aflamboyant Byzantine-style dome, it is sometimes called la grosse meringue ("the great meringue") by its detractors but it is nevertheless one of the most recognisable buildings in the capital.

notes.content: We know that au (to the) is the equivalent of ala for masculine nouns (lesson note 1). Aux is the plural form for both genders: Cet é té, nous allons aux É tats-Unis (masc.) / Je vais aux toilettes (fem.). Like all plural endings, the - xis silent [oh] unless it precedes a vowel.

Country names, like all nouns, are either masculine or feminine. Most of those ending in - eare feminine (la France, la Belgique (Belgium), l'Italie (Italy), etc.); the others are masculine. Some toponyms are plural, notably les É tats-Unis, the United States. There are afew exceptions, which we will see later.
Adjectives of nationality do not take an initial capital (l'ambassadeur amé ricain, the American ambassador), but nouns of nationality do: un(e) Amé ricain(e), an American man/woman.

The partitive articles du, de la and des give information about the quantity of the noun they precede. They are often translated by some/ any but, in some cases, can be omitted in English. Du and des are the combined forms of de le and de les, respectively (see lesson note 1). Il veut du pain, de la crè me et des champignons, He wants (some) bread, (some) cream and (some) mushrooms. If asingular noun following apartitive begins with avowel (or an h), the article becomes de l', whatever the noun's gender: (de l'argent, masc.; de l'é ducation, fem.). Yet another good reason for learning genders!

Despite the final - s, pays can be singular as well as plural (mon pays, my country, nos pays, our countries). The same applies to nouns ending in - x (le prix/les prix, price/prices) and - z, as we will see later on.

vrai(e), true, can also mean real (la vraie ré ponse, the real answer) The exclamation Ce n'est pas vrai !, It isn't true! can also be used (as in sentence 12) to mean I don'tbelieve it!, You're kidding! In everyday usage, careless speakers tend to drop the negative particle n', but don'tbe tempted to imitate them!

notes.content: ê tre, avoir and vouloir: These are three of the most common verbs in French. The first two - ê tre and avoir-are main verbs as well as auxiliaries, just like their English counterparts to be and to have. All three are irregular (or"strong") verbs. ê tre,to be: je suis, tu es*, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous* ê tes, ils/elles sont. avoir,to have: j’ai, tu as*, il/elle a, nous avons, vous* avez, ils/elles ont. vouloir,to want: je veux, tu veux*, il/elle veut, nous voulons, vous* voulez, ils/elles veulent. *tu is the familiar form (see below). French, like many languages, has both aformal and an informal way of addressing people. The corresponding pronouns are vous (formal) and tu (informal). For the time being, we will concentrate on using vous (the verb is vouvoyer), which is always the case when talking to astranger or aperson to whom we want to show respect. Vous is also the second person plural pronoun, used when addressing more than one person. Like all verbs, the negative of vouloir is formed with two words: ne (or n' before avowel or mute h) and pas (see lesson 7). Je ne suis pas libre demain, I'mnot free tomorrow. Elle n'apas de projets, She doesn'thave any plans. Nous ne voulons pas venir, We don'twant to come. The interrogative can be formed in three ways, depending on the context: - simply by raising the voice at the end of an affirmative sentence: Vous voulez venir? You want to come? This is very informal (but also very common); - by adding est-ce que (literally"is it that") before the pronoun: Est-ce que vous voulez venir? Do you want to come? (see lesson note 2). This is the usual construction in everyday spoken French; - by inverting the pronoun and the verb Voulez-vous venir? Do you want to come? This is the most formal of the three constructions. These negative and interrogative forms are used for all French verbs. Choosing the right one will depend on the person speaking and the context. For the time being, go back over the previous lessons and take note of the constructions we have used.

Agreement of nouns and adjectives: We know that adjectives agree in number and gender with the nouns they qualify. Here are some basic rules for identifying noun genders (though there are quite afew exceptions). 2.1 Nouns: In many cases, the gender can be identified by its ending. - Most nouns ending in -age and -eau are masculine. For example, l'â ge (age), un stage (atraining course), un bureau (an office/a desk), un cadeau (a gift). Two notable exceptions are une image (a picture) and l'eau (water). Another typical masculine ending is - er: le dé jeuner (lunch) or - ier, le quartier (the neighbourhood). Both these terminals are often found in the nouns for jobs or professions: un boulanger (a baker), un banquier (a banker), and so on. Finally, nouns that end in - in are generally masculine: un jardin (a garden), le matin (the morning). Possibly the most common exception is la fin (the end). - The majority of nouns ending in -ion and -te are feminine: une ré gion (a region), l'é ducation (education), la santé (health), la liberté (freedom, liberty). Two exceptions are le cô té (the side) and l'avion (the plane). Likewise, the -é e most ending is usually feminine, for instance la soiré e (the evening), une idé e (an idea). One of the very few exceptions is un musé e (a museum). There are several other"typical"endings, which we will see in lesson 28. 2.2 Adjectives: We have learned the basic rules for the agreement of adjectives, but some of them have an irregular feminine form. Here are three common ones: le lait frais (masc. fresh milk) → une fraise fraî che (fem. afresh strawberry) - note the circumflex on the i; le vin blanc (masc. white wine) → une carte blanche (fem. awhite card); un long moment (masc. along time/moment) → une longue avenue (fem. along avenue). To form the plural, simply add the final s. We saw in lesson that ahandful of the adjectives coming before anoun have two masculine forms, depending on the first letter of the following word: avowel (or h) or a consonant. In addition to beau and nouveau, the third commonly used adjective is vieux: un vieux monument (an old monument) but un bel endroit (apretty place or spot). Note that bel is pronounced in exactly the same way as the feminine form belle. Finally, twenty or so adjectives ending in - eare both masculine and feminine. In addition to superbe, facile, malade and moderne (lesson 16), vide (lesson 18) and honnê te (lesson 20), three others worth learning are fable, weak, pauvre, poor, and triste, sad. You will also recognise confortable, comfortable (note the n), drô le, funny (the origin of droll) and sincè re, sincere, genuine.

Days, months, and dates: The days of the week are: lundi Monday, mardi Tuesday, mercredi Wednesday, jeudi Thursday, vendredi Friday, samedi Saturday, dimanche Sunday. The final syllable, - di, is from the Latin dies, a day, found in the English equivalents (Monday, etc.). As for the weekend, most people in France (and Belgium) use the same word, le week-end (note the hyphen), rather than the preferred term la fin de semaine (litt."the end of week"), which is used in Canada. The months of the year are: janvier January, fé vrier February, mars March, avril April, mai May, juin June, juillet July, aoû t August, septembre September, octobre October, novembre November, dé cembre December. None of the day or month nouns take an initial capital (unless they start a sentence) and are all masculine. When giving the date, French uses acardinal number, not an ordinal, and puts the masculine definite article before the day, not the month, as in English: le lundi dix mai, Monday the tenth of May, le jeudi vingt et un aoû t, Thursday the twenty-first of August.

Telling the time: French has two main words for time: le temps (ameasured or measurable period) and l'heure, afeminine noun that literally means the hour but is used to give the precise time. To ask the time, always use the inverted question form (never est-ce que): Quelle heure est-il ? What time is it? (Here il is the impersonal pronoun, performing the same function as it in English.) - There is no equivalent of o'clock. Simply put heures (or heure for am or pm) after the hour: Il est une heure, It'sone o'clock, Il est quatre heures; It'sfour o'clock. - For minutes past the hour, use the cardinal and invert the word order: Il est trois heures dix, It'sten past three; Il est six heures vingt-cinq, It's twenty-five past six. - For minutes before the next hour, use moins (less, minus) after the cardinal: Il est une heure moins dix, It'sten to one, Il est onze heures moins vingt, It'stwenty to eleven. - For the quarter-hours, we use et quart and moins le quart, placed after the word heure(s): Il est deux heures et quart, It's aquarter past two, Il est huit heures moins le quart, It's aquarter to eight. Note the difference with the English word order. - The term for half past is et demie, placed after the hour. Demi means half, and, since une heure is feminine, we add afinal e (but no s): Il est neuf heures et demie, It'shalf past nine. - The words for midday (noon) and midnight are midi [meedee] and minuit [minwee]. - French uses the twenty-four hour clock, not only in official contexts such as appointments and travel or broadcasting schedules, but in everyday conversation, too: treize heures pm, quatorze heures pm, quinze heures pm, seize heures pm, dix-sept heures pm, dix-huit heures pm, dix-neuf heures pm, vingt heures pm, vingt et une heures pm, vingt-deux heures pm, vingt-trois heures pm, vingt-quatre heures midnight. The hour is followed simply by the number of minutes (et quart and moins le quart are not used): Il est seize heures trente, It'shalf past four (in the afternoon); Il est dix-neuf heures quarante, It'stwenty to eight in the evening.

notes.content: The double-lsound is pronounced in several ways. One of the trickiest is -ill-preceded by a consonant, which it is usually pronounced [eev]. We already know fille (fieeyy) and Bastille (basteeeyy). The same applies to grille (greeeyy). But there are exceptions: mille in line is [meef]. We recommend keeping alist of the various pronunciations so as not to get confused.

Most nouns ending in - eu form the plural with - x: un jeu, des jeux (game(s)), un feu, des feux (fire(s)). Another set of nouns with an irregular ending are those ending in - al. The Iis deleted and replaced by - ux: un cheval, des chevaux (horse(s)), un journal, des journaux (newspaper(s)). There are acouple more of these irregular forms, which we will learn later on.

tous is the masculine plural of the adjective tout, all. Placed before a noun, it is pronounced [too], just like the singular (tous les jeux, all the games → [too lay zheu]). But if tous comes after a verb, it means all of you/them/ everyone, and is pronounced [toos]: je les aime tous, Ilike all of them → [zhe layzem toos]. Always check the preceding word before trying to pronounce tous!

Mais non !, literally"But no!", is an emphatic contradiction, equivalent to Of course not! or Not at all! Vous ê tes malade ? - Mais non, je vais trè s bien ! Are you ill? - Not at all, I'mvery well! Another common exclamatory expression, in line and line 13, is Au fait, literally"to the fact."Placed at the beginning of a sentence, it means By the way. Au fait, quel est votre nom ? By the way, what'syour name?

é tablis is the first person singular of é tablir, to establish, to draw up. It belongs to the second major group of verbs, which end in - ir and are conjugated like this: j'é tablis, tu é tablis, il/elle é tablit, nous é tablis-sons, vous é tablissez, ils/elles é tablissent. Other common verbs in this group are choisir, to choose, finir, to finish, remplir, to fill, and ré flé chir, to think, reflect. (More details in the next lesson and an overview in lesson 28.)
choisissez is the second person plural and honorific singular form of choisir (see above). Note the pronunciation: [shwahzeessay].

gagner means to win: Elle gagne toujours quand elle joue, She always wins when she plays. But it also means to earn (money): Il gagne cinq mille euros par mois, He earns five thousand euros per month. Note the context whenever you come across this very common verb. Un(e) gagnant(e), awinner (male/female).

un sou is the name of an old French coin. It no longer exists, but the word still crops up in popular expressions –Je n’ai pas un sou, I don'thave a penny/a bean; Il est sans le sou, He doesn'thave a bean-as well as in the familiar term une machine a sous, aslot machine. (Pay attention to the context: sous is also apreposition meaning under).

notes.content: Pay attention when you come across a French word with the same spelling as an English word: the pronunciation is generally different. For example, la queue and le secret are pronounced [la kuh] and [luh suhkray], respectively.

Remember to always learn the preposition or adverb that usually follows a verb, particularly when the equivalent English verb does not have one. Here, jouer, to play, is followed by aif the object noun is feminine (jouer à la loterie, to play the lottery), au for amasculine singular noun (jouer au loto, to play the lotto) and aux for amasculine or feminine plural: jouer aux é checs, to play chess.

The negative particle pas is followed by de (or d' before a vowel) regardless of whether the following noun is singular or plural: I n'apas de billets, He doesn'thave any tickets; Elle n'apas d'argent, She doesn'thave any money.

The idiomatic adjective sympa is an abbreviated form of sympathique, equivalent to nice, pleasant, etc. Michel est une personne trè s sympa, Michel's areally nice person. Because the word in an abbreviation, it is invariable in the singular, but it takes afinal - sin the plural: Ce sont des personnes trè s sympas, They're really nice people. Note that sympa is as imprecise as nice - and just as common!

autre is an indefinite adjective, like tout, that is used to give ageneral description: Choisissez un autre chiffre, Choose another figure. When followed by aplural noun, it is preceded by the partitive d': Choisissez d’autres chiffres, Choose other figures. Now look back at lesson sentence 1, and lesson sentence 5.

dire (pronounced [deer]) is an important irregular verb that translates both to say and to tell. The present tense is je dis, tu dis, il/elle dit, nous disons, vous dites, ils/elles disent. Sami dit qu’il est dé solé, Sami says he’svery sorry. Dites-moi votre nom, Tell me your name. We’ll learn more about the subtle differences in construction later on.

tout à fait (“all to fact”) is acommon expression of agreement or a confirmation, equivalent to Exactly or Absolutely: Ê tes-vous prê t ? – Tout à fait, Are you ready? – Absolutely. It can also be used for emphasis: Je suis tout à fait d’accord, Itotally agree. Remember that French does not use an auxiliary to add emphasis (Ido like that game), so expressions such as tout à fait are very common.

toujours comes after the verb, in contrast to always: Nous jouons toujours aux mê mes jeux, We always play the same games. And whereas English makes adifference between always and still, toujours covers both notions: Est-ce que tu habites toujours à Toulouse ? Do you still live in Toulouse?

The terms for numbers, figures, digits and numerals are awkward to translate because the terms are not always used precisely. Thus un chiffre, which give us the English word cipher, refers to awritten figure or a digit: le chiffre sept translates as the figure 7, and un numé ro refers to aspecific unit such as aphone number or ahouse number (numé ro de té lé phone / de maison. To complicate matters slightly, there is also the word un nombre, which we will see later on.

Second-group verbs ending in - ir are characterised by their present participle, which ends in - issant (finir → finissant, applaudir → applaudissant, ré ussir → ré ussissant, etc.): Il choisit tous les numé ros finissant par huit, He chooses all the numbers finishing in eight.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Cafés are an essential feature of everyday life in France. The generic name, un café, is subdivided into several categories, notably un tabac (literally tobacco) or un bar-tabac, acafé that also sells tobacco products, newspapers, phone cards, postage and tax stamps and lottery tickets. That is where this 23rd lesson takes place. As the name un café implies, the basic drink is coffee, served either as an espresso or with milk (un café crème or un café au lait).

notes.content: More about the double-lsound (see lesson 22). If - ll-is preceded and followed by asingle vowel, it is pronounced simply as an [l] (mademoiselle, [mahduhmwazel]). When preceded by two vowels, it reverts to apalatised sound (like boy in English), which we have represented here by [yy]. The pronunciation of the previous syllable depends on the vowel combination. Thus oreille and vieille are pronounced [ohrayy] and [vyayy], while feuille is pronounced [feuyy]. Listen to the difference between the vowel sounds in the last syllables of fatigué and oreille. Now play the entire audio track again, repeating aloud feuille, oreille and vieille until you feel comfortable. Then add them to your - ll-list.

qu'est ce qui is an interrogative expression referring to the subject of the sentence: Qu'est-ce qui est important pour vous ? What'simportant for you? Compare it with qu'est-ce que, which refers to adirect object: Qu'est-ce que vous voulez ? What do you want?

We know that aller, to go, is used to talk about someone'shealth (see lesson 1). Je vais bien, I'm well. The negative form, Je ne vais pas bien means I'mnot well. To ask what is wrong, adoctor will say Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ? What'snot right?, or, more colloquially, What'sthe matter? / What'swrong ?

avoir mal ("to have bad") is an intransitive expression used to talk about pain or discomfort. It is generally followed by ala (or au/aux) and the painful body part: J'ai mal au ventre ("Ihave bad to the stomach"), Ihave astomach ache. The word order is often different to the English form: Elle amal ala tê te, She has a headache; Il amal aux pieds, His feet hurt. (Note that there is no distinction between ache and hurt in French.)

une fiè vre, literally a fever, is used in everyday speech, generally with de, to mean ahigh temperature: Mon fils ade la fiè vre, My son has a (high) temperature. In atechnical context, however, fiè vre is translated by the cognate: la fiè vre jaune, yellow fever. Note that the Fahrenheit scale is not used in most French-speaking countries (including Canada): all temperatures are in Celsius. So when the doctor says, as in line 6, Vous avez trente-huit (de fievre), You have atemperature of 38°C, the equivalent in Fahrenheit would be 100.4°F.

The masculine noun I'air means the air. But the meaning of the expression avoir I'air (de) is to look like or look as if. Marc a I'air fatigue, Marc looks tired. Elle a I'air d'une femme trè s sympa, She looks like very anice woman.

The direct object pronouns are me, me, te/vous, you, le/la, him/herit nous, us, and les, them. In contrast to English, they come before the verb: je les aime, Ilove them. Nous la voyons, We see her. Remember, though, that there are no neutral pronouns in French, so the last sentence can also mean We see it, if the pronoun is replacing afeminine noun.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Under France'shealth care system (le système de santé), the cost of medical care is covered by the national social security scheme (la Sécurité sociale, often shortened to la Sécu). In most cases, people are free to choose un médecin traitant, or ageneral practitioner. Once amedical consultation is complete, the doctor fills in une feuille de soins (literally"acare sheet"), which is forwarded - usually electronically - to the local health insurance branch. Note that un médecin means adoctor (see lesson 17), whereas the word doctor is used only as atitle (le Docteur Bellier, for example) or when addressing the practitioner directly: Bonjour docteur.

notes.content: Remember that French is syllable-timed, unlike English, where stress plays amuch greater role. For example: restaurant has three evenly-pronounced syllables in French: [res-toh-roeh"] but only two in English: [restront]. Try not to put too much emphasis on any one syllable in French words, however long they may be.

We know that the second person singular and plural are used in the imperative (lesson note 3). The same is true of the first person plural: Dé jeunons, Let'shave lunch. Faisons vite, Let'smake it fast. (Remember that the final - sis silent.) See lesson 18.

Most French words come from either Latin or Greek, whereas at least athird of English words are of Anglo-Saxon origin. Which means that one French word can often be translated in two ways. For example, accompanyer is either to accompany or to go/come with. For many English speakers, used to short phrasal verbs, French can sound very formal. It takes time to get used to this"double"vocabulary, so let'sstart now!

Don'tconfuse un quartier, adistrict or neighbourhood of acity (lesson 21) with un quart, a quarter. The noun can also be used attributively: un restaurant de quartier, aneighbourhood restaurant. (It is also used to refer to asegment of fruit or acut of meat.)

lequel (masc.), laquelle (fem.) and lesquels/lesquelles (plu.) are pronouns formed by combining the definite articles le/la/les and the interrogative adjectives quel/qu'elle/quels/quelles, meaning which/what. In this lesson and lesson 22, they are used as interrogatives: J'aime ces trois restaurants. - Lequel est-ce que vous pré fé rez? Ilike these three restaurants. - Which one do you prefer? Nous cherchons la crê perie. - Laquelle? - We're looking for the pancake house. - Which one? We will see later how to use these compounds as pronouns.

An idiom is an expression whose meaning can'tbe guessed from its various parts. For example, Ca m'est é gal ("It to me is equal") is equivalent to It'sall the same to me or I don't mind. Similarly, the interrogative Ca vous dit? (literally:"that you speaks") means something like Do you fancy that? Remember to make aspecial note of idioms and expressions whenever you come across them, because the meaning is not always obvious.

The adjective droit has two meanings: right (the opposite of gauche, left) and straight. Le genou droit, the right knee; un chemin droit, astraight path. Of course, both adjectives agree with their nouns: l'é paule droite, the right shoulder; deux lignes droites, two straight lines. The expression tout droit, straight ahead, is an adverb and therefore invariable.

venir de, to come from, followed by an infinitive, is an idiomatic way to express the immediate past. It is the translation of to have just + past participle in English: Je viens de voir Elsa, I've just seen Elsa. The expression is not used in the negative and is rarely found in the interrogative.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Une brasserie is a full-service restaurant offering traditional French cuisine throughout the day, and often late into the night. The word actually means abrewery (from brasser, to brew), because brasseries once brewed their own beer. Note how the - ie suffix, which generally denotes astatus or condition, is used to create nouns - most of them feminine-indicating an activity or profession: brasser → brasserie; une crêpe (a pancake) → une crêperie (apancake house), un sandwich → une sandwicherie (asandwich shop), etc. Similarly, many words for different kinds of businesses end in - erie: une boulangerie (a bakery), une fromagerie (acheese shop), une crèmerie (a dairy), etc. These are just afew examples of how to expand your vocabulary from acorpus of basic words.

notes.content: The verb suivre, to follow, is the root of la suite, the continuation (i.e. that which follows). The expression Si vous voulez bien me suivre is aformal way of asking someone to follow you. In aless formal setting, the server might say Suivez-moi (Follow me) as they lead you to your table. It'simportant to recognise the register, or level of formality, that is being used in order to respond accordingly.

convenir is another rather formal verb, meaning to suit, to be convenient/suitable for, etc. For the time being, just remember the interrogative expression Est-ce que ç a vous convient ?, Does that suit you? or, more idiomatically, Is that okay with you? And the response Ca me convient / Ca ne me convient pas, That'sfine / That doesn'tsuit me. Remember that idiomatic phrases can be translated in different ways, depending in the context, but the basic meaning is the same.

As we know, the verb avoir is used with several expressions whose English equivalents are formed with to be (J'ai trente ans, Iam thirty). Similar constructions include avoir faim, to be hungry (lesson 25), avoir soif, to be thirsty, avoir chaud, to be hot, and avoir froid, to be cold.
Remember that the present simple tense in French can express an immediate future (see lesson note 4). Je vous apporte la carte, I'll bring you the menu.

We saw in note that la suite, from suivre, to follow, means a continuation. But tout de suite is an idiomatic expression meaning immediately, at once. Faites-le tout de suite, Do it straight away. Note the pronunciation [foot-sweet].

In the previous lesson we learned agroup of compound pronouns (lequel, etc.). The root word is the interrogative adjective quel, what or, when used discriminatively, which, and its feminine and plural forms: quel plat... ?, which dish, qu'elle carte... ?, which card/menu, quels lé gumes... ?, which vegetables... ?, quelles tables... ?, which tables... ? All four adjectives are pronounced identically [kel], unless the following noun starts with a vowel, in which case the two are liaised: quelles é glises [kelz‿aygleez].
le sang (pron. [soehr]), blood, is the root of the verb saigner, to bleed, and the adjective saignant (fem. saignante) which literally means bleeding but, when applied to a steak, signifies rare.

une addition, literally"an addition,"also means abill in the context of food service. L'addition, s'il vous plaî t. The bill, please. Acommon synonym is la note (pron. [not]). The word for an invoice is une facture.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Most restaurants in France offer both une carte, a full-service menu (hence the expression manger àla carte, to eat àla carte), and un menu (literally"thin"or"slim"), a fixed-price or"slimmed-down"menu. Most menus feature un plat du jour, adish of the day. And since the wine list describes the full selection of bottles on offer, rather than ashort selection, the term is la carte (not le menu) des vins. Lastly, French restaurants include aservice charge (le service) in their menu prices (service compris, service"understood,"i.e. included), but it is customary to leave atip (un pourboire, literally"for-drink") if the dining experience is satisfactory.

notes.content: Although the initial hof hotel is silent, it is a"voiceless vowel,"so the rules governing liaisons apply. Thus the final sof quels runs into the oof hotel: [keizothel]. The same applies to the singular: quel hotel: [keilothel], un hotel: [ah'othel].
Be careful of the verb voler, which means to fly but also to steal. Thus un vol means either aflight or a theft, but hopefully the context will make the meaning clear!

In the transitive form, rater means to miss (a flight, an opportunity, etc.) Ne ratez pas votre avion ! Don’tmiss your plane! It does not, however, have the same emotional connotation of loss or absence as the English verb. For this we use another verb, manquer, which we will see later on.

The pronouns celui (masc. sing), celle (fem. sing.), ceux (masc. plur., see lesson 23) and celles (fem. plur.) are similar to the one/the ones (or those) in English, and perform the same function of avoiding the repetition of a noun. If adeux hô tels : celui prè s de l'aé roport est cher. There are two hotels: the one near the airport is expensive.

un avis (note the pronunciation: [ahnavee / ahnavee]) shares the same root as the English word advice (acredit or debit advice from abank is un avis de dé bit/cré dit). But the most common meaning is an opinion: Donnez-nous votre avis, Give us your opinion. The word is frequently used in expressions with the possessive adjectives: à mon avis, in my opinion, à son avis, in his or her opinion, etc. The plural is the same as the singular: Les avis sont partagé s, Opinions are divided.

As we saw in lesson note 6, some nouns are singular in English but plural in French, and vice versa. The collective masculine noun l'é quipement means equipment, but, when used in the plural, les é quipements has amuch broader meaning, similar to facilities or amenities.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Mince alors ! Like every language, French has many euphemisms that stand in for vulgarisms and swear words. This is especially true of exclamations and expletives. We already know Zut (see lesson 10). Now meet mince, an adjective meaning thin or slender. Used as apolite expletive, however, it replaces amuch stronger word, merde, equivalent in meaning to (but slightly less offensive than) shit. The reason for learning this kind of vocabulary is that many native speakers use such words on adaily basis, so it is important to be aware of them. However, we strongly recommend that you avoid using them, at least until you feel totally comfortable in French.

notes.content: The second group of verbs: -ir: Most verbs terminating in - ir form the second largest group of regular verbs, after the - er group seen in lesson 7. The conjugation endings are added to the stem, obtained by dropping the infinitive ending. Here are two very common - ir verbs: choisir, to choose: je choisis, tu* choisis, il/elle** choisit, nous choisissons, vous choisissez, ils/elles choisissent. finir, to finish: je finis, tu finis, il/elle finit, nous finissons, vous finissez, ils/elles finissent. * We will start using the familiar form, le tutoement, in the dialogues from lesson onwards. ** The third person singular is also used with the third person singular impersonal pronoun on. This is true for all verbs. As always, the final consonant (or double consonant) is silent. Note also that the nous and vous forms have an extra syllable (je chois, nous choisissons; tu finis, vous finissez). The negative is formed in the usual way, with ne...pas: je ne finis pas, vous ne finissez pas, etc. The interrogatives follow the same pattern (rising intonation, est ce que, inversion) as for - er verbs: Vous finissez votre cafe ?; Est-ce que vous finissez votre cafe ?; Finissez-vous votre cafe ? (Remember that the inverted interrogative is very formal and rarely used in everyday speech.) The distinguishing feature of regular second group verbs is apresent participle ending in - issant (finissant, finishing, etc.). This is important to remember because some - ir verbs actually belong to the third group. We will discuss these later.

Direct object pronouns: Here is the full table of direct object pronouns: me* me, te* you, le / la* him/her/it, nous us, vous you, les them. * The final vowel is elided if the next word in the sentence starts with a vowel. The main difference with English is that these pronouns come before the verb, not after it. Je le veux, Iwant it. Nous les achetons a l'aeroport, We buy them at the airport. Je l'ecoute tous les jours, Ilisten to him/her/it every day. Because of the elision, it is important to know the context of the sentence (in our example, je l'ecoute, the direct object pronoun could refer to aproper or personal noun that is feminine (la radio, the radio, la chanteuse, the singer) or masculine (le bruit, the noise, le guide, the guide). Finally, in aconstruction with an auxiliary like pouvoir or vouloir followed by an infinitive, the pronoun is placed between the two: Je peux le voir, Ican see him/it. Nous voulons vous aider, We want to help you.

Interrogative adjectives and pronouns: 3.1 Quel...? Quel can be used with a noun, in which case it serves as an adjective, or as apronoun to replace a noun: quel (masc. sing.), qu'elle (fem. sing.), quels (masc. plu.), quelles (fem. plu.) - what/which. Quel â ge avotre enfant ? How old is your child? Quelle heure est-il ? What time is it? Quels sont vos projets ? What are your plans? Quelles expositions sont inté ressantes ? Which exhibitions are interesting? Of course, the final plural - sis silent unless quels/quelles comes before aword starting with avowel quels‿enfants [kelzohr'fochr], quelles‿expositions [kelzekspozeessyohr] or with an h: quels‿hô tels [kelzohtel]. 3.2 Lequel...? Quel is used to ask questions about alarge group of things or people, but if the group is smaller or the choice relates to apredefined group, the adjective is combined with the definite article: lequel (masc. sing.), laquelle (fem. sing.), lesquels (masc. plu.), lesquelles (fem. plu.) - which one(s). Lequel de ces hô tels pré fé rez-vous ? Which of these hô tels do you prefer? Laquelle des deux montres voulez-vous ? Which of these two watches do you want? Prendre des comprimé s, d'accord, mais lesquels ? Take pills, okay, but which ones? J'ai des grandes et des petites bananes. - Lesquelles sont les moins chè res ? Ihave small and large bananas. - Which are the least expensive?

Demonstrative pronouns: celui: This family of pronouns is used to refer to something that has been mentioned previously, thus avoiding repetition: celui (masc. sing.), celle (fem. sing.), ceux (masc. plu.), celles (fem. plu.) - the one(s), those. Quel chemin prendre : celui de droite ou celui de gauche ? Which path to take, the one on the right or the one on the left? Les deux chambres sont chè res, mais celle du premier é tage n'est pas trè s confortable, Both rooms are expensive but the one on the first floor isn'tvery comfortable. Et celles du rez-de-chaussé e sont petites. And the ones on the ground floor are small. Les menus des crê peries sont moins chers que ceux des brasseries. The menus at pancake houses are cheaper than those at brasseries.

Avoir instead of"to be": Many expressions describing an emotional or physical state are formed with an auxiliary and adescriptive word. Whereas the majority of such expressions in English use to be and an adjective (I'm hungry), French uses avoir and anoun (J'ai faim). Here are some more examples: avoir faim: -Avez-vous faim? to be hungry; avoir soif: -J'ai trè s soif. to be thirsty; avoir chaud: -Avez-vous chaud? to be hot; avoir froid: -Il n'apas froid. to be cold; avoir raison: -Vous avez raison! to be right; avoir tort: -Ils n'ont pas tort. to be wrong; avoir peur: -Je n'ai pas peur. to be afraid; avoir sommeil: -Elle a sommeil. to be sleepy; avoir besoin (de): -Nous n'avons pas besoin de vous. to need; avoir de la chance: -Ils ont vraiment de la chance! to be lucky. Since the descriptive word in all these expressions is a noun, not an adjective, there is no need for agreement in gender or number: J'ai raison, Vous avez raison.

Numbers and figures: cardinals: Let'srevise the cardinal numbers, which you have assimilated naturally by reading them at the foot of each page. (If you've forgotten to do so, read on and then go back to the beginning of the book!) un1, deux2, trois3, quatre4, cinq5, six6, sept7, huit8, neuf9, dix10, onze11, douze12, treize13, quatorze14, quinze15, seize16, dix-sept17, dix-huit18, dix-neuf19, vingt20, trente30, quarante40, cinquante50, soixante60, soixante-dix70, quatre-vingts80, quatre-vingt-dix90, cent100. To form numbers above 20, use the multiple of ten followed by the second digit, e.g. 66 = soixante-six. However, this rule does not apply to 70, and 90, which are expressed in base-20 rather than base-10: - is 60 + 10 (soixante-dix), so soixante et onze (71), soixante-douze (72), soixante-treize (73), soixante-quatorze (74), soixante-quinze (75), soixante-seize (76), soixante-dix-sept (77), soixante-dix-huit (78), soixante-dix-neuf (79). – is 60+20: quatre-vingts, then quatre-vingt-un (81), quatre-vingt-deux (82), quatre-vingt-trois (83), etc. – is 80+10: quatre-vingt-dix, then quatre-vingt-onze (91), quatre-vingt-douze (92), quatre-vingt-treize (93), etc. This is the system used in France. It takes some practice at first, but soon becomes second nature. By contrast, Belgium and Switzerland have slightly different –and arguably more logical– systems. Both use septante for 70 (thus septante et un for 71, etc.) and nonante for 90 (nonante et un, etc.). In addition, Switzerland often uses huitante for 80. The rules governing the terminal - son vingt, in particular, the use of hyphens are quite complex, so for the time being concentrate on learning the numbers and acquiring the automatic reflex of seeing them, then saying them aloud. Lastly, there is only one word for in French: zero, which translates both zero and nought, as well as the oh used in phone numbers.

extras.content: You'll notice that, for the time being, the English translations are fairly literal. This is deliberate because we want you to concentrate on the French syntax, rather than systematically comparing the two languages. As we progress, however, the translations will become more idiomatic. And now that you are familiar with the basic rules on liaisons, we will no longer mark them with the undertie (vous‿avez) which has been used solely to get you used to this particular feature of spoken French.

notes.content: As always, the final smarking the familiar form of the verb (vas, fais, sais, vois, pense, etc.) is silent: [vah], [fay], [say], [vwah], [poeh's], etc.
Salut ! (the origin of salute) is afamiliar greeting, equivalent to Hil! As asingular noun, un salut is either awave (of the hand) or anod (of the head).
tu is the familiar pronoun for the singular you. It is used when talking to friends, family members and children. Toi, in this context, is the object pronoun.

la forme, meaning the form or shape, is also used to refer to fitness or health, as we saw in lesson 24. Louis est en forme aujourd'hui, Louis is on top form today. The polite expression J'espere que tu es en forme ? Ihope you're doing well? is often shortened to just La forme ?, with arising intonation, in familiar contexts.

You should be familiar with the two meanings of les courses: errands, shopping (lesson 13) and horse races (lesson 22). Similarly, un anniversaire can mean both abirthday and an anniversary. Remember to take special note of these homonyms, which can often be disconcerting.
Unlike English, French surnames do not take an - sin the plural: Monsieur et Madame Mercier → Les Mercier. Of course, this does not affect the pronunciation.
une patisserie refers to both apastry (the circumflex replacing the letter s) and the shop in which it is bought.
offrir, to offer, can also mean to give when used in the context of a gift. J'offre souvent des cadeaux à mes enfants, Ioften give my children presents. See also note 9.
See lesson note and lesson for more about the difference between savoir and connaî tre.

Singular nouns ending in - eau form their plural with a (silent) final x. They include un cadeau (a gift), un bureau (an office), un morceau (a piece, a bit, a slice), un gateau (a cake) and un tableau (a painting).

The adverb plutot, rather, instead, is auseful way of qualifying astatement or expressing a preference: je n'aime pas les tartes, je prefere plutot les gateaux, I don'tlike tarts, Iprefer cakes instead.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Chantilly is atown to the north of Paris, renowned for its chateau and gardens, an extensive library of illuminated manuscripts, and world-famous race horse training stables. But it is arguably better known for the delicacy that bears its name: la crème de Chantilly - or, more commonly la crème chantilly (whipped cream with vanilla and sugar) - as well as for la dentelle de Chantilly (handmade bobbin lace).

notes.content: un truc is afamiliar but very common placeholder word meaning a thing, a whatname, etc.

Allô comes from the English hello and, in France, is used only when answering the phone (in Quebec, it is also a greeting, like Hi!). The word is often found in the business names of emergency call-out services, such as Allo Serrurier for a 24/7 locksmith.

entendre, to hear, along with vendre (lesson 29) and several other verbs in this lesson, provide an introduction to Group Three, which comprises three types of endings divided into sub-categories. Verbs in the first sub-category end in - re. The inflexions are j'entends, tu entends, il/elle entend, nous entendons, vous entendez, ils/elles entendent. Note that the - sis usually dropped from the second person singular in the imperative form (but see note 5).

quitter, to leave, is the origin of the verb to quit. Quittez l’autoroute à la sortie trente, Leave the motorway at exit 30. On the telephone, Ne quittez pas, or Ne quitte pas in the familiar form, means Please hold (“Don’t leave”).

mettre, to put, is an important verb (je mets, tu mets, il/elle met, nous mettons, vous mettez, ils mettent). Unlike English, it does not usually take apreposition (mettre un manteau, to put on a coat).
Vas-yis the familiar form of Allez-y, Go ahead (lesson note 2). The terminal-sis retained in the imperative before the adverbial pronouns yand en to make pronunciation easier (Ivahzee).
vouloir bien (literally"to wish well") is used in polite expressions like Je veux bien or Si vous voulez / tu veux bien to express acceptance (similar to the formal If you will in English).

Used with the present or future tenses, the adverbial phrase à tout à l'heure ("to all to the hour") is equivalent to later on or, as a valediction, See you later: Je reviens dans quelques minutes. - Atout a l'heure. I'll be back in afew minutes. - See you later. It can also be used with apast tense, meaning earlier. (The phrase is probably the origin of the English slang term toodle-oo.)
