extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: For English-speakers, le tutoiement can be difficult to master at first (When to use it? With whom?). But in most cases, the context will help you: if someone addresses you in the tu form, you can respond likewise. If you're not sure which form of address (tu or vous) is appropriate, always opt for the formal one. For more information, see lesson 35.

notes.content: Here'sanother -ll-word. As usual after adouble vowel, the phoneme is pronounced [yy]: [booyy-wahr]. It'sworth repeating the word several times aloud in order to get to grips with the pronunciation.

We came across puis-je in the exercises in lesson 26. The term, derived from the old interrogative form of je peux, I can, is now used only in polite, formal questions, like may/might in English: Puis-je avoir votre nom ? Might Ihave your name? Que puis-je faire pour vous ? What may Ido for you? (Puis-je cannot be used in questions formed with est-ce que...?, which, by definition, are less formal than the inverted interrogative.)

The adverbial pronoun en was introduced in the previous lesson. It has several functions, notably to avoid repetition of a noun. En is frequently used with the partitives du/de la/des: J'ai du café. Vous en voulez ? / have coffee. Do you want some? See also note 5.

The demonstrative pronouns celui / celle / ceux / celles (lesson 28) can'tbe used on their own (Les tartes ?) 'aime celles aux fraises). But they can take the suffixes - ci (here, an abbreviation of ici, which has no cedilla under the c) and - la when indicating (or"demonstrating") aspecific thing that is either close to or distant from the speaker: Tu veux celui-ci ? Do you want this one (here)? Nous preferons celles-la, We prefer those ones (over there).

hors (pronounced [or]) means out of, away from. Followed by de, it is aprepositional phrase: Il est hors du bureau pour le moment, He'sout of the office for the moment. It can also be used in set expressions such as hors de question (see lesson 18), hors de prix ("out of price"), overpriced or outrageously expensive, as well as the culinary term hors d'œuvre, ("out of work"), a starter.

en is also apreposition meaning in. It can be used in phrases indicating either astate - en or, in/af gold-or a situation, en vacances, on holiday. For the time being, simply memorise the phrases you come across. We'll learn more as we go along.

We know that I'argent means money, but the other meaning is silver. In this case, it is preceded by de (la medaille d'argent, the silver medal) or en: Ma nouvelle montre est en argent, My new watch is in silver.

Don'tconfuse the preposition sur, on, with the adjective sur, safe, secure. Both words (and the feminine adjective sure) are pronounced identically, but the circumflex on the second word makes it easier to tell the difference between them.
tant pis is aset expression meaning Too bad or Never mind. (Pis aliterary form of pire, worse/worst, which we will see shortly).

Je vous en prie is the standard response to Merci, Thank you. The familiar (tu) form is Je t'en prie. Although the literal translation,"Ipray you,"is very formal (and rarely used) in English, the French expression - both the vous and the tu forms-is standard.

notes.content: The ligature œhas no equivalent sound in English. To pronounce un œil, an eye, use the 'open-u' sound found in the verb 'to purr' and add along 'y' sound (represented by [yy]) at the end: [uh-yy]. Listen carefully to the recording and try to imitate the speaker.
As we know, si means if, but it can also be an intensifier, like so. Ma collè gue est si fatigué e qu'elle ne peut plus continuer, My colleague is so tired that she can't continue.

This lesson looks at the second sub-category of third-group verbs; those ending in -oir: devoir, to have to / must; pouvoir, to be able to / can; recevoir, to receive; savoir, to know; and voir, to see. You have already come across most of them, but now you can see that they are conjugated in the same way.

Just like une dizaine, approximately ten (lesson note 3), une centaine means about a hundred. The indefinite plural can be used in the same way as hundreds in English: je reç ois des centaines de mails d'une dizaine de collè gues, Ireceive hundreds of emails from ten or so colleagues.

The indefinite pronouns chacun (masculine) and chacune (feminine) are compounds of chaque plus un/une: each one. Je regarde chacun des mails en dé tail, Ilook at each email (or, alternatively, each one of these emails) in detail. For emphasis, the pronoun can be placed at the end of the phrase, as in English: Ces bouillories coû tent cent euros chacune, These kettles costs 100 euros each. Don'tconfuse chacun(e) with chaque, which is followed by a noun: Chaque appareil coû te cent euros, Each device costs 100 euros. Obviously, neither chacun(e) nor chaque has aplural form.

The negative verb form is usually constructed with ne...pas. In some cases, however, pas can be replaced with an adverb, notably jamais and plus. Il ne ré pond jamais au té lé phone, He never answers the phone; Elle ne ré pond plus à mes messages, She is no longer answering my messages.

Another very common irregular plural is the masculine noun for the eye, l'œil, which becomes les yeux (pronounced yeu). Note also the idiom un coup d'œil, a glance, used with the verb jeter, to throw. (The expression donner un coup de main, used in line 11, is equivalent to the English idiom to give someone a hand.)

The indirect object pronouns are me, te, lui, nous, vous and leur. Max nous donne un coup de main, Max is giving us a hand. Peux-tu me prê ter dix euros? Can you lend me ten euros? They are identical to the direct object pronouns, except for the third persons singular and plural: lui and leur. Note that the singular lui can mean him or her. Je lui donne un cadeau: I'mgiving him OR her a present. Last, don'tconfuse the pronoun leur with the possessive adjective, spelled identically: leur travail, their work.
The plural of un mal, a pain, an ache, is des maux. See lesson note 3.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: The use of"franglais"- English words (or words derived from English)- is aperennial hot-button issue. Here's afirst example. The word email was imported directly into French decades ago as anoun (but not a verb). Efforts have since been made to find a home-grown equivalent - most notably un courriel, aportmanteau of le courrier électronique (electronic mail). However, many French speakers still prefer email or even mail. Asimilar debate has been waged over the terms for asmartphone (un smartphone) and tablet (une tablette). If you're unsure whether aword is accepted in French, check le site de l'Académie française, the official guardian of the language. (And don'tforget le tacos, which is masculine and singular, despite the s!)

notes.content: For internet addresses, French uses the nouns corresponding to the grammatical function of punctuation signs. Hence adot is called un point [pwah"], which means afull stop (or period).
Here is another example of the lexical links between French and English. Over the centuries, une garde-robe (plural garde-robes), literally"keep dress", evolved into a wardrobe.

Remember that the second person singular imperative of - er verbs has no final - s (tu entres ⇒ Entre ! you come in ⇒ Come in!). However, for all regular and most irregular - ir and - re verbs, the imperative is identical to the indicative: tu attends ⇒ Attends !
When used with the imperative, the direct object pronouns me and te become - moi and - toi: vous me donnez la clé → Donnez-moi la clé ! tu t'assié s → Assié s-toi !
We saw pas du tout, not at all, used on its own (lesson 3) as an emphatic negative. The phrase can also be used after a verb: je ne les connais pas du tout, I don'tknow them at all.

Here is another negative construction formed with ne and an adverb (see lesson note 5), in this case rein: Je n'ai rien à faire à la maison, Ihave nothing to do at home; Il ne voit rien la nuit, He can'tsee anything at night. Remember that pas is not used in this type of construction, otherwise it would create adouble negative.

This is another example of aword that can be singular in French but not in English (lesson note 5): les vê tements means clothes (Ses vê tements sont chics, His/her clothes are smart) whereas un vê tement is an item of clothing. Ce vê tement est trop petit, This piece of clothing is too small. In practice, we would generally use another, more precise word in English (this coat, etc.) but un vê tement is standard French.

mille is athousand so un millier is approximately a thousand, just like dix / une dizaine (lesson note 3) and cent / une centaine (lesson note 3). It, too, has aplural form: Des milliers de gens, Thousands of people. And it's masculine, not feminine.

The compound adjective bon marché ("good market") means inexpensive, cheap (with no negative connotation). It is invariable: Voici une liste des hô tels bon marché à Bordeaux, Here's alist of inexpensive hotels in Bordeaux. Asynonym is pas cher, not expensive, but in this case, the adjective agrees: des hô tels pas chers.

When used as adjectives, colours generally agree with the noun in number and gender: un manteau bleu, ablue coat, des jupes bleues, blue skirts. Of course, if the masculine adjective ends in - e, it does not change: un pull jaune, une robe jaune.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Le Bon Marche is the name of the world's first-ever grand magasin (department store), which opened in Paris in 1852. Although French uses the verbal expression faire ses courses to talk about shopping for food and other staples, the term faire du shopping is preferred when talking about browsing for and buying other goods, especially clothes. Naturally, purists dislike this import - they insist on faire des achats (to make purchases), while French-speaking Canadians say faire du magasinage-but it is largely (and unfortunately) unavoidable in everyday usage.

notes.content: The terminal -er of the masculine noun l'hiver is pronounced [air], as in cher (rather than [ay], as in aller). Don'tforget that the half-vowel his not pronounced (just like hour in English) so, with en hiver, the final nof en runs into the iof hiver: [œhneevair].
nez is pronounced [nay], like the final syllable of the second person plural of an -er verb: venez: [vuhnay].

This is final sub-category of third-group verbs which end in - ir but are irregular (unlike Group verbs). They include courir, to run; dormir, to sleep; sentir, to feel; servir, to serve; ouvrir, to open; souffrir, to suffer; offrir, to offer (see lesson note 7); and servir, to serve. The endings are, for example, je cours, tu cours, il/elle court, nous courons, vous courez, ils/elles courent.

Normally, the plural of nouns ending in - ou is formed by adding an s (un trou, a hole, des trous). But a handful, including un genou, a knee, un bijou, a jewel, and un caillou [kie-you], a pebble, take an - x. There are seven of these nouns in all, but these three are the most common.
rien can mean both anything or nothing (lesson note 5). Note the place of this pronoun, which, unlike English, comes before the verb: Il ne peut rien faire pour toi, He can'tdo anything for you.

mi-is ashortened form of demi, half. It is used in anumber of expressions, notably à mi-chemin ("half-path"), halfway: Sé lestat est à mi-chemin entre Colmar et Strasbourg, Sé lestat is halfway between Colmar and Strasbourg.

We know that the adverb ymeans there, as in il y a. But it can also be used to avoid repeating a noun, just like en (lesson note 2). Tu connais Colmar ? - J'y habite, Do you know Colmar? - Ilive there (instead of J'habite à Colmar). Like rien (note 3), ycomes before the verb. It can also be used in the expression y compris, including. Toute la famille est invité e, ycompris ton frè re, The whole family is invited, including your brother. In this case, yhas no intrinsic meaning.

Here'sanother very common vernacular word: un copain (feminine: une copine) means a pal, a mate. Depending on the context, the term can be used for a boyfriend/girlfriend. Le copain de Noé mie est un artiste qui s'appelle Florian, Noé mie'sboyfriend is an artist called Florian.

Like une course (lesson note 4), le temps has two meanings: the time and the weather (despite the final s, the word is singular). The context should make it easy to tell the difference, but remember this mnemonic just in case: Je n'ai pas le temps pour ce mauvais temps, I don'thave time for this bad weather. (Un temps can also mean a (verb) tense: Le futur simple est un temps de l'indicatif, The future simple is an indicative tense - see lesson note 3).

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Located in eastern France, Alsace is aregion with adistinct personality. Bordered by the Vosges mountains (les Vosges, pron. [vohzh]) to the west and the river Rhine (le Rhin, pron. [rahn]) to the east, it is part of the administrative area known as le Grand Est ("the great east"). Alsace has strong cultural ties with its immediate neighbour, Germany. It also has its own Germanic language, l'alsacien or Elsassisch, used alongside French on highway signage and street name signs, and still spoken by some Alsaciens (Alsatians). The region's capital, Strasbourg, is home to the European Parliament.

notes.content: The third group of verbs: -re, -oir and -ir: The third group is the most complex of the three, largely because the component verbs are all irregular. It can be divided into three sub-categories according to the endings: - re, -oir and -ir. 1.1 Verbs ending in -re: prendre, to take: je prends, tu prends, il/elle prend, nous prenons, vous prenez, ils/elles prennent. This sub-category includes common verbs such has attendre, to wait; mettre, to put; and boire, to drink. 1.2 Verbs ending in -oir: savoir, to know: je sais, tu sais, il/elle sait, nous savons, vous savez, ils/elles savent. Several key verbs come under this sub-category, particularly vouloir, to want; and pouvoir, to be able to. 1.3 Verbs ending in -ir: dormir, to sleep: je dors, tu dors, il/elle dort, nous dormons, vous dormez, ils/elles dorment. This sub-category, comprising irregular verbs such as sortir, to go out, souffrir, to suffer; partir, to leave (and repartir, to restart); and ouvrir, to open, is slightly disorienting because it can be confused with the second group of regular verbs. The difference can be seen in the present participle (suffering, leaving, etc.), which ends in - issant for Group but - ant for Group 3. Thus, finir, to finish, and choisir, to choose, are regular Group verbs with the present participle finissant and choisissant, whereas the present participle of the irregular dormir is dormant. The third group also contains one, very irregular - er verb: aller, to go. Since Group verbs are, by definition, irregular, they need to be learned by heart. There are, however, some recognisable patterns, which we shall see later on.

Plural nouns: an overview: By now, you should know how to form the plural of nouns and adjectives. Here is an overview. The basic rule is simply to add aterminal (and silent) -sto the singular: un croissant, deux croissants. There are, of course, several exceptions depending on the word ending: - ail: travail → travaux, work(s) (construction, etc.); - al: journal → journaux, newspaper(s); - eu: jeu → jeux, game(s); - eau: manteau → manteaux, coat(s). Singular nouns ending -s, -xor -zdo not change in the plural: un Francais → des Francais, one Frenchman, Frenchmen; une voix → des voix, a voice, voices; un nez → des nez, a nose, noses. The final letter is usually silent, but there are acouple of exceptions, notably un fils/des fils, a son/sons (listen to the dialogue in lesson 28).

yand en: The adverbial pronouns yand en have no direct equivalents in English. The meaning varies according to their function and where they are placed in the sentence. Here are some basic rules: 3.1 yis used to avoid repetition: Le musee ferme dans trois heures. On peut yaller maintenant. The museum closes in three hours. We can go there now. The noun does not have to refer to a place: J'aime mon travail et j'ypense tout le temps. Ilike my job and Ithink about it all the time. To form the negative, place the particle before the pronoun: je n'ypense pas. It'simportant to note that ycannot relate to a person: J'aime Annette : je pense aelle tout le temps. (The verbs in this type of sentence are generally followed by the preposition a: aller a, penser a, etc.). And of course, yis used in the phrase il y a ("it there has") to express the existence of something: Il y abeaucoup de neige cet hiver, There is alot of snow this winter. 3.2en replaces a word, often a verb, followed by de: En can be the equivalent of some / any: Avez-vous du lait ? Oui, j'en ai, Do you have any milk? - Yes, Ihave some. It always comes before the verb. While some is often dropped in this context in English (Yes, I have), en can never be omitted. It can also replace the partitive article (du / de la / des), meaning of or about it/them: Est-ce qu'elle ades enfants ? - Oui, elle en a trois. Does she have any children? - Yes, she has three [of them]. Alain connait bien l'Alsace : il en parle beaucoup. Alain knows Alsace very well: he talks about it a lot. As with y, the negative particle is placed before the pronoun: il n'en parle pas beaucoup. Idiomatically, en is used in the expressions Je vous en prie / Je t'en prie, Don'tmention it. Finally, en is also a preposition, usually translated as in: Ils habitent en Bretagne, They live in Brittany. Nous sommes en vacances la semaine prochaine, We're on holiday next week.

savoir and connaî tre: Both verbs mean to know, but they are used differently. In essence, savoir means to know afact or how to do something. It is usually used with a clause, introduced by que, qui, ou, quand, etc. For example, Je sais ou habite Emmanuel, Iknow where Emmanuel lives (note the word order, with the verb before the direct object). Used with an infinitive, savoir means the same as can: Il sait parler l'anglais et le franç ais, He can speak English and French. By contrast, connaî tre means to know or be familiar with aperson or a place. In a sentence, the verb is followed by adirect object noun: Je connais Emmanuel, Nous connaissons Paris. In sum, we would say Je connais Emmanuel mais je ne sais pas ou il habite, Iknow ("am acquainted with") Emmanuel but I don'tknow ("am not aware") where he lives. There are afew cases where either verb can be used in aspecific context, but these are few and far between.

Indirect object pronouns: Indirect object pronouns are used to avoid repeating a noun. They represent the person on whom an action is being performed. They are: me to me, nous to us, te to you, vous to you, lui to him / her, leur to them. me and te become m' and t' when followed by a vowel. In contrast to English, indirect object pronouns in French always come before the verb. In many cases, they are used with verbs followed by a (é crire à, to write to, donner à, to give to, parler à, to speak to), replacing both the noun and the preposition: Je vais parler au directeur = Je vais lui parler. One slight complication is when the equivalent verb in English takes adirect object: to phone someone / té lé phoner à quelqu'un. As a result, I'mphoning my sister is Je té lé phone à ma sœur, which becomes Je lui té lé phone. That'swhy it is so important to learn verbs together with their prepositions. Here are some examples: Dites à vos amis de venir → Dites-leur de venir. Tell your friends / Tell them to come; Il donne de l'argent à moi et ma femme → Il nous donne de l'argent. He gives money to me and my wife → He gives us money. The third person pronouns lui and leur replace both masculine and feminine nouns: Il faut demander au patron / à ma femme → Il faut lui demander. J'é cris à mes copains / à mes amies → Je leur é cris. The pronoun leur is invariable. Do not confuse it with the possessive adjective leur / leurs, which can agree with aplural noun (leurs amis). See lessons and note 7.

Le tutoiement: The"familiar"form of address no longer exists in English (thee and thou disappeared centuries ago), so mastering the equivalent in French, le tutoiement (from the pronoun tu) can be tricky at first. Here are some basic rules: - tu is used when talking with family, close friends, lovers, children and people in the same social group. Young people use tu (the verb is tutoyer) among themselves more so than older people; and you always tutoie pets, animals, God and inanimate objects that might irritate you (computer, car, etc.); - vous (le vouvoiement, vouvoyer) is the formal version, used in everyday interaction with people you don't know. It is also the plural pronoun, used collectively, even with family and friends; - using tu instead of vous outside these contexts can be seen as disrespectful or even rude. Tutoiement can even be aform of insult, for instance when used by two drivers involved in a fender-bender. In practice, however, the situations in which to use the familiar form vary according to anumber of factors. For instance, staff in abig company will use vous with superiors and tu with colleagues, whereas employees in atech firm will all use le tutoiement, regardless of rank or seniority. Similarly, an adult will address achild other than afamily member as tu but the child will respond with the vous form. And members of an online forum will tutoie each other even though they have never met. So, when in doubt, stick to the simple guideline that vous should always be used with strangers and in formal situations. You may then be invited to switch to the familiar form (On peut se tutoyer). Always take the lead from the person you are interacting with. Here are the vous and tu forms of each verb group: aimer: vous aimez / tu aimes; finir: vous finissez / tu finis; mettre: vous mettez / tu mets; boire: vous buvez / tu bois; dire: vous dites / tu dis. Two very common familiar phrases are Comment vas-tu ? How are you? and Vas-y ! Go ahead! Go for it! And since tu is the familiar form, it is often used in an informal register. In spoken French, tu as (you have) is frequently shortened to t'as (and tu n'as pas sometimes becomes t'as pas). Needless to say, you should not imitate these colloquialisms but it is important to recognise them because they are commonly used by native speakers.

extras.title: Smile!
extras.content: You have certainly noticed that the language content of our lessons is becoming alittle more idiomatic. This is deliberate because as soon as you start speaking in real-life settings, the people you interact with will rarely make an effort to confine themselves to"formal,"academic French. So, without venturing into hard-core slang, we will present you with language that is as realistic as possible while still allowing you to learn at arelaxed pace. Speaking of which, don'tforget to pick up the book or listen to the recordings every day, even if you only have ten minutes: C'est en forgeant qu'on devient forgeron,"It'sby forging that one becomes a blacksmith,"equivalent to the English proverb Practice makes perfect.

notes.content: The expression Ca yest ("that there is") is useful for acknowledging that something is about to happen - Ca yest : la pluie arrive, Here we go: the rain is on its way-or has happened: Ca yest : le week-end est terminé, That's it. The weekend is over. As usual, the translation will depend on the context, but the basic idea is that of recognition. As for the pronunciation, the three words are run together in asingle sound: [sayay].

This is the perfect tense -le passé composé-of verbs ending in -er. Generally formed with avoir, appropriately conjugated, and the past participle of the verb, it is used to describe an action that was completed ("perfected") in the past. Although similar in structure to the present perfect tense in English (Ihave ordered), it is not a one-on-one equivalent. (Some verbs form their passé compose with ê tre, as we will see later on.)

The interrogative form of the perfect tense can be constructed, like the present, in three ways: by raising the voice, inverting the auxiliary and pronoun or, as here, with est-ce que: Est-ce que vous avez fermé la fenê tre ? Did you have you closed the window?

When used with the perfect tense, tout is usually placed as an adverb between the auxiliary and the participle (ll atout fermé, He'sclosed everything). Remember that the adverb tout is invariable (ll atout fermé, ils ont tout fermé).

fermer means to close (Le magasin est fermé, The shop is closed) but also to lock. To avoid ambiguity, to lock can also be expressed as fermer aclé ("close to key"). The noun alock is une serrure. Doors and windows can also be secured with un verrou, a bolt, whence the verb verrouiller (vervoayy), to bolt.

We saw in lesson note that tout a l'heure, later on, could be used in reference to the past. In this case, it refers to an immediate or very recent event. J'ai verifie la cuisine tout a l'heure, Ichecked the kitchen just now / afeu minutes ago / earlier, etc. Remember that tout is used here as part of the expression, not an adverb, as in sentence 3.

The relative pronoun ce que, first seen in lesson 12, is equivalent to what / which. It functions as the direct object of asubordinate clause, often with asubject pronoun: Je mange ce que je veux, Ieat what I want. Prenez ce que vous voulez, Take what you want.

nettoyer is auseful verb that means to clean or clear up, depending on the context. Like fermer, it is often followed by anoun to make the action more specific, whereas English tends to use an entirely different verb. For example, J'ai nettoyé la piscine à l'é ponge, I've sponged down the swimming pool. We'll see more of these equivalent constructions (verb + noun in French vs. single verb in English) as we advance. The noun nettoyage asec means dry cleaning.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Words can teach us alot about a country'sculture and history. This is especially true of eponyms, or words derived from the proper names of real (or imaginary) people. The word for a dustbin, une poubelle, is named for Eugène Poubelle, a 19th-century city administrator who ordered refuse containers to be installed in all Parisian buildings for public health reasons. French is well-endowed with eponyms, notably in science and mathematics, yet many ordinary words originated from people who are often forgotten. For example, un martinet is atype of whip, named for the stern disciplinarian General Jean Martinet; la nicotine is named after the philologist Jean Nicot; while la guillotine was invented by a doctor, Joseph Guillotin, as a"humanitarian"form of execution! Tracking down the etymology of words, particularly eponyms, is an excellent way to build up a vocabulary.

notes.content: In many cases, pronouncing aliaison will depend on who is speaking. The expression pas encore is agood example. Acareful speaker will join the two words, pas‿encore [pahzohr'kor] whereas someone talking quickly will probably not [pah ohr'kor]. The first is more elegant; the second, more frequent.
Remember not to pronounce the hin bonheur. [boh-nuhr] (the same applies to the antonym malheur, misfortune : [mah-luhr]).

The perfect tense of Group verbs (regular, ending in - ir) is usually constructed with avoir and the past participle, formed by dropping the final - rfrom the infinitive. For example, grandir (to grow up) → grandi: j'ai grandi, tu as grandi, il/elle a grandi, nous avons grandi, vous avez grandi, ils /elles ont grandi. Simple!

Continuing the series of nouns that can be plural in French but not in English, la recherche has two meanings: research, in which case the noun is usually singular and has adefinite article - La recherche scientifique est trè s importante, Scientific research is very important - and, more generally, asearch or an investigation, in which case, it takes an indefinite article but can also be plural: Nous allons continuer nos recherches, We are going to keep searching. For web browsing (see lesson 27), we use un moteur de recherche, asearch engine.

le bonheur means happiness or good fortune. Aprè s, trois mariages, elle aenfin trouvé le bonheur : ê tre seule, After three marriages, she finally found happiness: being alone. The word can also be used in idiomatic expressions such as Est-ce que tu as trouvé ton bonheur ?, Have you found what you wanted or were looking for? The opposite of le bonheur is le malheur, unhappiness, misfortune. Remember this proverb: Un malheur n'arrive jamais seul, Misfortunes never come on their own, or, more colloquially, It never rains but it pours. (The his silent in both words.)

un appartement, aflat or an apartment (notice the difference in spelling), is one of the multisyllabic words that are frequently abbreviated in spoken French (lesson note 7). It becomes un apart, with the final t pronounced.

le moyen, in the singular, is the way or the means: Je connais un bon moyen d'apprendre une langue, Iknow agood way to learn a language. In the plural, it is equivalent to the singular English noun means, i.e. money. Nous n'avons pas les moyens d'aller en vacances cette anné e, We don'thave the money to go on holiday this year. In this case, avoir les moyens is agood paraphrase for to afford, which has no direct equivalent in French.

By now, you should be familiar with the comparatives of superiority and inferiority, where more is translated by plus and less by moins. In both cases the conjunction than is que. Lyon est plus grand que Toulouse mais plus petit que Paris, Lyon is bigger than Toulouse but smaller than Paris. To form the superlative, simply put the definite article le or la for the singular (depending on the gender of the noun) and les for the plural before plus or moins.

dessus and dessous mean above and below / beneath, respectively. They are used in different forms, but here we see them, with au-, as adverbs. J'habite au troisiè me é tage et ma copine habite à l'é tage audessus, Ilive on the third floor and my girlfriend lives on the floor above. La tempé rature est deux degré s au-dessous de zé ro, The temperature is two degrees below zé ro. (You will have recognised the adjective sous, under). In some cases, au-dessous is replaced with en dessous, but the meaning is exactly the same.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: L'île de France - literally"The Island of France" - is the official designation of the greater Paris area, the most populous of the country's 18 regions, but is often referred to simply as la région parisienne. The toponym is used to form an adjective, francilien(ne) (referring to the Paris region) and aproper noun, un Francilien / une Francilienne, alocal inhabitant. L'île de France comprises eight administrative areas, or départements, that are subdivided into two"rings,"an inner one (la Petite Couronne, or"small crown") and an outer one, la Grande Couronne,"big crown"). The region is circled by anetwork of motorways and expressways called... La Francilienne.

notes.content: Unlike in English, oo is not pronounced as along vowel but as two separate ones: [oh-oh]. This is particularly the case with the prefix co-Thus the first syllables of coordonné es and coopé ration are pronounced [koh-or] and [koh-op], respectively.

une part is apiece or a slice. Voulez-vous une part de gâ teau au chocolat ? Do you want apiece of chocolate cake? In atelephone conversation, however, the expression de la part de identifies the person on behalf of whom the call is being placed. The standard question is C'est de la part de qui ?, equivalent in register to Who shall Isay is calling? Giving one'sname is asufficient response. The caller can also say, for example, Je l'appelle de la part de Michelle, in which case, the caller may be Michelle herself or someone calling on her behalf.

Here is the perfect tense of certain Group verbs ending in -re, such as prendre, to take, and its derivatives: j'ai pris, tu as pris, il/elle a pris, nous avons pris, vous avez pris, ils/elles ont pris.

Another set of -re verbs, including dire, to say, lire, to read, and é crire, to write, form their past participle with afinal (and silent) -t: j'ai dit, tu as dit, il/elle a dit, nous avons dit, vous avez dit, ils/elles ont dit. Naturally, any verbs derived from these three, such as contredire, to contradict, are conjugated in the same way.

The adjective local has the same meaning as in English (un guide local, alocal guide). As a noun, however, it means premises. In contrast to English, it can be either singular or plural: un local commercial, des locaux commerciaux, commercial premises. The difference is merely aquestion of size, with the plural being used for alarger facility. (Remember that nouns and adjectives ending in - al form the plural with - aux.)

We are familiar with je vous en prie (see lessons and 35). In very formal contexts, however, the en can be dropped, particularly if the expression appears at the end of a sentence. Entrez, je vous prie, Please come in. You are unlikely to use je vous prie (and the tu form is very rarely used); however, you will probably hear it in certain circumstances, notably on the phone.

Afew nouns have two genders, each with adifferent meaning. One of the most common is poste. Une poste is apost office (lessons and 35) but un poste means aposition or job: Il quitte le poste de directeur en mai, He is leaving the position of director in May. The masculine word also means aswitchboard extension in atelephone system: Le poste ne ré pond pas, The extension is not answering. You can see why we insist on memorising not only the meaning of nouns but also their gender!

The adjective plein (feminine pleine, pronounced [plen]) means full or busy (think: plenty): Les hô tels sont toujours pleins en é té, The hotels are always full in summer. The invariable expression plein de means full of and, more broadly, lots of: Elle aplein de choses à faire, She has lots to do.

entendu is the past participle of entendre, to hear: J'ai entendu un bruit, Iheard a noise. But the word can be used alone in response to astatement that you acknowledge or agree with. Venez tô t demain. - Entendu. Come early tomorrow. - Will do. Of course, the actual translation will depend on the context but, in every case, avoid the (bad) French habit of saying OK instead of Entendu!

les coordonné es, coordinates, is the geographical term for distances or numbers identifying a position. By extension, it is commonly used to refer to a person'scontact details in the general sense. Thus Donnez-moi vos coordonné es can be translated as Give me your address / your contact details / your name and number, etc. If further details are needed, an adjective can be added - for instance, Donnez-moi vos coordonné es té lé phoniques or bancaires if you want the person'sphone number or bank details.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Job titles are often hard to translate because corporate structures differ from one country to another. Also, since English is widely used in the business world, many French companies anglicise to some extent their in-house vocabulary. Thus afirm may have both un directeur and un manager, who have different positions even though the second title is the translation of the first! But in most public companies, the top job is the same: le Directeur général, or managing director (also known as the chief executive). In some companies, le DG [day-zhay] as he (or she) is often called, can also be the chair of the company, in which case the title is le Président-directeur général, ("chairman and managing director") or le PDG [pay-day-zhay]. Note that most of the nouns used in French corporate job titles are still masculine, even if the person holding the office is female.

notes.content: In aformal register, careful speakers such as actors or newscasters tend to use linkage (see Introduction) more than would otherwise be the case. In this lesson, contrast the liaisons made in deux‿ou trois and films‿é trangers with je suis é tonné in line and sentence in the first exercise, both of which use the non-formal pronunciation found in everyday speech.

Most of this text is in aformal register, as used in the press, for example. In these contexts, French often shuns"ordinary"verbs such as ê tre and avoir, replacing them with fancier synonyms. Here, for example, La France aune longue tradition is rephrased using the regular verb possé der, to possess. Likewise, the cinema is known as le septiè me art, the seventh art. This tendency to"upgrade"simple concepts can be disconcerting at first, but it soon becomes afamiliar trope.

la diffusion comes from the verb diffuser, to diffuse but, more commonly, to spread or broadcast. The noun is used in terms such as la diffusion video, streaming, and la baladodiffusion, podcasting. These are relatively new coinages that have certainly not replaced the imported terms le streaming and le podcasting in everyday speech.

Here is agood example of how nouns are derived from verbs. From the verb mettre, to put, we get un metteur en scè ne ("aputter in stage"), afilm director or astage director, and la mise en scè ne, direction.

Another literary device used in formal writing is metonymy, the use of arelated term to stand in for an object or concept: les salles obscures ("the dark rooms") is used - always in the plural - to mean cinemas. However, the regular adjectives for dark are sombre (the absence of light, pronounced [sahbrruh]) or fonce (any colour approaching black): Mon nouveau pull est bleu fonce, My new sweater is dark blue.

We know that un rendez-vous means ameeting or an appointment (lesson 4, for example). But it can also be used figuratively when referring to an event attracting large numbers of people, Le Salon de l'automobile est le rendez-vous annuel des tous ceux qui aiment les voitures, The Motor Show is the annual get-together for everyone who loves cars. Because the final letters on both components of this compound noun are - sand - z, respectively, it does not change in the plural (des rendez-vous).

The Latin and Greek origins of French are evident in many everyday words. Here, for example, we have the suffix - phile (from the Greek philos, friend). With its Anglo-Saxon roots, English would translate this as lover: for example un bibliophile, a book-lover; un ciné phile, a film-lover or movie buff. The opposite suffix is - phobe (from phobos, fear): un aquaphobe: someone who is scared of water. These types of words are not considered formal.

suivi is the past participle of the Group verb suivre, to follow. Two other common verbs from the same group with the -iparticiple ending are finir → fini (to finish/finished) and dormir → dormi (to sleep/slept).
Here'sanother the past participle of a Group verb: voir → vu, to see → seen. Note also venir → venu, to come → came and avoir → eu, to have → had.

Introduced in lesson note 9, the present participle of all three verb groups ends in - ant: essayer → essayant (try → trying), finir → finissant (finish → finishing), rendre → rendant (give back → giving back). Note how the participle is used as an adjective: les arts vivants, the performing ("living") arts.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: In many French-speaking countries, the cinema is known as le grand écran ("the big screen") and the TV as le petit écran ("small screen"). One of France'stop film awards is la Palme d'Or, Golden Palm, presented to the best movie at le Festival de Cannes. And instead of the Oscars, the French movie industry organises its own annual awards, les Césars (named for the sculptor who designed the trophy). Foreign films are popular in France and are generally screened in two versions: en VO (version originale, with subtitles) or en VF (version française, dubbed into French).

notes.content: The familiar register in this lesson is in sharp contrast to the formality of the previous one. For example: the one-word exclamation Bof is aconcise idiomatic way of expressing indifference. It can be translated in several ways: Qu'est-ce que tu penses de ce film ? - Bof. What do you think of this movie? Not much!Meh/Whatever, etc.

In this lesson we come across two sets of Group verbs with their past participles: mettre → mis and prendre → pris; along with perdre → perdu, boire → bu, entendre → entendu, and plaire → plu. More details in lesson 42.

We saw the adjective é tranger, foreign, in lesson 39. The noun is identical: un é tranger / une é trangè re. It has two meanings: aforeigner and astranger (the latter derived directly from French). The context should make the meaning clear -for example, la Lé gion é trangè re, the Foreign Legion. Don'tconfuse the adjectives é tranger and é trange, strange: Quelle question é trange ! What astrange question!

dernier/derniè re means both last (lesson 14) and latest. Once again, context is key, because le dernier film de l'acteur can mean the actor'slast film (if he made no more movies or is deceased) and the actor'slatest film (their most recent performance). If in doubt, ask amovie buff or google the name!

Another familiar usage is nul (line 8). After a noun, the word literally means nil or null and void. But in idiomatic language, it indicates that the thing or person being described is useless, worthless, terrible, etc. Cet acteur est nul, That actor is terrible. Being an adjective, nul agrees with its noun: Cette actrice est nulle.

un truc, athing (lesson note 1), is used in the same way as in English to express something one likes or is keen on: Ce n'est pas mon/son/leur truc, It'snot my/his/her/their thing. Le sport, c'est son truc, He/she is into sports.

We know that si means both if and so (lesson note 1). It can also be used like oui when contradicting anegative statement, thus performing the same function as the repetition of the auxiliary in English: Il n'aime pas le chocolat - Si. He doesn'tlike chocolate. - Yes he does. To add extra insistence, the word is repeated: Si si, il l'adore, Oh yes he does, he loves it.

The suffix -erie, seen in lesson 25, can designate any place serving aspecific function: un billet → une billetterie, aticket / ticket office, une huile → une huilerie, oil (vegetable, etc.) / an oil mill or factory. Look for root word and work from there.

une bê te (the origin of beast) means an animal or a creature. As an adjective, it is used colloquially to mean silly or idiotie. Ton idé e est bê te, Your idea is silly. Auseful expression, in response to an acceptable suggestion, is Ce n'est pas bê te: Nous allons vendre notre voiture, - Ce n'est pas bê te. We are going to sell our car - That'snot abad idea.

un verre, aglass (lesson line 12) is used socially in the expression prendre un verre, to have / get a drink: Tu veux voir un film ou aller prendre un verre ? Do you want to see amovie or go for a drink?

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Identifying different registers in another language is difficult, particularly in the early stages of learning, and takes quite abit of practice. This lesson and the previous one are designed to underline some of the differences between formal and informal interactions in everyday French. For the time being, simply listen to the dialogues and do the exercises. You'll soon be able to differentiate between registers and take part actively in conversations using the appropriate language. Continuez le bon travail ! (Keep up the good work!)

notes.content: The terminal -euil has exactly the same sound as œil (lesson 32), so accueil is pronounced [ak-uh-yy]. In the verb accueillir, it precedes the ysound of the double-l, hence [ak-uh-yeer]. It'simportant to practise this sound, which does not exist in English.

accueillir has many different translations. Basically, it means to welcome, but it can be used in the broader sense of to meet, to pick up, etc. Mon amie Nadè ge m'aaccueilli à l'aé roport, My friend Nadè ge met me at the airport. The noun un accueil means a welcome, a reception, but the translation will depend on the context: Merci de votre accueil can mean Thanks for making me welcome or Thanks for having me. In apublic building, look for the sign Accueil, the reception desk.

The preposition depuis translates both for and since. It is used with the present tense, not the past: Je connais cet homme depuis vingt ans, Ihave known that man for twenty years. Elle est malade depuis Noë l, She has been sick since Christmas.

Here is another common example of apocope (lesson note 7), which mirrors English usage. The noun for asoftware routine, une application, is generally shortened to une appli, an app. This process of truncating long words is usual in technical contexts such as computing.

un fil, a wire, is often used in reference to telephones, even though landlines have almost vanished. Two common expressions are passer un coup de fil, to make phone call, give someone a ring, and au bout du fil, on the line. Do not confuse the plural les fils with the word for son: un fils / des fils. In the latter case, the singular and the plural are both pronounced [feess], compared with [fee/lfor fil / fils.

souhaiter is aformal verb meaning to wish (for) or to hope that. It is common in polite contexts: Aquelle heure souhaitez-vous venir ? What time do you wish to come? The noun, un souhait means a desire, a wish. The verbal response to someone sneezing is A tes/vos souhaits ! ("to your desires"), an exclamation inducted into English as Atishoo!

un couvert, from the verb couvrir, to cover, means a place-setting in culinary contexts, hence the expression mettre le couvert, to lay the table. In arestaurant context, the noun refers to acustomer or diner (known in the trade as"a cover"). Don'tconfuse un couvert with un couvercle, meaning alid or top of a container.

Remember that past participles used as adjectives must agree with their noun, so Gabriel est pris ce soir / Gabriel et Marc sont pris ce soir / Lucie est prise ce soir / Toutes les tables sont prises ce soir.

See lesson note 2. Using an inverted pronoun, rather than est-ce que, to ask aquestion is formal but quite common in formal social interaction. So instead of Est-ce que cela vous convient ? the restaurant owner enquires Cela vous convient-il ? (Listen to the liaison between the final tand the initial vowel.)
This is our first encounter with the future tense, which, in contrast to English, is formed not with an auxiliary but by changing the verb ending: chanter, to sing, → je chanterai.

Despite the prevalence of English, French has succeeded in coining"native"terms in the field of technology. One example is un texto, an SMS. Donne-moi ton numé ro et je t'envoie un texto tout à l'heure, Give me your number and I'll send you an SMS later. Even so, many young people in France opt for the English term un SMS. Which is unnecessary because the verb texter means"to text"!

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Léo Ferré (1916-1993) was a French singer, poet and composer who marked several generations of fans with his music, writing and politics. Ferré, along with his contemporaries Georges Brassens and Jacques Brel, was un auteur-compositeur-interprète ("author, composer, interpreter"), the nearest equivalent to the singer-songwriter typical of Anglo-American music. That tradition, known as la chanson (the song), attaches equal value to the music and the lyrics. More recently, the importance of the written word in French music has spawned several generations of rap and hip-hop artists who have become household names. Song lyrics can be hard to follow for language learners, but the pleasure of choosing asingle text and learning it by heart is definitely worth the effort.

notes.content: Participles: 1.1 Le participe pré sent - Present participle: Present participles, seen in lesson note and lesson note 6, are used less than in English because there is no progressive verb form in French. For most regular and irregular verbs, the participle is formed by dropping the ending from the first person plural of the present tense and adding -ant to the root: penser → pensons → pensant; dormir → dormons → dormant; perdre → perdons → perdant. (Remember that verbs ending -cer take acedilla in the first person plural, and thus in the participle (commencer → commenç ons → commenç ant), while -ger verbs take an e: manger → mangeons → mangeant). Present participles are used in two ways. First, as in English, to describe an ongoing action: Les personnes habitant prè s d'un aé roport souffrent souvent de maux de tê te. People living near an airport often get headaches. In this case, the participle does not agree with the noun. Asimilar usage is in aclause starting the preposition en: En vé rifiant la cave, j'ai trouvé la porte ouverte. While aliteral translation would be While checking the cellar, it is easier to recast the sentence: When Ichecked the cellar, Ifound the door open. The structure can be very different: Il arrive. En attendant, commenç ons à nettoyer la cuisine. He'son his way. In the meantime, let'sstart cleaning the kitchen. The other main use of the present participle is as an adjective, in which case it has to agree with the noun: C'est une histoire inté ressante. 1.2 Le participe passé - Past participle: In addition to functioning as adjectives, past participles are used to form le passé composé. They are therefore important. • For Group verbs (-er), simply drop the final -rand replace the -e-with -é. Hence commander → commandé, fermer → fermé, etc. There are no exceptions. • The rule for Group 2 (regular verbs ending in -ir with the present participle in -issant) is even simpler: simply drop the last letter: finir → fini, ré ussir → ré ussi. • For Group verbs (-re, -oir, -ir with apresent participle in -ant), the rules are: -re is replaced by -u: vendre → vendu; attendre → attendu; -oir verbs also end in -u: recevoir → reç u; vouloir → voulu; -ir behave mostly as regular Group verbs: partir → parti; sentir → senti. There are, however, many exceptions, notably frequently used verbs such as prendre → pris; faire → fait; dire → dit; courir → couru; mettre → mis; and, more importantly, the auxiliaries ê tre → é té, and avoir → eu. Two other common verbs with irregular past participles are pouvoir → pu, and savoir → su. When you learn anew verb, especially one from Group 3, always check the past participle. Finally, when apast participle is used alone as an adjective, it has to agree in number and gender with its noun: Toutes les tables sont prises, All the tables are taken; Cette robe est vendue en plusieurs couleurs, This dress is sold in several colours.

Le passé composé - the perfect tense: The perfect tense is known as le passé composé because it is"composed"of two parts: an auxiliary and apast participle. It is used in the spoken and written language to translate two English tenses: the past simple and the present perfect. There is an equivalent tense, le passé simple ("simple"because it consists of asingle word), which we cover only briefly at the end of this book because it is used chiefly in literature and, occasionally, very formal speech. The usual auxiliary is avoir, although some verbs take ê tre, as we shall see in the next set of lessons. The past participle sometimes has to agree with the direct object of the sentence, but we will look at this rule in more detail later on, particularly because it rarely affects the pronunciation. • Group 1: manger, to eat: j'ai mangé, tu as mangé, il/elle a mangé, nous avons mangé, vous avez mangé, ils/elles ont mangé. • Group 2: finir, to finish: j'ai fini, tu as fini, il/elle a fini, nous avons fini, vous avez fini, ils/elles ont fini. • Group 3: voir, to see: j'ai vu, tu as vu, il/elle a vu, nous avons vu, vous avez vu, ils/elles ont vu. The negative is formed by placing ne... pas around the auxiliary: je n'ai pas mangé, nous n'avons pas fini, ils n'ont pas vu. The three forms of the interrogative are (i) arising tone Tu as vu ? (ii) with est-ce que: Est-ce que tu as vu ? or (iii) inversion: As-tu vu ? The perfect tense relates to actions that took place in the past and are now complete. In this context, it is equivalent to the past simple tense in English: J'ai vu le notaire hier, Isaw the notary yesterday. But if we remove the time marker hier, the French verb remains the same (J'ai vu le notaire), whereas the English equivalent is either Isaw or the present perfect, Ihave seen the notary. When adverbs such as jamais and toujours are used with le passé composé, the verb is translated with the present perfect: J'ai toujours voulu / Je n'ai jamais voulu apprendre le franç ais. I've always/never wanted to learn French. In some cases, however, particularly with the preposition depuis, which translates both for and since, French uses the present rather than aperfect tense: Elle travaille ici depuis deux mois / depuis l'anné e derniè re. She has been working here for two months / since last year. Last, while English automatically uses the past tense to describe an action or sequence of actions that have taken place and are now complete, French tends to use the present form of the verb. This narrative device, known as le pré sent historique, brings the events to life and makes them more compelling: Hier, je vais au marché pour faire les courses mais j'oublie mon portefeuille. Yesterday, Iwent to the market to do the shopping but Iforgot my wallet. Of course, le passé composé can also be used in these cases, with absolutely no difference in meaning. To sum up, le passé composé does the work of both the simple past and the present perfect tenses in English and, for that reason, is easier to use. For instance: J'ai vu Max à Noë l mais je ne l'ai pas vu depuis. Isaw Max at Christmas but I haven'tseen him since.

Comparatives and superlatives: • The comparative of superiority is always formed with plus before the adjective and que after it: Londres est plus grand que Paris., London is bigger than Paris. Unlike English, the length of the adjective does not matter: Paris est plus cher que Bruxelles. Paris is more expensive than Brussels. • The same rule applies to comparisons of inferiority, formed with moins... que: Le film est moins inté ressant que le livre. The movie is less interesting than the book. • To form the superlative, simply put the definite article le or la for the singular (masculine/feminine) and les for the plural before plus or moins: Le bus est le moyen le plus rapide d'aller à Lille. The bus is the quickest way to get to Lille; C'est l'arrondissement le moins bruyant de la ville. It'sthe least noisy district in the city. Ahandful of adjectives are irregular, notably bon, bien and mauvais: bon, good → meilleur (que), better (than) → le meilleur / la meilleure, the best; bien, good/well → mieux (que), better than → le mieux / la mieux, the best; mauvais, bad → pire (que), worse (than) → le/la pire, the worst. Bien can be confusing at first because it is an adjective but also an adverb. As we will see later, it is invariable when used adjectivally: Elles sont trè s bien, tes nouvelles chaussures, Your new shoes are very nice. For adverbs, the superlative is formed with le (never la) before the comparative plus: le plus rapidement possible, as fast as possible.

On the phone: Using the telephone can be difficult, even in one'snative language, for many reasons. In aforeign language, those difficulties are compounded by rapid speech, an unfamiliar vocabulary and, usually, being unable to see the person you are talking to. And although texting, videoconferencing and other forms of digital communication are omni-present, being able to communicate by phone - té lé phone portable (mobile) or fixe (landline)- is still an important skill to learn. (Interestingly, although most communications today are wireless, the familiar expression for aphone call is still un coup de fil!) Here are some of the set phrases used in most conversations. • Allô is used when answering the phone or checking that the person you are calling can hear you. (One variant is Allô oui ?, although some people reply simply Oui ?, which is just as abrupt as Yes? in English.) To enquire about the identity of the caller, use the expression Qui est à l'appareil ? Who is calling? • To confirm that you have reached the right number, say Je suis bien chez... ? (for a person) or Je suis bien au/à la... (for a business, an administration, etc.) • If you ask to speak to someone other than the person answering, you will usually be asked: C'est de la part de qui ? Who shall Isay is calling? • Before transferring the call, the person will say Ne quittez/quitte pas (Hold the line) or Je vous le/la passe, I'll put you through to him/her, or both phrases together. • If the line is engaged, the message will be La ligne est occupé e or Ç a sonne occupé. If the person you wish to speak to is busy, you might want to leave them a message: Est-ce que je peux laisser un message ? or have them call you back Est-ce qu'il/qu'elle peut me rappeler s'il vous plaî t ? Or you can always say that you will call back later: Je rappellerai plus tard. • If you cannot hear the other person, tell them Je ne vous entends pas, parlez plus fort s'il vous plaî t. And if you have difficulty hearing or understanding, use one of these phrases: Je ne vous entends pas bien, I can'thear you very well, or Pouvez-vous ré pé tez lentement s'il vous plaî t ? Can you repeat slowly please? One slight difference between French and Anglo-American usage is that phone numbers are written and pronounced in two-digit groups. For example 06 32 72 would be given as zé ro six / trente-deux / soixante-douze / quatre-vingt-onze. Aword of advice: when taking down a number, pause if you hear soixante... because the next digit could be, for example, deux (62) or douze (72). The same applies to quatre-vingt..., which might be continued as quatre-vingt-quatre (84) or quatre-vingt-quatorze (94).

extras.title: Smile!
extras.content: In the past six lessons, you have expanded your knowledge of the different language registers that you're likely to encounter on aregular basis, either directly through conversation or indirectly through movies, books or videos. When you came back to this lesson series in the second part, or productive phase, of the learning process, you will realise just how much you have learned in arelatively short space of time.

notes.content: The names of many sports have been imported into French as masculine nouns. They include le tennis, le golf, le squash and le volley-ball. In acouple of cases, the names have been shortened. This is notably the case of le football → le foot and le basket-ball → le basket (the final tis pronounced). However, not all French sports have English names (for example, la natation, swimming) so always check in a dictionary.

When making the agreement between acompound noun and an adjective, always look for the root word, in this case é quipe, which is feminine (une é quipe fé minine, see line 15). With the noun l'é quipe de football, the adjective will agree with the head word, l'é quipe, not the second noun, football. By contrast, with asingle noun, the agreement is simple le football fé minin.

Certain verbs are conjugated in the perfect tense with ê tre instead of avoir when used intransitively. This lesson contains the main ones you will need to know, such as partir, to leave: je suis parti, tu es parti, il est parti, nous sommes partis, vous ê tes partis, ils sont partis. Another major difference with avoir-conjugated verbs is that the past participle agrees with the subject, thus Monsieur Gré goire est parti / Madame Gré goire est partie.

naî tre is avery irregular verb, meaning to be born. It is conjugated with ê tre in the perfect tense, so il est né / elle est né e means he / she was born. (The noun from naî tre is la naissance, birth, see lesson 23). The same conjugation rule applies to mourir, to die: je suis mort/morte, tu es mort/-e, il/elle est mort/-e, I / you / he died, etc.

plaire (past participle: plu) means to please but is used with the preposition à and an indirect object as asynonym for to like. In this case, the word is the reverse of English: La nouvelle maison plaî t à la famille, The family likes the new house (literally:"The new house is pleasing to the family"). If apronoun replaces the noun, it comes before the verb: Le film lui a plu, He liked the film. The same rule applies, for example, to demander à: Je vais demander à l'entraî neur → Je vais lui demander, I'mgoing to ask the coach. When learning anew verb, make sure to check the preposition, if any, that goes with it.

Masculine adjectives ending in -if form the feminine with -ive: sportif → sportive (sporty), cré atif → cré ative (creative), agressif → agressive (aggressive). Note how the feminine form is often used in English as an adjective.

quelque temps is an indefinite (and thus invariable) adjective describing ashort time period: a while, or the literal translation some time: Je ne les ai pas vus depuis quelque temps, I haven'tseen them for a while. Contrast this with longtemps (line 13), along time, written as asingle word.

Adding the definite article to bon, good, changes the meaning slightly, to correct, proper, or right: Tu es arrivé au bon moment, You came at the right time. Ce n'est pas la bonne question, That'snot the right question. One of the all-time classic guides to French grammar is Le Bon Usage, which translates as proper usage.

Here, personne is not anoun (lesson line 3) but an indefinite pronoun, meaning no one, nobody, anyone. It can be either the subject or the object of verb, and the accompanying verb is always in negative: Personne ne le sait, No one knows; Je ne connais personne ici, I don'tknow anyone here.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: The French school system is divided into four levels: l'école maternelle (nursery school), l'école primaire (primary school), le collège (roughly equivalent to middle school) and le lycée (secondary school). Students who graduate with the school-leaving certificate, le baccalauréat (known colloquially as le bac) can go on to l'université (university), which comprises several facultés (faculties). However, that word - often abbreviated to la fac - is also used in afamiliar register as asynonym for university.

notes.content: sens: the final sis pronounced: [sœhnss], as is the case for fils (son/sons) and for plus (more) at the end of a sentence.

We know that un titre means a title. By extension it also means adeed or a right, found in expressions like un titre de transport, aticket or travel card. As usual, context is all-important: when buying atrain ticket, you would ask for un billet but an inspector would likely ask you to show your titre de transport.

un quai is the origin of the English cognate quay. More broadly, it designates an embankment or riverside road. In atrain station, un quai is a platform, although the synonym une voie is also used, particularly in passenger announcements: Le train partira de la voie numé ro trois, The train will depart from platform number three.

In atravel context, un billet aller simple (or just un aller simple) means a one-way or single ticket. Areturn ticket is un (billet) aller-retour. The term for aseason ticket is une carte d'abonnement, literally"asubscription card,"or simply un abonnement.
In some cases, mauvais, bad, can mean wrong: Vous avez fait un mauvais numé ro, You've got the wrong number. There are several other ways of saying wrong, including faux, as we shall see later on.

un sens generally means a sense, but it can also relate to direction: Vous n'allez pas dans le bon sens, You're not going the right way. When buying atrain ticket, you can select aseat that faces forward: dans le sens de la marche, literally"the direction of walking,"i.e. movement.

The suffix -age can be added to the root of some verbs to make asubstantive noun. Thus composter means to time-stamp or punch a ticket, hence the noun le compostage: time-stamping. Likewise, afficher, to display gives us l'affichage, display or billposting.

marre, which is loosely related to la mer, the sea and hence the sense of discomfort brought on by sea-sickness, is found in the idiomatic expression en avoir marre, to be fed up. This can be used simply as an exclamation J'en ai marre !, I'mfed up!, or with adirect object: Il en amarre de son travail, He'sfed up with his job.

The adjective faux has several meanings, all related to things that are incorrect, fake or false. For example, un faux billet is aforged ticket while, in music, une fausse note is awrong note. The expression C'est faux means It'swrong or a falsehood. Remember, however, that to be wrong is avoir tort.
The opposite of ê tre d'accord avec, to agree with is ne pas ê tre d'accord avec, to disagree with: Je ne suis pas d'accord avec vous, Idisagree with you. It's simple!

vaut is the third person singular of the irregular valoir, to be worth: je vaux, tu vaux, il/elle vaut, nous valons, vous valez, ils/elles valent. Combien vaut ce tableau ? How much is this painting worth?

mal can be an adverb meaning badly as well as a noun, meaning pain or sickness. It can also be used figuratively, with du): J'ai du mal à le comprendre, Ihave difficulty understanding him. The expression prendre son mal en patience is equivalent to grin and bear it.

notes.content: The circumflex over the oof chô mage lengthens the vowel: [show-mahzh]; compare this sound with the oin dommage: [do-mahzh].

Most adjectives ending in -al, including social and royal, form their masculine plural with -aux: sociaux, royaux, etc. The feminine forms, sociale, royale, simply take an -s (sociales, royales). (Un ré seau, a network, forms its plural with an -x, as explained in lesson note 9.)

entendu, the past participle of entendre, to hear, can be used as a response, meaning Of course. The phrase Bien entendu has the same meaning but is more flexible and can be placed at the beginning, middle or end of acomplete sentence: Bien entendu, nous comprenons votre dé cision, Of course, we understand your decision.

qui and que are relative pronouns that can refer both to people and to things, qui as the subject and que as the direct object. It is important not to translate qui systematically as who because the subject can be inanimate: Prenez le bus qui part à dix heures, Take the bus that leaves at ten o'clock.

We know the noun un emploi, a job. Two related words are un mé tier, which, in addition to an occupation, can also mean atrade or craft, and une profession, a profession. The opposite, unemployment, is le chô mage. Ê tre au chô mage, to be unemployed.

ce qui and ce que are indefinite pronouns meaning which or what. They introduce asubordinate clause, in the same way as qui and que, but are used in sentences where the noun or phrase referred to by apronoun is not expressed.
voudrais is the first person singular of the conditional form of vouloir: je veux → je voudrais, Iwant → Iwould like.

Masculine job titles ending in -eur that are derived directly from averb have afeminine form ending in -euse - for example, un programmeur becomes une programmeuse - whereas -eur nouns that do not come from averb stem have the feminine ending -trice: un concept → un concepteur/une conceptrice.

The invariable phrase pas mal de is useful for describing afairly large quantity : Il y apas mal de neige ici en janvier, There'squite alot of snow here in January. Despite the adjective mal, bad, the term is not pejorative.

aussi... que is the comparative of equality, equivalent to as... as: Il est aussi grand que son pè re, He'sas tall as his father. The second noun can be replaced by astressed pronoun (but never asubject pronoun, as in English: Elle est aussi surprise que moi, She'sas surprised as I [am].

We know that French verbs do not have aprogressive form. Where necessary, though, the expression en train de, followed by an infinitive, allows us to insist on the ongoing nature of an action: Je ne peux pas venir, je suis en train de regarder le match, I can't come, I'mwatching the game. The important element is duration: Voici une bonne adresse pour votre prochain voyage ou votre voyage en cours si vous ê tes en train de voyager, Here's agood address for your next trip or your current trip if you are in the process of travelling. Don'tconfuse en train de with en train, by train!

The compound verb vouloir dire ("to want to say") translates as to mean, i.e. to imply or indicate. Only vouloir is conjugated: Qu'est-ce que tu veux / vous voulez dire ? What do you mean? However, in the sense to denote, we use the verb signifier: Que signifie ce mot ? What does this word mean?

notes.content: In formal language, monsieur and madame (but not mademoiselle) are used, along with an honorific, when addressing someone in an official position: monsieur le dé puté, ("mister member of parliament",) madame la directrice, ("madam director".) (Un agent de police, apolice officer; though masculine, l'agent can apply to officers of both sexes). Likewise, un é poux / une é pouse, a spouse, is used in official contexts, instead of un mari / une femme, to mean ahusband / a wife.

Remember that the past participle of verbs forming their perfect tense with ê tre (lesson note 3) agrees in number and gender with the subject, not the object, of the sentence. If aplural subject comprises both amale and afemale agent, as here, then the masculine takes precedence.

The stressed pronouns moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux and elles are used for emphasis, especially when acontrast is involved: Moi, j'aime le café au petit-dé jeuner, mais lui pré fè re le thé. In this context, the pronouns do not necessarily need to be translated into English: Ilike coffee for breakfast but he prefers tea. Note how the stressed pronoun is followed immediately by asubject pronoun (the second clause in our example could be phrased:... mais lui, il pré fè re le thé, in order to add even greater emphasis).

aucun is auseful adjective and pronoun, meaning not any, no, or none. As a determiner, it is not used in the plural and, in anegative construction, is not followed by pas: Ils n'ont aucun problè me de santé, They have no health problems. It must, however, agree with the singular noun it determines: Je n'ai aucune idé e, Ihave no idea. In informal language, asentence with the negative is often shortened: Aucune idé e.

Anumber of nouns are plural in French but singular in English. We already know les toilettes, the toilet, and en vacances, on holiday; another one is les cheveux, hair: Tes cheveux sont trop longs, Your hair is too long. The singular un cheveu is used in certain expressions, such as avoir un cheveu sur la langue ("to have ahair on the tongue"), to have alisp but rarely in the physical meaning of a hair.

In contrast to note 5, some nouns are plural in English but singular in French. This rule applies in particular to"two-legged"garments, which can be singularised in French: un jean, apair of jeans, un pantalon, apair of trousers. Logically, the plural two pairs of trousers is translated as deux pantalons.

meilleur, the comparative form of bon (lesson section 3), is an adjective and therefore agrees with its noun: J'ai une meilleure idé e, Ihave abetter idea. Ce café sert les meilleures crê pes et les meilleurs gâ teaux de Bretagne, This café serves the best pancakes and the best cakes in Brittany. Don'tconfuse meilleur with mieux, the comparative adverb of bien, well (see lesson section 3): Comment va ton frè re ? - Il va mieux.

The abstract noun la peine has several meanings, ranging from sadness to difficulty. Ce n'est pas la peine is an idiomatic expression meaning something like Don'tbother or Don'tworry about it. Vous voulez de l'aide ? - Ce n'est pas la peine, merci. Do you want help? - Don't bother, but thanks. In afull sentence, the expression is followed by the preposition de: Ce n'est pas la peine de chercher du sucre, il n'yen a plus. There'sno point looking for sugar, there'snone left.

Here'sanother idiomatic expression. Un souci is a concern, a worry. The common interjection Aucun souci is the equivalent of No problem or Don'tworry about it. An even commoner form is Pas de souci(s), in which case the noun can be in the plural.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: With asurface area of just 84.5square kilometres, the city of Paris is small compared with the likes of London or Los Angeles. One of the reasons is that it is surrounded by a 35km ring road called le Boulevard périphérique (in compound proper nouns, only the first word usually takes an initial capital). By contrast, the entire conurbation, known as le Grand Paris (greater Paris), is ten times larger. The city within le Périph' -the ring-road's nickname-is often referred to as Paris intra-muros, from the Latin phrase meaning"within walls."

notes.content: The terminal -er of the masculine noun l'hiver is pronounced [air], as in cher (rather than [ay], as in aller). Don'tforget that the half-vowel his not pronounced (just like hour in English) so, with en hiver, the final nof en runs into the iof hiver: [œhneevair]. nez is pronounced [nay], like the final syllable of the second person plural of an -er verb: venez: [vuhnay].

The English comparative phrase the more... the more has adirect equivalent in French: plus... plus. Typically, this type of construction uses the impersonal pronoun on: Plus on gagne de l'argent, plus on dé pense, The more money you earn, the more you spend. (Another well-known saying, Plus on est de fous, plus on rit -literally"The more madmen there are, the more we laugh"- is the equivalent of The more, the merrier.)

ce is both asingular demonstrative adjective (lesson note 1) and ademonstrative pronoun. It can replace il/elle est (→ c'est) but also ils/elles sont, (→ ce sont), in which case it is translated by they. Ce sont deux de mes films pré fé ré s, They are two of my favourite movies. The differences between il/elle est (ils/elles sont) and c'est (ce sont) are quite complex but, in this case, c'est / ce sont describes asituation ("they're lazy") as opposed to the specific person or object.

As we know, gros / grosse means fat (lesson section 5.2). But it has amuch broader meaning, including big (lesson line 11), thick (un gros manteau, athick coat), and serious (une grosse erreur, aserious mistake). To translate the adjective properly or find an idiomatic equivalent, always check the noun it is qualifying: Tu es un gros paresseux ! You're a slacker/ a lazybones! The expression en gros, usually placed at the beginning of asentence or clause, means broadly, basically, etc.

é ventuellement is a faux-ami. It expresses the idea of possibility: Je ne connais pas la ré ponse, mais vous pouvez é ventuellement la trouver en ligne, I don'tknow the answer but you may be able to find it online. Nicole vient à la fê te demain ? - É ventuellement, Is Nicole coming to the party tomorrow? - Maybe. (The adjective is é ventuel, possible). The adverb eventually is rendered finalement or enfin: Il afinalement acheté une nouvelle collection de timbres, He eventually bought anew stamp collection.)

courant is both anoun and an adjective: le courant means the current, while the adjective means ordinary, standard, common, etc. C'est un problè me courant, It's acommon problem. The expression ê tre au courant, first seen in lesson 32, means to be aware of something: Ma belle-sœur arrive demain. - Oui, je suis au courant. My sister-in-law is arriving tomorrow. - Yes, I'maware of that. Tenir au courant, to keep someone informed/posted.

Some verbs have no direct equivalent in other languages. That is the case for to charge (money). The most convenient equivalent is probably facturer, to invoice: Le plombier m'afacturé six cents euros de l'heure, The plumber charged me 600 euros an hour. Another possibility is prendre, to take, usually with amonetary amount or an adjective: Combien prend-il pour une leç on privé e ? How much does he charge for aprivate lesson?

When demi, half, comes before a noun, it is invariable: une demi-heure, un demi-kilo. After the noun, however, it can be feminine or masculine depending on the gender -une heure et demie, un kilo et demi-but never plural. In every case, the pronunciation is identical [duhmee].

We have seen bien used as an adverb meaning well, but it can also be an adjective, usually as part of an expression before a noun: Elle est trè s bien, cette chanteuse, She'svery good, that singer. In such cases, however, it does not agree with the subject: Les fauteuils sont trè s bien, The armchairs are very nice.

We know that indirect object pronouns come before the verb in French (lesson section 5). One slight complication is that some verbs taking an indirect object in English require adirect object in French. Among the most common of these are chercher, to look for, to fetch, and attendre, to wait for. In this case, the noun is replaced by adirect object pronoun: J'attends Didier et son collè gue → Je les attends (not Je leur attends).

le boulot is afamiliar but very common word for work, for which there is no one-on-one equivalent. Unlike its English counterpart, the noun is both countable and uncountable. J'ai beaucoup de boulot en ce moment, I've got alot of work at the moment; Jeanne commence son nouveau boulot ce lundi, Jeanne is starting her new job this Monday. The imperative expression Allez, au boulot ! means something like: Let'sget cracking! Another slang word that has no equivalent is un bouquin, a book, line 15, used in afamiliar register in the same way as un livre.
