extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: L'argot (slang) was once the language of thieves, footpads and other ne'er-do-wells. In its current acceptance, it means aset of non-technical words and expressions used by aparticular social group, whereas familiar language has amuch broader reach. In this book, we have largely avoided slang, while introducing familiar words and expressions, such as un bouquin and le boulot, which are widely used across all social classes and groups. Significantly, some of these colloquialisms have no direct equivalents in English, as these two examples show.

dialogue.french: Oh là là, pourquoi est-ce que tu fais cette tête ? Qu'est-ce qu'il t'arrive, ma pauvre amie ?
dialogue.english: Oh dear, why are you pulling that long face? What's happened to you, my poor friend?

dialogue.french: Je devais partir hier aux sports d'hiver avec une bande de copains.
dialogue.english: I was supposed to leave for winter sports yesterday with a bunch of friends.

dialogue.french: On allait faire la fête – et peut-être un peu de sport – dans un super chalet au pied des pistes.
dialogue.english: We were going to party – and maybe do a bit of sport – in a great chalet at the foot of the slopes.

dialogue.french: J'avais fait les valises, préparé mes affaires de ski et commandé un taxi pour cinq heures –
dialogue.english: I had packed my bags, prepared my ski gear and ordered a taxi for 5 a.m. –

dialogue.french: il n'est pas question de faire la grasse matinée quand on est en vacances à la neige !
dialogue.english: out of the question to lie in when on a winter holiday!

dialogue.french: Je quittais la maison quand j'ai reçu un message du bureau disant que ma présence était demandée.
dialogue.english: I was leaving the house when I received a message from the office saying that my presence was requested.

dialogue.french: J'avais fait le point avec mes collègues la veille, mais ils m'ont quand même fait venir aux aurores.
dialogue.english: I had updated my colleagues the day before, but they still made me come in at the crack of dawn.

dialogue.french: Du coup, j'ai dû faire une croix sur les vacances. Voilà pourquoi je fais la tête.
dialogue.english: As a result, I had to forgo the holidays. That's why I'm pulling a long face.

dialogue.french: Mais à vrai dire, ça me soulage un petit peu aussi car je devais partir avec Gaspard et Noé.
dialogue.english: But to tell the truth, I'm a little bit relieved, too, because I was supposed to leave with Gaspard and Noé.

dialogue.french: Partir avec ces deux-là, ensemble ? Il faut le faire !
dialogue.english: Leaving with those two, together? That's quite something!

dialogue.french: Gaspard s'est fait connaître pour son esprit de compétition bien développé.
dialogue.english: Gaspard made himself known for his well-developed competitive spirit.

dialogue.french: Pour ne pas dire esprit agressif ! Quand il est en compétition, celui-là, il ne fait pas de cadeau !
dialogue.english: Not to say aggressive spirit! When he's in competition, he gives people a tough time!

dialogue.french: D'ailleurs, il s'est fait un certain nombre d'ennemis à cause de ça.
dialogue.english: Moreover, he's made a number of enemies because of that.

dialogue.french: Mais il sait aussi se faire respecter. Gaspard est ami avec toutes les stars du sport, à qui il fait la bise.
dialogue.english: But he also knows how to make people respect him. Gaspard is friends with all the sports stars, with whom he's on kissing terms.

dialogue.french: Comment se fait-il qu'il soit devenu un si bon skieur ? Il a dû se faire aider par quelqu'un, non ?
dialogue.english: How is it that he's become such a good skier? He must have had help from someone, mustn't he?

dialogue.french: Non, il s'est fait tout seul, sans entraîneur, sans équipe et sans sponsor.
dialogue.english: No, he's self-made, without a coach, without a team and without a sponsor.

dialogue.french: Et Noé ?
dialogue.english: What about Noé?

dialogue.french: Il me fait de la peine, celui-là : c'est un désastre ambulant.
dialogue.english: I feel sorry for him: he's a walking disaster.

dialogue.french: On lui a souvent dit de faire gaffe mais il n'en fait qu'à sa tête.
dialogue.english: We've often told him to be careful but he does just as he pleases.

dialogue.french: L'année dernière, il n'a fait que quelques mètres avant de tomber et se fracturer les deux bras.
dialogue.english: Last year, he only went a few meters before he fell and broke both his arms.

dialogue.french: Il a dû se faire secourir par hélicoptère.
dialogue.english: He had to be rescued by helicopter.

dialogue.french: Cela dit, il a visiblement fait des progrès car l'année d'avant, il s'était cassé la cheville en descendant du train à la station de ski.
dialogue.english: Having said that, he has obviously made progress because the year before, he had broken his ankle getting off the train at the ski resort.

notes.content: chips, meaning crisps, is a faux-ami but, above all, aforeign import. Which is why the final sis pronounced. (Remember, too that ch-is pronounced as [sh].) The word is therefore pronounced [sheeps].

We have already seen dire used idiomatically to mean to fancy, like, etc. (lesson note 5). Arelated expression, Ç a ne me dit rien, expresses alack of interest or enthusiasm: Tu veux venir au ciné ma avec nous ? - Ç a ne me dit rien, Do you want to come to the movies with us? - I don'tfeel like it. As in our example (line 2), ç a can be replaced by a noun. The same structure can also express alack of recognition or familiarity: Ce nom ne me dit rien, I'mnot familiar with that name.

When describing temperature conditions, French does not use the same verbs as English. We already know avoir chaud and avoir froid (lesson note 3). Likewise, faire chaud / froid describes the ambient temperature: Il y aune grande diffé rence de tempé rature dans cette ré gion de France, il fait trè s chaud en é té et il fait trè s froid en hiver, There is abig difference in temperature in this region of France, it is very hot in summer and very cold in winter. When talking about the weather, chaud by itself can mean both hot and warm.

Like bien (lesson note 8), mal is usually an adverb -Je dors mal quand il fait chaud comme ç a, Isleep badly when it'shot like that-but it can sometimes be used as an adjective. In this case, it is usually invariable and can only be used with state-of-being verbs like ê tre: Je n'ai rien fait de mal, I haven'tdone anything wrong. Don'tconfuse mal with the adjective mauvais(e): C'est une mauvaise idé e, It's abad idea. And don'tconfuse avoir mal, to feel pain, with the idiomatic expression avoir du mal.

Remember that the adjective describes the head noun, in this case une salade, and not the complement, de riz. It therefore has to agree in the feminine plural. For example, une salade de fruits dé licieuse, adelicious fruit salad. This rule applies to all such compound nouns. (Note that English, which has no grammatical genders, is less precise than French in this respect: does delicious apply to fruit, salad or both? If we want to insist on the first noun, we would have to say asalad of delicious fruit, whereas French makes the distinction through adjective agreement une salade de fruits dé licieux.)
The preposition en is used between two nouns to describe what the first object is made of: une assiette en carton, acardboard plate, deux tasses en porcelaine, two china cups, etc.
supporter, to support, also means to tolerate. The verb is often used idiomatically in the negative: Je ne supporte pas cette é mission, I can'tstand that show.

When a BAGS adjective (lesson section 5.2) comes before aplural noun, the partitive article des becomes de (or d' before a vowel). For example, Nous achetons des produits sains, We buy healthy produce, but Nous achetons de bons produits sains, We buy good healthy produce.

Ceci and cela (line 14) are demonstrative pronouns meaning this, that, and, in impersonal sentences, it. Ceci is not widely used in everyday language, except when referring to something that is about to be mentioned or presented: É coutez ceci et dites-moi ce que vous en pensez, Listen to this and tell me what you think. Cela is usually abbreviated to ç a in informal language: Ç a te fait quelques centaines d'euros...

à is used in compound nouns to indicate the purpose of adesignated object, whereas English strings two nouns together: un panier à pique-nique, apicnic basket, un sac à dos, abackpack ("abag to the back"). Likewise, un verre à eau, awater glass, etc. Be careful not to confuse à with de (of) in this type of noun: un verre à vin, awine glass, un verre de vin, aglass of wine. The difference can be disappointing...

passer means to pass, which we have seen in lesson line 12, as well as in the idiom passer un coup de fil (lesson note 4). But se passer (literally:"to pass oneself") is areflexive verb. In this context, the idiom se passer means to happen: Qu'est-ce qui se passe ?, What's happening? / What'sgoing on?

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Fifty kilometres southeast of Paris, the city of Fontainebleau is famed for its huge forest, now classified as anational park, and its royal palace, le Château de Fontainebleau, dating from the 12th century.

dialogue.french: Qu'est-ce qu'il y a, Driss ? Tu as l'air complètement KO. Ça ne va pas ?
dialogue.english: What's up? You look completely exhausted. Things not going well?

dialogue.french: Si si, mais tout est sens dessus dessous en ce moment. J'ai le nez dans le guidon depuis cinq jours parce que j'écris un article sur les Dauphins.
dialogue.english: Yes, things are a little upside down right now. I've been totally immersed in things for five days because I'm writing an article about the Dolphins.

dialogue.french: Cette équipe de foot dont le capitaine, Dulong, a disparu dans la nature en 1980 ?
dialogue.english: That football team whose captain, Dulong, disappeared into the wild in 1980?

dialogue.french: Je m'en souviens bien. C'est une histoire qui a défrayé la chronique à l'époque.

dialogue.french: C'est vrai, elle a fait couler beaucoup d'encre mais, d'après moi, on n'a jamais su toute la vérité.
dialogue.english: It's true, a lot has been written about it, but in my opinion, we never knew the whole truth.

dialogue.french: Je n'ai pas réussi à parler avec Dulong, ou, plutôt, il a exigé une somme faramineuse pour une interview.

dialogue.french: Mais son ancien agent, Jacques Cartier, lui, a donné son accord tout de suite. Bingo !

dialogue.english: I asked him really precise questions, but each time he evaded the issue. He told me the truth, sure. But his truth!

dialogue.french: Tu aurais dû me demander de t'accompagner. « Au secours ! J'ai besoin d'aide ! »
dialogue.english: You should have asked me to come with you. "Help! I need assistance!"

dialogue.english: I would have come straight away. With guys like that, it's always the strongest who wins.

notes.content: Verbs conjugated with ê tre instead of avoir in the perfect tense: 1.1 The verbs: Agroup of verbs expressing either movement or achange of place or condition form their perfect tense with ê tre instead of avoir. There are sixteen main verbs, which can be remembered with asimple mnemonic: meet Dr and Mrs Vandertramp: Devenir (to become); Revenir (to come back); Mourir (to die); Retourner (to return); Sortir (to go out); Venir (to come); Arriver (to arrive); Naî tre (to be born); Descendre (to come down, descend); Entrer (to enter); Rentrer (to come back); Tomber (to fall); Rester (to rest); Aller (to go); Monter (to go up); Partir (to leave). Five of these have irregular past participles: venir → venu, and its derivatives devenir → devenu and revenir → revenu, as well as naî tre → né and mourir → mort (see lesson note 4). There are other members of this family, notably the verb passer, to pass, which can be both transitive and intransitive. We'll see these later on. 1.2 Conjugation: All these verbs are conjugated with ê tre instead of avoir in the perfect tense. This edifying little story might serve as another mnemonic (or acautionary tale). Ce lundi, Paul est arrivé trè s en retard pour son rendez-vous. Il est entré dans l'immeuble en courant et puis est monté au deuxiè me é tage. Personne. Il est descendu au premier é tage. Toujours personne. Il est retourné à l'accueil, où on lui a dit."Votre client ? Mais il est parti il y aune heure. Il est resté longtemps dans votre bureau mais vous n'ê tes pas venu. Il est devenu trè s impatient et il est sorti en colè re. Je pense qu'il est rentré chez lui. Ou il est peut-ê tre allé au café en face. Une chose est sû re : il n'est pas revenu ici". Paul est sorti tellement vite du bâ timent qu'il est tombé sous un camion. Pauvre Paul : il est né pour travailler mais il est mort au travail. This Monday, Paul arrived very late for his appointment. He ran into the building and then went upstairs to the second floor. No one was there. He went down to the first floor. Still no one. He went back to the reception desk, where he was told:"Your client? He left an hour ago. He was in your office for along time, but you didn'tshow up. He became very impatient and came out in an angry mood. Ithink he went home. Or maybe he went to the cafe opposite. One thing is sure: he didn'tcome back here."Paul ran out of the building so fast that he fell under a lorry. Poor Paul: he was born to work but he died at work. The past participle of these ê tre-conjugated verbs agrees in number and gender with the subject of the sentence. Returning to the above example: Marie est arrivé e trè s en retard pour son rendez-vous, Mary arrived very late for her appointment. Les deux hommes sont monté s au deuxiè me é tage, The two men went up to the second floor. Les deux femmes sont retourné es à l'accueil, The two women went back to the reception desk. If the plural subjects of an ê tre verb include amasculine and afeminine noun, then the participle agrees in the masculine: Paul et sa femme sont partis aprè s le diner. Paul and his wife left after dinner. Les hommes et les femmes sont arrivé s au mê me moment. The men and the women arrived at the same time. However, this centuries-old rule on masculine precedence -Le masculin l'emporte sur le fé minin, The masculine takes precedence over the feminine-is increasingly called into question in today'smore egalitarian world, and la rè gle de proximité, proximity rule, whereby adjectives (including participles) agree with the gender of the nearest noun, is making significant headway. Moreover, there is an ongoing debate about abolishing the rule on past-participle agreement altogether. In the meantime, however, we will stick to the established rule, albeit unenthusiastically.

Stressed, or emphatic, pronouns: These pronouns also exist in English but are not always used in the same way. moi (I, me), toi (you), lui (he, him), elle (she, her), nous (we, us), vous (you), eux (they, them - masc.), elles (they, them - fem.). They are used if the personal pronoun is emphasized (hence emphatic) or contrasted with another pronoun (or noun), which they generally precede. Toi, tu es un vrai ami, You're areal friend. Alain adore les pique-niques mais moi, je ne les supporte pas, Alain loves picnics but I can'tstand them. Stressed pronouns are also used in some imperative -or emphatic-constructions: Fais-le, toi ! You do it! Trouvez-la moi, Find her/it for me. The pronouns can also be used with amultiple subject: Ma femme et moi, nous aimons travailler ensemble, My wife and Ilike working together. In these examples, we can see that the pronoun seems disconnected from the sentence and could, theoretically, be omitted (which is why they are also called disjunctive pronouns). In French they are used almost systematically, which is why it'simportant to learn them in context. Finally, there is an impersonal third-person emphatic pronoun, soi, which we will see later on.

Relative pronouns: 3.1qui and que: Qui and que are used to avoid repeating anoun or pronoun. Learners often confuse the two because they can refer both to people and to things. First and foremost, it is important to avoid the common mistake of systematically translating qui as who and que as that. Think grammatically: qui is the subject and que the direct object. In asubordinate clause, the pronouns are equivalent to who (or whom), which and that. • Qui: The subject of asentence is often a person, but not always: L'homme qui nous aide pour le dé mé nagement est mon beau-frè re. The man who is helping us with the removal is my brother-in-law. J'ai horreur des couteaux qui ne coupent pas. Ihate knives that don't cut. Since qui refers to the subject, it is always followed by a verb. It can also be used with apreposition to replace an indirect object: Nous sommes une socié té à qui vous pouvez faire confiance. We're acompany that you can trust. La socié té pour qui j'ai travaillé n'existe plus. The company that Iworked for no longer exists. (In informal English, the preposition whom has all but disappeared, yet it is the equivalent of qui in this type of construction. Moreover, English prepositions are often placed alongside the verb ("the company that Iwork for"rather than"the company for which I work"). In French however, the preposition and the relative always stay together. Which is why, to an English-speaking ear, French often sounds formal. • Que: This pronoun replaces the direct object (thing or person) in arelative clause and is followed by anoun or pronoun: La Tour Eiffel, que tout le monde connaî t, est situé e prè s de la Seine. The Eiffel Tower, which everyone knows, is located near the Seine. Les personnes que nous allons rencontrer aujourd'hui vont nous aider. The people who[m] we are going to meet today are going to help us. Before avowel or the letter h, que become qu': La banane est le fruit qu'elle aime le moins. The banana is the fruit that she likes least; La chose qu'Henri dé teste le plus est la pluie. The thing (that) Henri hates the most is the rain. In every case, the relative pronouns and their subsequent clauses must be placed immediately after the antecedent, i.e. the word or words that they replace (la tour, les personnes, le morceau, etc.) 3.2ce qui and ce que: Like qui and que, the indefinite relative pronouns ce qui and ce que introduce asubordinate clause. They mean which/what and are used in sentences where the noun or phrase referred to by apronoun is not expressed. Ce qui relates to the phrase that is the subject of the verb: Mon mari a disparu, ce qui m'inquiè te, My husband has disappeared, which worries me. In this sentence, ce qui replaces the noun phrase his disappearance worries me. Ce que relates to the object of the verb: Je ne comprends pas ce que vous voulez dire. I don'tunderstand what you mean. The pronoun is often used for emphasis at the beginning of a sentence, just like What: Ce qu'il veut dire est que nous sommes en retard. What he means is that we're late. Note that only ce que is abbreviated to qu' before a vowel.

Singular versus plural: Some nouns that are always singular in French are plural in English, and vice versa (lesson 46). In some cases, a French noun exists in both the singular and the plural (i.e. it is countable), for instance une information, apiece of information, les informations, information in general (or the news, see below). One of the most obvious examples concerns garments"with two legs."In addition to un pantalon, this rule also applies to un collant, tights; un jean, jeans; un maillot de bain, swimming trunks; un pyjama, pyjamas; un short, shorts; and un slip, underpants. To form the plural -for example, three pairs of shorts-simply add an sto the noun: trois shorts. Other common examples of this singular-to-plural shift include l'actualité, current affairs, l'escalier, the stairs, la politique, politics, and la vaisselle, dishes; as well as certain sciences, such as la physique, physics and la linguistique, linguistics. Conversely, nouns that are generally plural in French but singular in English include les affaires, business; les conseils, advice; les toilettes, the toilet; les bagages, luggage, and les connaissances, knowledge. It is important to remember these nouns because, in some cases, the singular and plural forms can have slightly different meanings. For example, les affaires, business, une affaire, a firm; la recherche, research, les recherches, searches; or l'actualité, current affairs, les actualité s, the news (bulletin) -asynonym of les informations. We'll see some more examples in upcoming lessons.

Prepositions: Prepositions are vitally important because they connect different parts of asentence and alter the meaning of verbs. French has no equivalent of the phrasal verbs that are so hard to learn in English (go up, down, in, out, through, etc.) but even so it is important to learn the preposition that normally accompanies a verb, especially where there is adifference between English and French: é couter, to listen to, for example. Here is atable showing the main prepositions (some of which, marked with an asterisk, are also adverbs). You have already seen all of them. à to: Passe le carton à Jé rô me. Pass the box to Jé rô me. aprè s* after: Aprè s vous, madame. After you, madam. avant* before: Venez avant neuf heures. Come before o'clock. avec* with: Elle sort avec mon meilleur ami. She'sgoing out with my best friend. chez to/at (the home of): Je reste chez moi ce soir. I'mstaying at home this evening. contre* against: Le tableau est contre le mur. The painting is against the wall. dans in: Ils connaissent un bon restaurant. They know agood restaurant. de of,from: Sorya vient de Marseille. Sorya is from Marseille. depuis* since, from: Je suis là depuis ce matin. Ihave been here since this morning. derriè re* behind: Le magasin est derriè re l'é glise. The shop is behind the church. devant* in front of: Le Louvre est devant vous. The Louvre is in front of you. en in: Ê tes-vous libre en avril ou en mai ? Are you free in April or May? entre between: Il y aun match entre la France et l'Espagne. There's amatch between France and Spain. par by: J'ai ré ussi à la joindre par té lé phone. Imanaged to reach her by phone. pendant during, for: Elle aré flé chi pendant quelques secondes. She thought for afew seconds. pour for: Avez-vous un secret pour le loto ? Do you have asecret for the lotto? prè s de near: Ils sont assis prè s de la fenê tre. They're sitting near/by the window. sous under: Tes clé s sont sous la table. Your keys are under the table. sur on: On afait des recherches sur Internet. We searched on the Internet. vers towards: Il va vers la gare. He'sgoing towards the station. Use this table to revise the prepositions from time to time, until you can recognise them instantly.

extras.title: Smile!
extras.content: You have now completed the receptive phase of the method. Lesson 50 marks the beginning of the productive phase, when you start to generate your own phrases and sentences. When you reach the end of anew lesson from 50 to 100, go back to the beginning of the book and study alesson you have already seen, as instructed, and translate the main dialogue and the first exercise into French. For more information, see the Introduction. Maintenant, continuons (Now, let's continue!).

dialogue.french: Je me réveille à la même heure et je me connecte à Internet pour lire les messages dans ma boîte de réception.
dialogue.english: I wake up at the same time and I log on to the internet to read the messages in my inbox.

dialogue.french: Si j'ai vraiment envie, j'écoute les informations à la radio – je me méfie des journaux télévisés
dialogue.english: If I really want to, I listen to the news on the radio – I'm wary of TV news broadcasts

dialogue.french: car je trouve qu'ils se trompent constamment et, de toute façon, les infos me dépriment.
dialogue.english: because I find that they constantly get things wrong and, in any case, the news depresses me.

dialogue.french: Moins on les écoute, plus on est tranquille.
dialogue.english: The less you listen to it, the calmer you feel.

dialogue.french: De temps à autre, je lis un magazine sur ma tablette, mais je le finis en cinq minutes.
dialogue.english: From time to time, I read a magazine on my tablet, but I finish it in five minutes.

dialogue.french: Au bout d'un quart d'heure, je me lève très lentement – je ne me dépêche pas –
dialogue.english: After a quarter of an hour, I get up very slowly – I don't hurry –

dialogue.french: puis je vais dans la salle de bains, où je me rase, me lave et me brosse les dents.
dialogue.english: then I go into the bathroom, where I shave, wash, and brush my teeth.

dialogue.french: Ensuite je m'habille et me prépare à partir au travail, en centre-ville.
dialogue.english: Then I get dressed and prepare to leave for work, in the town centre.

dialogue.french: J'y vais en voiture, jamais en bus ou en métro, et j'y suis en vingt minutes.
dialogue.english: I go by car, never by bus or by metro, and I'm there in twenty minutes.

dialogue.french: En arrivant, je m'installe dans mon bureau et ferme la porte à clé.
dialogue.english: When I arrive, I settle in my office and lock the door.

dialogue.french: Je fais semblant de travailler, mais j'essaie surtout de ne pas m'endormir.
dialogue.english: I pretend to work, but I try above all not to fall asleep.

dialogue.french: Le travail, c'est dur, vous savez. Je me demande si je suis fait pour ça.
dialogue.english: Work is very hard, you know. I wonder whether I'm made for it.

dialogue.french: C'est très stressant de ne rien faire. Je dois me détendre autant que possible.
dialogue.english: It's very stressful doing nothing. I must relax as much as possible.

dialogue.french: Mon médecin m'a conseillé de ne pas m'énerver et de me reposer quand je peux.
dialogue.english: My doctor advised me not to get annoyed and to rest when I can.

dialogue.french: Mais vous vous amusez quand même un peu ? En fait, quel métier faites-vous ?
dialogue.english: But you enjoy yourself a little anyway? In fact, what job do you do?

dialogue.french: Je suis Président-directeur général d'une des entreprises de mon père.
dialogue.english: I'm Chairman and Managing Director of one of my father's companies.

dialogue.french: Ça ne m'étonne pas !
dialogue.english: That doesn't surprise me!

notes.content: tranquille: Despite the seemingly feminine ending (-lle), the adjective tranquille is masculine, so the last syllable is pronounced [-eel].

This lesson looks at pronominal verbs and, more specifically, reflexive verbs, where the subject is the person or thing performing the action. Indicated by se (or s' in the infinitive: s'ennuyer, for example), these verbs always take reflexive pronouns in French, though not necessarily in English. Thus the transitive verb ennuyer quelqu'un, to bore someone, requires apronoun in the reflexive form: je m'ennuie, which translates as Iam bored ("Ibore myself") or, in some contexts, Iget bored. Likewise, Je connecte mon ordinateur à mon té lé phone, I'mconnecting my computer to my phone, requires apronoun if the subject and object are the same person: Je me connecte à Internet, I'mconnecting to the internet.

à with the definite article (au with amasculine noun) translates on in the case of communications media such as the TV, radio or phone: à la radio, à la té lé vision, au té lé phone. Be careful not to use sur.

se mé fier (de) means to mistrust or be suspicious of (it is the negative form of se fier à, to trust). Elle se mé fie des informations qu'elle lit en ligne, She mistrusts the news that she reads online. (Remember: de becomes des because informations is plural). The imperative Mé fiez-vous ! is commonly used as awarning - Mé fiez-vous du chien !, Beware of the dog - and in certain proverbs: Il faut se mé fier de l'eau qui dort ("You need to be wary of water that sleeps"), i.e. Still waters run deep.
Here is another apocope (lesson note 7): les informations, the news, is shortened in everyday speech to les infos.

me is one of the reflexive pronouns, along with te, se (the same as the infinitive), nous and vous. But it is also adirect object pronoun (lesson note 6). For example, Je me ré veille à midi, Iwake up at noon, but Le bruit me ré veille toutes les nuits, The noise wakes me every night.

en, as we know, can be both an adverbial pronoun (lesson note 2) and apreposition meaning on, in, to, etc. Note how it is used in this lesson, and how it contrasts with dans (lines and 12). In particular, en is used with modes of transport -en bus, en voiture, etc.- but not for walking: aller à pied (lesson line 10). We'll look at en vs. dans in greater detail in the next revision lesson.

Many verbs that are reflexive in French but not in English concern everyday actions such as getting up (se lever), shaving (se raser), dressing (s'habiller), brushing one'steeth (se brosser les dents), but also taking ashower (se doucher), applying make-up (se maquiller) and brushing one'shair (se brosser les cheveux).
See lesson section 1.1.

The noun semblant, the origin of semblance, is commonly used in the expression faire semblant (de), to pretend or act as if. Mon enfant fait semblant de ne pas m'entendre quand je dis non, My child pretends not to hear me when Isay no.

demander (à), to ask, is used in the pronominal form, se demander, to mean to wonder ("to ask oneself"): Je me demande ce qu'il faut faire, Iwonder what to do. The verb is rarely used in the negative.
Note that the English idiom I don'twonder means I'mnot surprised and is translated with the verb s'é tonner (the root of to astonish): Ç a ne m'é tonne pas, That doesn'tsurprise me.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Job titles are often hard to translate because corporate structures differ from one country to another. Also, since English is widely used in the business world, many French companies anglicise to some extent their in-house vocabulary. Thus afirm may have both un directeur and un manager, who have different positions even though the second title is the translation of the first! But in most public companies, the top job is the same: le Directeur général, or managing director (also known as the chief executive). In some companies, le DG [day-zhay] as he (or she) is often called, can also be the chair of the company, in which case the title is le Président-directeur général, ("chairman and managing director") or le PDG [pay-day-zhay]. Note that most of the nouns used in French corporate job titles are still masculine, even if the person holding the office is female. Today we start the productive phase of our method, as explained at the end of lesson 49. Productive phase: 1st lesson

dialogue.french: Tout le monde est là ? Non, il manque Brice. Où est-il ?
dialogue.english: Is everyone there? No, Brice is missing. Where is he?

dialogue.french: Toujours au lit, mais ne l'attendons pas. Tu sais très bien qu'il ne se lève jamais avant midi.
dialogue.english: Still in bed, but let's not wait for him. You know very well that he never gets up before noon.

dialogue.french: Dépêchons-nous ! Nous perdons du temps.
dialogue.english: Let's hurry up! We're wasting time.

dialogue.french: La pièce commence dans vingt minutes et nous allons manquer le début.
dialogue.english: The play starts in twenty minutes and we're going to miss the beginning.

dialogue.french: On n'est pas encore prêts et le théâtre n'est pas tout près. Comment faire ?
dialogue.english: We're not yet ready and the theatre isn't very close by. What shall we do?

dialogue.french: Il est trop tard pour y aller en transports en commun, donc on va prendre la voiture.
dialogue.english: It's too late to go there by public transport, so we're going to take the car.

dialogue.french: Nous y serons en dix minutes si nous partons dans deux minutes.
dialogue.english: We'll be there in ten minutes if we leave in two minutes.

dialogue.french: Tu plaisantes ! On n'a pas le droit de se garer dans les rues autour du centre.
dialogue.english: You're joking! You're not allowed to park in the streets around the centre.

dialogue.french: Ne vous inquiétez pas : c'est facile comme tout.

dialogue.french: Je m'arrête dix secondes dans une place de livraison mais je n'arrête pas le moteur.

dialogue.french: Vous descendez vite et je vais garer la voiture dans le parking public qui se trouve du côté droit du tribunal.
dialogue.english: You get out quickly and I go to park the car in the public carpark on the right side of the court house.

dialogue.french: Pendant ce temps, vous achetez les billets et on se retrouve dans le foyer.
dialogue.english: Meanwhile, you buy the tickets and we meet up in the foyer.

dialogue.french: Bon, on y va. Bougez-vous !
dialogue.english: Right, let's go. Move yourselves!

dialogue.french: Euh, attendez un instant. Il y a un petit problème.
dialogue.english: Um, wait a moment. There's a slight problem.

dialogue.french: Qu'est-ce qui se passe ? Nous allons être en retard !
dialogue.english: What's happening? We're going to be late!

dialogue.french: Je ne trouve pas mes clés de voiture.
dialogue.english: I can't find my car keys.

dialogue.french: Je ne me souviens pas où je les ai mises. Elles ne sont pas dans ma poche,
dialogue.english: I don't remember where I put them. They're not in my pocket,

dialogue.french: ni dans le tiroir du meuble en bas de l'escalier, où je les mets d'habitude.
dialogue.english: nor in the drawer of the piece of furniture at the bottom of the stairs, where I usually put them.

dialogue.french: Pourquoi souris-tu ?
dialogue.english: Why are you smiling?

dialogue.french: Parce qu'elles sont dans ta main, idiot ! Vite, dépêche-toi. En route !
dialogue.english: Because they're in your hand, dummy! Quick, hurry up. Let's get moving!

notes.content: Despite the different spellings, the adjective prê t (ready) and the adverb prè s (near) are pronounced identically [pray]. The cof the adjective and noun second(e) is pronounced as a hard"g" [suhgoh"/suhgoh"d].

We saw manquer, to miss, in lesson note 2 (and below, in line 4). Here, however, the verb is used in the impersonal form, so il can be translated in different ways: Il manque un mot dans cette phrase, There's aword missing in this sentence. The pronoun is invariable, even if the subject is plural: Il manque trois personnes, Three people are missing. Compare this with Où est-il ?, were il, of course, means he.

As we saw in the previous lesson, the negative of areflexive verb is formed by placing the particle ne before the pronoun and pas (or an adverb, lesson note 5) after the verb: Je ne me souviens pas où tu habites, I don'tremember where you live, Ils ne s'arrê tent jamais de travailler ! They never stop working!

The imperative form of reflexive verbs depends on whether the sentence is negative or affirmative. In the negative, the pronoun comes before the verb, as usual: Ne nous inquié tons pas, Let'snot worry. In the affirmative, however, the pronoun comes afterwards: Dé pê chez-vous !, Hurry up!. Remember also that te becomes toi in an affirmative command: Dé pê che-toi !; but it does not change if the command is negative: Ne te dé pê che pas.

Comment faire ? (literally"How to do?") is a useful, short way of asking what to do or how to do something. It can be used alone -J'ai perdu mon mot de passe. Comment faire ? I've lost my password. What should I do?- or with a complement: Comment faire pour fermer une boî te de dialogue ? What do you do to close adialogue box?

You know some of the differences between en and dans, summarised in lesson 50. With an expression of time, the difference is quite subtle but very important. While en expresses the time taken to do something -Je peux le faire en cinq minutes, Ican do it in five minutes-dans indicates when the action takes, or will take, place: Elle peut le faire dans cinq minutes, She can do it in five minutes' time. Look again at sentence 7: en describes the duration of the trip to the cinema whereas dans specifies when that trip will begin.

le droit means the law (lesson line 7) but also the right (lesson line 6). Thus the expression avoir le droit (de) means to have the right (to) but also, in everyday speech, to be allowed to: Vous n'avez pas le droit de vous garer ici, You're not allowed to park here. (Remember that droit is also an adjective, meaning right, as opposed to gauche, left.)

Here is an example of averb used in the transitive and the reflexive forms: Où est-ce que tu gares ta voiture ? Where do you park your car? If we drop the direct object of the sentence (i.eif the subject and object are the same), we use a reflexive: Où est-ce que tu te gares ?, Where do you park/Where are you parking?

Some verbs have aslightly different meaning when used in the reflexive form. In this case, Je m'arrê te means Ipull up (in a car, for example) whereas J'arrê te le moteur means Iturn off the engine. Similarly, se trouver ("to find itself/oneself"), the reflexive form of trouver, means more or less the same as to be: Trouville se trouve en face de Deauville, Trouville is opposite Deauville.

retrouver (literally"to find again") means to find something that one has lost. But it is often translated simply by to find: J'ai retrouvé mes clé s, I've found my keys. The reflexive form generally means to meet up with: On se retrouve au restaurant à vingt heures, We're meeting up at the restaurant at pm.

We know that the pronominal verb se passer means to happen (lesson note 10). The actual translation will depend on the context, though, and is often very simple: La fê te se passe chez nous demain soir, The party is at our place tomorrow evening.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Simple verbs like être and avoir are often shunned - especially in written French-in favour of more complex synonyms such as se trouver and posséder, which have the same meaning but sound more"elegant"than simply be or have. Thus Ils possèdent une grande maison is preferred to Ils ont une grande maison, even though the two sentences are synonymous. This stylistic habit, which underlines the impression of formality discussed in Lesson 7, can be disconcerting at first, but it soon becomes second nature. Productive phase: 2nd lesson

dialogue.french: J'ai accepté de répondre à un sondage sur « les attentes des Français dans le domaine de l'audiovisuel ».
dialogue.english: I've agreed to answer a survey on "the expectations of the French in the field of broadcasting."

dialogue.french: Voulez-vous participer ou, au moins, donner votre point de vue sur cette première question :
dialogue.english: Do you want to take part or, at least, give your point of view on this first question:

dialogue.french: « Quelle est votre série préférée, celle qui vous a fait rire ou pleurer le plus ? »
dialogue.english: "What is your favourite series, the one that made you laugh or cry the most?"

dialogue.french: La mienne est l'émission d'humour « Puissance faible ».
dialogue.english: Mine is the comedy show "Low Power."

dialogue.french: Et la tienne, Mathilde ? La vôtre, Léon et Adèle ?
dialogue.english: And yours, Mathilde? Yours, Léon and Adèle?

dialogue.french: Moi, je ne suis pas fan de séries. Je préfère les magazines et les documentaires.
dialogue.english: Me, I'm not a fan of series. I prefer magazine programmes and documentaries.

dialogue.french: Et vous deux, vous préférez les divertissements ou les débats politiques ?
dialogue.english: And you two, do you prefer entertainment shows or political debates?

dialogue.french: Ni l'un ni l'autre. Nous regardons la télévision pour nous distraire, pas pour nous instruire !
dialogue.english: Neither one nor the other. We watch television for entertainment, not for education!

dialogue.french: Je ne vous ai pas autorisé à me tutoyer, jeune homme. Un peu de politesse, je vous prie.
dialogue.english: I didn't authorise you to use the familiar form of address, young man. A little politeness, please.

dialogue.french: La jeunesse est une belle chose ; quel crime de la laisser gâcher par les jeunes !
dialogue.english: Youth is a beautiful thing; what a crime to let it be spoiled by the young!

dialogue.french: Tu empoches une prime à chaque fois que tu recycles les bons vieux gags ?
dialogue.english: Do you pocket a bonus every time you recycle the good old gags?

dialogue.french: Ne perdons pas de vue notre thème. Peut-on – doit-on – trouver de l'humour dans tout ?
dialogue.english: Let's not lose sight of our theme. Can we – should we – find humour in everything?

dialogue.french: La grossesse, la vieillesse, la richesse : ne faudrait-il pas plutôt de la gentillesse et de la tendresse ?
dialogue.english: Pregnancy, old age, wealth: shouldn't we have kindness and affection instead?

dialogue.french: Faut-il s'affoler si quelqu'un plaisante sur des étrangers, par exemple ?
dialogue.english: Should we panic if someone jokes about foreigners, for example?

dialogue.french: On se permet de taquiner les Lillois, les Alsaciens, les Toulousains, ou les Marseillais.
dialogue.english: We allow ourselves to tease the people of Lille, Alsace, Toulouse, or Marseilles.

dialogue.french: Alors pourquoi pas des gens plus lointains ? Ce n'est pas de la méchanceté, c'est de la rigolade.
dialogue.english: So why not people further away? It's not meanness, it's fun.

dialogue.french: Non : vous rhabillez de vieux préjugés avec des mots nouveaux, monsieur.
dialogue.english: No: you are dressing up old prejudices with new words, sir.

dialogue.french: Et je te dis qu'il faut se fier à ses instincts et se méfier comme de la peste des idées reçues.
dialogue.english: And I'm telling you that you must trust your instincts and be wary of preconceived ideas.

dialogue.french: L'humour adoucit les mœurs et allège notre quotidien grisâtre je te – je vous – le garantis.
dialogue.english: Humour soothes our manners and lightens our greyish daily lives – I guarantee you.

dialogue.french: Notre débat touche à sa fin, messieurs, et nous ne disposons pas de suffisamment d'éléments
dialogue.english: Our debate is coming to an end, gentlemen, and we don't have enough information

dialogue.french: pour arriver à une conclusion ferme et définitive, mais...
dialogue.english: to come to a firm and final conclusion, but...

dialogue.french: Si si. Tu sais ce qu'on dit : on peut rire de tout – mais pas avec tout le monde.
dialogue.english: Oh yes we do. You know what they say: you can laugh at everything – but not with everyone.

notes.content: The phoneme euille is pronounced like the noun œil : [uhyy] (see lesson 32).

une attente, from attendre, to wait, has aliteral meaning, found in terms such as une salle d'attente, awaiting room, and also in sentences: L'attente à la caisse est trop longue, The wait at the checkout is too long. But it can also mean an expectation: Nous essayons toujours de ré pondre aux attentes de nos clients, We always try to meet our customers' expectations.

When used as adverbs, the superlatives le plus, the most, and le moins, the least, can be placed before the verb as well as after it: Quelle est l'é mission qui vous ale plus fait rire ? Pre-placement is more literary but nevertheless quite common.

Possessive pronouns (yours, mine, etc.) are formed with adefinite article (le, la, les) and apronominal word (mien, tien, etc.). Like possessive adjectives, they agree in number and gender with the noun(s) they replace, not with the possessor. The pronoun vô tre takes acircumflex over the oto distinguish it from the possessive adjective votre: Ceci est votre clé → C'est la vô tre.

The adjective fan, an abbreviation of fanatique, fanatical, is used idiomatically to mean wildly enthusiastic. Je suis fan de foot, I'm afootball fanatic. The word can also be used as a noun: C'est un fan de l'é quipe de Bordeaux, He's afan of the Bordeaux team. Both adjective and noun are pronounced [fan] (with ashort [a]) because they come from the English word.

We have seen ni used in anegative construction to mean nor (lesson line 78). If the negative verb applies to two things (like neither... nor), simply repeat the conjunction instead of using pas: Mes enfants n'aiment ni les fruits ni les lé gumes, My children like neither fruit nor vegetables. Be careful: unlike in English, the verb must always be negative. Ni l'un ni l'autre can often be translated simply as neither: Ni l'un ni l'autre n'est venu, Neither came.

The adjective faible means weak (see lesson 27) but can be used in abroader sense of lacking: Elle aune faible chance de ré ussir, She has aslim chance of succeeding; Ces lé gumes sont faibles en calories, These vegetables are low in calories. The corresponding noun is la / une faiblesse, (a) weakness: Ma faiblesse en franç ais est un problè me dans mon travail, My weakness in French is aproblem in my job. By contrast, the expression avoir un faible pour means to have aweakness for or, idiomatically, asoft spot for: J'ai un faible pour les é missions d'humour, Ihave asoft spot for comedy shows.

While many verbs can take areflexive pronoun if the subject and object are identical, others are always (or"essentially") pronominal. For example, se souvenir (de) means to remember and, in everyday usage, is always pronominal: Est-ce que tu te souviens de cette é mission ?, Do you remember that show? A near-synonym of se souvenir de is se rappeler (with no partitive article): Je me rappelle cette é mission, Iremember that show. (In the non-reflexive form, rappeler means to remind: Rappelez-moi votre nom, Remind me of your name.)

The agreement of past participles in pronominal verbs is complex. If the reflexive pronoun (me, se, etc.) is the indirect object of the sentence, the participle does not agree with the reflexive pronoun: Ma femme s'est coupé la main, My wife has cut her hand. But if the pronoun is the direct object, then the participle agrees in gender and number: Ma femme s'est coupé e, My wife has cut herself. In some cases, notably first-group verbs, there is no difference in the pronunciation of the past participle (coupé and coupé e are both pronounced [koopay]). However, this is not the case for the other verb groups, as we shall see.

The concrete noun une / la cuisine, a/the kitchen (lesson line 6), has an abstract use that means cooking/cookery -or even cuisine! J'adore la cuisine basque, Ilove Basque cooking/cuisine. Faire la cuisine means to cook, or, more precisely, to do the cooking. Je fais toujours la cuisine pour mes amis, Ialways cook / do the cooking for my friends.

Used with the past tense and followed by atime period, il y ais the equivalent of ago: J'ai vu ce pré sentateur il y avingt ans, Isaw that presenter years ago. The action described is always complete.

An idiosyncratic use of manquer (see lesson 57) is when the verb to miss expresses afeeling or regret or sadness. The French sentence structure is the reverse of English: Imiss you is Tu me manques (or Vous me manquez), literally"you me are missing."Thus the person (or thing) missed is the subject of the sentence in French but the object in English. Thus if Maï ka misses me, Iwould say Je manque à Maï ka.

notes.content: This is the first person singular of the future tense of the irregular verb faire, to do/make: je ferai, tu feras, il/elle fera, nous ferons, vous ferez, ils feront. In most cases, this tense corresponds to the English future with will. Note the difference between this tense and the"immediate"future formed with aller before the infinitive (in line 4, for example).

The future tense of verbs in the first two groups (ending in -er and -ir) is formed by adding the endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont to the stem. (See lesson note 9). In some cases, the stem changes slightly. For example, with acheter, to buy, the first etakes agrave accent (j'achè terai, etc.) while the yin essayer changes to an i (j'essaierai, etc.). Neither of these changes makes anoticeable difference to the pronunciation.

Verbs ending in -re form their future from the infinitive, but drop the final -e. Thus the future tense of prendre, to take, is je prendrai, tu prendras, il/elle prendra, nous prendrons, vous prendrez, ils/elles prendront.

un rayon means aray or abeam (Enfin un rayon de soleil ! At last aray of sunshine!). In ashopping context, however, it means a department, section or counter in astore or supermarket. In this case, there is no need for apreposition between rayon and the qualifying noun: le rayon frais, the fresh [food] section.

une promotion has many meanings, including the cognate apromotion (i.e. professional advancement). In stores, it means aspecial offer. Les meubles de jardin sont en promotion cette semaine, Garden furniture is on special offer this week. The word is often abbreviated to en promo.

Bonjour, Good morning, is used in several idioms, notably C'est simple comme bonjour, It'sas easy as pie. It can also be found in the idiomatic exclamation Bonjour les dé gâ ts ! ("Hello the damage"), equivalent to What a mess!

tout, all, everything (see line 18) is also used as an adverb of degree, as seen in lesson line 5. Nous habitons tout prè s d'ici, We live very near here. As such, it refers not only to physical distance but also to position or intensity: Ton nom est tout en haut de la liste, Your name is right at the top of the list. In this function, tout is invariable.

aucun(e), none, not any (lesson note 4) can also mean neither when followed by de / des and a determiner. The accompanying verb is always negative: Elle n'aime aucune de ces robes, She likes neither of these dresses. (Compare with ni l'un... ni l'autre, lesson 52).

Here is the future tense of the irregular verb aller, to go: j'irai, tu iras, il/elle ira, nous irons, vous irez, ils/elles iront. Note that only the stem is irregular, while the endings are exactly the same as for regular verbs (see note 1).

Another irregular future: ê tre, to be, becomes je serai, tu seras, il/elle sera, nous serons, vous serez, ils/elles seront. The negative is formed, as usual, with ne... pas: Les commandes ne seront pas livré es demain matin, The orders will not be delivered tomorrow morning.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: La charcuterie (from the term la chaire cuite, or cooked flesh) is ablanket term for cooked products made from pork (le porc) including ham (le jambon), pâté (le pâté), and sausage, for which French has two words: une saucisse, the generic term for any type of sausage eaten hot, and un saucisson, a hard, cooked sausage usually consumed when cold. The word charcuterie can refer to both the products (deli meats or cold cuts) and the shop where they are bought. The term for a grocery, une épicerie, comes from the noun une épice, a spice, which is what these shops originally sold. (The initial syllable ép-is often -but not always-the equivalent of sp-in English: une éponge, a sponge, les épinards, spinach, épier, to spy, etc.) Productive phase: 4th lesson

notes.content: The abstract noun le doute means doubt. Je n'ai pas de doute sur leur ré ponse, Ihave no doubt about their answer. The root verb is douter (de). Il doute de tout, He doubts everything. The phrase sans doute, without a doubt, can be used to mean probably: Elle araison sans doute, mais nous devons ê tre certains, She'sprobably right but we have to be certain.

The singular noun la politique, seen in lesson 49, means politics: La politique est l'art du possible, Politics is the art of the possible. In this context, the noun is never plural. But it can also mean a policy: une politique é conomique, an economic policy, in which case, it takes aregular plural -s: les politiques é conomiques. Un(e) politique can also mean a (male or female) politician, although the loan word un(e) politicien(ne) is frequently used nowadays. (Remember that politique is also an adjective, see lesson line 7).

The noun un meeting is used to describe apolitical gathering or assembly. It is also used in athletics (un meeting d'athlé tisme). Like most loan words, meeting is masculine. (Don'tconfuse it with une ré union, abusiness meeting, lesson line 15).
The demonstrative adverb -ci (lesson note 3) can be used with time periods to emphasise proximity: Ce mois-ci, This coming month. It does not have aplural form: ces jours-ci, [in] the coming days.

The adjective cé lè bre (the origin of celebrity and celebrated, lesson line 11) means famous or well-known. But fameux has amuch broader meaning, often relating to quality: Son pâ té est fameux !, His (or Her) pâ té is fantastic! The word can also be used to describe something that has been widely discussed: C'est ç a, ton fameux plan ? C'est nul ! Is that the plan that you've been talking about? It's rubbish!

In asubordinate clause beginning with atime expression, such as quand, the verb is in the future tense if the verb in the main clause is also in the future. This contrasts with English, which uses the present. Nous serons tous là quand il arrivera, We will all be there when he arrives.

Remember that adjectives always agree in gender with the person they refer to, but those ending in -e (like triste, sad) in both masculine and feminine agree only in the plural: des choses tristes, sad things. (See lesson 14).

devoir is a verb, must (lesson note 5), but also amasculine noun meaning duty: C'est mon devoir de vous le dire, It'smy duty to tell you. In aschool context, it is used in the plural (les devoirs) to mean homework (because the student is obliged to do the work).

l'homme is used in the general sense to mean mankind. For that reason, it is often written with an initial capital: Le Musé e de l'Homme à Paris est fermé le mardi, The Museum of Mankind in Paris is closed Tuesdays. Aconcerted effort is underway in France to move towards more gender-neutral language, especially in official contexts. So the expression les droits de l'homme (or l'Homme),"the rights of man"is making way for les droits humains, the back translation of human rights. (The Canadian francophone community has long used the term les droits de la personne.)

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Politics is aperennial topic of conversation in France. The country is organised constitutionally as une république, arepublic (the current regime, dating from 1958, is fifth republic, la cinquième république, since 1792). It is headed by le Président de la République, elected by universal suffrage every five years (the term of office is known as un quinquennat [kahnkenah], from the Latin word for five). Les élections législatives (ageneral election) are also held every five years to elect les députés, representatives who sit in the lower house of parliament, la Chambre des députés (although the president has the right to seek an early dissolution of parliament, le parlement). The members of the upper house, le Sénat, are called les sénateurs and are elected every nine years. Productive phase: 5th lesson

notes.content: un monstre sacré ("aholy monster") is an admirative term similar to the English epithet agiant or alegendary figure: Gé rard Gé rard Gé rard Gé rard Gé rard Gé rard Gé rard Gé rard Gé rard Gé rard Gé rard Gé rard is agiant of French cinema. The expression applies to both men and women. However, the noun un monstre is used pejoratively, as in English: C'est un monstre horrible qui fait peur aux enfants, He's adreadful monster who scares children.

amuser means to amuse (someone): Il m'amuse avec ses histoires drô les, He amuses me with his funny stories. The pronominal form, seen in lesson line 2, generally means to enjoy or to have fun. Il joue mal de la guitare mais il s'amuse, He plays the guitar badly but he enjoys himself.

entendre means to hear (and we know the past participle entendu, lesson note 8, meaning, Isee or I understand). And, as asimple reflexive, s'entendre means to hear oneself. Faites moins de bruit, je ne m'entends pas parler au té lé phone, Make less noise, I can'thear myself speaking on the phone. As an idiomatic pronominal verb, s'entendre means to reach an agreement with or, more commonly, to get on well with someone. Je m'entends trè s bien avec le frè re de Jacques, Iget on well with Jacques' brother.
See lesson note 8.

se tromper (lesson line 5), to make a mistake, is the pronominal form of tromper, to deceive or mislead: Le vendeur m'atrompé sur le prix des appels té lé phoniques, The salesman misled me about the price of phone calls. The transitive verb can also mean to be unfaithful to, cheat on: Si une femme trompe son mari, c'est souvent parce que le mari trompe sa femme: If awife is unfaithful to her husband, it'soften because the husband is cheating on his wife.

We have already seen un coup in several expressions (un coup d'œil, un coup de main, lesson 32, for example). Here we have the original meaning, a blow, a knock, etc.: J'ai pris un coup sur la tê te, Ibanged my head. In these contexts, English is more flexible than French. For instance, donner un coup de poing/de pied ("to give ablow of the fist/foot") is to punch/kick. The expression à coups de describes the thing delivering the blow: Elle le battait à coups de brosse, She was hitting him with a brush.

un(e) gosse, acommon informal word for a child, is the equivalent of a kid: Ils vont en vacances sans les gosses ce mois-ci, They're going on holiday without the kids this month. Like monstre sacré (note 4), the noun is masculine but can apply to both sexes. Two common related idioms are un sale gosse (a brat) and un beau gosse, a good-looker. (Be careful: in Canadian French, gosse is atesticular slang word!)

notes.content: Pronominal verbs: Pronominal verbs are divided into two classes: reflexive, where the subject and object of an action are the same, and reciprocal, used when two or more subjects do the same thing to each other. Both classes are preceded by se (s' before an initial vowel or h) in the infinitive and are conjugated in the same way, with asubject pronoun and areflexive pronoun: se laver, to wash: je me lave, tu te laves, il/elle se lave, nous nous lavons, vous vous lavez, ils/elles se lavent. In the perfect tense, pronominal verbs are conjugated with ê tre and the past participle, which generally agrees with the subject: je me suis lavé/-é e, tu t'es lavé/-é e, il s'est lavé / elle s'est lavé e, nous nous sommes lavé s/-é es, vous vous ê tes lavé/lavé s/-é es, ils se sont lavé s / elles se sont lavé es. To form the negative, place ne before the reflexive pronoun and pas (or jamais, etc.) after the verb: Il ne se lave pas. The first interrogative (rising intonation) is formed with the subject pronoun followed by the reflexive pronoun: Tu te laves ? For the second interrogative, place est-ce que before the subject pronoun: Est-ce que tu te laves ? The third interrogative (inversion, Te laves-tu ?) is slightly more complex and less common. For the imperative, the position of the pronoun depends on whether the command is affirmative or negative. In both cases, the subject pronoun is dropped. With anegative imperative, beginning with Ne..., the reflexive pronoun comes before the verb, as usual: Ne te lave pas. In the affirmative, however, the reflexive pronoun is replaced by astressed pronoun, placed after the verb and joined with a hyphen: Lave-toi ! Reflexive verbs: These are much more common in French than in English. In particular, those indicating achange of state (se ré veiller, to wake up, s'endormir, to go to sleep) or describing an everyday action or movement (se laver, to wash, s'habiller, to get dressed, se promener, to go for a walk) are not reflexive in English. Some of these verbs are"exclusively pronominal,"so that without the reflexive pronoun, they have no meaning. Among the most frequently used are s'absenter, (to leave, go away from), s'enfuir (to run away, to flee), s'envoler (to fly away), se fier (to rely on), and se mé fier (to be wary of). In the past tense, the past participle always agrees in number and gender with the subject. By contrast, some verbs are"occasionally pronominal"and can be used transitively or reflexively depending on the direct object. For example: Je lave ma voiture, I'mwashing my car; Je me lave le visage, I'mwashing my face. Reciprocal verbs are used when the subject or subjects are acting on each other. For example: se comprendre: Nous ne nous comprenons pas, We don'tunderstand each other. Other common reciprocals include se dé tester (Ils se dé testent, They hate each other), se regarder (Nous nous regardons, We are looking at each other) and se sourire (Elles se sourient, They're smiling at each other). Some pronominal verbs have aslightly different meaning when used non-reciprocally, as we saw in lesson 55. These include passer (to pass, to spend time) and se passer (to happen); entendre (to hear) and s'entendre (to get on well with); tromper (to deceive) and se tromper (to make a mistake).

Future tense: The future tense is used in very much the same way as its English equivalent (but remember that French makes no difference between the simple and the progressive). To form the future of regular verbs, the endings of avoir are added to the stem, which, for the first two verb groups, is usually the infinitive: ajouter, to add: j'ajouterai, tu ajouteras, il/elle ajoutera, nous ajouterons, vous ajouterez, ils/elles ajouteront. finir, to finish: je finirai, tu finiras, il/elle finira, nous finirons, vous finirez, ils/elles finiront. Verbs ending in -re use the same endings but drop the final -efrom the infinitive: vendre, to sell: je vendrai, tu vendras, il/elle vendra, nous vendrons, vous vendrez, ils/elles vendront. There are afew spelling changes when the future endings are added to certain -er verbs, as we saw in lesson with acheter and essayer. The same changes occur with lever, to lift (the initial etakes agrave accent) and payer, to pay (the ychanges to i): j'achè terai, je lè verai; j'essaierai, je paierai. Another change concerns verbs such as jeter and appeler, which double the first letter of the last syllable: je jetterai, j'appellerai. Some important irregular verbs, particularly the two auxiliaries avoir and ê tre, change significantly in the future. Here they are, for reference purposes: j'aurai, tu auras, il/elle aura, nous aurons, vous aurez, ils/elles auront; je serai, tu seras, il/elle sera, nous serons, vous serez, ils/elles seront. Two other important irregular verbs are faire and aller (see lesson notes and 9). Amajor structural difference between French and English concerns subordinate clauses linked to a future-tense main clause by atime conjunction, particularly quand, when. In French, the verbs in both clauses are in the future: Quand je saurai ce qu'il veut, je te le dirai, When Iknow what he wants, I'll tell you. The same rule applies to the future perfect, which we see at the end of the course.

Possessive pronouns: Possessive pronouns -the equivalent of yours, mine, etc.- are formed with adefinite article and apronominal word. le mien, la mienne, les miens, les miennes (mine); le tien, la tienne, les tiens, les tiennes (yours); le sien, la sienne, les siens, les siennes (his/hers/its); le nô tre, la nô tre, les nô tres (ours); le vô tre, la vô tre, les vô tres (yours); le leur, la leur, les leurs (theirs). Like possessive adjectives, these pronouns agree in number and gender with the noun(s) they replace, not with the possessor. For example: C'est mon stylo, It'smy pen → C'est le mien, It's mine; C'est ma voiture, It'smy car → C'est la mienne, It's mine. Because of the agreement, it is not possible to identify the gender of the possessor in third person singular (le sien, la sienne). C'est son manteau → C'est le sien can mean his or hers. Note that the circumflex over the oon nô tre and vô tre makes it possible to distinguish between the pronoun and the possessive adjective (votre, notre): Ceci est votre clé → C'est la vô tre.

Prepositions: en, dans and à: While most French prepositions are easy to master, these three are often confused (in addition, en is also an adverbial pronoun, like y). Let'srevise the different prepositional uses we have seen since you started this course. 4.1 Dans and en: • One basic difference is that en is never followed by adefinite or partitive article (except in anumber of fixed expressions, such as en l'air, in the air). It is used, among others, to talk about languages (en franç ais, en anglais), modes of transport (en avion, en train, etc.), materials (en papier, en or), periods and dates (en 1789, en avril), and seasons with the exception of spring: (en é té, en automne, en hiver but au printemps). En can also be used with places, Il est en prison, and countries that are feminine nouns: Je vis en France (masculine countries take au, see lesson 57). Last, it is used before apresent participle: en arrivant, on arriving. • In contrast to en, dans has to be followed by an article, whether definite (le/la/les), indefinite (un/une) or partitive (du, de la, des). Dans designates the location of something (dans ma poche) and, in this context, is more precise than en. For example, you would say Mes vacances en montagne, My holidays in the mountains but Mes vacances dans les montagnes du Jura, My holidays in the Jura mountains. When followed by an article and a noun, dans means in: Elle est dans son bureau, She is in her office. Dans is also used for aspecific measure of time (dans dix minutes), but remember (lesson note 5) that en can also be used in this context, but with aslight difference in meaning: Je peux faire le travail en vingt minutes, Ican do the job in minutes (i.e. it will take me minutes) compared with Je peux faire le travail dans vingt minutes, Ican do the job in minutes' time (i.e. in the future). 4.2 Dans and à: Here, too, the differences are subtle. The one that seems to most confuse English-speakers is the use of à to translate in when the pronoun does not mean inside. Atypical usage is à la maison, at home. Où est Rosie ? - Elle est à la maison, Where's Rosie? - She'sat home. By contrast, J'entends quelqu'un dans la maison, Ican hear someone inside the house. Likewise, J'ai vu le film au ciné ma, Isaw the movie at the cinema, versus, J'ai perdu ma montre dans le ciné ma, Ilost my watch in (i.e. inside) the cinema. One big difference with English, and asource of many mistakes, concerns parts of the body: Il aun couteau à la main, He has aknife in (not inside) his hand, compared with Tiens-le dans ta main, Hold it in your hand (i.e. close your fingers around it). À is also used to talk about cities or towns: Elle habite à Paris, She lives in Paris. (Remember that à becomes au/aux with le/les: Elle habite au quatriè me é tage, She lives on the fourth floor.) Last, à is used with certain communications media: à la té lé vision, à la radio, au té lé phone.

notes.content: commerç ant [komairssœhn]: Note how the cedilla beneath the letter cchanges the pronunciation from ahard [k] to a sibilant, or soft, [s]. The ç is used only before the vowels a (ç a), o (garç on) and u (reç u) because cis automatically sibilant before e, iand y.

Comment ç a se fait ? ("How that does itself") is an idiomatic way of asking a question, alittle like How come.... Il n'est pas parti en vacances cette anné e - Comment ç a se fait ? He didn'tgo on holiday this year? - How come? The expression can also be used in afull sentence: Comment ç a se fait que le train est en retard ? How come the train is late? In this case, however, it is often necessary to put the main verb into the subjunctive, which we will learn later on.

French does not have aword for both, relying on various constructions according to the grammatical function. As an adjective, you can use les/des/aux deux: J'ai mal aux deux genoux, Both my knees hurt. As a pronoun, use tous les deux: Ils sont bretons, tous les deux, They're both Breton.

Here is the imperfect tense, glimpsed in lesson line 7. It is used to describe situations or actions in the past, without specifying when they began or ended. The imperfect form of the irregular verb ê tre is j'é tais, tu é tais, il/elle/on é tait, nous é tions, vous é tiez, ils/elles é taient. The nearest equivalent in English is was / were.

The imperfect tense of all verbs other than ê tre is formed by dropping the -ons ending from the nous form of the present and adding the following endings: enseignons: j'enseignais, tu enseignais, il/elle enseignait, nous enseignions, vous enseigniez, ils/elles enseignaient. Depending on the context, the translation uses was teaching or used to teach. In this same sentence, travaillait is the third-person singular imperfect of travailler.

un commerç ant comes from the noun le commerce, trade. (Here is another example of Latin/Anglo-Saxon variations: trade concerns the exchange of goods and some services, whereas commerce encompasses abroader range of ancillary activities). Depending on the context, un(e) commerç ant(e) can be atrader but also ashopkeeper or merchant.
This is the imperfect of savoir: savons → je savais, tu savais, il/elle/on savait, nous savions, vous saviez, ils/elles savaient.
baragouiner is afamiliar verb meaning to talk gibberish or, less insultingly, to speak alanguage badly, mumble afew words: Il baragouinait le russe, He was speaking bad Russian.

We know that apprendre means to learn and enseigner to teach. However, when used with adirect object and an indirect object in the same phrase, apprendre means to teach (something to someone). So, j'apprends le franç ais, I'mlearning French but Je leur apprends le franç ais, I'mteaching them French. By contrast, enseigner means only to teach: Je leur enseigne le franç ais. The idiomatic expression Vous m'apprenez / Tu m'apprends quelque chose is the equivalent of That'snews to me (or, more simply, I didn'tknow that).

We know that adjectives of nationality do not take an initial capital, whereas nouns do (lesson note 3). Logically, the lower-case rule applies to adjectives derived from regions, towns, etc., as well as to languages: C'est un Normand qui parle mal l'anglais, He's a Norman who speaks bad English. Be careful not to confuse nouns and adjectives of nationality: Ce sont des Bretons but Ils sont bretons. (Alternatively, Ils sont d'origine bretonne, They're of Breton origin.)

We know that the adverbial pronoun yrefers back to apreviously mentioned indirect object, usually athing or place, generally introduced by à (see lesson section 3.1). Thus, in the idiomatic phrase on n'ycomprend rien, yreplaces that indirect object: À la fin du film, on n'ycomprend rien (i.e. au film), By the end of the movie, nobody understands anything. If the indirect object comes after the verb, however, yis not used, and rien returns to its usual place, directly after the verb: On n'arien compris au film.
To remind yourself of how to use connaî tre (line 18) and savoir (line 10), look back at lesson section 4.

dialogue.french: Allons à Auxerre ce week-end, puisque mardi est férié.

dialogue.french: « La vieille ville, la Tour de l'Horloge, l'abbaye, les beaux hôtels particuliers,

dialogue.french: D'abord, il faudra partir au petit matin car la plupart des Parisiens seront sur la route, et il y aura un monde fou.
dialogue.english: First, we'll have to leave in the early hours because most Parisians will be on the road, and there'll be loads of people.

dialogue.french: La dernière fois que je suis allé en Bourgogne, j'ai mis une demi-journée à faire cinquante kilomètres !

dialogue.french: Je suis resté coincé dans les embouteillages pendant quatre heures et demie, et ce n'était pourtant pas un jour férié.

dialogue.french: Pire, il faisait un froid de canard et il tombait des cordes.

dialogue.french: Selon la météo, il fera beau, chaud et ensoleillé toute la semaine.

dialogue.french: et je n'ai pas les moyens de jeter l'argent par les fenêtres.

dialogue.french: J'abandonne ! Tu es têtu comme une mule.
dialogue.english: I give up! You are as stubborn as a mule.

notes.content: enthousiaste: remember that the phoneme th is always pronounced as a t: [œh"tooziast]. a à: the two letters are pronounced identically and each must be sounded: don'ttry to elide the second one.

Although une chouette means an owl, the word is often used as afamiliar adjective meaning great, cool, nice, etc. Il est vraiment chouette, ton nouveau sac, Your new handbag is really nice. Chouette can also be used as an exclamation, sometimes followed by alors: On ira à Auxerre demain. - Chouette alors ! We'll go to Auxerre tomorrow. - Great!

The idiom Qu'est-ce qu'il y a ? means What's wrong? or What's up? Unlike Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ? (lesson line 1), where something is visibly wrong, Qu'est-ce qu'il y a ? is often amore general way of making an enquiry: Qu'est-ce qu'il y a ? - Je veux vous parler, What is it? - Iwant to talk to you.

Here are two false friends. The adjective particulier, particular, distinctive, can also mean private when used in the compound noun un hô tel particulier, aprivate mansion. (In this context, un hô tel takes no guests!) The noun un particulier means aprivate individual, as opposed to a company. Website contact pages often ask the question: Ê tes-vous un particulier ou une entreprise ? Are you an individual or a business?

Here is another use of the third person of valoir (lesson line 18): the impersonal expression Ç a vaut... followed by anoun means It'sworth.... Ç a vaut la peine, It'sworth the trouble (see lesson note 8). Some tourist guides rate important monuments, sites and even restaurants simply as Vaut le voyage, Worth the trip.

The feminine noun la flemme is derived from the medical term le flegme, phlegm and conveys the idea of laziness. It is used almost exclusively in the expression avoir la flemme: J'ai la flemme de faire le lit, I can'tbe bothered to make the bed.

We know that le monde, the world, is asynonym for people (tout le monde, beaucoup de monde). The idiomatic expression Il y aun monde fou ("amad world") means It'sreally crowded / There are loads of people, etc. Il y aun monde fou dans les magasins à Noë l, The shops are really crowded at Christmas.

The adverb pourtant, seen in the previous lesson, is auseful way of expressing a contradiction, like yet or however. It can be used directly after a verb: Il reste pourtant beaucoup de choses à faire, But there'sstill alot to do, or at the beginning of a sentence, usually with Et, as a rejoinder. Tu es en retard. - Et pourtant, je me suis levé tô t, You're late. - And yet Igot up early.

un canard means a duck: Suzanne vend des poulets et des canards au marché depuis dix ans, Suzanne has been selling chickens and ducks at the market for ten years. Since ducks are apparently easier to hunt in the winter, they have become synonymous with bitter cold: Il fait un froid de canard dehors, It'sfreezing outside.

une corde means arope or, on amusical instrument, a string. Since streams of heavy rain can resemble thick ropes, the expression tomber (or pleuvoir) des cordes means to pour with rain. (The English noun acord is generally translated by un cordon.)

un bulletin mé té orologique is the official term for aweather forecast. For simplicity, it is usually abbreviated to la mé té o, another example of the tendency to shorten longer phrases in the everyday language (lesson note 7). As-tu entendu la mé té o pour aujourd'hui ? Have you heard today'sweather forecast? And la mé té o can also mean simply the weather. Si la mé té o est mauvaise, nous ne sortirons pas le bateau, If the weather is bad, we won'tget the boat out.
