extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Although France is asecular country (un pays laïc), it has astrong Catholic tradition, and many public holidays -in addition to Noël (Christmas) and Pâques (Easter)- are religious in origin. Chief among them are le quinze août or l'Assomption, the Assumption on 15 August, and le premier novembre, or la Toussaint, All Saints' Day on 1 November. These, and other holidays, are known collectively as les jours fériés (from a Latin word for leisure). Similarly, une fête, generally translated as a party, is also afeast day or saint's day. The tradition of wishing aperson Bonne fête, or"good name-day"on the feast day of the saint after whom they are named is rapidly disappearing as France becomes increasingly multicultural. (For the expression faire le pont, see the Culture Note in lesson 18.) Productive phase: 9th lesson

dialogue.french: Quand mon père était jeune, les moyens de communication que nous avons aujourd'hui n'existaient pas.
dialogue.english: When my father was young, the means of communication that we have today did not exist.

dialogue.french: S'il voulait contacter un parent ou un ami, il devait écrire une lettre ou, en cas d'urgence, envoyer un télégramme...
dialogue.english: If he wanted to contact a relative or a friend, he had to write a letter or, in case of emergency, send a telegram...

dialogue.french: Un quoi ? Je pensais qu'un télégramme était un journal breton !
dialogue.english: A what? I thought a telegram was a Breton newspaper!

dialogue.french: Non, imbécile, les télégrammes permettaient...
dialogue.english: No, idiot, telegrams allowed...

dialogue.french: Laisse tomber, tu n'étais même pas né.
dialogue.english: Drop it, you weren't even born.

dialogue.french: Je disais donc que papa ne pouvait jamais s'attendre à une réponse instantanée.
dialogue.english: So I was saying that dad could never expect an instant answer.

dialogue.french: Il ne pouvait pas non plus obtenir une information immédiatement.
dialogue.english: Neither could he get information immediately.

dialogue.french: Comme c'est affreux ! Il n'avait pas le téléphone ? Ça existait alors, non ?
dialogue.english: How awful! He didn't have a phone? It existed back then, didn't it?

dialogue.french: Bien sûr, mais les appels coûtaient très cher donc on ne téléphonait que rarement.
dialogue.english: Of course, but calls were very expensive and people telephoned only rarely.

dialogue.french: Si j'ai bien compris, les forfaits illimités n'existaient pas encore ?
dialogue.english: If I have understood correctly, unlimited phone plans didn't yet exist?

dialogue.french: C'est ça. Et on utilisait des pigeons voyageurs pour communiquer. Non, je plaisante.
dialogue.english: That's right. And we used homing pigeons to communicate. No, I'm joking.

dialogue.french: À cette époque, papa jouait au Tiercé toutes les semaines.
dialogue.english: At that time, dad used to play the Tiercé every week.

dialogue.french: Comme lui et maman vivaient loin du village voisin, il prenait son vélo pour aller au PMU.
dialogue.english: As he and mum lived far from the neighbouring village, he would take his bike to go to the betting office.

dialogue.french: Il ne gagnait jamais mais ça l'amusait de jouer et il aimait bien se balader à la campagne.
dialogue.english: He never won but he enjoyed playing and he liked riding around the country.

dialogue.french: Je suis sûr que tes parents espéraient toucher le gros lot.
dialogue.english: I'm sure that your parents were hoping to get the jackpot.

dialogue.french: C'est possible mais j'en doute. Malheureusement, mon père choisissait ses chevaux au hasard.
dialogue.english: It's possible but I doubt it. Unfortunately, dad used to choose horses at random.

dialogue.french: Il lançait des dés ou jouait à pile ou face, c'est pourquoi il perdait toujours.
dialogue.english: He would throw dice or flip a coin, which is why he always lost.

dialogue.french: Enfin, presque toujours. Une nuit, pendant qu'il dormait, il a fait un rêve...
dialogue.english: Well, almost always. One night, while he was sleeping, he had a dream...

dialogue.french: Le lendemain, il ne se souvenait pas exactement du nom du gagnant mais pensait qu'il s'appelait « Fortune ».
dialogue.english: The next day, he didn't remember exactly the name of the winner but he thought it was called "Fortune".

dialogue.french: Mais ce jour-là il pleuvait tellement fort que papa n'a pas pu aller au village.
dialogue.english: But that day, it was raining so hard that dad was unable to go to the village.

dialogue.french: Et heureusement, car il n'y avait pas de « Fortune ».
dialogue.english: And fortunately, because there was no "Fortune".

notes.content: alors, seen several times with the meaning so or then, literally means at the time, back then (from lors, which we will see later): Je l'ai connue à la fac. Elle é tait alors é tudiante, Iknew her at uni. Back then, she was a student. A shorter, more elegant way of saying à cette é poque (line 12), alors is never used at the beginning of asentence in this context.

We know that les moyens can mean financial resources (lesson note 6) but it is also the word for means i.e. amethod for achieving something. However, while the English word takes an s, even in the singular, un moyen / les moyens depends on the context. J'ai trouvé un moyen de le contacter, I've found ameans of contacting him. Contrast that with Il y adeux moyens de payer : par té lé phone ou par carte, There are two means of payment: by phone or by card.

un parent means aparent but also arelative (cousin, niece, etc.). So mes parents et amis can mean my parents OR my relatives and friends. The word is also used in the expression le parent pauvre: Le changement climatique est le parent pauvre des politiques de ce gouvernement, Climate change is the poor relative of this government's policies. Always check the context!

The feminine noun urgence means urgency, and, in some cases, rush: Il n'y apas d'urgence, ç a peut attendre, There'sno rush; it can wait. With the partitive d', it means emergency: La mairie apris des mesures d'urgence, The town hall has taken emergency measures. And the emergency department of a hospital, le service des urgences, is often referred to simply as les urgences.

The compound verb laisser tomber ("to allow to fall") means to drop: Attention, il va laisser tomber le sac par terre !, Watch out, he'sgoing to drop the bag on the floor! Idiomatically, the expression can mean -as in English-to abandon: Il alaissé tomber ses é tudes de mé decine, He dropped his medical studies. (Note the construction; we'll meet it again shortly.) As an interjection, Laisse(z) tomber ! is equivalent to Forget it, expressing irritation or boredom: Cet exercice est trop difficile. - Laissez tomber, This exercise is too hard. - Forget it. In this context, there is no need for adirect object.

un forfait basically means an all-in financial package or afixed sum. It is widely used in two contexts: travel (for example, un forfait avion-hô tel, aflight and hotel package) and telephony, where the basic meaning is aphone plan: J'ai dé passé mon forfait, I've exceeded my plan limit.

papa and the feminine equivalent maman are the equivalents of mum(my) and dad(dy). Papa et maman sont marié s depuis plus de trente ans, Dad and mum have been married for more than years. In everyday usage, une maman is more common that une mè re.

un voisin means aneighbour (we saw the feminine form in lesson 36) but the word can also be an adjective, meaning neighbouring, nearby, etc. Ils habitant dans le rue voisine, They live in the next street. By extension, le voisinage means the neighbourhood.

The little-used English word velocipede, aforerunner of the bicycle, comes from the French un vé locipè de, which passed long ago into everyday language as un vé lo, a bike. The"technical"term is une bicyclette. Such is the longstanding popularity of cycling in France that the affectionate term for the machine is la petite reine ("little queen").

un hasard (lesson line 1) is another faux-ami, meaning chance or luck. Je l'ai rencontré par hasard dans la rue hier, Imet him by chance in the street yesterday. extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: France has a state-operated system for horse race betting. It is controlled through an organisation called le Pari mutuel urbain, or PMU, named for amutual betting system (un pari, a bet) also used in North America (although un PMU can also mean abetting office). Bets were originally placed on acombination of three horses, hence the name Tiercé. Although the system has since been expanded to four (Quarté) or five (Quinté) winners, le Tiercé is widely used as ageneric term for horse betting. Most punters would love to win le gros lot ("fat prize"), also known as le jackpot ... Although telegrams were phased out in France in 2018, the word is used on the masthead of several popular newspapers in Brittany, notably Le Télégramme de Brest. Productive phase: 10th lesson

notes.content: The pronunciation of the adverb plus changes according to its function. Listen carefully to the text and recorded exercise. Detailed rules can be found in lesson 63. province : Note the open vowel [ahn] in the second syllable: [provahnss]. Don'tconfuse this word with Provence, the beautiful region of southeastern France, pronounced [provœh"ss].
The adverb peu is used in numerous contexts. On its own in atime clause, it means shortly or just: Je suis arrivé peu avant la fermeture du magasin, Iarrived shortly before the shop closed.

We know that environ means about, approximately (lesson line 7). As an adverb, it does not agree. However, it can take an sin the expressions dans les environs, meaning in the vicinity, Il habite dans les environs, He lives in the vicinity/neighbourhood. If further information is added, we need the preposition de: Ils habitent dans les environs de la gare, They live somewhere around the station. When the idea of approximation applies to time we use the expression aux environs de: Il est arrivé aux environs de midi, He arrived at around noon...

We saw un peu de, a little, abit of, in lesson 11. Do not confuse the noun un peu with the adverb peu de, which means little/few (remember that French makes no difference between countable and uncountable nouns in this context). Here's asimple mnemonic: J'ai peu d'argent mais un peu de temps, Ihave little money but abit of time.
The conjunction lorsque, when, is asynonym of quand. There is no difference in meaning between the two, but lorsque is more elegant. (The root word is lors, seen in alors, lesson note 5.)

depuis with the present tense, meaning for or since, is generally followed by aspecific time period (lesson note 2). But it can also be followed by less precise adverbs such as peu and longtemps. In the first case, Je la connais depuis peu, the English equivalent would use either anegative verb or an affirmative with only: Ihave not known her for long / Ihave known her for only ashort time. With longtemps, the translation is more straightforward: Je les connais depuis longtemps, Ihave known them for along time. Note the grammatical simplicity of the French constructions.

The reflexive verb se rendre compte ("to render account to oneself") means to realise or be aware. When followed by adirect object, it takes de: Est-ce qu'il se rend compte de la situation ? Is he aware of the situation? (Because compte is the direct object of the reflexive verb, rendu does not agree in number or gender: Elle s'est rendu compte...) The verb ré aliser is a faux-ami, meaning to do or to carry out.
When plus is used at the end of asentence to mean more, the final sis pronounced. The pronunciation rules for plus are quite complex (see lesson 63).

The verb importer means to import (goods, etc.) but also to matter, to be important (as in English: amatter of import). It is often found in the exclamation Peu importe, It doesn'tmatter or Never mind. C'est trè s cher ! - Peu importe. It'svery expensive! - Never mind.

pendant followed by aperiod of time means during (see table, lesson 49). Followed by the conjunction que it means while. In a past-tense sentence, the verb that follows is generally in the imperfect tense: Le té lé phone asonné pendant qu'ils dormaient, The phone rang while they were sleeping (i.ethe action lasted acertain period of time).

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Les secours d'urgence or, more commonly, les secours (the origin of the English word succour), is the blanket term for the emergency services. In addition to la police, the police force, which in France is organised on anationwide basis, whence the official name la Police nationale, the other main service is the fire brigade, les sapeurs-pompiers (although the first part of the title -the root of the English word a sapper-is generally omitted in everyday speech). The origin of the term un pompier is une pompe, a pump. Productive phase: 11th lesson

title: La célébrité ne me dit pas grand-chose

dialogue.french: Mon invitée est la photojournaliste Isabelle Rossi, pour son nouveau livre « Une réputation injuste, une vie écourtée », dans lequel vous superposez deux Marie-Antoinette : une princesse inconstante et dépensière et une femme courageuse et sous-estimée.
dialogue.english: My guest is photojournalist Isabelle Rossi, for her new book 'An Unfair Reputation, A Life Cut Short', in which you superimpose two Marie Antoinettes: a fickle and spendthrift princess and a brave and underestimated woman.

dialogue.french: Je suis tenté de vous demander : pourquoi un livre de plus – qui n'est pas un roman – sur un personnage qui a déjà fait couler énormément d'encre ?
dialogue.english: I'm tempted to ask you: why another book – which isn't a novel – on a character about whom so much has already been written?

dialogue.french: N'est-ce pas un peu irréaliste d'essayer de rétablir la réputation d'un personnage si controversé ?
dialogue.english: Isn't it a bit unrealistic to try to restore the reputation of such a controversial character?

dialogue.french: Bien au contraire. On ne cesse de revisiter l'histoire de notre pays, nous, les historiens, et de réexaminer la vie de celles et ceux qui en étaient les acteurs principaux.
dialogue.english: Quite the contrary. We historians are constantly revisiting the history of our country, and re-examining the lives of those who were the protagonists.

dialogue.french: Dans le cas de Marie-Antoinette, on a souvent essayé de défaire et de refaire la réputation de celle que l'on traitait de « Madame Déficit ».
dialogue.english: In Marie Antoinette's case, attempts have often been made to undo and rebuild the reputation of the woman who was referred to as 'Mrs Deficit'.

dialogue.french: Je crois sincèrement qu'elle a été maltraitée par ces historiens, dont la plupart sont des hommes.
dialogue.english: I sincerely believe that she has been mistreated by those historians, most of whom are men.

dialogue.french: Je pensais qu'il fallait la réévaluer d'un point de vue féministe, non pas comme une femme irresponsable et écervelée mais comme un personnage fort, en avance sur son temps – et injustement méprisée.
dialogue.english: I thought she should be re-assessed from a feminist point of view, not as an irresponsible and scatterbrained woman but as a strong character, ahead of her time – and unjustly despised.

dialogue.french: Sa réputation est entachée depuis des siècles par un certain nombre de légendes dont la fameuse « Qu'ils mangent de la brioche », une phrase qu'elle n'a jamais prononcée.
dialogue.english: Her reputation has been stained for centuries by a number of legends including the famous 'Let them eat cake', a phrase she never uttered.

dialogue.french: Mais, en lisant votre ouvrage, on a l'impression d'avoir affaire à une sainte. Je cite : « Elle passa son enfance en Autriche, une fille heureuse qui fit le bonheur de sa famille. »
dialogue.english: But, reading your book, one gets the impression of dealing with a saint. I quote: 'She spent her childhood in Austria, a happy girl who delighted her family.'

dialogue.french: « Elle épousa le Dauphin, devenant une épouse irréprochable et une excellente mère. » On dirait un ange !
dialogue.english: 'She married the Dauphin, becoming an irreproachable wife and an excellent mother.' She sounds like an angel!

dialogue.french: Mais dans l'avant-propos, j'écris « Elle fut au cœur de nombreux scandales, et elle dépensa des sommes faramineuses en robes et bijoux. »
dialogue.english: But in the foreword, I write 'She was at the centre of many scandals, and she spent enormous sums of money on dresses and jewellery.'

dialogue.french: Ainsi, elle fut tour à tour adorée et haïe, mais elle était tenue éloignée du monde des hommes.
dialogue.english: Thus she was both loved and hated, but she was kept away from the world of men.

dialogue.french: Savez-vous quels ont été ses derniers mots ?
dialogue.english: Do you know what her last words were?

dialogue.french: Euh, « Vive le Roi ! » ? « Que Dieu bénisse la France ! » ? Quelque chose de ce genre ?
dialogue.english: Uh, 'Long live the King!'? 'God bless France!'? Something like that?

dialogue.french: Vous n'y êtes pas du tout. Écoutez bien : « Ayant marché par mégarde sur le pied de son bourreau, elle le regarda doucement et lui dit 'Excusez-moi, Monsieur, je ne l'ai pas fait exprès'. »
dialogue.english: You're wide of the mark. Listen carefully: 'Having inadvertently stepped on her executioner's foot, she looked at him gently and said, "Excuse me, sir, I didn't mean to do it."'

dialogue.french: Peut-on dire vraiment que celle qui a écrit dans son testament « Que mon fils ne cherche jamais à venger notre mort », peut-on vraiment dire que cette femme n'était qu'une tête de linotte ?
dialogue.english: Can it really be said that she who wrote in her will 'May my son never seek to avenge our death', can we really say that this woman was just a scatterbrain?

dialogue.french: Vous avez sans doute raison, mais connaissant le sort réservé à Marie-Antoinette, à votre place, j'éviterais le mot « tête »...
dialogue.english: You are undoubtedly right, but knowing the fate that befell Marie Antoinette, if I were you, I would avoid the word 'head'...

notes.content: Since an initial his a half-vowel, it is usually mute when liaised to final consonant of the previous word. Thus bonne heure is pronounced identically to bonheur [bonuhr].

We are familiar with falloir, to be necessary / to have to. This impersonal verb is also defective, meaning that it has only once conjugation in each tense: the third person singular. The imperfect form is fallait: Il ne fallait pas inviter ce journaliste, That journalist shouldn'thave been invited.

fré quenter is agood example of a French verb with both a Latin-based and an Anglo-Saxon translation, depending on the level of formality. De nombreux oiseaux fré quentent cette ré gion; Numerous birds frequent this region or, less formally, É vite de fré quenter les bars du centre-ville, Avoid going to the bars in the city centre. The verb can also be translated as to keep company with, spend time with, etc. By contrast, the adjective fré quent simply means frequent.

We know that the adjective grand, big, can also mean great, eminent, etc. (lesson note 2). It can also mean main, principal. Note the subtle difference in meaning in this sentence: La grande difficulté est de trouver une salle assez grande, The main difficulty is finding aroom that is big enough. In short, grand designates anything of size, importance, value or seniority.

In the expression faire la connaissance, to make the acquaintance of, connaissance is still abstract. But it can also be aconcrete noun: Simon n'est pas un ami, plutô t une connaissance, Simon is an acquaintance rather than a friend. (The noun remains feminine, regardless of the acquaintance's sex.) Remember that the root verb is connaî tre.

We know laisser tomber means to drop (lesson note 5). In the perfect tense, it is not possible to put two participles together, so, in any two-word compound verb -faire cuire, to cook, for example-the second verb stays in the infinitive: J'ai fait cuire des pommes de terre, I've cooked some potatoes, or, as in lesson 59, Il alaissé tomber son sac, He dropped his bag.

Faux-ami alert: un(e) photographe, a photographer, une photographie, aphotograph (often abbreviated to une photo, a photo), and la photographie (or la photo), photography. The latter is classified as either numé rique (digital) or argentique, aneologism from l'argent, silver, usually translated as film or analogue.

à la fois means at the same time, at once: N'essaie pas de faire trop de choses à la fois, Don'ttry to do too many things at once. The expression can also translate both in the case of two nouns: La solution est à la fois simple et pas chè re, The solution is both simple and inexpensive. In alonger construction, however, the expression can simply be dropped, but the meaning remains: La solution est à la fois simple, rapide et pas chè re, The solution is simple, quick and inexpensive.

dû is the past participle of devoir: Nous avons dû partir car nous é tions en retard, We had to leave because we were late. The circumflex is important in order to distinguish the word from the partitive du, just as the grave accent allows us to distinguish between ou (or) and où (where). In neither case does the accent change the pronunciation.
valait is the imperfect of valoir (lesson note 10).

The expression pas grand-chose means not much, nothing much. On ne sait pas grand-chose de lui, We don'tknow much about him. / Not much is known about him. The expression Ç a ne me dit pas grand-chose means It doesn'tmean very much to me or, in amore familiar register, It doesn'tgrab me. Note that we use grand even though the noun is feminine. The same form is found in acouple of other nouns, notably une grand-mè re, agrandmother (the masculine being un grand-pè re, grandfather).

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: La Corse (Corsica both in English and the Corsican language: le corse) is an island 170 kilometres off the Mediterranean coast of France. Known as l'île de Beauté the Isle of Beauty, it is famed for dramatic scenery, mountainous terrain, sandy beaches and lush vegetation. Corsica has its own language (le corse -note the masculine gender) and avery strong cultural identity combining influences from all over the Mediterranean and beyond. Corsicans -among others-often refer to mainland France as la Métropole ("metropolitan France"), often without acapital m, since the word was once used to differentiate acountry from its colonies or possessions. Productive phase: 12th lesson

title: J'ai mis le doigt sur ton problème ...

dialogue.french: Au secours ! Qu'est-ce que j'ai fichu ?
dialogue.english: Help! What the heck have I done?

dialogue.french: Je faisais des tableaux tranquillement avec mon tableur quand je me suis arrêté pour chercher à manger à la cuisine.

dialogue.french: Au retour, je me suis remis devant l'écran, et patatras ! Panne totale.

dialogue.english: Now nothing works: not the computer, nor the wifi, nor the keyboard, nor the plug, nothing at all.

dialogue.french: Aïe ! C'est embêtant. Mais tu aurais dû faire plus attention – ou plus de ménage : t'as vu le fouillis dans ton bureau ?
dialogue.english: Ouch! That's annoying. But you should have paid more attention – or more cleaning: have you seen the mess in your office?

dialogue.french: Mais par où commencer le rangement quand tout est sens dessus dessous ?
dialogue.english: But where do you start the tidying when everything is topsy-turvy?

dialogue.french: C'est pas vrai ! Il y a juste un petit peu de désordre, c'est tout, deux ou trois choses de travers.
dialogue.english: It isn't true! There's just a little bit of clutter, that's all, a couple of things out of place.

dialogue.french: Je l'aurais rangé hier si j'avais eu le temps mais je travaillais contre la montre.
dialogue.english: I would have tidied it yesterday if I'd had the time, but I was working against the clock.

dialogue.french: À ta place, j'aurais fait le ménage tous les jours. Comme ça tu n'aurais pas eu ce problème.
dialogue.english: If I were you, I would have cleaned it every day. That way you wouldn't be having this problem.

dialogue.french: Comment tu vas faire pour t'en sortir ? Tu n'es ni électricien, ni réparateur informatique.
dialogue.english: What are you going to do to sort things out? You're not an electrician or a computer repairman.

dialogue.french: J'ai tenté de contacter le service d'assistance en ligne mais l'attente était interminable.
dialogue.english: I tried to contact the online helpdesk but the wait was endless.

dialogue.french: Tu aurais pu demander à Driss, c'est un as de l'ordinateur. Il aurait remis tout en ordre en moins de deux.
dialogue.english: You could have asked Driss, he's a computer whizzkid. He would have sorted everything out in no time.

dialogue.french: Mais il est parti ce matin à Toulouse pour assister à un atelier.
dialogue.english: But he left this morning for Toulouse to attend a workshop.

dialogue.french: Zut ! Si j'avais su, je l'aurais appelé sur le champ mais je pensais qu'il était toujours dans le coin.
dialogue.english: Damn! If I'd known, I would have called him on the spot but I thought he was still in the neighbourhood.

dialogue.french: Je suis certain qu'il serait venu tout de suite si je lui avais demandé. Il est très serviable.
dialogue.english: I'm sure he would have come right away if I had asked him. He's very helpful.

dialogue.french: Quand même, il aurait pu me dire qu'il partait et qu'il n'était pas disponible !
dialogue.english: Even so, he could have told me that he was leaving and that he wasn't available!

dialogue.french: Là, tu te livres à ton passe-temps favori : te plaindre après coup. Sniff !
dialogue.english: Now you're indulging in your favourite pastime: complaining after the fact. Boo-hoo!

dialogue.french: Et toi, tu me critiques toujours : « T'aurais dû faire ci, tu n'aurais pas dû faire ça » et patati et patata.
dialogue.english: And you're always criticizing me: 'You should have done this, you shouldn't have done that,' and so on and so forth.

dialogue.french: Peut-être bien, mais j'aurais été contente si tu m'avais appelée. J'aurais pu t'aider.
dialogue.english: Maybe so, but I would have been happy if you had called me. I could have helped you.

dialogue.french: Comment cela ? Toi non plus, tu n'es pas un crack de l'informatique, que je sache.
dialogue.english: What do you mean? You're not a computer expert either, as far as I know.

dialogue.french: Peut-être pas, et je n'aurais pas su réparer l'équipement. Mais j'ai de bons yeux et je sais regarder.
dialogue.english: Maybe not, and I wouldn't have been able to fix the hardware. But I have good eyesight and I know how to look.

dialogue.french: Ta machine est débranchée : tu as dû te prendre les pieds bêtement dans le cordon d'alimentation.
dialogue.english: Your machine is unplugged: you must have stupidly got your feet caught in the power cord.

notes.content: The adjective doux (fem. douce; adverb doucement) means gentle, sweet, mild, soft, etc. (Think dulcet). Il fait un temps doux et sec, The weather is mild and dry. Ce savon laisse vos mains douces, This soap leaves your hands soft. The idiomatic expression faire les yeux doux (à) is the equivalent of to make eyes at someone. By extension it can mean to woo, to cosy up to, etc. L'é quipe fait les yeux doux au jeune joueur marocain, The team is eyeing up the young Moroccan player.

avoir les dents longues ("to have long teeth") means to be ambitious: Il ira loin, Jean, il ales dents longues. Jean will go far. He's ambitious. Be careful: it is not the translation of to be long in the tooth, translated by ne pas ê tre tout jeune ("not to be very young").

avoir un coup de cœur (pour quelque chose / quelqu'un) ("have ablow of the heart") means to fall in love with or have acrush on (something or someone) or, more abstractly, to be taken with. Acommon usage of the noun un coup de cœur is as synonym for a favourite. Nos coups de cœur de cette semaine: This week's favourites.

The adjective sourd means deaf. Faire la sourde oreille, to turn adeaf ear to. (French can use adjectives as nouns, which is not always possible in English: un sourd, adeaf person, un jeune, ayoung person, etc. We will see more examples in another lesson.)

la tê te, the head, is used in many French idioms. With the reflexive form of the verb creuser, to dig, se creuser la tê te is the equivalent of to rack one's brains. Je me suis creusé la tê te mais je ne m'en souviens pas, I've racked my brains but I can't remember. By contrast, se casser la tê te ("to break one's head") means to worry or fret. The verb is often used in the expression Ne te casse / vous cassez pas la tê te, Don'tworry (about it).

prendre ses jambes à son cou ("take one'slegs to one's neck") paints acartoonish image of aperson running away quickly: to take to one's heels. Note that, unlike many other idioms, this one does not use the reflexive form of the verb.

Another idiom that resembles its English equivalent: mettre les pieds dans le plat, to put one'sfoot in it. Spot the little differences: aplural noun (pieds) and an extra bit of detail (le plat, the dish).

Despite the final -s, le dos, the back (lesson 48), like le bras (lesson 61), is singular and does not change in the plural. The expression faire froid dans le dos means to send shivers down the spine. It can be used impersonally (Ç a fait froid dans le dos) or with an indirect object pronoun: Ce qu'ils ont trouvé leur fait froid dans le dos, What they've found sends shivers down their spine.

Here are two more French words that have passed into English: une é paule, ashoulder (think an epaulette, a shoulder-worn decoration) and un fusil, agun (a fusilier, atype of soldier). The idiom changer son fusil d'é paule ("to change one'sgun to the other shoulder") means to shift one's stance, to have achange of heart: Le ministre n'est pas prê t à changer son fusil d'é paule au sujet de la santé, The minister isn'tprepared to shift his stance on the health issue.

Many idioms are formed from un œil / les yeux. If something is obtained à l'œil, it is free (tradespeople used to judge a person'seligibility for free credit by casting an eye over them). By contrast, if something is exorbitantly expensive, il coû te les yeux de la tê te, it costs the earth ("eyes of the head"). Interestingly, British English has integrated the American expression to cost an arm and a leg, which French has now transformed into coû ter un bras.
une barbe, abeard (the origin of barber) is used as an exclamation La barbe ! / Quelle barbe !, What a drag! Whence the idiomatic adjective barbant, boring.

If you sleep soundly, you hear nothing. This is probably the origin of dormir sur ses deux oreilles ("to sleep on both ears"), which also means to rest easy. And while English-speakers sleep like a log, afrancophone will dormir comme une souche, literally"to sleep like atree stump"!

extras.content: We're now beginning to learn the kinds of idiomatic expressions that are used on aregular basis by native speakers. Some of the ones in this lesson will look familiar; others may surprise you. But once you get the hang of them (vous en prenez l'habitude), you'll be speaking truly colloquial French. Productive phase: 13th lesson

notes.content: L'imparfait: the imperfect tense: The imperfect is used to describe actions performed regularly or for an extended period in the past, with no mention of when they began or ended. (The tense owes its name to the fact such actions are not"perfected,"or completed). There is no direct equivalent in English. Depending on the context, the imperfect can be translated by the past continuous (Iwas teaching) or the past habitual (Iused to teach, Iwould teach). In some cases, particularly descriptions, the best equivalent is the past simple. The imperfect for all three verb groups (including irregular verbs) is formed from the first person plural of the present tense, deleting the -ons ending and adding -ais, ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, and -aient to the stem. Here are examples from the three groups: enseigner, to teach → enseign-: j'enseignais, tu enseignais, il/elle enseignait, nous enseignions, vous enseigniez, ils/elles enseignaient. finir, to finish→ finiss-: je finissais, tu finissais, il/elle finissait, nous finissions, vous finissiez, ils/elles finissaient. savoir, to know→ sav-: je savais, tu savais, il/elle savait, nous savions, vous saviez, ils/elles savaient. The only exception is ê tre: j'é tais, tu é tais, il/elle é tait, nous é tions, vous é tiez, ils/elles é taient. There are two special cases: the impersonal verb falloir and the defective verb pleuvoir, to rain, are both used in the third person singular only: il fallait; il pleuvait. The negative and interrogative forms of the imperfect are formed in the usual way: tu ne connaissais pas ?; est-ce-que tu connaissais ? / connaissais-tu ?, etc. In some case, the stem changes very slightly. In the case of -er verbs like lancer, to throw (lesson 59), the ctakes acedilla before the letter a: il lanç ait (if not, the cwould be ahard k). Likewise, in verbs such as manger, to eat, and dé ranger, to disturb, the gbecomes ge before aand o: tu mangeais, il dé rangeait (otherwise, the gwould be hard g). The imperfect tense is used for continuous or habitual actions in the past, notably those that, in English, are in the past continuous (Elle vivait à Lyon à l'é poque, She was living in Lyon at the time). It is used particularly in sentences where acontinuing action is interrupted by asingle action in the past: Elle dormait quand son té lé phone a sonné. She was sleeping when her phone rang. One very common use is narration: Quand nous habitions à Grenoble, j'enseignais le franç ais et mon ami travaillait à Colombe. Nous avions beaucoup de chance car nous habitions à trente kilomè tres de la montagne. En é té, j'allais faire de la randonné e toutes les semaines. In this case, the imperfect is translated by the past simple tense or with would because the actions are all habitual: When we lived in Grenoble, Itaught French and my friend worked at Colombe. We were very lucky because we lived thirty kilometres away from the mountains. In summer, Iwould / used to go hiking every week. Note the difference between En é té, j'allais faire de la randonné e toutes les semaines and this sentence: En é té, je suis allé faire de la randonné e quatre fois, In summer, Iwent hiking four times. In both cases, there is arepetitive action, but the first sentence describes ahabitual (and less precise) action.

valoir and falloir: These two irregular verbs, which are sometimes confused, are used idiomatically. Let'stake a look: • valoir: Present: je/j' vaux, tu vaux, il/elle vaut, nous valons, vous valez, ils/elles valent. Future: je/j' vaudrai, tu vaudras, il/elle vaudra, nous vaudrons, vous vaudrez, ils/elles vaudront. Imperfect: je/j' valais, tu valais, il/elle valait, nous valions, vous valiez, ils/elles valaient. Past: j'ai valu, tu as valu, il/elle a valu, nous avons valu, vous avez valu, ils/elles ont valu. Valoir means to be worth: Cette maison vaut deux millions, This house is worth two million. The derived noun, value, is la valeur: Je n'ai aucune idé e de la valeur de ce produit. Ihave no idea of the value of this product. Pecuniary value aside, valoir conveys the notion of merit or quality: Que vaut ce nouveau jeu ? How good is this new game? Ces nouvelles mesures ne valent pas grand-chose. These new measures don'tmean very much. In this context, the impersonal idiom valoir par is used to emphasise the main quality of something, expressed in a noun: Cet hô tel vaut par son ambiance. The good thing about this hotel is its atmosphere. The impersonal third-person singular, vaut, is coupled with the comparative mieux, better, to talk about something preferable or more desirable: Il vaut mieux partir de bonne heure. It'sbetter to leave early. Another common impersonal use is the expression Ç a vaut la peine, It'sworth it, or, more idiomatically, Ç a vaut le coup. There are many other idiomatic uses of valoir, some of which we will see in future lessons, but the underlying theme is that of worth or value. Try to learn as many as you can: Ç a vaut le coup ! • falloir (with adouble l) is an impersonal verb whose basic meaning is to need or to be necessary. It is conjugated only in the third person singular: Present: il faut. Future: il faudra. Imperfect: il fallait. Past: il a fallu. The verb is impersonal -it can never take a subject-and is generally followed by anoun or an infinitive, just like need. The translation depends, as always, on the context. For example, Il faut beaucoup d'argent pour voyager can be translated formally with one or informally with the impersonal"you": One needs / You need alot of money to travel. Another possibility is to use the passive: Alot of money is needed, etc. To personalise falloir, add an indirect object pronoun (me, lui, etc.) before the conjugated form: Il me/lui faut de l'argent (see lessons line and line 5). And just as American English uses need to when giving instructions, so French uses falloir: Il vous faut tourner à gauche. You need to take a left. In the interrogative, the inverted question form is very common, particularly in apolite register. When shopping, for instance, you might be asked: Vous faut-il autre chose ? Do you need anything else? rather than Est-ce qu'il vous faut autre chose ? Naturally, falloir is used in idiomatic expressions, many of which concern the idea of appropriate action. For example: Il adé pensé une fortune ! - Il faut ce qu'il faut. He spent afortune - Whatever it takes ("it'snecessary what is necessary"). Another concise expression -so concise that it has been imported into English-is comme il faut, suggesting proper or necessary behaviour: Le travail doit ê tre fait comme il faut. The work has to be done properly. Keep an eye out for other falloir expressions, and make anote of them.

When to pronounce the"s"in plus: The pronunciation, or not, of the final sin the adverb and noun plus depends, among other things, on the word'sgrammatical function and position in the sentence or expression. Abasic rule is that sis voiced if plus has apositive meaning and unvoiced if negative. • Pronounced: The sis pronounced [plewss] when plus means more: Il faut plus de moyens... More resources are needed... Similarly, at the end of a sentence: Ce n'est pas assez ; il faut un peu plus. It'snot enough; you need alittle more.... and as a noun: Ce stage est un plus pour ta carriè re. That course is aplus for your career. More generally, it is pronounced -always as a [z]- when followed by adjective starting with a vowel: plus‿inté ressant, [plewzah"teressœh"]. • Silent: The sis silent ([pl/ew]) when plus is used in the negation ne... plus or, at the end of aphrase in non plus: Nous n'avons plus d'argent, We have no more money. - Et nous n'en avons pas, non plus, And we have none either. Likewise, it is silent in the comparative form if the adjective it precedes starts with a consonant: Ils sont plus grands, They are bigger. However, in the intensifier plus en plus, the first sis pronounced (as a z) to make the liaison: [duh plewz-œh"-plew]. In short, it is very important to remember the grammatical function of plus: Est-ce qu'il y aun peu plus ([plewss]) de lait ? - Non, je n'en ai plus ([plew]).

Conjunctive adverbs (pourtant, cependant, etc.): Conjunctive adverbs can modify or qualify the statements or sentences they precede or follow. Here are some of the ones you have met so far: • Pourtant is used to contrast or contradict, in the same way as yet, however, still, or even so. Je ne la connais pas bien. Pourtant, je lui fais confiance. I don'tknow her well, and yet Itrust her. The contrast is often highlighted with mais: C'est difficile à croire mais pourtant vrai. It'shard to believe and yet it's true. or, especially, et:"Et pourtant elle tourne!"disait Galilé e."And yet it moves ("turns"),"said Galileo. The adverb is often used before the verb, rather than after it, or at the beginning of the phrase, as in English: Il faut pourtant le faire. It has to be done even so / And yet it has to be done. • Cependant has almost exactly the same meaning but is more formal than pourtant. Most importantly, it is not preceded by et: C'est difficile à croire, cependant c'est vrai. It'shard to believe, and yet it'strue (see above). • Né anmoins is almost adirect translation of nevertheless (né ant means nothingness): J'espè re né anmoins que vous vous ê tes amusé s. Ihope you had fun nevertheless. • Alors has several meanings. As an adverb of consequence, it means so or then. In the same way that many English speakers begin asentence with So..., francophones will say: Alors, tu viens ?, So, are you coming? The adverb is frequently used in exclamations, too: Alors ç a, ç a me fait plaisir, Now that makes me happy. But alors also refers back to the past, like at that time, back then: Je l'ai connu en 2018. Il é tait alors mon directeur. Iknew him in 2018. At that time, he was my director. In every case, the translation will depend on the context, the register and the person speaking. (And remember, there may be no precise English equivalent.) We recommend that you note down any examples of usage that surprise you.

Idioms (1): body parts: Idioms are avital part of a language, but they can be hard to understand because their overall meaning is different from the literal meaning of the individual words they are composed of. Because of the similarities between French and English, some idioms are common to both languages, as seen in lesson 62 (s'arracher les cheveux); others are almost the same but vary slightly (mettre les pieds dans le plat); and still others are either totally different (avoir les dents longues) or have no direct equivalent (à l'œil). One of the best ways of learning idioms is to group them by category. In the last few lessons, we saw some of those in the"body part"category: accueillir (quelqu'un) les bras ouverts (welcome someone with open arms), baisser les bras (give up, abandon), coû ter un bras (cost an arm and a leg), s'arracher les cheveux (tear one'shair out), avoir un coup de cœur (fall in love with / be smitten by), mettre de l'huile de coude (use elbow grease), serrer les dents (grit one's teeth), ne pas lever le doigt (not lift a finger), mettre le doigt sur quelque chose (put one'sfinger on something), faire froid dans le dos (make one'sblood run cold), changer son fusil d'é paule (change one's stance), prendre ses jambes à son cou (take to one's heels), donner un coup de main (à quelqu'un) (give someone a hand), avoir quelque chose à l'œil (get something for free), dormir sur ses deux oreilles (sleep soundly), faire la sourde oreille (turn adeaf ear), mettre les pieds dans le plat (put one'sfoot in it), se casser la tê te (worry / fret about), se creuser la tê te (rack one's brains), passer au-dessus de la tê te de quelqu'un (go over someone's head), coû ter les yeux de la tê te (cost the earth), faire les yeux doux (à) (make eyes at).

dialogue.french: Entrez, entrez monsieur. Est-ce que je peux vous renseigner ?
dialogue.english: Come in, come in sir. Can I give you some information?

dialogue.french: Il me faut des vacances parce que je suis épuisé. Qu'est-ce que vous pouvez me proposer ?
dialogue.english: I need a holiday because I'm exhausted. What can you offer me?

dialogue.french: Tout dépend : combien de temps pouvez-vous partir ? À quelles conditions et à quel moment ?
dialogue.english: It all depends: how long can you go away for? On what terms and at what period?

dialogue.french: Si vous partez avant le mois de juillet, normalement vous serez tranquille, mais si vous attendez les grandes vacances, ça sera réellement l'enfer.
dialogue.english: If you leave before the month of July, you should have some peace and quiet, but if you wait for the summer holiday, it really will be hellish.

dialogue.french: Tout est bondé en cette période, les prix grimpent et les températures aussi.
dialogue.english: Everything is crowded during that period, prices climb and temperatures too.

dialogue.french: Les moments les plus agréables sont soit début-juin soit fin-septembre.
dialogue.english: The nicest times are either early June or late September.

dialogue.french: Ce sont les moments où il y a le moins de monde. Pour moi, ce sont les plus beaux mois.
dialogue.english: These are the times when there are fewer people. For me, they are the nicest months.

dialogue.french: Et quel est le pire mois de l'année, d'après vous : juillet ou août ?
dialogue.english: And what's the worst month of the year, according to you: July or August?

dialogue.french: Ils sont aussi mauvais l'un que l'autre, mais je pense qu'août est pire que juillet.
dialogue.english: Each is as bad as the other, but I think that August is worse than July.

dialogue.french: S'il fait beau, les plages sont saturées de touristes, et s'il fait mauvais on ne peut pas se baigner.
dialogue.english: If it's fine, the beaches are inundated with tourists, and if the weather's bad you can't go swimming.

dialogue.french: Pour éviter ça, si vous avez envie, vous pourrez essayer quelque chose de plus original.
dialogue.english: To avoid that, if you want to, you can try something more original.

dialogue.french: Par exemple, vous pourrez faire de la plongée sous-marine dans le Var, ou bien de la randonnée à cheval dans le Massif central.
dialogue.english: For example, you can go underwater diving in the Var, or horse trekking in the Massif Central.

dialogue.french: C'est merveilleux à cette période de l'année.
dialogue.english: It's wonderful at that time of year.

dialogue.french: Non, aucun des deux ne me tente. Je ne sais pas nager, je ne sais pas monter à cheval, et je n'ai pas envie de prendre des cours non plus.
dialogue.english: No, neither of the two tempts me. I can't swim, I can't ride, and I don't want to take lessons either.

dialogue.french: J'ai une autre possibilité, qui est très reposante, très confortable mais pas donnée.
dialogue.english: I have another possibility, which is very relaxing, very comfortable, but not cheap.

dialogue.french: Une semaine dans un grand hôtel, Le Domaine des Dieux, sur la Côte d'Azur.
dialogue.english: A week in a grand hotel, the Domain of the Gods, on the Riviera.

dialogue.french: C'est un des plus beaux palaces de la région.
dialogue.english: It's one of the nicest luxury hotels in the region.

dialogue.french: Il y a une offre de dernière minute avec une réduction exceptionnelle de deux pour cent.
dialogue.english: There is a last-minute offer with an exceptional reduction of two per cent.

dialogue.french: Et c'est combien ? Je crains le pire...
dialogue.english: And how much is it? I fear the worst...

dialogue.french: La formule tout compris est à dix mille euros, hors taxes pour quatre jours en demi-pension.
dialogue.english: The all-in package is at ten thousand euros, before tax for four days at half-board.

dialogue.french: Mm, je vois. Et des cours de plongée, ça serait combien ?
dialogue.english: Mm, I see. And how much would diving lessons cost?

notes.content: grand hô tel: Since his a half-vowel, the pronunciation rule explained in lesson applies here, i.e. the terminal dis pronounced [t]: [grœh"t-ohtel].

renseigner is the verb from which the masculine noun renseignement (lesson line 7) is derived. It means to give information or directions to. Pouvez-vous me renseigner ? is aformal way of asking for information. The question Est-ce que je peux / Puis-je vous renseigner ? is used by service industry staff to greet customers: Can Ihelp you? The information desk in apublic building is signposted RENSEIGNEMENTS.

Here is the first, or"zero,"conditional which, like English, uses the present+future construction: Si vous partez maintenant, vous arriverez avant midi, If you leave now, you'll arrive before noon. In some cases, the si clause introduces asimple observation, in which case the present is used in both parts of the sentence, and can be replaced by quand: S'il fait / Quand il fait mauvais, les plages sont vides, If/when the weather is bad, the beaches are empty.

normalement, normally (lesson line 4) is also used to express a condition: Il vient tout à l'heure ? - Normalement oui, Is he coming later? - Yes, he should do. In this context, it can be understood as under normal circumstances or if all goes well.

The construction of asuperlative clause depends on whether the adjective comes after the noun, which is the general rule, or before it (the BAGS rule, lesson 14). In the first case, the article is repeated: les mois les plus agré ables; but not in the second: les plus beaux mois.

aprè s vous means after you, Je suis arrivé(e) aprè s vous, Iarrived after you. It is also apolite way of allowing someone to go ahead of you. But d'aprè s with anoun or pronoun means according to: D'aprè s Jarnel, il y abeaucoup de monde au mois d'aoû t, According to Jarnel, August is very crowded.

faire is used when talking about sports or physical activity, whereas in English we generally use to go: Je fais du ski deux fois par an, Igo skiing twice a year. In other cases, faire du/de la/de l' + sport can be translated by asingle verb in English, faire de la natation: to go swimming OR to swim; faire du cheval, to go horse-riding OR to ride. Quand elle é tait au lycé e, elle faisait de la natation tous les jours, When she was at school, she used to swim every day.

Another difference with English is the use of savoir to translate the notion of ability (i.e. to know how to): Je ne sais pas nager et ma femme ne sait pas conduire, I can'tswim and my wife can't drive.
un cours (singular, despite the s) is asynonym of une leç on, a lesson. We can say un cours de franç ais or une leç on de franç ais.

The idiom Ce n'est pas donné means It'snot cheap ("not given [away]"). And, as in our example, pas donné can be incorporated into a sentence: Leurs produits ne sont pas donné s mais ils sont de trè s bonne qualité, Their products aren'tcheap but the quality is very good.

The technical term une formule, a formula, is frequently used in acommercial context to mean a package, an offering: Notre formule"tout compris"comprend les vols, les hô tels et les repas, Our all-in deal or package includes flights, hotels and meals. The term is commonly found in restaurants offering une formule dé jeuner, the equivalent of the"English"term aprix fixe lunch.

notes.content: pareille the feminine and the masculine (pareil) are pronounced identically in both the singular and the plural: [parayy].

This is the second conditional, expressing the possible result of ahypothetical action. Pouvoir is an irregular verb, the conditional mood being je pourrais, tu pourrais, il/elle pourrait, nous pourrions, vous pourriez, ils/elles pourraient. In an if-then sentence, French uses the imperfect tense (never the conditional) after si, instead of the past simple in English: Il pourrait t'aider si tu voulais, He could help you if you wanted.

The present conditional of aller is j'irais, tu irais, il/elle irait, nous irions, vous iriez, ils/elles iraient. There is no need for an auxiliary (e.g. would). The first person singular is pronounced identically to the future form (j'irai), i.e. the final sis silent. The same rule applies to all verbs.
The conditional of avoir is j'aurais, tu aurais, il/elle aurait, nous aurions, vous auriez, ils/elles auraient. (Remember j'aurais is ahomophone of the future form j'aurai.)

With most ordinary verbs, the conditional is formed by adding the endings of the imperfect tense to the infinitive. Thus the conditional of coû ter is je coû terais, tu coû terais, il/elle coû terait, nous coû terions, vous coû teriez, ils/elles coû teraient.
The conditional of ê tre is je serais, tu serais, il/elle serait, nous serions, vous seriez, ils/elles seraient.
You'll find the conditional of vouloir in lesson 70. See also lesson note 6.
For the conditional of -re verbs, the final eis dropped (like for the future): Thus dire → je dirais, tu dirais, il/elle dirait, nous dirions, vous diriez, ils/elles diraient.
The conditional of the defective verb falloir (see lesson note 2) is il faudrait.

la mode generally means fashion (clothing, etc., see lessons and 61), so the adjectival phrase à la mode means fashionable, trendy: Les investissements verts sont à la mode cette anné e, Green investments are fashionable this year.

The masculine adjective pareil (fem pareille) means the same or similar. Les deux mots sont pareils, The two words are the same. The basic difference between pareil and mê me is that the former is used alone while the latter requires an article and a noun, usually chose. Tu viens jeudi ou vendredi ? - Pour moi, c'est pareil / c'est la mê me chose. The expression C'est du pareil au mê me ("It'sfrom the same to the same") means It'sthe same thing, etc. Lire ou é couter un livre audio, c'est du pareil au mê me, Reading or listening to an audio book is six of one, half adozen of the other.

extras.content: Les Pyrénées, the Pyrenees, is arange of mountains forming anatural border between France and Spain and spanning several départements, including les Pyrénées Orientales ("eastern Pyrenees"), les Hautes-Pyrénées ("high Pyrenees") and les Pyrénées-Atlantiques (bordering the Atlantic Ocean). One section of the range is abeautiful national park, le parc national des Pyrénées. Productive phase: 16th lesson

dialogue.french: Les élèves d'un lycée lyonnais sont invités à participer au débat sur le climat à l'Assemblée nationale, avec, comme thème, « Que feriez-vous si vous étiez Président de la République ? »
dialogue.english: The students from a high school in Lyon are invited to take part in the debate on the climate in the National Assembly, on the theme 'What would you do if you were President of the Republic?'

dialogue.french: « Mesdames et messieurs les députés, j'invite Mademoiselle Noura Bouris à prendre la parole. Alors, Noura, si vous étiez présidente, que feriez-vous pour combattre le changement climatique ? »
dialogue.english: 'Fellow Members of Parliament, I invite Ms Noura Bouris to take the floor. Well, Noura, if you were president, what would you do to fight climate change?'

dialogue.french: « Est-ce qu'il serait possible, à votre avis, de prendre rapidement des mesures efficaces ? »
dialogue.english: 'Would it be possible, in your opinion, to quickly take effective measures?'

dialogue.french: Nous croyons que oui, et il faudrait en effet agir vite car nous sommes tous en danger.
dialogue.english: We believe so, and we should act quickly because we are all in danger.

dialogue.french: « Que feriez-vous ? Interdiriez-vous à tous les véhicules à essence et diesel de rouler en ville ? »
dialogue.english: 'What would you do? Would you prohibit all petrol and diesel vehicles from driving in cities?'

dialogue.french: Je n'interdirais pas les petits véhicules utilitaires car les artisans ont besoin de se déplacer, mais je ne permettrais pas aux camions de livraison de circuler pendant la journée.
dialogue.english: I wouldn't prohibit small goods vehicles because artisans need to travel, but I wouldn't allow delivery trucks to drive during the day.

dialogue.french: « Et que feriez-vous pour approvisionner les magasins ? Interdiriez-vous n'importe quel camion à n'importe quelle heure, n'importe où dans la ville ? Ça ne serait pas très pratique. »
dialogue.english: 'And what would you do to supply the shops? Would you prevent any lorry at any time, anywhere in town? That wouldn't be very practical.'

dialogue.french: Peut-être, mais je n'aimerais pas que mes enfants respirent constamment de l'air pollué.
dialogue.english: Perhaps, but I wouldn't like my children to constantly breathe polluted air.

dialogue.french: « Tout le monde est contre les voitures particulières, mais elles sont un mal nécessaire, non ? »
dialogue.english: 'Everybody is against passenger cars, but they are a necessary evil, aren't they?'

dialogue.french: Nous ne sommes pas contre les voitures, monsieur, mais contre le réchauffement planétaire.
dialogue.english: We're not against cars, sir, but against global warming.

dialogue.french: Tous les véhicules polluent mais certains sont pires que d'autres, et de loin.
dialogue.english: All vehicles pollute but some are worse than others, and by far.

dialogue.french: Et, au bout d'un certain temps, les résultats seront catastrophiques.
dialogue.english: And, after a certain time, the results will be disastrous.

dialogue.french: Il faut à tout prix réduire notre empreinte carbone.
dialogue.english: It's necessary to reduce our carbon footprint at all costs.

dialogue.french: « N'importe quoi ! Si nous savions comment éliminer les gaz à effet de serre, nous l'aurions fait il y a longtemps. »
dialogue.english: 'Nonsense. If we knew how to eliminate greenhouse gases, we would have done it a long time ago.'

dialogue.french: Nous avons la nette impression que vous ne nous écoutez pas.
dialogue.english: We have the distinct impression that you are not listening to us.

dialogue.french: « Mais si, mais si, ma petite. Sinon, nous ne vous aurions pas invités aujourd'hui. Maintenant, deux autocars attendent dehors pour vous ramener à la maison. »
dialogue.english: 'But yes, but yes, my little one. Otherwise, we wouldn't have invited you here today. Now, two coaches are waiting outside to take you home.'

dialogue.french: C'est bien ce que nous pensions ! Vous ne nous prenez pas au sérieux.
dialogue.english: That's exactly what we thought! You don't take us seriously.

notes.content: net is irregular because the final tis pronounced, exactly the same as the feminine nette: [net].

We know that adjectives do not take an initial capital. This applies not only to nationalities (lesson 65: la Suisse → suisse) but also to adjectives of location, here the city of Lyon → lyonnais. Like all adjectives, agreement is obligatory: les é coles lyonnaises, schools in Lyon. But remember that, with an indefinite article (often preceded by un(e)), such words are nouns, and therefore take a capital: Notre magazine est lu par un Lyonnais sur deux, Our magazine is read by one Lyonnais in two.
The third interrogative (inversion) is commonly used with the conditional form because it is easier on the ear than the est-ce que form (qu'est-ce que vous feriez), which is nevertheless used.

une parole, like un mot, means a word, but refers more to the underlying thoughts or meaning than to the words themselves. Combien de mots y a-t-il dans cette phrase ? How many words are there in this sentence, but Je te donne ma parole, Igive you my word. Prendre la parole ("to take the word") is aformal way of saying to speak or to take the floor, usually in apublic forum.

As in English, croire, to believe, can be asynonym for penser, followed by que if used in a clause: Je pense/crois qu'il é tait surpris, I think/believe that he was surprised. The relative is also used when either verb is followed by oui or non: Je crois/pense que non, I believe/think not.

interdire means to forbid (the origin of the English technical word interdict) and is usually used in the impersonal form with de: Il est interdit de fumer dans la plupart des lieux publics, Smoking is forbidden in most public places. If the verb has adirect object, however, it needs the preposition à: Je vais interdire à mon fils d'utiliser son té lé phone le soir, I'mgoing to forbid my son to use his phone in the evening. The past participle, interdit, is used in warning signs: INTERDIT DE VAPOTER, NO VAPING.

circuler literally means to circulate: L'air circule partout dans la chambre, Air circulates throughout the bedroom. But the verb is used more broadly in the sense of to walk or move around, or, for traffic, to drive: N'oubliez pas qu'en Grande-Bretagne, on circule à droite, Don'tforget that in Great Britain, they drive on the right. (Thus la circulation can mean traffic (see lesson 44): La circulation est dense ce soir, Traffic is heavy this evening.) The difference with conduire, seen in the previous lesson, is that circuler is intransitive.

In lesson line 19, we saw the indefinite pronominal expression n'importe où, anywhere. N'importe can be followed by other prepositions or pronouns: Choisissez n'importe qu'elle carte, Choose any card. N'importe qui peut entrer dans mon bureau, Anyone can come into my office. In such cases, the basic meaning is any. N'importe quoi ! is adismissive exclamation: Nonsense!

We know that un mal can mean a pain, an ache, harm, etc. (lesson note 3). But the root is le mal, evil (think: malevolent, etc.). So un mal né cessaire is anecessary evil. Less diabolically, le mal means wrong: le bien et le mal, right and wrong or even just a difficulty: Nous avons ré ussi à la joindre, mais non sans mal, We managed to get hold of her, but not without difficulty.

certain means not only certain (as in line 16: un certain temps, acertain time) but, more broadly, some. In this case, the adjective must agree with its noun: Certaines personnes, notamment des é cologistes, sont vé gé tariennes, Some people, particularly ecologists, are vegetarian. In some cases, either translation is appropriate (dans certains cas, in some/certain cases), but you should be aware of the basic difference.

net (feminine nette) means neat or tidy (see nettoyer, to clean, lesson line and lesson note 8). By extension, the adjective can mean clear, sharp or precise. Je n'aime pas les photos numé riques car les images sont moins nettes, I don'tlike digital photos because the pictures are less sharp.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Inhabitants of villages, towns and cities throughout France can all be referred to by a gentilic, derived from the place name and usually formed by adding the suffix -ien(ne) or -ais(e): un(e) Parisien(ne), un(e) Lyonnais(e), etc. When mayors make aformal address to their fellow citizens, they will begin with these proper nouns (always putting the feminine first):"Parisiennes, Parisiens, je compte sur vous". The nearest English equivalent would be"My fellow Parisians, Iam counting on you."l'Assemblée nationale (National Assembly) is the lower house of France's two-chamber parliament. Its lawmakers, les député(e)s, sit in le Palais Bourbon, the official seat, on the left bank of the River Seine. (The upper house is le Sénat, as we saw in lesson 54.) Productive phase: 17th lesson

dialogue.french: Madame Claudie Marchand est rentrée à la maison lundi dernier après avoir passé un mois à l'hôpital.
dialogue.english: Mrs Claudie Marchand came home last Monday after having spent a month in hospital.

dialogue.french: Claudie est toujours coincée dans son appartement au douzième étage, la pauvre.
dialogue.english: Claudie is still stuck in her flat on the twelfth floor, the poor thing.

dialogue.french: Comment ça ? Qu'est-ce qui s'est passé ?
dialogue.english: How so? What happened?

dialogue.french: L'ascenseur est tombé en panne il y a trois semaines et il ne marche toujours pas.
dialogue.english: The lift broke down three weeks ago and it still isn't working.

dialogue.french: C'est pénible – surtout pour elle, qui n'est pas sortie de chez elle depuis trois jours.
dialogue.english: It's annoying – especially for her, who hasn't left her house for three days.

dialogue.french: Quand je suis rentré hier, je suis monté la voir pour savoir si elle avait besoin de quelque chose.
dialogue.english: When I got back yesterday, I went up to see her to find out if she needed anything.

dialogue.french: J'ai rentré ses plantes, qui étaient sur le balcon depuis un mois et demi, et j'ai descendu sa poubelle.
dialogue.english: I brought in her plants, which had been on the balcony for a month and a half, and I took down her rubbish bin.

dialogue.french: J'ai même sorti son petit chien pour le promener.
dialogue.english: I even took out her little dog to walk it.

dialogue.french: Moi, je suis passée la voir ce matin. J'ai monté quelques courses et son courrier.
dialogue.english: I went by to see her this morning. I brought up some shopping and her mail.

dialogue.french: Après, j'ai passé l'aspirateur, fait un peu de ménage et rangé le désordre.
dialogue.english: After, I passed the vacuum cleaner, did a bit of housework and cleared up the mess.

dialogue.french: Magali, sa voisine du dessus, est descendue la voir et elles ont bavardé pendant une bonne heure.
dialogue.english: Magali, her upstairs neighbour, came down to see her and they chatted for a good hour.

dialogue.french: Je suis sûr que, à son âge, Claudie n'a pas d'ordinateur.
dialogue.english: I'm sure that, at her age, Claudie doesn't have a computer.

dialogue.french: Sinon, elle aurait pu entrer sa liste de courses dans une appli et demander à être livrée à domicile.
dialogue.english: Otherwise, she could have entered her shopping list into an app and asked to be delivered at home.

dialogue.french: Tu serais surpris ! Madame Marchand est très bien équipée pour une sénior.
dialogue.english: You'd be surprised! Mrs Marchand is very well equipped for a senior.

dialogue.french: La première fois que je suis allée chez elle, je suis entrée dans une petite pièce à côté de la cuisine et j'ai vu qu'elle avait un nouveau portable, une imprimante, et même une connexion Internet.
dialogue.english: The first time I went to her place, I went into a little room next to the kitchen and I saw that she had a new laptop, a printer, and even an internet connection.

dialogue.french: Le problème, c'est qu'après un mois à l'hôpital, Claudie a oublié ses identifiants.
dialogue.english: The problem is that after a month in hospital, Claudie has forgotten her login details.

dialogue.french: Je suis retournée avant-hier et j'ai regardé partout, sur les étagères, dans ses classeurs et ses boîtes de rangement, mais je n'ai rien trouvé.
dialogue.english: I went back the day before yesterday and I looked everywhere, on the shelves, in her filing cabinets and storage boxes, but I didn't find anything.

dialogue.french: En dernier ressort, j'ai retourné son tapis de souris.
dialogue.english: As a last resort, I turned over her mouse mat.

dialogue.french: Bingo ! Les codes et les mots de passe étaient collés là-dessous.
dialogue.english: Bingo! The code and passwords were glued underneath.

dialogue.french: Comme on dit : « L'encre la plus pâle vaut mieux que la meilleure mémoire » !
dialogue.english: As they say: 'The palest ink is worth the strongest memory'!

notes.content: verrouillé looks difficult to pronounce, but take the word apart: verr is pronounced as in very, -ou-is [oo], the ifeeds into the double-l, pronounced [yy], and the final acute é is [ay]: [verooyay]. Because French is syllable-timed, it'seasier to hear the different sounds that make up a word.

Ahandful of verbs can be conjugated with both avoir and ê tre, but with aslight change of meaning. In the intransitive form, rentrer means to go / come back: Tu es rentré(e) tard hier soir ! You came back late last night! The transitive form means to bring in: As-tu rentré ta voiture au garage ? Did you bring your car into the garage?

The interrogative Comment ç a se fait ? (lesson note 1) is often shortened to Comment ç a ? in idiomatic French when asking for an explanation: Il n'est pas dans son bureau. - Comment ç a ? He'snot in his office. - How come?. Other, similar forms can be used, notably Où ç a ? - Regarde ce petit chien ! - Où ç a ? Look at that little dog? - Whereabouts?

The adjective pé nible, from la peine (lesson note 8) describes something that is difficult, laborious, etc. Le voyage en avion é tait pé nible, The flight was difficult. When used to describe a person, it means tiresome, irritating, etc. Qu'est-ce qu'il est pé nible !, He'sso annoying!

Used intransitively for to go out (lesson section 1.3), sortir is conjugated with ê tre (Elle est sortie, She'sgone out). The transitive form -note the direct object (clé s)- means to put / take out: Il asorti ses clé s de sa poche, He took his keys from his pocket.

The intransitive monter, to go up, has asimilar meaning in the transitive form: to bring / take up: J'ai laissé mes lunettes en bas. Peux-tu les monter s'il te plaî t ? I've left my glasses downstairs. Can you bring them up please? (Remember that monter à cheval means to ride).

The opposite of monter is descendre, to get off / to go/come down (lesson line 10). It follows the same pattern when used with adirect object: Pouvez-vous m'aider à descendre ma valise ? Can you help me bring down my suitcase?

We know the intransitive use of passer: Aquelle heure passe le bus pour le centre-ville ?, What time does the bus for the town centre come by? The transitive form is self-evident: Passe-moi le savon, Hand me the soap. Remember the difference between passer and se passer, to happen (lesson section 1).

The regular verb bavarder means to chat or, depending on the context, to gossip. On abavardé un bon quart d'heure, We chatted for agood half hour. However, both the adjective (bavard(e)) and the noun (un(e) bavard(e)) are slightly more judgmental: Qu'est-ce qu'il est bavard !, What a chatterbox!
The transitive form of entrer is used, as in English, to mean to introduce or insert something: Entrez votre code PIN et validez, Enter your PIN and press OK.

In the intransitive form, retourner (generally with à) means to return, to go back (to): Nous sommes retourné s à notre hô tel aprè s la ré union, We went back to our hotel after the meeting. The transitive verb means to turn over, up, etc. Retournez le poisson au bout de deux minutes et ajoutez les lé gumes, Turn the fish over after two minutes and add the vegetables.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: You will have noticed that we are gradually whittling down the pronunciation section because, by now, you should be familiar with most of the sounds in French, and, in particular, the various verb tenses. From now on, we will indicate only the new words that we introduce and any unusual or irregular pronunciations. You can gauge yourself just how much progress you have made so far. (If in doubt about how aparticular word or group of words is pronounced, listen carefully to the recordings.) Productive phase: 18th lesson

dialogue.french: Salut Papy, salut Mamie. Ça fait longtemps que je ne vous ai pas vus !
dialogue.english: Hi Grandad, hi Granny. I haven't seen you for a long time!

dialogue.french: Vous allez bien tous les deux ? En tout cas, vous avez bonne mine.
dialogue.english: Are you both well? In any case, you look well.

dialogue.french: Bonjour ma petite ! C'est très gentil de nous rendre visite. Ton grand-père et moi sommes tous les deux contents.
dialogue.english: Hello my dear! It's very kind of you to visit us. Your grandfather and I are both happy.

dialogue.french: On te voit si peu ces jours-ci : tu dois être très occupée.
dialogue.english: We see so little of you these days: you must be very busy.

dialogue.french: Oui, je fais un tas de choses et je cours à droite et à gauche, comme toujours, mais dès que j'ai un moment, je viens vous voir, vous le savez bien.
dialogue.english: Yes, I'm doing loads of things and I'm running around left, right and centre, as always, but as soon as I have a moment, I come and see you, as you know very well.

dialogue.french: Mais tu viens toujours seule : tu n'as pas un amoureux ? Un petit-ami ? Ou même une petite-amie ?
dialogue.english: But you always come on your own: don't you have a sweetheart? A boyfriend? Or even a girlfriend?

dialogue.french: Tu sais bien que tu peux nous présenter qui que ce soit : nous sommes des vieux jeunes !
dialogue.english: You know very well that you can introduce us to anyone: we're young old people!

dialogue.french: Mamie, je t'en prie ! Chaque chose en son temps.
dialogue.english: Granny, please! Everything in its own time.

dialogue.french: J'ai une blague à te raconter : « Un muet dit à un sourd qu'un aveugle les espionne, en se cachant derrière les cheveux d'un chauve ». C'est drôle, non ?
dialogue.english: I've got a joke to tell you: 'A dumb person says to a deaf person that a blind person is spying on them, hiding behind the hair of a bald person.' That's funny, isn't it?

dialogue.french: Papy, comment te dire... ? Je ne suis pas morte de rire.
dialogue.english: Grandad, how can I put this? I'm not dying of laughter.

dialogue.french: Tu devrais savoir que notre vocabulaire a changé depuis que toi et Mamie étiez jeunes.
dialogue.english: You should know that our vocabulary has changed since you and Granny were young.

dialogue.french: Par exemple, on ne dit plus un aveugle mais un « non-voyant » ; et « un malentendant » est plus juste que « un sourd », tu comprends ?
dialogue.english: For example, we no longer say 'a blind person' but a 'non-sighted person'; and 'a hearing impaired person' is more accurate than 'a deaf person', you understand?

dialogue.french: Bon, changeons de sujet : comment vas-tu rentrer à Paris ?
dialogue.english: Right, let's change the subject: how are you going to get back to Paris?

dialogue.french: Une amie m'a déposée ici en voiture mais je vais rentrer en train.
dialogue.english: A friend dropped me here by car but I'm going to go back by train.

dialogue.french: Je crois qu'il y en a un vers dix-huit heures. Avez-vous un horaire ?
dialogue.english: I think that there is one around 6pm. Do you have a timetable?

dialogue.french: Oui il circule toutes les heures dès treize heures. Je t'amènerai à la gare.
dialogue.english: Yes, it runs every hour from 1pm onwards. I'll take you to the station.

dialogue.french: Merci, je reviendrai dès que possible, c'est promis. Au fait, peux-tu me prêter vingt euros ?
dialogue.english: Thanks, I'll come back as soon as possible, I promise. By the way, can you lend me twenty euros?

dialogue.french: Je suis temporairement sans ressources. Autrement dit, fauchée.
dialogue.english: I'm temporarily without resources. In other words, broke.

notes.content: un tas: as usual, the final sis silent [ta]. Of course, the plural is pronounced identically. [puhteet-amee / puhteet-amee]. Both the masculine and the feminine forms have the same pronunciation so it is important to listen to the article (un/une).

une petite-fille (masc. un petit-fils) means agranddaughter (resp. grandson). The hyphen is essential because both words are compound nouns; without it, une petite fille (un petit fils) would mean asmall girl (resp. small son). The plural forms are petites-filles and petits-fils. There is almost no difference in pronunciation between the compound noun and the adjective+noun formation, in both the singular and the plural, so context is all-important.

papy (or papi) et mamie are the equivalents of grandad and granny. As in English, the terms are sometimes used pejoratively (old man, old woman) or humorously: le papy boom, the grey boom (retirement of the baby boomers).

Ç a fait... can introduce atime clause (lesson line 1). On its own Ç a fait longtemps means It'sbeen along time. It can also be used in a sentence, usually with the present or the perfect: Ç a fait longtemps que tu apprends le franç ais ? Have you been learning French for long? Ç a fait longtemps qu'elle aquitté son pays, She left her country along time ago. Note how the clause comes at the beginning of the French sentence but the end of the English one.

We know that there is no word for both (lesson note 2). Where English uses the word as an adverb (both you and I, for example), we translate it as tous les deux / toutes les deux, generally after the verb: Michel et moi aimons tous les deux la campagne franç aise, Both Michel and Ilove the French countryside. (Note that French uses the stressed pronoun moi, not the subject pronoun je.)

une mine refers to a person'sface or physical aspect: Elle amauvaise mine. Qu'est-ce qu'elle a ? She doesn'tlook well. What'sthe matter with her? Ne faites pas cette mine triste, Don'tpull that sad face. (Une mine also means a mine, but the context will clear up any ambiguity.)

Adjectives can easily be used as singular nouns in French. Mon petit (fem. ma petite) is usually affectionately to address ayounger person, abit like my dear. Other examples in this lesson of adjectives used as nouns include: Il est amoureux de toi, He'sin love with you → C'est un amoureux de la musique, He's a music-lover. In many cases, English needs to add anoun to convey the same idea: aveugle, blind → un(e) aveugle, ablind man/woman; sourd, deaf → un(e) sourd(e), adeaf man/woman.

un tas means aheap or pile. Il yavait un grand tas de livres dans le coin de la chambre, There was abig pile of books in the corner of the bedroom. In afamiliar register, though, un tas de means loads of or heaps of: J'ai un tas de choses à vous raconter, I've loads of things to tell you. The plural is des tas: J'ai des tas de choses...

Used in atime clause, the preposition dè s -note the grave accent-means (as) from: L'agence ouvrira ses portes dè s midi, The agency will open its door from noon onwards. Dè s always marks the start of the action but is not used in a from-to context (L'agence ouvrira ses portes de midi à dix-huit heures.) Dè s que means as soon as or as early as: Donne-moi des nouvelles dè s que possible, Send me news as soon as possible.

soit is the third person singular subjunctive of ê tre (the equivalent of est in the present tense). The phrase... que ce soit, preceded by apronoun like qui, quoi or où, has the indefinite sense of any+pronoun: La rè gle est la mê me, où que ce soit en France, The rule is the same, anywhere in France. We'll learn more about the subjunctive later on.

The verb faucher literally means to mow, reap or cut down. However, the adjectival participle fauché(e) is used idiomatically to mean broke or hard up. The link between the literal and metaphorical meanings is evident in the expression ê tre fauché comme les blé s, i.e. to be stony-broke.
