extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Imported from the US and the UK, terminology designed to avoid offence to particular groups of people has entered French. This mode of expression applies in particular to certain forms of physical and mental disadvantage (for example non-voyant, non-seeing, rather than aveugle, blind). Culturally sensitive language is increasingly common, particularly in the media, and is worth paying close attention to. In Canada, in particular, amajor effort has been made to find appropriate terminology in French. Productive phase: 19th lesson

dialogue.french: Oh là là, pourquoi est-ce que tu fais cette tête ? Qu'est qu'il t'arrive, ma pauvre amie ?
dialogue.english: Oh dear, why are you pulling that long face? What's happened to you, my poor friend?

dialogue.french: Je devais partir hier aux sports d'hiver avec une bande de copains.
dialogue.english: I was supposed to leave for winter sports yesterday with a bunch of friends.

dialogue.french: On allait faire la fête – et peut-être un peu de sport – dans un super chalet au pied des pistes.
dialogue.english: We were going to party – and maybe do a bit of sport – in a great chalet at the foot of the slopes.

dialogue.french: J'avais fait les valises, préparé mes affaires de ski et commandé un taxi pour cinq heures – il n'est pas question de faire la grasse matinée quand on est en vacances à la neige !
dialogue.english: I had packed my bags, prepared my ski gear and ordered a taxi for 5 a.m. – out of the question to lie in when on a winter holiday!

dialogue.french: Je quittais la maison quand j'ai reçu un message du bureau disant que ma présence était demandée.
dialogue.english: I was leaving the house when I received a message from the office saying that my presence was requested.

dialogue.french: J'avais fait le point avec mes collègues la veille, mais ils m'ont quand même fait venir aux aurores.
dialogue.english: I had updated my colleagues the day before, but they still made me come in at the crack of dawn.

dialogue.french: Du coup, j'ai dû faire une croix sur les vacances. Voilà pourquoi je fais la tête.
dialogue.english: As a result, I had to forgo the holidays. That's why I'm pulling a long face.

dialogue.french: Mais à vrai dire, ça me soulage un petit peu aussi car je devais partir avec Gaspard et Noé.
dialogue.english: But to tell the truth, I'm a little bit relieved, too, because I was supposed to leave with Gaspard and Noé.

dialogue.french: Partir avec ces deux-là, ensemble ? Il faut le faire !
dialogue.english: Leaving with those two, together? That's quite something!

dialogue.french: Gaspard s'est fait connaître pour son esprit de compétition bien développé.
dialogue.english: Gaspard made himself known for his well-developed competitive spirit.

dialogue.french: Pour ne pas dire esprit agressif ! Quand il est en compétition, celui-là, il ne fait pas de cadeau !
dialogue.english: Not to say aggressive spirit! When he's in competition, he gives people a tough time!

dialogue.french: D'ailleurs, il s'est fait un certain nombre d'ennemis à cause de ça.
dialogue.english: Moreover, he's made a number of enemies because of that.

dialogue.french: Mais il sait aussi se faire respecter. Gaspard est ami avec toutes les stars du sport, à qui il fait la bise.
dialogue.english: But he also knows how to make people respect him. Gaspard is friends with all the sports stars, with whom he's on kissing terms.

dialogue.french: Comment se fait-il qu'il soit devenu un si bon skieur ? Il a dû se faire aider par quelqu'un, non ?
dialogue.english: How is it that he's become such a good skier? He must have had help from someone, mustn't he?

dialogue.french: Non, il s'est fait tout seul, sans entraîneur, sans équipe et sans sponsor.
dialogue.english: No, he's self-made, without a coach, without a team and without a sponsor.

dialogue.french: Et Noé ? Il me fait de la peine, celui-là : c'est un désastre ambulant.
dialogue.english: What about Noé? I feel sorry for him: he's a walking disaster.

dialogue.french: On lui a souvent dit de faire gaffe mais il n'en fait qu'à sa tête.
dialogue.english: We've often told him to be careful but he does just as he pleases.

dialogue.french: L'année dernière, il n'a fait que quelques mètres avant de tomber et se fracturer les deux bras.
dialogue.english: Last year, he only went a few meters before he fell and broke both his arms.

dialogue.french: Il a dû se faire secourir par hélicoptère.
dialogue.english: He had to be rescued by helicopter.

dialogue.french: Cela dit, il a visiblement fait des progrès car l'année d'avant, il s'était cassé la cheville en descendant du train à la station de ski.
dialogue.english: Having said that, he has obviously made progress because the year before, he had broken his ankle getting off the train at the ski resort.

notes.content: Asymbol of strength or size, un cheval, ahorse (plur. des chevaux, lesson 22) turns up in many idioms and similes, like une fiè vre de cheval, araging fever, and its antidote un remè de de cheval, adrastic remedy or cure.

un lapin means a rabbit, and poser, to put or place (lesson line 12). The idiomatic expression poser un lapin (à quelqu'un) means to stand someone up or, simply, not to show up: La chanteuse Nala aposé un lapin à ses fans, The singer Nala didn'tturn up to meet her fans.

un fouet means a whip, whence the verb fouetter (note the double t). Avoir d'autres chats à fouetter ("to have other cats to whip") is one of several idioms using different animals to convey the same idea as an English equivalent: to have other fish to fry.

un cafard is the universally unpopular insect a cockroach. And since aroach infestation can cause depression, avoir le cafard means to be feeling low or down in the dumps. Another common expression is avoir un coup de cafard, to have afit of the blues.

The idiomatic adjective moche is useful for describing ugliness (Il est moche comme un pou ("ugly as a louse"), He'sas ugly as sin), or unpleasantness in general: Le match contre Lyon é tait assez moche, The game against Lyon was pretty awful. The word is often used to describe bad weather.

In French as in English, dogs feature in many idioms, generally expressing drudgery, hardship etc. Une vie de chien, a dog's life. Likewise, J'ai eu un mal de chien à le convaincre, Ihad atough time convincing him.
une pie, a magpie, features in the metaphor ê tre bavard comme une pie, which can be translated simply as to be a chatterbox.

Some French idioms are confusing because they resemble English expressions but mean something different. Here, reprendre du poil de la bê te shares the same origin as to take ahair of the dog but has nothing to do with hangovers. It means to regain strength, to pick up, etc. Le marché arepris du poil de la bê te depuis le dé but du mois, The market has rallied since the start of the month. Note that un poil / des poils refers to body and animal hair, whereas un cheveu / des cheveux is used for human head hair.

The link (or lack of one) between the two animals in this expression -un coq, acock (rooster), and un â ne, a donkey-is lost in the mists of time, but the expression passer (or sauter) du coq à l'â ne means to go or jump from one subject to another, unrelated one.

The adjective malin (fem maligne) comes from le mal, evil, seen in lesson note 8 (whence the English cognate malignant). In everyday French, though, it means clever, smart: Ce n'est pas trè s malin, ce que tu viens de faire, What you've just done isn'tvery clever. Because of the word's"devilish"origins, the emphasis is on shrewdness rather than just intelligence. Un singe, a monkey.

vachement, from une vache, a cow, is an idiomatic intensifier commonly used both with adjectives, Elle est vachement intelligente, She'sreally smart, and with verbs, Il pleut vachement, It'sraining really hard. The word should be used with caution because it is quite familiar.

une liè vre means a hare. The verb courir, to run or to race, has entered English as to course, i.e. to hunt, as in hare coursing."Hunting several hares at a time" -courir plusieurs liè vres à la fois-means to concentrate on more than one thing, or to have several irons in the fire. (One can also have trop de liè vres, too many irons.)

donner sa langue au chat ("to give one'stongue to the cat") means to give up or stop guessing: Si tu donnes ta langue au chat, je te donnerai la ré ponse, If you give up, I'll tell you the answer. The same idea of being unable to speak is found in the English idiom Has the cat got your tongue? but the scope is broader than in French.

notes.content: Le conditionnel: the conditional: So far, we have seen three types of conditional sentence formed with asi (if) clause and amain clause: • The"zero conditional"simply expresses ageneral truth, using the same verb tenses as in English: S'il fait froid, les plages sont vides, If it is cold, the beaches are empty. In most case the first part of the proposition can be introduced by quand (when) rather than si (if). • The first conditional describes a cause-effect proposition (i.e. if the condition is fulfilled, then the result is certain). In this case, the verb in the si clause is in the present tense and the second verb is in the future, as in English: Si vous achetez ce sac en ligne, vous le payerez plus cher. If you buy that bag online, you will pay more for it. • The second conditional is a hypothetical, describing what would happen if acondition were satisfied. In an"if → then"construction, the verb governed by si is in the imperfect tense (see lesson 63) and the verb in the main clause is in the conditional. To form the conditional tense, the imperfect endings (-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient) are added to the infinitive of the verb. For Group verbs ending in -re, the final letter is omitted before adding the endings: gagner: je gagnerais, tu gagnerais, il/elle gagnerait, nous gagnerions, vous gagneriez, ils/elles gagneraient. finir: je finirais, tu finirais, il/elle finirait, nous finirions, vous finiriez, ils/elles finiraient. boire: je boirais, tu boirais, il/elle boirait, nous boirions, vous boiriez, ils/elles boiraient. This rule applies to all verbs. However, four of the most important irregular verbs change their stems: avoir: j'aurais, tu aurais, il/elle aurait, nous aurions, vous auriez, ils/elles auraient. ê tre: je serais, tu serais, il/elle serait, nous serions, vous seriez, ils/elles seraient. aller: j'irais, tu irais, il/elle irait, nous irions, vous iriez, ils/elles iraient. vouloir: je voudrais, tu voudrais, il/elle voudrait, nous voudrions, vous voudriez, ils/elles voudraient. These are not the only exceptions forms -major verbs such as devoir, pouvoir, venir and voir are all irregular-so please check the appendix. As regards spelling, ahandful of Group verbs change very slightly. This applies to verbs ending in -eler and -eter, which double the final consonant: j'appellerais, vous appelleriez; je jetterais, vous jetteriez, etc. As we saw with the future (lesson section 2), verbs such as acheter and lever take agrave accent (j'achè terais, tu lè verais). Finally, the conditional of -ayer verbs, like essayer, can be spelled in two ways: j'essayerais or j'essaierais. Both forms are correct and are pronounced identically. The most important thing to remember with a second-conditional construction is that the verb following si is in the imperfect, not the conditional. This is easy to see in asentence with ê tre: Si j'é tais vous, je serais content de partir. If Iwere you Iwould be happy to leave. As in English, the conditional is used in many expressions of politeness (Je voudrais un café s'il vous plait). However, for the"tag"response to an invitation (Would you like to come? - Yes I'dlike to.), we do not use the conditional in French because it would suggest a reserve: (Iwould like to but I can't). The usual answer to such an invitation, Voudriez-vous venir ? is usually Avec plaisir. Similarly, where English uses would to express ahabitual action in the past (When we were young we would go on holiday together), would go is not areal conditional; in French we use the imperfect for both actions: Quand nous é tions jeunes, nous allions en vacances ensemble. There is afourth construction, the past conditional, which we will not see in this course.

Verbs that can be conjugated with ê tre and avoir: As we saw in lesson 67, the passé composé of some common verbs can be formed with ê tre or avoir, depending on the meaning. The basic difference is between transitive and non-transitive usage. To remember the difference, meet acolleague of Dr Vandertramp's: DR PRE MS: Descendre, Rentrer, Passer, Retourner, Entrer, Monter, Sortir. Il est descendu du bus. (He got off the bus). Il adescendu l'escalier. (He went down the stairs). Nous sommes rentré s tard. (We came back late). Nous avons rentré la poubelle. (We've brought in the bin). Elle est passé e tout à l'heure. (She came by earlier). Elle m'apassé le sel. (She passed me the salt). Je suis retourné en Bretagne. (Iwent back to Brittany). J'ai retourné la crê pe. (Iturned over the pancake). Ils sont entré s sans payer. (They went in without paying). Ils ont entré toutes les donné es. (They entered all the data). Elles sont monté es au premier é tage. (They went up to the first floor). Elles ont monté les courses. (They brought up the shopping). Je suis sorti trop tard. (Iwent out too late). J'ai sorti la voiture du parking. (Ibrought the car out of the carpark). In each pair, the two meanings are related but different. In terms of construction, the intransitive form is followed immediately by apreposition or an adverb while the transitive form takes adirect object. Like entrer and rentrer, some of these dual-auxiliary verbs can take a prefix: descendre / redescendre (to come down again), monter / remonter (to go back up), and passer / repasser (to come by again -although repasser can also mean to iron!). All these prefixed verbs follow the same rules.

All about tout: Tout, meaning all or every (and in some cases very), can be confusing because it has several functions and can be used as an adjective, adverb, pronoun or noun. • As an adjective, tout always precedes and agrees in gender and number with the nouns it qualifies. The four forms are tout (masculine singular), toute (feminine singular), tous (masculine plural) and toutes (feminine plural). Here's asimple sentence to help you remember: Tout le temps et toute la journé e, tous mes frè res et toutes mes sœurs sont à la maison. (Where tout refers to two nouns of different genders (here, frè res, sœurs), it must be repeated in the appropriate form.) In addition to nouns, tout can qualify adjectives, both possessive: Toute ma famille vit à Marseille, All my family lives in Marseille; and demonstrative: Tous ces gens sont ici pour nous aider, All these people are here to help us. Regarding pronunciation, the adjectives tout and tous are identical ([tao]) as are toute and toutes ([foot]). • As an adverb, tout is usually invariable: Allez tout droit et tourner au feu rouge. Go straight on and turn at the traffic light. If used with another adverb, tout means very or quite: Je commence tout doucement à m'ennuyer. I'mvery slowly getting bored. Three other common expressions in which tout is an adverb are tout à fait, absolutely (lesson 23), tout droit, straight on (lesson 25), and tout à l'heure, later (lesson 30). • As a pronoun, there are only three forms: tout, tous and toutes. The singular pronoun means everything, anything, all, etc. Tout est possible ! Everything/Anything is possible! Les enfants sont tous dans la chambre, The children are all in the bedroom. Les commandes sont toutes arrivé es en retard. All the orders arrived late. In terms of pronunciation, tout and toutes are pronounced in the same way as the adjectival forms but the final sof tous is voiced: [tooss]: Tous [too] les hommes sont pareils. / Les hommes sont tous [tooss} pareils. All men are the same / Men are all the same. When tout is followed by arelative clause starting with que, we have to add ce, whereas English usually omits the relative that/which: Tout ce que vous voulez, Everything you want. • Other expressions seen so far include: tout le monde, everybody (lesson 20), tout de suite, right away (26), tout le temps, all the time (34), tout à l'heure, earlier/later (30), en tout cas, in any case (54), also written en tous cas, and rien du tout, nothing at all (66). C'est tout pour le moment, That'sall for now!

N'importe: We know (lesson note 8) that importer means to be important / of import / to matter. In the affirmative, the verb is quite formal and often used with the subjunctive. But in the negative, it is included in many common indefinite expressions. The simplest are N'importe and Peu importe. Generally used in response to a question, they mean No matter, I don't mind, etc. Que voulez-vous boire ? - N'importe. What do you want to drink? - Anything. (i.e."It matters not.") Anumber of indefinites are formed simply by adding apronoun or adverb after n'importe -the equivalent of anyone, anywhere etc. J'irais n'importe où avec lui, I'dgo anywhere with him. N'importe qui peut y aller, Anyone can go there. Tu peux venir à n'importe qu'elle heure ou n'importe quel jour. You can come at any time or on any day. En fait, tu peux venir n'importe quand, In fact, you can come anytime. Il faut cliquer sur une page, n'importe laquelle. You have to click on a page, any one. With quoi, there are several possibilities. The literal meaning is anything at all: Il ferait n'importe quoi pour attirer mon attention. He would do anything to attract my attention. En ligne, on trouve tout et n'importe quoi. You can find anything and everything online. But n'importe quoi can also refer to something that is absurd or nonsensical. Tu dis n'importe quoi, You're talking rubbish. In this sense, it is often used as an exclamation to criticise or dismiss aprevious statement: Les Franç ais sont les meilleurs ! - N'importe quoi ! The French are the best! - Rubbish. Alonger form, but with the identical meaning, is C'est du n'importe quoi.

Idioms (2): animals: As we saw in the last revision lesson, it is agood idea to learn idiomatic expressions in thematic groups. This second instalment looks at animal-based idioms, which feature in most languages. ê tre doux comme un agneau (be as gentle as a lamb), reprendre du poil de la bê te (pick up, to recover), avoir le cafard (be down in the dumps), donner sa langue au chat (give up), avoir d'autres chats à fouetter (have other fish to fry), avoir une fiè vre de cheval (have araging fever), ê tre malade comme un chien (be as sick as a dog), faire un temps de chien (be / have lousy weather), passer / sauter du coq à l'â ne (jump from one thing to another), poser un lapin (stand someone up), courir plusieurs liè vres à la fois (have several irons in the fire), dormir comme un loir (sleep like a log), avoir une faim de loup (be famished), avoir un appé tit d'oiseau (eat like a bird), ê tre bavard comme une pie (be a chatterbox), ê tre heureux comme un poisson dans l'eau (be as happy as alark / clam), s'ennuyer comme un rat mort (be bored to tears), ê tre malin comme un singe (be as smart as a whip). One word seen in lesson is the adjective vachement, which apparently comes from une vache, a cow. The word was originally an adverb meaning nastily or unpleasantly (the adjective vache still has that meaning: une remarque vache, anasty comment) but is now used as an intensifier. Although very common, vachement is nevertheless familiar and, depending on the register of language, can be the equivalent of bloody or damned. Thus, as with slang and idioms in general, it should not be used by anyone who does not already have agood grasp of standard French.

dialogue.french: « Le quatorze juillet mil sept cent quatre-vingt-neuf marqua un tournant majeur dans l'histoire de France.
dialogue.english: '14 July 1789 marked a major turning point in the history of France.

dialogue.french: En effet, la prise de la Bastille annonça la fin de la monarchie et les débuts de la République.
dialogue.english: The storming of the Bastille heralded the end of the monarchy and the beginnings of the Republic.

dialogue.french: Mais qu'en fut-il vraiment ? Que se passa-t-il exactement en ce « jour de gloire » ?
dialogue.english: But what was it really like? What exactly happened on that 'day of glory'?

dialogue.french: Combien de misérables prisonniers furent libérés de ce lieu morne par ces révolutionnaires de fortune ?
dialogue.english: How many miserable prisoners were freed from that gloomy place by those makeshift revolutionaries?

dialogue.french: Le récit est palpitant, même si le bilan de la libération n'est pas à la hauteur du mythe.
dialogue.english: The story is thrilling, even if the result of the liberation does not live up to the myth.

dialogue.french: En juillet de cette année fatidique, Louis Seize subissait les pressions de la toute nouvelle Assemblée nationale.
dialogue.english: In July of that fateful year, Louis XVI was under pressure from the brand-new National Assembly.

dialogue.french: Le roi fit semblant d'accepter leurs exigences, mais en réalité, il fit venir les troupes à Paris et les concentra tout autour de la capitale.
dialogue.english: The king pretended to accept their demands, but in reality he brought troops up to Paris and concentrated them all around the capital.

dialogue.french: Les Parisiens s'inquiétèrent de la situation, et l'agitation grandit de minute en minute, d'heure en heure.
dialogue.english: The Parisians were worried about the situation, and the agitation grew from minute to minute, from hour to hour.

dialogue.french: Le douze juillet une émeute éclata dans la ville et de violents combats firent rage.
dialogue.english: On 12 July a riot broke out in the city and violent fighting raged.

dialogue.french: Peu à peu, les citoyens descendirent dans la rue, assoiffés de liberté et de justice.
dialogue.english: Gradually the citizens took to the streets, thirsty for freedom and justice.

dialogue.french: La foule grossit, les voix s'élevèrent de plus en plus fort, les citoyens prirent les armes.
dialogue.english: The crowd grew larger and larger, the voices grew louder and louder, and the citizens took up arms.

dialogue.french: Les armes, soit, mais il manquait des munitions ! Où en trouver ? Dans une forteresse, forcément !
dialogue.english: Arms, all very well, but there was no ammunition! Where could it be found? In a fortress, of course!

dialogue.french: Alors s'éleva le cri « À la Bastille, citoyens ! La liberté ou la mort ! » et, comme un seul homme, la foule se dirigea vers l'effroyable prison, déterminée à en faire tomber ses murs sinistres.
dialogue.english: Then the cry went up, 'To the Bastille, citizens! Freedom or death!' and, as one man, the crowd went to the dreadful prison, determined to bring down its grim walls.

dialogue.french: En débouchant de la rue Saint-Antoine, les révoltés marquèrent un temps d'arrêt, tant l'édifice était menaçant, mais la colère et la passion l'emportèrent et toute la fureur du peuple se concentra sur ce symbole de leur oppression.
dialogue.english: When the rebels emerged from Rue Saint-Antoine, they paused for a moment, for the building was so threatening, but anger and passion took over and all the wrath of the people focused on this symbol of their oppression.

dialogue.french: Cependant, la Bastille ne fut pas prise, elle se rendit ; et les révolutionnaires – car il s'agit bien d'une révolution, pas d'une révolte – ne tuèrent qu'un seul homme.
dialogue.english: However, the Bastille was not taken, it surrendered; and the revolutionaries – for it was a revolution, not a revolt – killed only one man.

dialogue.french: Ainsi, notre Fête nationale ne commémore ni la violence ni la haine, mais la France libérée des traîtres et des menteurs de l'Ancien régime.
dialogue.english: Thus, our National Day commemorates neither violence nor hatred but France liberated from the traitors and liars of the Ancien Régime.

dialogue.french: Au fait, au moment de la prise, le donjon funeste ne contenait qu'une petite poignée de prisonniers ! »
dialogue.english: By the way, at the time of the capture, the fateful dungeon contained only a handful of prisoners!'

notes.content: The pin baptisé is not pronounced in any of the verb'sdifferent forms: here, [bateezay]. The masculine adjective fier and the feminine fiè re are both pronounced [fyair].

French often uses the present tense to describe past actions (le pré sent historique, lesson 42). Here, ê tre is the auxiliary of the passive voice, along with the past participle, as in English: Eiffel construit son monument en deux ans → Le monument est construit en deux ans par Eiffel. Eiffel built the monument in two years → The monument was built in two years by Eiffel. Since the past participle behaves as an adjective, it has to agree with the subject: Eiffel construit sa tour... → Sa tour est construite...

à peu prè s ("at little near") is auseful adverbial phrase meaning approximately. Il est à peu prè s huit/vingt heures, It'saround o'clock. Although asynonym of environ (lesson note 2), it can also be used to qualify adverbs, replacing presque: Cet acteur est connu à peu prè s partout, That actor is known almost everywhere.

The idiom bon an, mal an ("good year, bad year") means year in, year out, in other words, the average of good and bad years taken together. Bon an, mal an, la tour attire des millions de touristes, Year in, year out, the tower attracts millions of tourists. Always use an, never anné e, in this expression.

The impersonal pronoun on often does the same job as the passive voice. Thus Il est appelé l'Homme de fer and On l'appelle l'Homme de fer both mean He'scalled the Iron Man. Look again at the first sentence: Le guide qu'on m'a recommandé, The guide that was recommended to me. In neither case would on be the equivalent of the impersonal one in this type of passive-equivalent construction.

The adjective vif (fem. vive) means lively or keen. The adverb vivement means keenly, vividly, sharply, etc. En ville, il est vivement recommandé d'utiliser les transports en commun, In town, it is strongly/highly recommended to use public transport.

Proverbs in French often use old or literary constructions. Rira bien qui rira le dernier is the equivalent of He who laughs last laughs longest. Note how the two clauses are inverted in the French proverb.

As you already know, les affaires can mean business in the sense of an economic activity (lesson 47) or personal affairs (lesson 61). In the singular, une affaire generally means a matter, acase or an affair. The expression une bonne affaire means agood deal, a bargain. It is often used with faire: Nous avons fait une bonne affaire en vendant notre maison, We got agood deal when we sold our house.

The adjective fier (fem. fiè re) means proud. Elle est fiè re de ses origines basques, She'sproud of her Basque heritage. The word can also be used with the subjunctive mood, as we will see later on. One very common, invariable expression, similar to its English counterpart, is Il n'y apas de quoi ê tre fier, That'snothing to be proud of. The noun is la fierté, pride. (Do not confuse fier with the verb se fier, pronounced [feeyay], to trust, lesson note 3.)

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: One of France's - and the world's - biggest tourist attractions, the Eiffel Tower was inspired by the work of two American engineers who wanted to design and build a 300-metre-tall tower. Completed to coincide with the hundredth anniversary of the 1789 French Revolution, the monument was to have been dismantled after adecade but Gustave Eiffel made every effort to ensure that his work would endure, despite opposition from writers, architects and intellectuals, who likened it to afactory chimney. The anecdotes about the tower being sold off for scrap metal by aconfidence trickster and being wedded to an eccentric American are both true. And although acertain British politician once tried to make the Iron Lady sobriquet her own, there is really only one Dame de fer! Productive phase: 22nd lesson

dialogue.french: Éric Camus nous quitte à la fin du mois et nous allons organiser un pot de départ avec tous ses amis pour lui souhaiter bonne chance dans les années à venir.
dialogue.english: Éric Camus is leaving us at the end of the month and we're going to organise a farewell drinks party with all his friends to wish him good luck in the years to come.

dialogue.french: Depuis combien de temps est-ce qu'il gère le service ? On me dit qu'il est là depuis des lustres.

dialogue.french: Auparavant, il était salarié dans une compagnie d'assurances en province, mais on lui a fait comprendre qu'il n'aurait pas d'avancement parce qu'il était trop jeune.
dialogue.english: Beforehand, he was an employee in an insurance company in the provinces, but he was made to understand that he wouldn't get a promotion because he was too young.

dialogue.french: C'est un de ses amis qui a mentionné notre entreprise : Éric a postulé et on l'a embauché aussitôt.

notes.content: province: Note the open vowel [ahn] in the second syllable: [provahnss]. Don'tconfuse this word with Provence, the beautiful region of southeastern France, pronounced [provœh"ss].

un pot means apot - un pot de fleurs, apot of flowers - or a jar, un pot de confiture ajar of jam. (Remember the important difference between à and de in this case, lesson note 9). In afamiliar register, un pot means adrink (usually alcoholic): Tu viens boire un pot avec nous ? Coming for adrink with us? In awork context, it means adrinks party, or, specifically, un pot de dé part or d'adieu, an office farewell/leaving party.

un lustre means shine (or lustre). However, the familiar expression depuis des lustres (from the Latin word for a five-year period, and always plural) simply means for along time / for ages. Il est ici depuis des lustres, He'sbeen here for ages.

One way of avoiding the passive voice in asentence is to put the emphasis on the subject (the person performing the action). For this, we use c'est (sing.) or ce sont (plur.) at the beginning of the clause followed by qui/que. So instead of Votre entreprise aé té mentionné e par un ami we say C'est un ami qui amentionné votre entreprise. In English, c'est / ce sont... qui does not need translating: Afriend mentioned your firm.

The adverb aussitô t, formed from aussi, as, and tô t, early, is an elegant way of saying straight away, immediately. La neige est tombé e cette nuit mais adisparu aussitô t, The snow fell last night but disappeared immediately. It can often be replaced by immé diatement. One common and easy-to-remember expression is Aussitô t dit, aussitô t fait, No sooner said than done.

The passive agent is generally introduced with par: La dé cision aé té prise par le directeur, The decision was taken by the manager (See lesson note 1). But if the verb expresses afeeling or emotion, par may be replaced by de: Il est aimé par or de ses collè gues, He is liked by his colleagues. There is no difference in meaning.

Be careful not to confuse the masculine noun l'humour, humour (see lesson for pronunciation) with the feminine l'humeur, mood. Elle est de bonne humeur ce matin, She'sin agood mood this morning. The word can also refer to a person's temperament: Il est d'humeur changeante depuis qu'il aarrê té de fumer, He'sbeen moody since he stopped smoking. Another"animal"expression (lesson 69) is ê tre d'une humeur de chien: Le chef est d'une humeur de chien depuis deux jours, The boss has been in afoul mood for two days.

We know that grand means not only big but also great, eminent (lesson note 2). Thus faire / accomplir de grandes choses means to do / accomplish great things. Don'tconfuse this adjective-plus-noun construction with the idiom ne pas faire grand-chose (always singular), seen in lesson 61.

un appel, from the verb appeler, to call, means acall (phone, appeal, etc., lesson 38, 16). Thus to make aphone call is passer un appel (té lé phonique). The expression faire appel à thus means to call upon or appeal to. The direct object of the verb can be aperson - Nous avons fait appel à un expert pour nous aider, We called on an expert for help - but also an abstract noun: Je fais appel à vos connaissances en informatique, I'mcalling on your computer skills.

Another way to avoid the passive is with the pronominal verb form in the third person singular: Tout se fait en franç ais dans notre entreprise, Everything is done in French in our company. This workaround is generally used in situations where the agent is unknown or unimportant: Le billet s'achè te en ligne, The ticket is bought online. It can also be used if the agent is"understood,"notably when addressing them directly, in which case the previous sentence means You buy the ticket online. The expression Ç a ne se fait pas, meaning That'snot the done thing, can be used in avariety of contexts (it's a no-no, You can'tdo that, etc.)

notes.content: In informal French, the adverb ne is often omitted from anegative construction when speaking quickly. Thus, j'en peux plus, pronounced [zhoeh"puh plew], is the informal way of saying je n'en peux plus [zhuh noeh"puh plew]. Similarly, c'est pas possible (line 10) replaces ce n'est pas possible. You will find these grammatically incorrect forms written out in song lyrics, blog entries, social media postings and the like. Needless to say, do not imitate them, but do be prepared for amissing ne.

We saw le dos, the back, in lesson note 8. The idiomatic expression en avoir plein le dos basically means to be fed up, to be sick and tired. It can be used as an exclamation, as here, or with adirect object, in which case it takes de: J'en ai plein le dos de leurs excuses, I'msick and tired of their excuses. Likewise, Je n'en peux plus expresses inability to deal with unpleasantness, using the same image as English expressions like I can'ttake any more, I've had it up to here.

une grè ve means a strike, awork stoppage. It is generally used either with faire (sometimes without an article) or ê tre en (never with the article): Les ouvriers font [la] grè ve / L'usine est en grè ve, The workers are striking / The plant is on strike.

un bouchon means a cork. While English uses abottleneck to describe traffic congestion, French prefers the image of abottle stopper. Un bouchon is more or less synonymous with une embouteillage (lesson line 13), which literally means bottling and is generally used to describe urban congestion. However, only bouchon can be used in a verb: Ç a commence à bouchonner sur la route des vacances, Traffic jams are starting to form on holiday roads.

une galè re is literally agalley (an oar-propelled vessel). The sheer effort and exertion made by the ship'soarsmen provides the context for aword that describes anything from hardship and difficulty to ahellish journey. For now, simply learn the exclamation Quelle galè re !, What a pain/mess/nightmare!

The idiom casser les pieds ("break the feet") is an idiomatic way of saying that someone is importuning you, i.e. to bore, annoy, irritate, pester, etc. Il me casse les pieds avec toutes ces questions ! He'spestering me with all those questions! There is also aderived adjective - C'est casse-pieds de changer son mot de passe chaque mois, It's adrag to change your password every month - and noun: Mon nouveau voisin est un vrai casse-pieds, My new neighbour is areal pain.

The familiar adjective dingue, derived from an old slang word for malaria, basically means crazy, barmy, incredible, etc. Ce truc me rend dingue ! This thing is driving me nuts! In this sense, it is asynonym for fou (lesson 58). Derived meanings include unbelievable, extraordinary, etc. Les prix dans ce restaurant sont dingues ! That restaurant charges unbelievable prices! The nominal form is un(e) dingue: C'est un dingue de moto, He's amotorcycle nut.
en avoir marre, as we saw in lesson note 7, means to be fed up with. Il yen amarre ! is an impersonal exclamation that translates roughly as That's enough!

The adverbs dessus, on top of, and dessous, underneath, are combined in the expressions sens dessus dessous, upside down, the word order being the same as in English (or, in some cases, topsy-turvy): Tu as mis ma vie sens dessus dessous, You have turned my life upside down. Note the order of the two adverbs: the one with the extra letter (o) comes second.

plaindre means to pity, feel sorry for: Si vous n'avez pas encore la ré ponse, je vous plains, If you still don'thave the answer Ifeel sorry for you. The pronominal form se plaindre, with its past participle plaint, is the origin of to complain and acomplaint (une plainte). Il se plaint de maux de tê te, He'scomplaining of headaches. It can also mean to grumble, moan, etc. Arrê te de te plaindre tout le temps, Stop moaning all the time. The expression On ne peut pas se (or Je ne peux pas me) plaindre is the equivalent of the stoic response Mustn't grumble.

le moral means morale, i.e. enthusiasm, confidence: Qu'est qu'il y a ? Tu n'as pas le moral ? What'sthe matter? Are you feeling down? Be careful not to confuse it with la morale, morals, moral standards.

s'en faire, to worry / to be concerned about, is asynonym of s'inquié ter (lesson line 9). It is mainly used in the expression Ne vous en faites pas (fam. Ne t'en fais pas): Don't worry. Adirect object, introduced by pour, can be added: Ne t'en fais pas pour lui, il va bien, Don'tworry about him, he's fine.

extras.content: We often stress the importance of etymology and association in building up asubstantial vocabulary. Take une grève, a strike. Until the 18th century, one of the main public gathering places in Paris was apatch of sandy ground on the right shore, or strand (grève), of the River Seine, where jobless labourers would gather in search of a day'swork unloading barges at the nearby docks. The place became known as Place de Grève (just as London's Thames riverbank was named The Strand), and the name eventually became synonymous with idleness and, ironically, with deliberate work stoppages. More ominously, the square was also the venue for public executions. (It was renamed Place de l'Hôtel de Ville, i.e. City Hall Square, at the beginning of the 19th century.) Productive phase: 24th lesson

notes.content: The verb haï r, to hate, is awkward. The diaresis, showing that both aand imust be pronounced, is present in the infinitive [eye-ear] and the three present-plural forms (haï ssons, [eye-eessoh"], haï ssez [eye-eessay], haï ssent [eye-eess]) but not the singular: hais and hait, both of which are pronounced [ay].

The masculine noun les soldes, usually plural in this context, means sales (reduced-price goods). The singular, un solde, means a balance, i.e. aremaining amount. Thus le solde des marchandises means remaining goods. The verb solder means to wind up or pay off a balance, while the participle adjective soldé generally means reduced in price: Cette veste est soldé e à moins quinze pour cent, This vest is reduced by 15% in the sales.

The expression tomber bien ("to fall well") is used in two ways. Applied to clothing (coat, skirt, etc.), it means to hang well (line 16). By extension, the idiomatic meaning is to come at the right moment. Ce chè que tombe bien : j'ai besoin d'argent: This cheque has arrived at just the right moment. Ineed cash. Auseful exclamation is Ç a tombe bien ! meaning That's convenient! or Great timing! The opposite, of course, is Ç a tombe mal.

un plan means amap (lesson line 3) or aplan (lesson note 5). But the idiomatic expression un bon plan has asimilar meaning to une bonne affaire (lesson note 7). Depending on the context, it can mean agood deal or bargain or, in tourism, atop tip or recommendation, etc. On est dé jà vendredi ! Voici nos bons plans pour le week-end, It'salready Friday. Here are our top tips for the weekend.

la / une pagaille means mess, shambles, chaos. À cause de la grè ve, c'est la pagaille dans les transports en commun, Public transport is amess because of the strike. Preceded by the preposition en, the meaning is huge amounts or loads of: Elle ades idé es en pagaille, She has loads of ideas. (An alternative spelling is une pagaï e, but this should be avoided because it is too similar to une pagaie [pagay], apaddle or short oar.)

quant à means with regard to, as for: Quant à lui, il n'est mê me pas venu, As for him, he never came. This adverb is often used to stress a contrast, in which case it does not need to be translated: J'aime les sports mais mon mari, quant à lui, les hait, Ilove sports but my husband hates them. Do not confuse quant with quand, when (tip: it'salways followed by à).

Merci, Thank you, is also apolite way to express refusal. Vous voulez un thé ? - Merci. Do you want some tea? - No thanks. This can be confusing for English-speakers, who often use merci thinking that it is apositive response (yes thank you). If in doubt, you can always insist: Non merci.

Here is acommon example of how the masculine gender dominates the feminine. If two nouns with different genders are used together, any subsequent pronoun - especially lequel/laquelle, etc. - is in the masculine form: Je peux vous montrer un passeport ou une carte d'identité. Lequel voulez-vous ? Ican show you apassport or an identity card. Which one do you want?

French has no direct equivalent of to suit. Convenir can be used to express the notion of being acceptable or convenient (lesson note 2). But, if the meaning is to enhance or look good on, we use aparaphrase such as aller bien: Cet impermé able bleu vous va trè s bien, That blue raincoat really suits you. The usual preposition is à, so the pronoun is indirect: La parka lui va bien, The parka suits him/her.

se trouver, to be located (lesson note 8) can also be used in the third person to express acoincidence or occurrence, like to happen or turn out (that). Il se trouve que j'ai le mê me pré nom que leur mè re, It turns out that Ihave the same first name as their mother. As a rule, if the usual translation of aword doesn'thelp you to understand the sentence (like tomber bien in note 2), always look at the broader context. And, of course, check in agood dictionary!

le bricolage, from the root verb bricoler, is an institution in France. It is the nearest equivalent to the English concept of home repairs and do-it-yourself (DIY). Le dimanche, j'adore bricoler / faire du bricolage, Ilove doing stuff around the house on Sundays. Used disparagingly, the meaning is to do something hastily, mess about with: Le travail est mal fait: c'est du bricolage, The work is badly done; it's arush job.

notes.content: The regular verb entamer literally means to cut / slice into (la tranche d'entame is the first slice of aloaf or ham). It is often used as asynonym for commencer, i.e. to begin an action lasting acertain length of time (Nous avons commencé / entamé notre voyage). But while commencer can be both transitive and intransitive (Le voyage a commencé), entamer is transitive only.

Time periods are not used as preceding adjectives in French. For example, a three-year programme is un programme de trois ans. But they can be used with the partitive de to add extra information: longue de trois ans. (See also lesson 77.)

The regular verb dé cerner (the root of discern) means to award: Le Prix Goncourt aé té dé cerné à Proust en 1919, The Goncourt Prize was awarded to Proust in 1919. Moreover, un prix, aprize (lesson line 12), can also be translated as an award. In certain contexts, especially music and business prizes, French has unfortunately adopted les Awards. To be avoided at all costs!

douter (the root of doubt) can be used transitively and pronominally, with aslight difference in meaning. The transitive form (lesson line 16) means to doubt and, with adirect object, is followed by de: Malgré trois excellents albums, elle a toujours douté de ses qualité s de chanteuse, Despite three excellent albums, she has always doubted her abilities as a singer. By contrast, se douter de means to suspect or guess something: Je ne savais pas mais je m'en suis douté, I didn'tknow but Isuspected it. Auseful expression, used as a rejoinder, is Je m'en doute ! Ican imagine, I'msure you do/are!, etc.

Remember that the past participle behaves as an adjective and agrees with the direct object (here, the feminine plural choses) if it comes before the verb. Compare that with Il autilisé des mots (m.) que je n'aurais jamais imaginé s, He used words that Inever would have imagined. Of course, the two forms of the participle are pronounced identically.

Another commonly used idiomatic noun is un pote, a mate, a buddy. Unlike un copain (lesson note 6) it does not imply aromantic interest. Formerly used only in closed circles, the word came back to prominence in the late th century with the anti-racist catchphrase Touche pas à mon pote, Don'ttouch my buddy, now the official slogan of an NGO collective.

toucher means to touch: Cette armoire touche le plafond, This cupboard is touching the ceiling. As atransitive indirect verb (which acts on or for its object), it requires the preposition à: Il n'apas touché à sa nourriture, He hasn'ttouched his food. The idiom meaning toucher à tout means to try one'shand at everything.

Yet another common slang word, bosser means to work and is used instead of travailler. Depending on the context, it can also mean to slog away, to swot, etc. Tu viens ? - Non, je bosse mes cours, Are you coming? No, I'mswotting up on my lessons.

The pronominal form of mettre, like most common verbs, has several meanings. When followed by à (thus au/aux) and either an object or an infinitive, it can mean to start or get down to something: Je vais me mettre au travail dè s demain, I'mgoing to get down to work tomorrow. (See lesson for more about difference between base and pronominal verbs.)

The impersonal third-person emphatic pronoun soi (referenced in lesson section 2) means one or oneself but is much less formal in French than in English. It is often used with an indefinite pronoun: Chacun pour soi, Every person to themselves or in asentence with no antecedent: Il faut tout faire soi-mê me, You have to do everything yourself (very formally, One has to do everything oneself). This impersonal context is underlined by the use of the indefinite pronoun on: On est toujours mieux chez soi, There'sno place like home.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Marcel Proust (1871-1922) is one of the greatest French novelists and prose stylists. His masterwork, Àla recherche du temps perdu (In Search of Lost Time aka Remembrance of Things Past), was published between 1913 and 1927. Proust coined the term la mémoire involontaire, involuntary memory, to describe the recollections triggered by cues encountered by chance, specifically the memories of childhood triggered when the novel'sprotagonist dips a cake, une madeleine, into his tea. Today, the expression la madeleine de Proust refers to atiny event that stirs up strong emotions. Proust was afan of an English game called Confessions, where seemingly trivial questions (Quel est votre animal préféré ? What'syour favourite animal?) are framed to discover a person'sinner nature. The game subsequently became known as le questionnaire de Proust and is often used today by chat show hosts to find out more about their guests. Productive phase: 26th lesson

notes.content: Two common adverbial suffixes are -emment, formed from adjectives ending -ent (frequent → fré quemment), and -amment, from adjectives ending in -ant (brillant → brillamment). In both cases, the initial vowel of the suffix (e, a) is pronounced as an open [a]: [breeyahmœhn] / [fraykahmœhn]. Listen carefully to sentences and 15.

We know the adjective pré cis (lesson line 8) and the adverb pré cisé ment (lesson line 9). But the regular verb pré ciser has no direct equivalent. It means to specify, clarify, etc. Nous voudrions pré ciser quelques dé tails, We would like to clarify afew details. Thus, while the general noun la pré cision means precision, accuracy, the countable form means a clarification, detail, etc.: J'ai besoin d'une pré cision, Ineed a clarification.

Unlike pré cis/pré cisé ment, some adverb formations are slightly irregular. Adjectives ending in -ant form their adverb by replacing the last two letters with mthen adding the usual -ment suffix: brillant → brillamment (lesson line 19). See also note and the pronunciation notes.

Unlike in English, the French passive voice can'tbe used with an indirect object. So asentence like My question has been answered by the audience is not directly translatable. The options are to use the impersonal pronoun: On aré pondu à ma question, in which case the indirect object public is dropped, or the demonstrative c'est... + qui: C'est le public qui aré pondu à ma question.

faire place à means to make way for or give way to: La croissance é conomique rapide afait place à une expansion plus modé ré e. Rapid economic growth has made way for amore moderate expansion. The expression Place à (Place aux jeunes, Make way for the young) is often used as an introduction. Et maintenant, place à la fê te, Now it'sparty time.

Dimensions, such as height (la hauteur), length (la longueur) and width (la largeur), are among the kinds of information introduced by de (lesson note 2). For example: L'horloge de la gare mesure neuf mè tres de hauteur, The station is meters high. But we can also use the adjectives haut, large and long as (masculine) nouns:... neuf mè tres de haut. There is no difference in meaning between the two forms.

que can be used, like quel, to introduce an exclamatory expression, often as the equivalent of how: Que c'est beau ! How beautiful! When followed by apersonal pronoun, however, que is not necessarily translated: Que je suis fatigué ! I'mreally tired!

Literally, se connaî tre means to know oneself: Je me connais : si je ne le fais pas maintenant, je ne le ferai pas du tout, Iknow myself: if I don'tdo it now, I won'tdo it at all. But with the pronoun y, the meaning is to know about or be skilled in something. Elle s'yconnaî t en litté rature franç aise, She knows alot about French literature. Note the use of en to introduce the complement.
Adjectives ending in -ent form their adverb by replacing the last two letters with mthen adding the usual -ment suffix: patient → patiemment. See also note and the pronunciation notes.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Victor Hugo (1802 - 1885), a novelist, poet, dramatist, politician and social historian, is one of France'sgreatest literary figures. Outside his home country, he is best known for his novels Notre-Dame de Paris (The Hunchback of Notre Dame), published in 1831, and Les Misérables (literally:"the wretched poor," "the dispossessed," 1862). The latter book is so sweeping in its scale and scope (one chapter even recounts the Battle of Waterloo) that is justifiably known as une épopée du peuple, a people's epic. (To answer the first quiz question, the world'slargest painting is La Fée Électricité, The Electricity Fairy, by Raoul Dufy, which hangs in le Musée d'Art Moderne in Paris.) Productive phase: 27th lesson

notes.content: Le passif: the passive voice: The passive is used if the object - aperson or thing - of an active statement is more important than the subject. The French passive voice is almost identical to its English counterpart in terms of construction. But it is used less frequently, for various reasons. 1.1 Formation: The passive voice of averb is formed with ê tre and the past participle. Les gens l'aiment, People love him → Il est aimé, He's loved. In the past tense, ê tre becomes é té and the two participles follow each other: Ils ont fermé le pont hier, They closed the bridge yesterday → Le pont aé té fermé hier, The bridge was closed yesterday. In these two examples, the passive is used because the fact of being loved or closed is more important than whoever is doing the loving or closing. One slight difference with the English construction is that the past participle, being an adjective, has to agree with the subject of the passive verb: Ils ont fermé la fenê tre → La fenê tre aé té fermé e. (Now'sthe time to revise your past participles!) If the active subject is incorporated as an agent into the passive sentence, it is preceded by par, by: Le maire afermé le pont, The mayor closed the bridge → Le pont aé té fermé par le maire, The bridge was closed by the mayor. Of course, the participle agreement rule does not change (L'é cole aé té fermé e par le maire). Where the agent is mentioned, par is used for almost all verbs. However, those expressing afeeling or an emotion (aimer, respecter, admirer) or astate (entourer, couvrir, dé corer, etc.) tend to use de rather than par: Le metteur en scè ne est respecté de tout le monde. The director is respected by everybody. There are only ahandful of such verbs, so they are easy to learn. The negative and first and second interrogatives follow the usual rules: Le pont n'apas é té fermé ; Est-ce que le pont aé té fermé ? The third interrogative is slightly more complicated - Le pont a-t-il é té fermé ? - but is used much less than the other two forms. 1.2 Use: The passive is used less in French than in English, firstly because active forms are preferable when describing actions, and secondly because French has several ways of sidestepping passive constructions. There are three main workarounds: with on, with the pronominal form, and with c'est... qui. • with on: The third-person impersonal pronoun on is used when the subject is implied or unimportant. It replaces nous, ils/elles, quelqu'un, tout le monde, etc. So asentence like Ici, on parle anglais can be used by ashop to inform potential customers that all its staff speak English (We speak English here), or by residents of an area to insist that everyone is anglophone (Everyone here speaks English). As you know, on is also commonly used instead of nous, simply because the first-person plural verb form often sounds too formal. In very formal situations, on can be translated by its English cognate, one. For example, On dit que... can be the equivalent of One says that... but it would generally be rendered by the passive It is said that... In amore colloquial setting, the usual equivalent is They say that... • with the pronominal verbs, formed with se: These are more common in French than in English precisely because they are used instead of the passive voice. In this case, there is no notion of myself, itself, etc. For example: Ce plat se mange chaud ou froid means This dish is eaten hot or cold. This form is possible only with the third person singular or plural: Les voitures neuves se vendent bien cette anné e, New cars are selling well this year. One very common set of short passive phrases is formed with ç a (or, more formally, cela) followed by apronominal verb: Il est franç ais. - Ç a s'entend, He's French. - You can hear it. Elle atrè s mal. - Cela se voit, She'sin great pain. - That's obvious, etc. • with c'est (plural: ce sont)... qui: This workaround avoids the passive by emphasising the subject. So asentence like The report was written by my German colleague can be translated literally by Le rapport aé té é crit par mon collè gue allemand, which is grammatically correct, or, more colloquially, by C'est mon collè gue allemand qui aé crit le rapport. A word-for-word translation ("It'smy German colleague who...,"etc) does not have the same resonance, precisely because French prefers the active to the passive. The main difference between the two languages is that the passive cannot be used with an indirect object in French, unlike English. For example, the English sentence Someone has sent me an email can, if necessary, be turned into apassive by converting the indirect object to a subject: Ihave been sent an email by someone. This is not possible in French. In cases like this, on can be used as a workaround: On m'aenvoyé un mail, Ihave been sent an email. Likewise, if an English passive sentence does not contain adirect object (for example, The email has been answered), it cannot be passive in French: On aré pondu au mail.

Adverbs of time: Let'sreview this important category of adverbs, most of which you have already learned and assimilated. Remember that many adverbs are formed from the feminine form of adjectives (dernier → derniè re → derniè rement). They are placed after averb consisting of asingle word and between the component parts of two-word verbs or aconjugated verb and its auxiliary. Now that you have been using most of these words for several months, the etymological explanations below will make them clearer and help you remember them. - actuellement, now, at present, at the moment, currently: From the adjective actuel, current: Elle travaille actuellement à Brest, She'scurrently working in Brest. Do NOT confuse actuellement and actually (en ré alité / en fait). - alors: From the adverb lors (see below), alors means at the/that time: Il é tait alors directeur de l'usine, He was the factory manager at the time. It also means so, then: Alors, tu viens ? So, are you coming? - aprè s, next or after(wards): Je l'ai revue longtemps aprè s, Isaw her along time afterwards. - auparavant, before(hand), previously, earlier: Elle avait annoncé son dé part une semaine auparavant. She had announced her departure aweek earlier. Asynonym of avant (as an adverb, not a preposition), auparavant is more common in writing than in speech. - aussitô t: asynonym of immé diatement, meaning straight away: J'ai appelé un taxi et il est arrivé aussitô t. Icalled ataxi and it came immediately. Formed from aussi and tô t but always written as asingle word. - autrefois, formerly, in the past: Autrefois, on vivait diffé remment, In the past, people lived differently. (from autre, other, and fois, time). Synonyms include dans le passé, in the past and avant (see below) - avant: as an adverb, avant is aless formal synonym of autrefois and auparavant (with which it shares an etymology). See doré navant. - bientô t, soon, shortly: On arrive bientô t, We'll be arriving shortly. Used commonly in the expression à bientô t, See you soon. - d'abord, first (of all): Nous allons d'abord t'acheter une casquette. First we're going to buy you a cap. When citing the main reason for something, d'abord means in the first place: D'abord tu es trop jeune, In the first place, you're too young. - dé jà, already: Il est dé jà dix-sept heures ! It's pm already. - depuis, for / since, depending on the context: depuis Noë l, since Christmas; depuis dix ans, for ten years. - derniè rement, lately, recently: Je ne l'ai pas vue derniè rement, I haven'tseen her lately. - doré navant, from now on: Doré navant, c'est moi qui prendrai les dé cisions, From now on, I'll take the decisions. (Note the root word, avant.) - enfin, at last, finally: Ils sont enfin arrivé s, They've arrived at last. (en + fin, in the end). Also used in declarative or explicative contexts: C'est mon mari, enfin, mon copain, He'smy husband, well, my boyfriend. - ensuite, next, afterwards: Je té lé phonerai d'abord et j'é crirai ensuite. I'll phone first, then afterwards I'll write. (suite, from suivre, means continuation, follow-up). - jamais, never: Elle n'ajamais lu"Notre Dame de Paris", She has never read"The Hunchback of Notre Dame". In some cases, jamais can be used without ne : Jamais plus ! Never again. - longtemps, for along time, (for) long: Je n'ai pas attendu longtemps, I didn'twait long. The root adjective (long) is masculine; it cannot be used as an adverb, unlike in English. - lors de, during, at the time of: L'ascenseur aé té installé lors de la construction de la tour. The lift was installed during the construction of the tower. In modern French, lors is not used alone.

Base and pronominal verbs with different meanings: We know that French uses pronominal (i.e. reflexive or reciprocal) verbs extensively in order to avoid the passive voice. In some cases, there are slight idiomatic differences in meaning between the base verb and its pronominal form. As always, the most important factor is context. - Faire: The base verb means to do or make, so the literal meaning of the reflexive form is to make oneself: Je me fais un sandwich au jambon, I'mmaking myself aham sandwich. Idiomatically, se faire un film or un restaurant means to go out to amovie or for a meal. Another very common idiom is s'en faire, to worry, be concerned about. It is often used in the negative: Ne t'en fais pas, je t'aiderai, Don't worry, I'll help you. And the expression Ç a se fait / Ç a ne se fait pas states what is or is not aproper thing to do: Chez nous, ç a ne se fait pas, We don'tdo that sort of thing at our house. (See also lesson note 1). - The reciprocal form of mettre, to put, is used in relation to clothing: Je n'ai rien à me mettre, I've got nothing to wear. It can also indicate movement towards something: Mettez-vous au chaud, Get into the warm. Followed by à, se mettre means to take up (an activity): Il s'est mis au tennis, He'sstarted playing tennis (see lesson note 9). And where the object is understood, it is replaced by y. Je vais m'y mettre, I'll get started on it. - Other common verb pairs with slight differences include attendre, to wait, and s'attendre, to expect (lesson 59); entendre, to hear, and s'entendre, to get along with (lesson 55); plaindre, to pity, and se plaindre, to complain; douter (de), to doubt, and se douter (de), to guess or suspect (both in lesson 73). Asimple rule of thumb is that if you can'textrapolate the meaning of apronominal verb from its base form, then look in agood bilingual dictionary.

Adjectives of dimension: Dimensions can be expressed in several ways. The adjectives long(ue), haut(e), large and profond(e) are placed before the noun, along with the partitive de: Le bâ timent est haut de trente é tages, The building is stories high. Of course, they have to agree: La Tour Eiffel est haute de trois cent vingt mè tres. The Eiffel Tower is 320 meters high. Another possibility is to put the nouns la longueur (length), la hauteur (height), la largeur (width) and la profondeur (depth), preceded by de, after the noun: Le salon fait trois mè tres de largeur or Une tour de cent mè tres de hauteur. In this case, however, we still use an adjective when translating into English: The living room is three metres wide, A 100-metre high tower. Lastly, and slightly confusingly, long, haut and large are also masculine nouns (le haut du visage, the upper part of the face, for example) and can be used in the same predicative position as the equivalent adjectives. Thus twenty kilometres long is either vingt kilomè tres de long or de longueur; one metre high is un mè tre de haut or de hauteur; and two centimetres wide is deux centimè tres de large or de largeur. The exception to this duality is profondeur, depth: trois mè tres de profondeur (*de profond is incorrect). The only, slight difference is register: the substantive is considered slightly more elegant than the adjective. In practical terms, though, the two are equivalent.

Proverbs and sayings: Maxims are an integral part of any language and are used regularly, either directly or obliquely ("You know what they say about rolling stones..."). In any case, they are an important part of popular culture. Because French and English are closely related, many proverbs are identical or very similar in both languages. We've learned Rira bien qui rira le dernier, He who laughs last laughs longest. Here are five more: Pierre qui roule n'amasse pas mousse, Arolling stone gathers no moss; À mauvais ouvrier point de bons outils, Abad workman always blames his tools; Tout ce qui brille n'est pas or, All that glitters is not gold; Mieux vaut tard que jamais, Better late than never; Il ne faut pas mettre tous ses œufs dans le mê me panier, Don'tput all your eggs in one (or the same) basket. We have also learned an axiom which, though not identical, does have adirect equivalent: C'est l'hô pital qui se moque de la charité ("It'sthe hospital that is mocking the charity"), The pot calling the kettle black. In upcoming lessons, we'll learn more about sayings with the same meaning but slightly different wording.

dialogue.french: Vous avez des projets pour le pont de l'Ascension ? Je suis à la recherche d'inspiration.
dialogue.english: Do you have plans for the long weekend of the Ascension? I'm looking for inspiration.

dialogue.french: Nous allons rendre visite à mes neveux et ma nièce à Nîmes, enfin pas à Nîmes même, mais juste à côté.
dialogue.english: We're going to visit my nephews and niece in Nîmes, well not in Nîmes itself, but just next door.

dialogue.french: Vous y allez avec les enfants, j'imagine. Quelle chance ils ont !
dialogue.english: You're going with the children, I imagine. How lucky they are!

dialogue.french: Non, pas cette fois-ci. Nous le leur avons proposé mais ils n'étaient pas très chauds.
dialogue.english: No, not this time. We suggested it to them, but they didn't seem too keen.

dialogue.french: Ils sont difficiles, vos gamins. Moi, je sauterais sur l'occasion de visiter la Provence.
dialogue.english: Your kids are difficult. Me, I'd jump at the opportunity to visit Provence.

dialogue.french: Je ne leur en veux pas. On les y a souvent emmenés quand ils étaient jeunes. Ils s'y sont beaucoup amusés.
dialogue.english: I don't hold it against them. We often took them there when they were young. They had a lot of fun there.

dialogue.french: Mais maintenant ils préfèrent s'amuser avec les copains plutôt que de rester avec leurs parents !
dialogue.english: But now they prefer to have fun with their friends rather than stay with their parents!

dialogue.french: Et pourtant, les voyages forment la jeunesse, dit-on.
dialogue.english: And yet, they say that travel broadens the mind.

dialogue.french: Je le leur ai dit mais ils n'en ont rien à faire et je n'arrive pas à les convaincre.
dialogue.english: I told them that, but they don't care and I can't manage to convince them.

dialogue.french: Ils me disent qu'ils ont peur de s'embêter avec les vieux, qu'ils trouvent trop ennuyeux.
dialogue.english: They tell me they are afraid of getting bored with old people, whom they find too boring.

dialogue.french: Je leur réponds que c'est dans les vieux pots qu'on fait la meilleure soupe.
dialogue.english: I tell them that the best wine comes in old bottles.

dialogue.french: Qu'importe. Ce sont eux les perdants dans l'histoire.
dialogue.english: It doesn't matter. It's they who are the losers in the story.

dialogue.french: Revenons à notre sujet. Vu que vous serez dans la région nîmoise, est-ce que vous pouvez m'acheter du miel de lavande et des herbes de Provence ?
dialogue.english: Let's get back to the subject. Since you'll be in the Nîmes region, can you buy me some lavender honey and Provence herbs?

dialogue.french: Bien sûr, on en rapporte aussi pour Alex et Théo. Nous leur en avons promis.
dialogue.english: Of course, we're also bringing some back for Alex and Théo. We promised them some.

dialogue.french: Et si vous voyez un beau vase en céramique avec un motif de cigales dessus – le souvenir touristique par excellence –, vous pouvez me le prendre ?
dialogue.english: And if you see a beautiful ceramic vase with a cicada design on it – the ultimate tourist souvenir – can you get it for me?

dialogue.french: Oui, je connais une boutique qui en vend : nous y en avons déjà acheté pour d'autres amis.
dialogue.english: Yes, I know a shop that sells them: we've already bought them there for other friends.

dialogue.french: Mais vu les prix, ça risque de te revenir cher, tu sais.
dialogue.english: But given the prices, it could cost you a lot, you know.

dialogue.french: Alors je vais te faire un chèque tout de suite.
dialogue.english: So I'll do you a cheque right away.

dialogue.french: Ne me le donne pas maintenant ; donne-le-moi à la fin du mois.
dialogue.english: Don't give it to me now; give it to me at the end of the month.

notes.content: la recherche, research (see lesson note 3) is used in the expression à la recherche de, to be in search of or, simply, to be looking for: Nous sommes à la recherche de nouveaux locaux, We're looking for new premises.

It is important not to confuse rendre visite, to visit or to go and see aperson (see lessons line and line 10), and visiter, to visit aplace (lesson line 8). One way of avoiding rendre visite is simply to say aller voir: Nous sommes allé s voir Thé o hier, We went to see Thé o yesterday.

When asentence contains both adirect object pronoun and an indirect object pronoun, they have to follow astrict order. In an affirmative sentence, the direct object le has to precede the indirect leur (In the singular, and with afeminine direct object, the sentence would read Nous la lui avons proposé e.) In anegative sentence (line 23), ne precedes the first pronoun and pas follows the verb: Ne me la propose pas.... Look at the examples in this lesson (noted 3), then check lesson for afuller explanation.

ê tre chaud pour has nothing to do with temperature; it means to be enthusiastic about or keen to do something. Fabien est chaud pour venir avec nous à Nî mes, Fabien is enthusiastic about coming with us to Nî mes. Arguably, the expression is used more often in the negative. Tu viens ? - Je ne suis pas trè s chaud. You coming? - I'mnot too keen. (Of course, to be hot is avoir chaud.)

un gamin is asynonym of un(e) gosse, (lesson note 10), both of which mean a kid. (The feminine form, une gamine, is the origin of our word gamine, meaning an attractively boyish girl or woman.) The two words are familiar, not slang.

Here'syet another idiomatic construction with faire: n'en avoir rien à faire means not to care or be bothered. Ils sont trop occupé s ou, peut-ê tre, ils n'en ont rien à faire, They're too busy, or perhaps they don't care. The clue to the idiomatic nature of the expression is en, because Ils n'ont rien à faire simply means They have nothing to do.

Another meaning of arriver, to arrive, is to manage or succeed. In this case, it is followed à, and any subsequent verb is in the infinitive: Je n'arrive pas à la joindre par té lé phone, I can'tget through to her on the phone.

Here is another verb that changes meaning slightly in the pronominal form (see lesson 77): embê ter means to pester, annoy, etc.: N'embê tez pas votre frè re, il travaille, Don'tpester your brother, he's working. But s'embê ter, asynonym of s'ennuyer, means to be or get bored: Elle s'embê te en cours d'anglais, She gets bored in English lessons. In the sense of to bother, the pronominal and base forms can have the same meaning: Ne vous embê tez pas avec ç a, Don'tbother with that.
Qu'importe is amore elegant form of Peu importe. Both mean It doesn'tmatter (lesson note 8).

vu, the past participle of voir, to see, is useful way of saying in view of (or, more simply, since). It can be followed by a noun: Vu le temps, on restera à la maison, In view of the weather, we'll stay at home, or by que and averb clause: Vu qu'il fait beau, on ira à la plage, Since the weather's fine, we'll go to the beach. In the que construction, vu que can be used like puisque (lesson line 1).

revenir, to come back, is used idiomatically to talk about cost: Avec l'essence, le voyage reviendra à cent euros, With petrol, the journey will work out at 100 euros. Acommon expression is Ç a revient cher. That costs a lot.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: L'Ascension ("the Ascension") is a Christian holiday celebrated forty days after Easter. Since it always falls on a Thursday, many people take advantage of along weekend. (See Culture Note, lesson 18). Your knowledge of French is becoming not only broader, with more grammatical content, but also deeper and more colloquial. In this lesson, you learned two more axioms: Les voyages forment la jeunesse and C'est dans les vieux pots qu'on fait la bonne/meilleure soupe, that are used regularly by native speakers. In other words, you are learning"real"French! Productive phase: 29th lesson

title: Il faut que je trouve une bonne excuse ...

dialogue.french: Allô, c'est toi, Thomas ? Je suis content que tu sois là.
dialogue.english: Hello, is that you, Thomas? I'm glad that you're there.

dialogue.french: Il faut que je te parle, et il faut que tu sois franc avec moi. Je ne te dérange pas ?
dialogue.english: I have to talk to you, and you have to be frank with me. I'm not disturbing you?

dialogue.french: Non, non. Je suis heureux que tu m'appelles, Martin. C'est à quel sujet ?
dialogue.english: No, no. I'm happy that you're calling, Martin. What's this about?

dialogue.french: C'est à propos d'Alexis, l'associé de mon père. Il veut que je l'aide à peindre son salon et sa salle à manger.
dialogue.english: It's about Alexis, my father's business partner. He wants me to help him paint his living room and dining room.

dialogue.french: Et alors ? Qu'est-ce qui t'en empêche ? Tu es bien peintre professionnel, non ?
dialogue.english: So what? What's stopping you? You're a professional painter, aren't you?

dialogue.french: Oui, c'est vrai, mais tu connais Alexis : il est aussi exigeant que maniaque.
dialogue.english: Yes, that's true, but you know Alexis: he's as demanding as he is finicky.

dialogue.french: Par exemple, il aimerait que je sois là à l'aube et que je passe toute la journée avec lui.
dialogue.english: For example, he'd like me to be there at dawn and spend the whole day with him.

dialogue.french: Il faut que j'apporte le matériel – pinceaux, rouleaux, couteaux et tout et tout – mais aussi que j'amène mon employé pour faire les plafonds et les endroits les plus délicats.
dialogue.english: I have to bring the material – brushes, rollers, scrapers and all that – but also that I bring my employee to do the ceilings and the most awkward places.

dialogue.french: Et, quand on aura terminé, il faudra sans doute que j'emporte les déchets à la déchetterie !
dialogue.english: And, when we're finished, I'll probably have to take the rubbish to the waste collection centre!

dialogue.french: En résumé, je ne sais pas quoi lui dire. Je ne veux pas qu'il soit fâché contre moi.
dialogue.english: In short, I don't know what to say to him. I don't want him to be angry with me.

dialogue.french: Tu permets que je sois tout à fait honnête et que je te donne un bon conseil ?
dialogue.english: Do you mind if I'm completely honest and give you some good advice?

dialogue.french: Il suffit de le regarder droit dans les yeux et lui dire, gentiment mais fermement : « Je préfère que vous trouviez quelqu'un d'autre, Alexis. »
dialogue.english: All you have to do is look him straight in the eye and say to him, gently but firmly: 'I'd rather you found someone else, Alexis.'

dialogue.french: À défaut, il vaudrait mieux que tu ne sois pas disponible ce jour-là, que toi et ton apprenti, vous soyez sur un autre chantier.
dialogue.english: Failing that, it would be better if you weren't available that day, that you and your apprentice were on another job site.

dialogue.french: Ou, au pire, que vous soyez malades tous les deux. Rien de trop grave, bien sûr, mais des épidémies de rougeole ou de scarlatine sont bien utiles dans des cas pareils !
dialogue.english: Or, at worst, that both of you were sick. Nothing too serious, of course, but epidemics of measles or scarlet fever are very useful in such cases!

dialogue.french: N'empêche, j'ai peur qu'il soit vexé quand même.
dialogue.english: Even so, I'm afraid he'll be offended anyway.

dialogue.french: Il ne t'en voudra pas. Il sera triste que tu ne puisses pas l'aider, c'est tout.
dialogue.english: He won't hold it against you. He'll be sad that you can't help him, that's all.

dialogue.french: Et comment le sais-tu ?
dialogue.english: And how do you know that?

dialogue.french: Parce qu'il m'a posé exactement la même question hier et je lui ai donné exactement la même excuse.
dialogue.english: Because he asked me exactly the same question yesterday and I gave him exactly the same excuse.

notes.content: This lesson deals with the subjunctive mood, used to express feelings or doubts about asituation or action. It is used with certain verbs in two-part sentences having different subjects. The verbs in our examples (ê tre content, falloir, ê tre heureux, ê tre triste, avoir peur, etc.) are followed by que, which links (or"sub-joins") them to the second, subjunctive verb in the sentence: J'ai peur qu'il soit fâ ché, I'mafraid he may be angry.
The full, irregular conjugation of ê tre in the subjunctive is (que) je sois, tu sois, il/elle soit, nous soyons, vous soyez, ils/elles soient.

See lesson note 1. Since falloir is impersonal, the invariable pronoun il is equivalent to it. In principle, the English subjunctive can be used here to translate sentences like Il faut que nous soyons à l'heure (It is necessary that we be on time). In practice, though, alternative constructions are used (We have to/must/need to be on time).

The subjunctive form of regular -er verbs is the same as the present tense, except for the first and second persons plural, which add an i: (que) j'appelle, tu appelles, il/elle appelle, nous appelions, vous appeliez, ils/elles appellent. Remember: since the second verb is subjoined to an initial verb, it is preceded by que: Il faut que nous appelions notre bureau, We have to call our office.

empê cher means to prevent or stop: On m'aempê ché de sortir, Iwas prevented from leaving. The associated noun, un empê chement (the root of impeachment), means a difficulty, an obstacle, a hitch, often unexpected: Elle voulait yaller mais elle aeu un empê chement, She wanted to go but something came up. The invariable expression n'empê che, quite informal, is the equivalent of even so, all the same: N'empê che, ils auraient pu té lé phoner, All the same, they could have called. Later we'll see how to use the expression in aless informal context.

See lesson note 9. Aussi... que can also be used to compare two adjectives: Elle est aussi intelligente que sympathique, She'sas intelligent as she is nice. In contrast to English, there is no need to repeat the verb. (While the adjective maniaque means fussy, finicky, the noun un maniaque means amanic or a fanatic.)

The verbs apporter (lesson 26), amener (68) and emmener (78), basically meaning to bring or to take, are often confused. The basic rule is that apporter/emporter means to take something to the place where you are going, amener means the same thing but applies to people or animals that are taken, and emmener means to take someone or living beings away from the place of origin: J'apporte mes outils, j'amè ne mon assistant et j'emporte les dé chets, Ibring my tools and my assistant and Itake away the rubbish. More details in alater lesson.
Here, Thomas switches from tu, used when chatting with his friend, to vous because he is talking about two people: Martin and his apprentice.

Here'sanother use of acommon verb: en vouloir à means to hold something against (see lesson line 7) or to be mad at someone. Martin m'en veut parce que j'ai oublié son anniversaire, Martin is mad at me because Iforgot his birthday. Auseful expression, used apologetically, is Vous ne m'en voulez pas ? You won't resent/hold it against me?
The subjunctive of the irregular verb pouvoir is (que) je puisse, tu puisses, il/elle puisse, nous puissions, vous puissiez, ils/elles puissent.
