extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: You're certainly aware that we have been scaling down the figurative pronunciation section beneath the main dialogue. By now you should be familiar with French sounds and be able to extrapolate from, say, an infinitive like aimer to its past participle aimé or the imperfect aimait. We will continue to provide guidance for new or unusual sounds, but the aim now is to remove the crutch on which you've been relying for the past 79 lessons. What's more, the grammar is becoming more complex. But because you've already assimilated many of the constructions before they are explained in the revision lessons, you will find it easier to understand and acquire the underlying mechanisms. Bonne continuation ! (Onward and upward!) Productive phase: 30th lesson

title: "Notre action ne dépend que de vous"

dialogue.french: Les syndicalistes de l'SSP, le Syndicat des services publics, ont déposé un préavis de grève pour la fin janvier.
dialogue.english: The members of the SSP, the Public Services Union, have given advance notice of a strike for the end of January.

dialogue.french: Ils réclament des augmentations de salaire, mais leurs exigences vont au-delà de la seule question salariale et des négociations sur les conditions d'accès aux congés maladie.
dialogue.english: They are demanding wage increases, but their demands go beyond the wage issue alone and negotiations on the conditions of access to sick leave.

dialogue.french: Le SSP exige que ces réclamations soient entendues par le gouvernement et le patronat dans le cadre de la réduction du temps de travail.
dialogue.english: The SSP demands that these claims should be heard by the government and employers as part of the reduction in working time.

dialogue.french: Pour l'instant, la grogne est limitée à une trentaine de grandes entreprises mais elle pourrait devenir un mouvement massif touchant plusieurs secteurs, y compris la sidérurgie et l'agroalimentaire.
dialogue.english: For the time being, the discontent is limited to some thirty large companies but it could become a massive movement affecting several sectors, including the steel industry and food processing.

dialogue.french: Ce matin, un des leaders syndicaux a prononcé un discours devant ses militants.
dialogue.english: This morning, one of the union leaders gave a speech to his activists.

dialogue.french: « Camarades, notre action ne dépend que de vous ! Il faut que nous élargissions et durcissions le mouvement pour qu'il ne faiblisse pas dans les semaines à venir. »
dialogue.english: 'Comrades, our action depends only on you! We must broaden and toughen the movement so that it does not weaken in the weeks to come.'

dialogue.french: « En matière de congés maladie, il est flagrant que les employeurs nous imposent deux poids, deux mesures. »
dialogue.english: 'As regards sick leave, it is flagrant that employers are imposing double standards on us.'

dialogue.french: « Si un ouvrier oublie de faire quelque chose, il est paresseux ; mais si son patron l'oublie, c'est simplement parce qu'il est trop occupé. »
dialogue.english: 'If a worker forgets to do something, he's lazy; but if his boss forgets, it's simply because he's too busy.'

dialogue.french: « Il est dommage que vous n'ayez pas la reconnaissance que vous méritez. »
dialogue.english: 'It's a pity that you don't get the recognition you deserve.'

dialogue.french: « Supposez que vous ayez la grippe et que vous choisissiez de ne pas aller au boulot pour ne pas incommoder vos camarades. Qu'est-ce qui va se passer ? »
dialogue.english: 'Suppose you have the flu and you choose not to go to work so as not to inconvenience your comrades. What's going to happen?'

dialogue.french: « Le patron ne va pas attendre que vous finissiez votre traitement et que vous soyez guéri ; il va exiger que vous reveniez travailler dans les plus brefs délais ! Quelle honte ! »
dialogue.english: 'The boss isn't going to wait for you to finish your treatment and get better; he will demand that you come back to work as soon as possible! It's disgraceful!'

dialogue.french: « Car si c'est lui qui est malade, ses collègues vont insister pour qu'il obéisse au médecin du travail, et qu'il y réfléchisse à deux fois avant de revenir au bureau. »
dialogue.english: 'Because if it's he who is sick, his colleagues will insist that he obey the occupational physician, and think twice before coming back to the office.'

dialogue.french: « Cela démontre bien que tous les hommes sont égaux, mais que certains sont plus égaux que d'autres ! »
dialogue.english: 'This goes to show that all men are equal, but that some are more equal than others!'

notes.content: The regular verb ré clamer is a faux-ami, meaning to demand or call for: Les syndicats ré clament des ré sultats, The unions are demanding results. In alegal context, it can mean to lodge a complaint, hence the noun une ré clamation. If aconsumer wishes to complain about a company'sproducts or services, they can contact le service / le bureau des ré clamations.

un congé, often translated simply as aholiday (lesson line 12), also covers the notion of leave, i.e. absence from work, and is used in compound nouns such as les congé s payé s, paid leave, un congé de maladie, sick leave, or un congé de maternité, maternity leave. (In common usage, de is often omitted: un congé maladie, etc.).

This lesson builds on the constructions explained in lesson note 1. Verbs such as exiger que, to demand that, ê tre dommage que, be ashame that and attendre que, to expect that all imply an element of uncertainty or contingency about the action described in the second, subordinate-clause verb, which is therefore in the subjunctive. (Note that insister requires pour before que: J'insiste pour que tu choisisses entre nous deux, Iinsist that you choose between the two of us.)

The masculine noun l'acier means steel: Cette porte est en acier, This door is made of steel. The noun la sidé rurgie covers both steel and iron (le fer, see lesson 71) and thus refers to the metalworking or the iron and steel industry.

Although French has perfectly good native nouns like un dirigeant or un responsable, meaning aleader or an official, it often uses un leader in apolitical or managerial context (along with the horrible le leadership).

The negative form ne... que means only: Elle ne m'appelle qu'une fois par semaine, She calls me only once a week. The construction can be used instead of seulement (Elle m'appelle seulement une fois par semaine). Que can also be used with another two-part negative construction, such as ne... pas, with the same meaning: Il ne reste plus que trois candidats, There are only three candidates left.

The present subjunctive endings of regular -ir verbs are slightly more complex than for -er verbs. Thus é largir, to broaden (from large, broad, wide): (que) j'é largisse, tu é largisses, il/elle é largisse, nous é largissions, vous é largissiez, ils/elles é largissent. Remember that the subjunctive form is usually preceded by que.

le poids, the weight, takes an -sin the singular as well as the plural: Quel poids faites-vous ?, How much do you weigh? Une mesure means ameasurement as well as ameasure (lesson line 5). The expression deux poids, deux mesures means adouble standard: Le gouvernement applique deux poids, deux mesures sur cette question, The government is applying double standards to this issue.
The present subjunctive of avoir is (que) j'aie, tu aies, il/elle ait, nous ayons, vous ayez, ils/elles aient.

la honte means shame, disgrace. Leurs actions sont une source de honte pour nous tous, Their actions are asource of shame for all of us. However, it does not translate the notion of shame or pity contained in English expressions like What a pity, which is Quel dommage (lesson line 19). C'est une honte ! It's a disgrace!

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Even acasual reading of French news media will reveal an entire vocabulary of words and terms relating to employment (l'emploi), joblessness (le chômage) and labour relations (les relations de travail, literally"work relations"). The adjective social refers to interactions between employers and employees, referred to collectively as les partenaires sociaux ("social partners"). Key players include management (la direction) and staff representatives (le/la délégué(e) du personnel), who seek to maintain labour relations (le dialogue social) and avert any industrial action (un mouvement social). Productive phase: 31st lesson

dialogue.french: Bon, il n'est pas certain que nous puissions tenir cette réunion si l'autre partie ne fait pas un pas vers nous.
dialogue.english: Well, it's not certain that we can hold this meeting if the other side doesn't take a step towards us.

dialogue.french: Vous avez raison. Bien que nous fassions tous les efforts nécessaires, nous sommes dans un dialogue de sourds.
dialogue.english: You're right. Although we're making all the necessary efforts, we're in a dialogue of the deaf.

dialogue.french: Nous nous sommes fait attaquer par les médias qui nous désignent comme les méchants.
dialogue.english: We've been attacked by the media who are pointing at us as the villains.

dialogue.french: C'est ridicule, bien entendu. Il n'empêche que nous devons être très attentifs.
dialogue.english: It's ridiculous, of course. Nevertheless, we must be very careful.

dialogue.french: Leur déléguée du personnel, Inès Laurent, est très adroite et, de plus, c'est une négociatrice expérimentée.
dialogue.english: Their staff representative, Inès Laurent, is very skilful and, moreover, she's an experienced negotiator.

dialogue.french: Il n'est pas certain qu'elle attende la fin des pourparlers avant de déclencher un grand mouvement social.
dialogue.english: It's not certain that she'll wait for the end of the talks before launching a major social movement.

dialogue.french: Quoi qu'il en soit, ses idées gagnent du terrain et on doit être sur le qui-vive.
dialogue.english: Be that as it may, her ideas are gaining ground and we have to be on the alert.

dialogue.french: Je suis d'accord. Il faut qu'on fasse très attention car tout peut arriver.
dialogue.english: I agree. We have to be very careful because anything can happen.

dialogue.french: Il est peu probable que Madame Laurent comprenne notre stratégie ou qu'elle connaisse notre vraie position.
dialogue.english: It's unlikely that Mrs Laurent understands our strategy or knows our real position.

dialogue.french: En revanche, il est tout à fait probable qu'elle suspendra les négociations si elle n'obtient pas ce qu'elle veut.
dialogue.english: On the other hand, it's quite likely that she'll suspend negotiations if she doesn't get what she wants.

dialogue.french: De toutes les façons, les délégués du personnel en général nous en veulent à tous.
dialogue.english: In any case, the staff representatives generally resent all of us.

dialogue.french: Ce qui est sûr c'est que nous ne pouvons pas nous tourner les pouces en attendant que le problème se règle tout seul.
dialogue.english: What's certain is that we can't twiddle our thumbs waiting for the problem to sort itself out.

dialogue.french: Au contraire, il faut patienter jusqu'à ce que Laurent soumette un document avec ses propositions.
dialogue.english: On the contrary, we need to be patient until Laurent submits a document with her proposals.

dialogue.french: Si elle ne le fait pas dans un délai de quarante-huit heures, nous aurons le droit de rompre les négociations sans préavis.
dialogue.english: If she doesn't do so within forty-eight hours, we'll have the right to break off negotiations without notice.

dialogue.french: Disons d'ici à vendredi ? Pourvu que nous soyons tous du même avis,
dialogue.english: Let's say by Friday? Provided we're all of the same opinion,

dialogue.french: je préparerai un communiqué de presse, comme prévu et on le publiera plus tard.
dialogue.english: I'll prepare a press release, as planned, and we'll publish it later.

dialogue.french: Avant que tu finisses, Yann, j'ai une anecdote qui illustre le genre d'individus à qui nous avons affaire.
dialogue.english: Before you finish, Yann, I have an anecdote that illustrates the kind of individuals we're dealing with.

dialogue.french: Un jeune homme, fraîchement sorti d'une école de commerce, me sollicite pour un poste de commercial et me demande le salaire.
dialogue.english: A young man, fresh out of a business school, asks me for a sales position and asks me about the salary.

dialogue.french: Je lui propose le salaire minimum pour commencer,
dialogue.english: I offer him the minimum wage to start with,

dialogue.french: en lui disant qu'il serait augmenté de manière conséquente au bout de sa période d'essai de six mois.
dialogue.english: telling him it would be increased substantially at the end of his six-month probation period.

dialogue.french: Vous savez ce qu'il m'a répondu ?
dialogue.english: You know what he answered?

dialogue.french: « D'accord, dans ce cas je reviendrai dans vingt-quatre semaines ».
dialogue.english: 'All right, in that case I'll come back in twenty-four weeks.'

dialogue.french: C'est inadmissible, sans doute, mais c'est logique.
dialogue.english: It's inadmissible, no doubt, but it's logical.

notes.content: Some conjunctions introducing acondition or conjecture (although, etc.) are followed by averb in the subjunctive. For example, bien que, usually placed at the beginning of asentence or clause, means although, etc. Bien que nous soyons souvent absents, nous pensons à toi, Even though we are often away, we think of you. Note once again how the subjunctive is introduced by que. Be careful, though, to distinguish between the conjunction bien que and the adverb bien introducing adependent clause starting with que (lesson line 22).
The present subjunctive of the irregular verb faire is (que) je fasse, tu fasses, il/elle fasse, nous fassions, vous fassiez, ils/elles fassent.

The adjective mé chant literally means nasty, unkind, etc. Il faut que tu apprennes à ne pas ê tre mé chant avec les autres, You have to learn not to be nasty to other people. We will see other uses later on. The personal noun un(e) mé chant(e) means anasty or unpleasant person and, by extension,"abad guy"in anovel or movie. Dans les tous premiers films, le mé chant portait toujours un chapeau noir, In the very early movies, the baddy always used to wear ablack hat.

Il n'empê che que has the same meaning as n'empê che, seen in lesson note 5, but is alittle more formal (be that as it may). Any verb following the expression is in the indicative, not the subjunctive: Je sais que vous ne les aimez pas. Il n'empê che qu'ils ont raison, Iknow that you do not like them. Be that as it may, they are right.

When used in the negative, impersonal verbs such as ê tre certain / ê tre sû r indicate doubt and therefore require the subjunctive: Il n'est pas sû r qu'elle soit d'accord avec nous, It'snot sure that she'll agree with us. In the indicative, however, the doubt disappears, as does the subjunctive. In such cases, the verb is often in the future tense: Il est certain qu'elle sera accord avec nous, She'sbound to agree with us. The same applies, of course, to probability: see lines 10 (subjunctive) and 11 (indicative).

This is the subjunctive of Group verbs (in -re): (que) j'attende, tu attendes, il/elle attende, nous attendions, vous attendiez, ils/elles attendent. Be careful not to confuse the subjunctive with the imperfect in the first and second persons plural, which are identical.

See lesson note 9. This expression, formed with the relative pronoun and the subjunctive, means whatever, no matter what. Quoi que nous fassions, nous aurons toujours tort, Whatever we do we will always be in the wrong.

Afew time conjunctions also take the subjunctive. The most common are jusqu'à ce que, until, and avant que (note the tell-tale que in both cases): Avant que tu partes, j'ai quelque chose à te dire, Before you go, I've got something to say to you. Tu peux le garder jusqu'à ce que je revienne ? Can you keep it until Icome back?

un dé lai is a faux-ami (a delay, un retard). It basically means atime period or limit: Il faut le faire dans un dé lai de dix jours, It has to be done within a ten-day period. The actual translation depends on the context -for example Quel est le dé lai pour ce travail ? What'sthe deadline for this job?- but the underlying notion is the passage of time. (In some expression, dé lai can be plural, see lesson line 19).

notes.content: The vowel middle sound in veuille / veuillez is pronounced the same as the ligature in œil (see lesson 32). In conversational French, the ne is usually elided (see the note in lesson 73). Thus you'll probably hear some people say j'en connais aucun [zhœh"konay okah"].

que can be used at the beginning of an adverbial clause to introduce an alternative, like whether... or. In this case, the following verb is in the subjunctive: Que vous l'aimiez ou non, il tient à vous, Whether you like him or not, he'sfond of you. The negative non can be replaced by pas (Que tu l'aimes ou pas... ) with no change in meaning.

The subjunctive of the irregular verb vouloir is (que) je veuille, tu veuilles, il/elle veuille, nous voulions, vous vouliez, ils/elles veuillent. As with Group verbs, be careful not to confuse the subjunctive with the imperfect in the first and second persons plural (lesson note 6).
The plural indefinite pronoun certains can be used for agroup of people (lesson line 18), like some or some people. Certains sont d'accord, d'autres pas. Some (people) agree, others don't.

The impersonal verb s'agir de, usually found in the third person singular il s'agit de, can be hard to pin down. The nearest equivalent is: it has to do with or it's aquestion of. Je dois vous parler : il s'agit de votre salaire, Ihave to talk to you. It has to do with your salary. We'll return to this later on.

Remember that the negative form ne... que means only: Le gouvernement n'aque deux choix : accepter ou dé missionner, The government has only two choices: accept or resign. In this context, ne... que can be replaced by seulement, with no change in meaning: Le gouvernement aseulement deux choix, etc.

The questions asked by the pollster are formal, which is why the type interrogative is used. To avoid the juxtaposition of two initial vowels (a il), the letter tis placed between hyphens: a-t-il ? This rule is not confined to avoir or to the present tense. See line 12, dure-t-il, and line 17, arrivera-t-il.

là-dessus, on there, can be used literally to describe aphysical position or idiomatically to replace sur cela/ç a: Tu peux compter sur ç a → Tu peux compter là-dessus, You can count on that. By extension, it can also mean thereupon, with that: Charles amarmonné quelque chose et, là-dessus, il est parti en courant, Charles muttered something and, with that, he ran away.

The adverbial phrase tout court ("all short") is useful for indicating brevity or sufficiency: Ne m'appelez pas Madame la Pré sidente mais Madame, tout court, Don'tcall me Madam President, just Madam. The translation changes depending on the context: L'opposition veut le pouvoir, tout court, The opposition wants power, pure and simple. In short, keep the translation short!

The meaning of tenir, to hold, shifts slightly when followed by à: to value, to be attached to or fond of. Ils tiennent à leur indé pendance, They value their independence. The direct object can be replaced by y: C'est mon mari qui m'adonné cette é charpe et j'y tiens, It'smy husband who gave me this scarf and I'mvery fond of it. The expression si tu ytiens / si vous ytenez means If you insist (i.e."if you are attached to"or"value that thing"), which can also be expressed by si tu insistes / si vous insistez.

Just as qu'est-ce que is dropped in a type-3 interrogative, so it can be omitted from an exclamation: Qu'est-ce qu'il est pé nible ! (lesson note 3) → Qu'il est pé nible ! If asubject noun is added, it comes after the exclamation: Qu'ils sont sympathiques, ces gens ! How nice those people are!

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: French-speakers often refer to aplace or an institution by using aword closely related to it (the technical term for this is metonymy). Le Palais de l'Élysée (the Elysée Palace), usually shortened to l'Élysée, is the official residence of the French president, located at the bottom of les Champs-Élysées (Culture Note, lesson 15). Thus l'Élysée is ametonymy for the presidency, while le locataire (literally"the renter"or tenant) de l'Élysée is the president himself or (one day) herself. Productive phase: 33rd lesson

notes.content: The subjunctive of the irregular verb savoir is (que) je sache, tu saches, il/elle sache, nous sachions, vous sachiez, ils/elles sachent.

The masculine plural les é pinards means spinach (the singular is rarely used). Butter adds alittle something to spinach, making it more palatable. So the idiom mettre du beurre dans les é pinards means to top up one's income, add/earn alittle extra: Souvent les é tudiants cherchent des petits travaux afin de mettre du beurre dans les é pinards, Students often look for odd jobs in order to earn alittle extra.

une planche means aplank or board, as in une planche à dé couper, achopping ("cutting up") board. The expression avoir du pain sur la planche ("have bread on the board") resembles to have one'swork cut out, to have alot on one's plate: J'ai du pain sur la planche si je veux finir avant midi, I've got my work cut out if Iwant to finish by noon.
une pê che, apeach (lesson line 3), apparently gives plenty of energy because avoir la pê che means to be on top form or, to use afood idiom, to be full of beans.

The idiom en faire tout un fromage ("make awhole cheese of it") means to make abig fuss or song and dance. Elle en afait tout un fromage parce que j'avais dix minutes de retard, She made asong and dance because Iwas ten minutes late.
une andouille is acold sausage made of pork. The idiom faire l'andouille has nothing to do with butchery, however, because it means to act the fool. Used as an interjection, Andouille ! means Nitwit!

une poire, a pear, is used in the idiom couper la poire en deux ("to cut the pear in half"), meaning to compromise or meet someone halfway. Coupons la poire en deux : tu prends les enfants cette semaine et moi je les prendrai le week-end, Let'smeet halfway: you take the children this week and I'll take them for the weekend.

une auberge, an inn, is often found on restaurant signs, and also in the name of the youth hostel movement (les auberges de jeunesse). The expression ne pas ê tre sorti de l'auberge (always the negative form) means not to be out of the woods.

tomber dans les pommes ("fall into the apples") means to pass out, faint: Hier, elle é tait tellement fatigué e qu'elle est tombé e dans les pommes, She was so tired yesterday that she passed out. (The expression probably derives from se pâ mer, to swoon.)
The subjunctive of the irregular verb aller is (que) j'aille, tu ailles, il/elle aille, nous allions, vous alliez, ils/elles aillent.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: One problem arising from the shortage of French epicene nouns - those having only one form for the male and the female - is the need to use both forms, notably in public address. In these contexts, particularly speeches and media commentary, a noun'sfeminine and the masculine forms (in that order) are used jointly to ensure gender inclusivity (see lesson 66 line 3). TV presenters, for example, often start their shows with the greeting Chères téléspectatrices, chers téléspectateurs (whereas the English equivalent would be Dear viewers), and radio presenters say Chères auditrices, chers auditeurs (Dear listeners). Likewise, amagazine director might start an editorial with Chères lectrices, Chers lecteurs (Dear readers), while apublic official in, say, Lyon, might start ablogpost with Chères Lyonnaises, Chers Lyonnais. Cumbersome as they might seem, these dual forms are very important, for political reasons. Productive phase: 34th lesson

dialogue.french: Je vous appelle à propos des travaux de peinture que vous nous avez commandés.
dialogue.english: I'm calling you about the painting work you ordered from us.

dialogue.french: Je crains une mauvaise nouvelle... Dites-la-moi.
dialogue.english: I fear bad news... Tell me.

dialogue.english: Nobody warned you? I thought my colleague had called.

dialogue.english: Well, it's not certain that we can come next week.

dialogue.french: Je suis désolé de ne pas pouvoir être plus précis, mais ça ne dépend pas que de moi.

dialogue.french: Je vais faire appel à un collègue, mais il est sur un autre chantier en ce moment.

dialogue.english: I feel like we're not out of the inn (out of the woods)!

notes.content: Le subjonctif: the subjunctive: The subjunctive mood describes ahypothetical situation. It is generally used in asubordinate clause to talk about actions or events that are desirable, imagined or possible, and that generally depend on an initial verb in the indicative. The subjunctive exists in English but, being almost identical to the indicative, is rarely identified as such (except in phrases such as Iwish Iwere on holiday). In French, however, it is both common and obligatory. This is especially the case in subordinate clauses where the subject is different from the one in the main clause and where the action being described is in some way conditional, theoretical or subjective. In this case, the subordinate verb is preceded by que. For example, Je veux que tu sois heureuse, Iwant you to be happy (i.e. the person I'mtalking to seems miserable -my subjective opinion-and Iwish they weren't). There are four subjunctive tenses (present, past, imperfect and pluperfect) but in modern, conversational French, we generally use the present form (and occasionally the past). 1.1 Formation: The present subjunctive is formed by taking the third person plural of the present tense, dropping the final -ent and adding the endings shown below. aimer: j'aime, tu aimes, il/elle aime, nous aimions, vous aimiez, ils/elles aiment. finir: je finisse, tu finisse, il/elle finisse, nous finissions, vous finissiez, ils/elles finissent. attendre: j'attende, tu attendes, il/elle attende, nous attendions, vous attendiez, ils/elles attendent. Note that the first and second persons plural of the subjunctive are identical to the equivalent imperfect forms, but the structure of the sentence (and, often, the presence of que) should make it easy to distinguish between the two. The negative follows the usual pattern (vous n'aimiez pas, etc.), while the interrogative is almost never used. These rules apply to all regular and most irregular verbs. Nevertheless there are some irregular forms, especially with major verbs, which have to be memorised: ê tre: (que) je sois, tu sois, il/elle soit, nous soyons, vous soyez, ils/elles soient. avoir: (que) j'aie, tu aies, il/elle ait, nous ayons, vous ayez, ils/elles aient. faire: (que) je fasse, tu fasses, il/elle fasse, nous fassions, vous fassiez, ils/elles fassent. pouvoir: (que) je puisse, tu puisses, il/elle puisse, nous puissions, vous puissiez, ils/elles puissent. vouloir: (que) je veuille, tu veuilles, il/elle veuille, nous voulions, vous vouliez, ils/elles veuillent. aller: (que) j'aille, tu ailles, il/elle aille, nous allions, vous alliez, ils/elles aillent. There are other, stem-changing verbs, which we will see in the coming lessons. 1.2 Use: One of the most common uses of the subjunctive is when the subject of asentence expresses apersonal feeling, such as regret, hope, preference or expectation, about an action performed -or not-by another person. In this case the first verb is in the indicative, followed by que, and the second is in the subjunctive. Here are some examples: Je suis content / heureux / ravi que vous veniez ce soir. I'mpleased / happy / delighted that you're coming this evening. Elles veulent que vous té lé phoniez tout à l'heure. They want you to phone later on. Il espè re que son film puisse ê tre distribué en France. He is hoping that his movie can be distributed in France. Nous pré fé rons que vous leur demandiez. We prefer you to ask them. Similar verbs include aimer que (to wish that), attendre que, s'attendre à ce que (expect), demander que (ask that), douter que (doubt that), ê tre dé solé que (be sorry that), ê tre triste que (be sad that), ê tre dommage que (be ashame that), exiger que (demand that) and insister pour que (insist that). Go back to lesson and review these verbs in context, noting how the subjunctive in the subordinate clause is"sub-joined"to the indicative verb in the main clause. - The subjunctive is also obligatory with impersonal verbs, especially falloir: to be necessary that, etc. Il faut que tu finisses rapidement, You have to finish quickly. Other impersonal forms, such as ê tre certain / ê tre sû r que, logically take the indicative in the affirmative: Il est certain que nous pouvons les aider, We can certainly help them. In the negative, however, the outcome is in doubt, so the subjunctive is used: Il n'est pas certain que puissions les aider. It'snot certain that we can help them. - The subjunctive is used after subordinating conjunctions, such as bien que, quoi que and pourvu que, that introduce ahypothesis or condition. These, too, are followed by the subjunctive. Bien que nous soyons amis, je ne peux pas vous aider. Even though we're friends, I can'thelp you. Quoi que tu fasses, rien ne changera. Whatever you do, nothing will change. Pourvu qu'il vienne ! As long as he comes! We'll see other examples in the coming lessons. - Similarly, the subjunctive is necessary if we use an imperative to posit a condition: Supposons que quelqu'un vienne te dire :"Vous avez gagné au loto". Que ferais-tu ? Let'sassume that someone comes along and says:"You've won the lotto."What would you do? - The subjunctive is also obligatory with certain time conjunctions: Faites-vite, avant qu'elle parte en vacances. Do it quickly, before she leaves on holiday. Je reste ici jusqu'à ce que tu me dises la vé rité, I'mstaying here until you tell me the truth. In the next six lessons, we will look at other types of construction in which the subjunctive is obligatory, as well as cases where it may or may not be used, depending in the shade of meaning.

Pronoun order: When several indirect pronouns are used before a verb, they have to follow astrict order. You are already familiar with the basic patterns, seen in the course of previous lessons. One way to remember the proper sequence is to visualise asoccer team playing in a 5-3-2 formation, with agoalkeeper (y) and the ball (en). The sequence is: me / te / se / nous / vous, le / la / les, lui / leur, y, en. The sequence is actually easier than it might seem. In most cases only two indirect pronouns are ever used together (the maximum is three), with the most usual combination being Column and Column 2. The pronouns in the first and third columns never go together. Similarly, pronouns in the same column cannot be placed together. For example, Ils se pré sentent à nous, They introduce themselves to us (never *Ils nous se pré sentent). Look at these examples, all of which start with asubject pronoun, which is closest to the verb. Je te donnerai l'adresse de la boutique. → Je te la donnerai. I'll give you the address of the shop. → Iwill give it to you. Elle veut donner le vase à Alex. → Elle veut le lui donner. She wants to give the vase to Alex. → She wants to give it to him. Nous avons proposé le voyage à nos enfants. → Nous le leur avons proposé. We offered the trip to our children. → We offered it to them. Vous me parlez souvent de vos amis. → Vous m'en parlez souvent. You often tell me about your friends. → You often tell me about them. Nous emmenons nos enfants à Nî mes demain. → Nous les yemmenons demain. They're going to Nî mes tomorrow. → They're going there tomorrow. In the negative, the pronouns come immediately after the first negative particle, ne, while pas, comes after the verb, as usual: Je ne te le donnerai pas, Il ne la lui donnera pas, etc. With an imperative, the word order is slightly different. First, we know that me and te become moi and toi (lesson note 3). Second, the second-column pronouns precede those in the first column: Passez-moi la tablette. → Passez-la moi. Donnez-lui le miel. → Donnez-le lui.

Negative constructions: The simple way to negate averb is with ne... pas (Il comprend → Il ne comprend pas). But there are other constructions in which pas is replaced by an adverb. Let'sreview them: • ne... jamais, never: Ils ne veulent jamais venir en vacances avec nous. They never want to come on holiday with us. For emphasis, the adverb sometimes comes first: Jamais ils ne veulent venir en vacances... Never do they want to come on holiday. • ne... plus, no longer, no more: On ne peut plus continuer comme ç a, We can'tgo on like this any longer. Remember that adefinite or indefinite article coming after plus becomes de: Il y aune grè ve / Il y ades grè ves → Il n'y aplus de grè ve/grè ves. • ne... que, only: Je n'ai que deux minutes à vous accorder, Ican only give you two minutes. In some cases, ne... que can be replaced by seulement: J'ai seulement deux minutes à vous accorder, but this is considered less elegant. • ne... aucun(e), no, none: Nous n'avons aucune nouvelle de lui, We have no news from him. Aucun(e) can be used alone in response to a question: Avez-vous des nouvelles de lui ? - Aucune. Have you had any news from him? - None at all. • ne... rien, nothing: Je n'ai rien à vous dire, I've got nothing to say to you. When negating acompound verb, such as avoir besoin, rien comes after the partitive article: Je n'ai besoin de rien. However, where rien is used as the direct object of a sentence, it is not part of the negative construction: Elle ne mange jamais rien, She never eats anything. • ne... personne, no one / anyone, nobody / anybody: Il n'aime personne, He doesn'tlike anyone. If personne is the subject of the sentence, then the verb needs only the particle ne (remember the rule against double negatives): Personne ne l'aime, No one likes him/her. • ne... ni... ni, either... or: Je n'ai ni le temps ni l'envie, Ihave neither the time nor the inclination. As with ne... personne, ni... ni... can negate the subjects of the sentence. In this case, unlike English, the verb is generally in the plural: Ni la pluie ni la neige ne me gê nent. Neither the rain nor the snow bothers me. In some cases, though, the singular can also be used, especially if each of the subjects is considered individually (Ni Rachida ni Anne n'est la mè re de cet enfant). But the rules for this are quite complex, so, if in doubt, use the plural. In some cases, two negative adverbs can be used together -for example, Je ne l'ai plus jamais revu, Inever saw him again-but the meaning will always be clear. Finally, in spoken French, the ne part of anegative construction is often"swallowed,"leaving only the adverb ("il vient jamais", for example). Of course, this is incorrect and should not be imitated, but you will certainly hear it.

The euphonic tin the interrogative: Whereas est-ce que is the most common interrogative construction in everyday French, especially for oral expression (Est-ce qu'il vit à Paris ?), the inverted interrogative is more frequent in written and formal contexts. In terms of pronunciation, this poses no problem if the verb form ends in aconsonant (vit-il...), which can be liaised with the initial vowel of the pronoun ([veet-eel]); but if the verb ends in a vowel, Il parle le franç ais, the liaison is impossible and an inverted form would be hard (and ugly) to pronounce. So, to avoid this, aeuphonic t, which does not change the meaning, is inserted between the verb and the pronoun and joined to them by hyphens: Parle-t-il le franç ais ? (In the third person plural, however, this device is unnecessary: Parlent-ils ?). Lastly, if the third person singular ends in d (il prend, for example), asimple inversion is sufficient (prend-il); however, that dis pronounced as aeuphonic t: [prœhn-teel].

More idioms: food: Since France has an enviable gastronomic reputation, it is hardly surprising that many of the idioms in its language are concerned with food and eating. Here is abrief recap of what you have learned: avoir du pain sur la planche (have one'swork cut out), avoir la pê che / frite (be full of beans / on top form), couper la poire en deux (meet halfway, compromise), ê tre dans les choux (be in atough spot, in trouble), faire l'andouille (act the fool), en faire tout un fromage (make asong and dance), mettre du beurre dans les é pinards (earn alittle extra), ne pas ê tre sorti de l'auberge (not to be out of the woods), ne pas gagner un radis (not to earn a bean), tomber dans les pommes (pass out). All these expressions are used in everyday communications. Two other common expressions relating to food are un navet (literally aturnip but, idiomatically, applied to a film, a flop, a turkey, etc.: Son dernier film est un vrai navet, His/Her latest movie is rubbish) and avoir un cœur d'artichaut, (literally"to have an artichoke's heart") to be flighty, to fall in love easily. In the latter expression, the person so described (Il aun cœur d'artichaut, celui-là) has as many paramours as an artichoke heart has leaves. And don'tforget the two proverbs seen in lesson 78: Les voyages forment la jeunesse, Travel broadens the mind, and C'est dans les vieux pots qu'on fait la bonne/meilleure soupe. The best wine comes in old bottles.

title: Comment ça, je massacre le français ?

dialogue.french: Tu sors par ce temps, Michel ? Tu ne vois pas qu'il fait un froid glacial ?
dialogue.english: You're going out in this weather, Michel? Can't you see it's freezing cold?

dialogue.french: Et ils annoncent à nouveau de gros orages pour tout à l'heure.
dialogue.english: And they're forecasting big thunderstorms again for later.

dialogue.french: Il est où ton pardessus ? Et, de toute façon, où tu vas à cette heure-ci ?
dialogue.english: Where's your overcoat? And, anyway, where are you going at this hour?

dialogue.french: Pourquoi tu veux savoir ? Ce ne sont pas tes oignons, mon frère.
dialogue.english: Why do you want to know? It's none of your business, brother.

dialogue.french: C'est quoi, ton problème ? Pourquoi tu es si grognon ce matin ?
dialogue.english: What's your problem? Why are you so grumpy this morning?

dialogue.french: Je vais à ma banque, si tu veux savoir. Ça te va comme explication ?
dialogue.english: I'm going to my bank, if you must know. Does that work as an explanation?

dialogue.french: On m'a appelé et on m'a demandé de passer à l'agence au plus vite.
dialogue.english: They called me and asked me to come to the branch as soon as possible.

dialogue.french: Il paraît que mon compte est à découvert. Je suis tombé des nues quand je l'ai appris.
dialogue.english: It seems my account is overdrawn. I was gobsmacked when I heard.

dialogue.french: Ils t'ont appelé quand ? C'est quand le rendez-vous ?
dialogue.english: When did they call you? When's the appointment?

dialogue.french: Tu pars à quelle heure ? Ton conseiller de clientèle sera là-bas, au rendez-vous ?
dialogue.english: What time are you leaving? Will your account manager be there at the meeting?

dialogue.french: Tu poses toutes ces questions pourquoi ? Tu mets ton nez partout.
dialogue.english: Why are you asking all these questions? You stick your nose in everywhere.

dialogue.french: Tu ne sais pas qu'il ne faut pas être curieux et se mêler des affaires des autres ?
dialogue.english: Don't you know you shouldn't be nosy and meddle in other people's business?

dialogue.french: Bon, assez discuté. Quelle heure il est ? Il faut que je file.
dialogue.english: Right, enough chat. What time is it? I need to get going.

dialogue.french: Arrêtez, vous deux, pour l'amour du ciel ! Où avez-vous appris le français ?
dialogue.english: Stop it, you two, for heaven's sake! Where did you learn French?

dialogue.french: Je vous écoute depuis cinq minutes, et vous massacrez la langue de Molière !
dialogue.english: I've been listening to you for five minutes, and you're massacring the language of Molière!

dialogue.french: On doit dire « Où allez-vous ? » ou « Quand est ton rendez-vous ? ».
dialogue.english: You should say 'Where are you going?' or 'When is your appointment?'.

dialogue.french: De même, on ne dit pas « Il est arrivé quand ? » mais « Quand est-il arrivé ? ».
dialogue.english: Likewise, you don't say 'He arrived when?' but 'When did he arrive?'.

dialogue.french: Et « À quelle heure pars-tu ? » est dix fois plus élégant que « Tu pars à quelle heure ? ».
dialogue.english: And 'What time are you leaving?' is ten times more elegant than 'You're leaving at what time?'.

dialogue.french: Pour en revenir à toi, Michel. Pourquoi tu vas... euh... vas-tu à la banque ?
dialogue.english: To come back to you, Michel. Why are you going... er... are you going to the bank?

dialogue.french: C'est-à-dire que j'ai emprunté ta carte de crédit et je me suis acheté quelques petits trucs...
dialogue.english: That is to say I borrowed your credit card and bought myself a few little things...

dialogue.french: Tu as dépensé combien, espèce de petit voyou ? Pardon : combien as-tu dépensé, mon frère adoré ?
dialogue.english: How much did you spend, you little rascal? Sorry: how much have you spent, my beloved brother?

dialogue.french: Occupe-toi de tes affaires. Je veux dire : La curiosité est un vilain défaut, cher ami.
dialogue.english: Mind your own business. I mean: Curiosity is an ugly flaw, dear friend.

dialogue.french: Vilain défaut ? Et comment !
dialogue.english: Ugly flaw? You can say that again!

notes.content: The verb haï r, to hate, is awkward. The diaresis, showing that both aand imust be pronounced, is present in the infinitive [eye-ear] and the three present-plural forms (haï ssons, [eye-eessoh"], haï ssez [eye-eessay], haï ssent [eye-eess]) but not the singular: hais and hait, both of which are pronounced [ay].

comment, how, is used as an interjection to express surprise, annoyance or disbelief (lesson line 15), just like What... ?. Comment, tu as perdu mes clé s de voiture ? What, you've lost my car keys? It can be used like Comment ç a (lesson note 2): Comment ç a, je parle trop fort ? What do you mean, I'mtalking too loudly? Comment can be used as apositive intensifier, Et comment !, in response to acomment or question, like Ishould say so!, You bet!, etc. Donc tu as aimé le jeu ? - Et comment ! So you enjoyed the game? - Didn't I just! (Don'tconfuse the intensifier and the interrogative: see the exercises below.)

un pardessus is an overcoat. The word comes from the hyphenated preposition par-dessus ("by above"), meaning over: Mets un pull par-dessus ta chemise, il fait un froid glacial, Put asweater over your shirt, it'sfreezing cold.

In afamiliar register, where the subject of an interrogative sentence is apersonal pronoun (je, me, etc), the question can be formed simply by starting with an interrogative word and avoiding the inversion or est-ce que: Où vous allez ? Where are you going? instead of Où allez-vous / Où est-ce que vous allez ? Though not recommended, particularly when writing, these idiomatic interrogatives are very common.

un oignon (sometimes spelled ognon), an onion, is used in several idiomatic expressions where the English equivalent is business. The most common are Ce ne sont pas (or simply Ce n'est pas) mes oignons, It'snone of my business, and Occupe-toi de tes oignons, Mind your own business.

Another idiomatic way of forming aquestion is to precede the interrogative word (qui, comment, etc.) with C'est... : C'est qui, ton meilleur ami ? Who'syour best friend? Comment tu es venu ce matin ? How did you get here this morning? These idiomatic forms are often used in advertisements, song lyrics, etc. to reflect everyday speech.

dé couvrir, (from couvrir, to cover, see lesson 41, note 5), means both to discover and to uncover. The past participle, dé couvert, is used as an adjective: une piscine dé couverte, an open-air swimming pool. But the noun un dé couvert means an overdraft (i.e. outgoings not covered by incoming amounts). The adjective is ê tre à dé couvert, to be overdrawn, to have an overdraft.

The adjective nu means naked, bare (and, of course, nude), etc. Il faisait tellement chaud que nous é tions torse nu, It was so hot that we were shirtless ("bare torso"). However, in the expression tomber des nues, it is the plural of an old word for acloud (un nuage in modern French). The meaning of the idiom is to be flabbergasted, stunned: Je suis tombé des nues quand j'ai appris la nouvelle, Iwas flabbergasted when Igot the news.

filer literally means to spin (cotton, etc.), hence un fil a thread, awire (remember passer un coup de fil, lesson note 4). Used idiomatically, the verb means to leave, run off, etc. Avery common expression is Il faut que je file, Ihave to dash.

In technical French, une espè ce is a species. But in ordinary conversation, it means a sort/kind of. La galette est une espè ce de crê pe au blé noir, The"galette"is asort of buckwheat pancake. The word is also used in afamiliar register, without the indefinite article and followed by an interjection (just like you little... in English). Espè ce d'idiot ! You little idiot! (Un voyou means alout or ruffian, and, when applied to a child, a rascal.)

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Molière, the stage name of Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, is one of France'sgreatest playwrights, who lived from around 1622 to 1673. In works such as Tartuffe (The Imposter), Le Misanthrope (The Misanthropist) and L'Avare (The Miser), he skewered pretention, power and hypocrisy with biting satire and brilliant wit. His influence on the language is such that French is often referred to figuratively as la langue de Molière (for comparison, English is la langue de Shakespeare). Much of the language you will be learning in these last sixteen lessons is idiomatic and colloquial. By now, you should be able not only to detect these registers but also to recognise more or less instinctively when and where they are used. Nevertheless, you can count on us to continue informing and advising you. Amusez-vous ! (Enjoy!) Productive phase: 36th lesson

notes.content: Remember that, in arelative clause, qui replaces the subject and que the object (lesson section 3). Both can refer to either people or things. And whereas the relative can often be omitted in English (one of the markets we have been trying to penetrate), this is not the case in French (un des marché s que nous essayons de pé né trer). Qui can also replace the indirect object after a preposition: la personne à qui nous confierons le poste, the person to whom we will give the job.

The relative pronoun dont, seen in lesson line 20, basically means of whom, whose or of which, in reference to the object of arelative clause: Je suis fier de cette jeune é quipe → L'é quipe dont je suis fier est jeune. The team of which Iam proud is young. Dont can also be used, as in line 17, to translate including (or of which): Deux chambres d'hô tel, dont une avec une salle de bain, Two hotel rooms, one of which with a bathroom.

The idiomatic construction il se peut que (from pouvoir) indicates a possibility, like it may be that, etc. And because of the conditionality, the accompanying verb is in the subjunctive: Il se peut que je sois en retard car j'ai une ré union à midi, Imay be late because Ihave anoon meeting.

une piste means atrack or trail. Among the many other meanings are an airport runway (piste d'aé roport), adance floor (piste de danse) or, for skiers, a run, slope (or... piste!). But the noun is often used figuratively, as in Il faut trouver une solution rapidement, et nous avons plusieurs pistes à explorer, We need to find asolution quickly and there are several avenues to explore. In short, une piste is something that leads somewhere!

The regular verb privilé gier (the root of privilege) is a faux-ami, meaning to favour: Notre socié té privilé gie une approche é thique, Our company favours an ethical approach. However, the past participle retains the idea of privileged or special: La France aune relation privilé gié e avec plusieurs pays du sud, France has aspecial relationship with several southern countries. As always, the context will dictate the appropriate translation.

une cause, a cause, a reason, features in anumber of expressions, notably à cause de, because of (lesson line 6) and en tout é tat de cause ("in any state of cause"), in any case, anyway: En tout é tat de cause, vous devez prendre vos vacances avant la fin du mois de dé cembre, In any case, you must take your holidays before the end of December. The expression is synonymous with quoi qu'il en soit (lesson note 7), and both are quite formal.

In many ways, French is more grammatically precise than English. Here is agood example: les marché s suisse et belge refers to the Swiss market and the German market, each considered individually, whereas les marché s suisses et belges implies several markets in both countries. In both cases, the English translation is the Swiss and German markets. In spoken French, there is no difference in pronunciation between the singular and plural forms, but the difference is obvious in the written language.

When penser means to think about, consider, it can be followed directly by an infinitive: Je pense acheter une voiture neuve, I'mthinking about buying anew car. Of course, if we repeat the pronoun, the verb that follows penser has to be conjugated: Je pense que je vais acheter une voiture neuve, but there is no difference in meaning between the two constructions. Another common verb that can be followed by the infinitive is croire, to believe: Je crois savoir que vous ê tes avocat, Iunderstand that you are a lawyer.

Here'sanother example of averb that is formed from an adjective and can be tricky to translate: fidè le means faithful, so fidé liser ("make faithful"), means something along the lines of to develop/build loyalty: Nous devons fidé liser notre clientè le et analyser ses besoins, We need to develop our customers' loyalty and analyse their needs. As is often the case with this type of verb, there is no word-for-word translation. You need to identify the root word in order to find the right shade of meaning.

This is the personalised form of falloir (lesson section 2) with the indirect object pronoun (me) and the direct object pronoun replacing the noun (here, la femme, line 18). So, for example, if the direct object is masculine plural (les atouts) and the indirect object pronoun is nous, the sentence is Il nous les faut, We must have them. When faced with asentence containing multiple pronouns, always try to break it down into its component parts.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: René Descartes was a 17th century mathematician and philosopher who argued that knowledge can be achieved only through rational reasoning. His most famous formulation, Je pense, donc je suis (I think, therefore I am), is part of French culture, both highbrow and popular. Descartes' influence and his reputation for rational reasoning is such that the nation prides itself on being cartésien (Cartesian), that is to say dispassionate and logical. Productive phase: 37th lesson

notes.content: Beware of words that are spelled the same in both languages. Although you may know the rules, it'sso easy to confuse the English and French pronunciations. Thus assassin and suspect are pronounced [assassahn] and [sewspay], respectively.

Remember that descendre is one of those verbs that can used transitively and intransitively (lesson section 2). Among its transitive meanings, based on the notion of to lower, is to shoot down or, in slang, to bump off.

Like its English cognate, super can be used as an (invariable) adjective - Elle est super, la nouvelle pharmacienne, The new pharmacist is great - and an intensifier, before an adjective: Elle est super sympa, She'ssuper nice. The word can also be used as an exclamation: Super ! Excellent! Great, etc. Don'tconfuse it with another invariable adjective, superbe, superb, glorious, etc. Quelle journé e superbe !, What aglorious day!

With some verbs, ne is used as an expletive, aword that fills out asentence without adding to the meaning. This usage is often found in subjunctive constructions: Le mauvais temps aempê ché qu'ils ne partent, The bad weather prevented them from leaving. More details in an upcoming lesson.

This is the pluperfect tense, formed with the imperfect of avoir (or ê tre, depending on the verb) and the past participle. It is used in more or less the same way as its English counterpart: Elle é tait dé jà partie quand je suis arrivé, She had already left when I arrived.

The irregular verb se taire means to be/fall silent or keep quiet: Quand je demande qui va payer, tout le monde se tait, When Iask who is going to pay, everyone keeps quiet. The imperative Taisez-vous (familiar: Tais-toi) means Be quiet or Shut up, depending on the context. The past participle (following the same pattern as plaire, plu, to please/pleased) is tu: Tout à coup, il s'est tu, Suddenly, he fell silent.

Don'tconfuse the feminine noun la fin, the end, with the adjective fin(e), meaning thin: Ajoutez une fine couche de chocolat, Add athin layer of chocolate. By extension, it can also mean fine, delicate, high-class, etc. Notre magasin propose une gamme complè te de vins fins, Our shop offers afull range of fine wines. Fin can also be used as an intensifier, meaning last and final: Ils habitent au fin fond de la campagne, They live deep in the countryside. Whence the meaning of the expression le fin mot de l'histoire,"the last word of the story,"i.e. the real truth, the bottom line.

The adverb tant que means as long as: Tant que vous buvez avec modé ration, vous n'avez pas de soucis, As long as you drink in moderation, you have nothing to worry about. In some contexts, tant que can also mean until: Vous ne pouvez pas accé der à votre compte tant que vous n'avez pas payé, You can'taccess your account until you have paid. In this case, it has the same meaning as jusqu'à ce que:... jusqu'à ce que Laurent soumette un document... (see lesson line 14).

Formed from vrai, true, and sembler, to seem, la vraisemblance means likelihood. It is generally used in the expression selon toute vraisemblance, in all likelihood/probability. The adjective vraisemblable therefore means likely: Il est trè s vraisemblable qu'elle perdra son travail, It'svery likely that she will lose her job.
We know that drô le means funny (lesson line 15). And, as in English, the underlying meaning can be strange, peculiar: C'est un drô le de type, ton ami, Your friend is astrange guy.

One way to avoid the subjunctive is to change the structure of the sentence. For example, Avant qu'il soit un espion, notre agent é tait comptable, Before he was a spy, our agent was an accountant can be recast as Avant de devenir espion, etc. We'll see more ways of getting around the subjunctive later on.

extras.content: French uses the present tense for narrative and descriptive purposes when talking about past events, as Gaëtan'sstory shows. Known as le présent historique, or historical present, this usage is not confined to spoken or colloquial contexts, as is often the case in English (though both languages use the tense in news headlines). One of the reasons for the historical present - apart from bringing past events vividly to life - is to avoid le passé simple (also known as le prétérit), which is used almost exclusively in written prose, particularly literature. We will look briefly at the passé simple in the last set of lessons. Productive phase: 38th lesson

notes.content: Certain adverbs are always followed by the subjunctive. We have already seen quoi que (lesson note 7); others include qui que, whoever, où que, wherever, and quel que, whatever (the latter agreeing in number and gender with the following noun).

This lesson is based around anumber of common slang terms, which are explained in detail in lesson 91. For now, just read the translation of the dialogue, bearing in mind that many colloquial terms in French have no direct equivalents in English, and vice versa.

un gars is afamiliar word, derived from un garç on, and is sometimes used like a lad. But the most common usage is as asynonym of un type, aguy (lesson note 9), especially in the plural: Venez voir, les gars, Hey guys, come and look. Asynonym is un mec: Ce mec n'ajamais lu un bouquin de sa vie, That guy'snever read abook in his life. (Note how the use of the familiar un bouquin, seen in lesson note 10, reinforces the familiar register of the sentence.) Un mec can also be used in the sense of boyfriend: Elle aquitté son mec, She'sleft her man.

Derived from un carré, a square, the adverb carré ment means candidly, bluntly, etc.: Je lui ai dit carré ment ce que je pensais de lui, Itold him straight out what Ithought of him. The word is widely used as an intensifier: Ce gars est carré ment dingue, That's guy'stotally nuts. (The"standard"word would be complè tement, completely). Lastly, carré ment can be used as an assertion expressing agreement or support: Tu aimes ce chanteur ? - Carré ment ! Do you like that singer? - Totally!

une fleur, aflower (seen in lesson line 1), is used in several familiar expressions where, as in English, it embodies something prime or excellent. Les deux comé diens sont dans la fleur de l'â ge, The two actors are in the prime of life. Thus faire une fleur (à quelqu'un) means to do someone agood turn or favour. L'hô tel nous afait une fleur, en nous donnant une suite au lieu d'une chambre double, The hotel did us afavour by giving us asuite instead of adouble room.

In afamiliar register, ficher (which, in standard French means to put on file) replaces standard verbs, particularly faire, meaning to do, to get up to, etc. Qu'est-ce qu'il fiche, Georges ? Il est en retard, What's Georges up to? He's late. The pronominal form, s'en fiche(r) (line 21), is usually found in expressions such as Je m'en fiche, I don't care. But the past participle, fichu, used with ê tre, means to be finished, done for, etc. Si les joueurs entrent sur le terrain avec la peur au ventre, ils sont fichus, If the players are afraid when they take to the field, they're done for.

The familiar adjective dingue (see lesson note 6) means crazy, and, as in English, can be both meliorative - On apassé une soiré e dingue chez eux, We had acrazy evening at their house - and pejorative: Cette assurance nous coû te un fric dingue, That insurance is costing us astupid amount of money. The noun un dingue means a nutcase.

The subjunctive is used in relative clauses with superlatives (le plus gros, le meilleur) and other expressions of uniqueness (le seul, l'unique). For example, C'est l'hiver le plus froid qu'on ait connu depuis longtemps, It'sthe coldest winter we have known in a while; or Tu es la seule personne qui puisse m'aider, You're the only person who can help me.
The imperative form of ê tre is identical to the subjunctive. Il faut que vous soyez / tu sois là à midi, You must be there at noon; Soyez / Sois là à midi, Be there at noon.

notes.content: The idiomatic expression faire la tê te means to sulk, pull along face, etc. Pourquoi est-ce qu'il me fait la tê te ? Je ne lui ai rien fait ! Why'she sulking? I haven'tdone anything to him! You can also use an indirect object: Pourquoi est-ce que tu me fais la tê te ? Why are pulling that face at me? See also note 10.

Derived from le gras, fat, blubber, etc. (and the origin of grease), the adjective gras(se), greasy, means fatty (and, by extension, fatty foods): É vitez de manger gras avant une activité physique, Avoid eating fatty foods before physical activity. The expression faire la grasse matiné e, to lie in, sleep late: J'aime faire la grasse matiné e le dimanche, Ilove lying in on Sundays.

faire un/le point is anavigational term meaning to take aprecise bearing. That notion of precision is echoed in the expression'scolloquial usage, where the basic meaning is to review or sum up a situation, to bring someone up to date, etc. Nous allons faire un point sur les orages dans le Midi, We're going to update you on the storms in the south of France. Logically, the idiom is often used in connection with news coverage.

une croix, a cross, is found in the idiomatic expression faire une croix sur, meaning to forgo, write off, say goodbye to, etc. (like avaledictory sign of the cross): On devra faire une croix sur les vacances à la montagne cette anné e, We'll have to forgo our mountain holiday this year. If the object noun has already been mentioned, it is replaced by dessus, on it, to avoid repetition: Si tu lui prê tes ta moto, tu peux faire une croix dessus, If you lend him your motorbike, you can kiss it goodbye.

Il faut le faire literally means It has to be done: Si vous voulez le faire, il faut le faire maintenant, If you want to do it, you've got to do it now. Used as an exclamation, however, the meaning is something like That takes some doing/beating! It can be admirative or ironic, depending on the context: Il aperdu non seulement ses clé s mais aussi son portefeuille : il faut le faire !, He'slost not only his keys but also his wallet. That'squite an achievement. (In spoken French, the third-person pronoun is often dropped: Faut le faire !)

This"causative"form of the reflexive, se faire followed by an infinitive (lesson line 17), tells us that the subject of the sentence is acted upon by something or someone. As often with the reflexive, the equivalent structure in English uses got: Il s'est fait aider par un journaliste pour é crire l'article, He got help from ajournalist to write the article.

faire cadeau de means to give something away, often as a present: Mon copain m'afait cadeau de cette ceinture, My boyfriend gave me this belt. In the negative, the expression is used figuratively with the meaning not to spare someone or let off lightly. L'é quipe n'apas fait de cadeau à ses adversaires, The team gave their opponents ahard time.

This is the inverted -hence, more elegant-form of comment ç a se fait... ? (lesson note 1). Here, however, the following verb is in the subjunctive because the speaker is expressing doubt or uncertainty.

The fishery term une gaffe, agaff or hook, is used in the expression faire une gaffe, to make ablunder (lesson line 3). However, faire gaffe (without adefinite article) means to pay attention to or be wary of: Il faut faire gaffe parce que l'é tagè re est trè s lourde, We have to be careful because the shelf is very heavy. The verb is more commonly used as an imperative: Faites/Fais gaffe : c'est vachement lourd ! Be careful, it'sdamn heavy. Whatever the context, the expression is familiar, replacing the more formal faire attention (lesson line 8).

The idiomatic expression n'en faire qu'à sa tê te has nothing to do with sulking (note 1): it means to do exactly as one pleases/wants (listening only to what'sin one's head, presumably): Quoi qu'on lui dise, elle n'en fera qu'à sa tê te, Whatever we say to her, she'll do exactly as he wants.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Among the cultural specificities of the French lifestyle, la bise holds aspecial place. The term faire la bise literally means to give ("make") a kiss, (and, by extension, to be on familiar terms with someone), and refers to the habit of greeting friends with apeck on both cheeks. Just how many pecks? The number varies between two (possibly the most common) and four, but it all depends on the relationship with the person, their age, and even the region of France. notes.content: There is no difference in pronunciation between the masculine and feminine forms of the nouns reviewed in this lesson. Context aside, the only way to distinguish between them is through the preceding article. The"h"in haricot is aspirated (in contrast to heure, for example), which is why the vowel in the definite and partitive articles is not elided (le / de / des haricots : [luh / duh / day areekoh]. Remember that, despite the name, an aspirated"h"in is not pronounced.

The regular verb ignorer is a faux-ami, meaning not to know or to be unaware of. J'ignore tout de sa vie, Iknow nothing about his/her life. Thus, in the negative, it means not to be unaware of! L'ex-pré sident n'ignore pas comment il aperdu les é lections, The former president is not unaware of how he lost the elections. However, the feminine noun l'ignorance means ignorance.

The coordinating conjunction et... et is one of the constructions used to translate both... and (lesson note 2): J'aime et les petits pois et les haricots, Ilike both peas and beans. In spoken French it is not as common as à la fois (lesson note 7), probably because the open [ay] sound is harder to hear.

Yet another use of un coup (lesson note 3). The set phrase du coup, generally found at the beginning of aspoken sentence or clause, means as a result: Le match est annulé ; du coup, ils ne viennent pas samedi. The match has been cancelled. As a result, they're not coming on Saturday.

First seen in lesson line 17, pour autant is the equivalent of the phrase for all that: Il apris sa retraite, mais sa vie ne s'est pas arrê té e pour autant, He has retired but his life hasn'tstopped for all that. If the sentence contains acontrastive conjunction, such as mais, but, there is often no need to translate pour autant directly (He may have retired but his life hasn't stopped).

See lesson note 4. The past participle can be used without the auxiliary in elliptical clauses introduced by adverbs such as aussitô t: Aussitô t le dernier invité parti, nous avons é teint toutes les lumiè res, As soon as the last guest had left, we turned off all the lights. This type of construction is generally used in written rather than spoken French.

We know that un dé faut is aflaw (hence a defect, lesson line 22) and is also used in the expression à dé faut, failing that (lesson line 16). The same notion of lack or defect crops up in the expression faire dé faut, to be lacking, to be short of or failed by, etc. Le temps me fait dé faut, I don'thave enough time. By extension, another meaning is to be let down by: C'est un bon joueur mais son manque de vitesse lui afait dé faut, He's agood player but he was let down by his lack of speed.

un manche means ahandle or shaft (un manche à balai, a broomstick). The word can be used idiomatically to indicate clumsiness or inability: Tu es rentré dans un arbre ! Tu conduis comme un manche, You've hit a tree! You're auseless driver. Thus s'yprendre comme un manche means to go about something badly, make amess of things.

We know the verb marier (one"r") and the past participle/adjective marié(e). The derived noun un(e) marié(e) means agroom / a bride. J'ai pris plein de photos de la marié e et du marié, Itook loads of photos of the bride and groom. Don'tconfuse these words with un mari (a husband) and une femme (a wife). (We have also learned the formal term un é poux / une é pouse, lesson note 7).

In the masculine un physique refers to physical appearance (or... physique!), particularly in phrases like Elle aun physique agré able, She's nice-looking. Un jeune premier is aromantic male lead in a movie, hence the expression avoir un physique de jeune premier, to have movie-star good looks.

The indefinite adjective quelque chose is occasionally used as amasculine noun in the expression un petit quelque chose, alittle something (even if the thing in question is feminine): Cette comé dienne aun petit quelque chose en plus, That actress has alittle something extra.

Every French schoolchild learns the three nouns that are masculine in the singular and feminine in the plural: un amour, a love; un dé lice, a delight; un orgue, an organ (instrument). The reasons are obscure and, in our case, any mistakes would be easily excused.

extras.content: France comprises not only the country on the mainland (Culture Note, lesson 61) but also anumber of overseas territories and départements, known collectively as la France d'autre-mer. Because of its shape, the continental European part is often referred to, especially in the media, as l'Hexagone. Productive phase: 41st lesson

notes.content: Formal and informal interrogatives: We know that the first, raised-intonation interrogative (1-1) is customary in everyday and colloquial speech but is not usually written, while the second form, (1-2 est-ce que), can be written and spoken. The third, inverted interrogative, is more formal. Acommon feature of 1-1questions is to place the interrogative word at the end of the question, instead of at the beginning in 1-2and 1-3. Que and quoi behave slightly differently. Choosing which form to use depends on the context and the person speaking. Non-native speakers are often granted less latitude and must therefore abide by all the rules.

The causative: This construction is used where the subject causes the action of the verb to happen. Often rendered in English with get and apast participle, the causative is formed with faire, conjugated according to the subject, and an infinitive. The reflexive form of the causative describes an action performed on the subject. If adirect object is used, it comes after both parts of the verb. With both the non-reflexive and the reflexive causative form, the direct object may be replaced by a pronoun, placed before faire.

The subjunctive: afew last details: The subjunctive is used in clauses containing superlative adjectives or descriptions of uniqueness, as well as indefinite expressions. With superlative adjectives: the subjunctive is used after asuperlative asserting the unrivalled status of the thing being referred to. Descriptions of uniqueness: Il est le seul qui puisse me comprendre. Indefinite expressions: où que, qui que, quoi que, quel que. The subjunctive is not always obligatory; the choice of tense depends on several factors and the speaker's perceptions.

The do'sand don'ts of dont: The relative pronoun dont translates of which, of who(m) in relative clauses. It relates to the object, whether animate or inanimate, replacing the partitive de. Dont also translates whose and can refer to an animate or inanimate object. Dont is used when singling out elements in a group.

Le plus-que-parfait: The pluperfect is formed with the imperfect of avoir or ê tre as an auxiliary and the past participle of the verb. There are no particular problems of usage because the plus-que-parfait is very similar to its English equivalent.

Slang: Using slang can be tricky because it implies an intimate knowledge of the culture. Here is aselection of terms: bagnole, caisse (car); balaise/balè ze, costaud (brawny); baraque (house); bé cane (scooter); causer (talk); dingue (crazy); fichu (done for); flingue, flingueur (gun, gunman); fric, pognon, blé, thune (money); fringues, fringuer (clothes, to dress); gars, mec, type (guy); indic (informer); pinard (wine); pote (mate); ré glo (above-board); tifs (hair); toubib (doctor); Top ! / Nickel ! (Great!).

notes.content: This lesson shows how prefixes are used to alter the meaning of verbs, nouns and adjectives. For example, é-can indicate distance (loin, far → é loigné(e), remote, distanced) or achange of state (court, short → é courté(e)). The noun le cerveau, the brain, forms the basis of é cervelé, scatterbrained (line 10). Be careful, though, because é-is not always astandalone prefix, for example: é pouse, wife, spouse (line 16).
We know that surnames do not take aplural s (lesson note 5); neither do first names. Nous avons deux Robert dans le studio ce soir, We have two Roberts in the studio with us this evening.

Prefixes are used, among other things, to form negative adjectives (constant → inconstant, ré aliste → irré aliste, traiter → maltraiter), to express adegree of intensity (estimer → sous-estimer, line 3), and to denote repetition (examiner → ré examiner - see lesson section 2).

If the impersonal pronoun on follows aword ending in a vowel, especially qui, que and ou/où, we sometimes add l' to facilitate pronunciation (... où l'on habite rather than... où on habite, for example). This is generally used only in formal written language or by careful speakers.
Here are some more examples of the imperative use of the subjunctive: Vive les Bretons (lesson 57), Long live the Bretons. Qu'il parte immé diatement, Let him (or He should) leave immediately.

This is the past simple tense, or passé simple. Equivalent in meaning to the passé composé, it is used almost exclusively in written French. The conjugation for regular -er verbs, such as passer, to pass (or spend time) is: je passai, tu passas, il/elle passa, nous passâ mes, vous passâ tes, ils/elles passè rent. Thus Elle passa sa jeunesse en Autriche is identical in meaning to Elle apassé sa jeunesse en Autriche → She spent her youth in Austria.
The passé simple of faire is je fis, tu fis, il/elle fit, nous fî mes, vous fî tes, ils/elles firent.
The passé simple of ê tre is very irregular: je fus, tu fus, il/elle fut, nous fû mes, vous fû tes, ils/elles furent.

une linotte is a linnet, and the expression avoir/ê tre une tê te de linotte means to be abird brain. Aless pejorative equivalent is avoir la tê te en l'air / ê tre tê te en l'air ("to have / to be (one's) head in the air"). Il oublie toujours tout, Carl. Il avraiment la tê te en l'air, Carl always forgets everything. He's areal scatterbrain.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Born in Austria in 1755, Marie-Antoinette de Habsbourg-Lorraine married the heir-apparent (Le Dauphin -though the word also means dolphin) to the French throne, Louis-Auguste, later Louis XVI. Loved and hated in equal measure, she was acontroversial figure who, despite her lavish expenditures - which earned her the nickname Madame Déficit - was possibly more sinned against than sinning. It is popular myth that, when informed that the people were starving for want of bread, she answered Alors qu'ils mangent de la brioche (usually translated as Let them eat cake, although la brioche is akind of sweet pastry). Cited by Rousseau, the phrase was attributed to"une grande princesse"and may be actually have been the author'sown invention. Marie-Antoinette met her end on the guillotine in 1793. Productive phase: 43rd lesson

notes.content: This lesson contains anumber of words, such as munitions, combats and ré volution, that are identical or remarkably similar to the English words derived from them. Before using these loan words in spoken French, always check the pronunciation because the differences between the two languages can be considerable (for example, the double sin passion / passion is pronounced as asibilant in French rather than [sh] in English).

une fortune, afortune (lesson line 27), is the root of the adjective phrase de fortune, meaning makeshift or improvised: J'ai un bureau de fortune dans mon salon, Ihave amakeshift office in my living room. By extension the phrase means chance (i.e. unplanned): Gilles n'est pas un vé ritable ami, c'est un compagnon de fortune, Gilles isn'treally a friend, he's achance companion.

un bilan is afinancial term meaning abalance sheet (aka astatement of financial position). The underlying notion of assessment is found in many contexts, such as un bilan de santé, amedical checkup ("health statement"). The word is also used in news reports about injuries or fatalities: Le bilan de l'accident est de trois morts et deux blessé es, The accident resulted in three dead and two injured. Amuch broader meaning, as in line 2, is an outcome, a result.

la hauteur, height (lesson line 8), is another example of anoun used in afigurative expression: ê tre à la hauteur, to be up to or equal to (a situation, etc.): Nos athlè tes paralympiques se sont montré s à la hauteur du dé fi, Our Paralympic athletes proved equal to the challenge.

The past simple of grandir and other regular -ir verbs is: je grandis, tu grandis, il/elle grandit, nous grandî mes, vous grandî tes, ils/elles grandirent. We saw the le passé simple of regular -er verbs in the previous lesson.

The past simple of descendre and other regular -re verbs is identical to that of regular -ir verbs: je descendis, tu descendis, il/elle descendit, nous descendî mes, vous descendî tes, ils/elles descendirent.

We know that soit is the third person singular subjunctive of ê tre (see lesson note and lesson note for the full conjugation). But in line 16, it is an invariable adverb, and the final tis pronounced. In aformal register, soit is used like the English phrase Be that as it may, or, less formally, Very well. Cette brioche est chè re, soit, mais elle est dé licieuse ! This brioche may be expensive, but it'sso good! (Be careful not to confuse this adverbial usage with the conjunction soit... soit, lesson line 7.)

dé boucher is another example of aprefixed verb: boucher means to block (up): L'é vier est bouché ; il faut le dé boucher, The sink is blocked; it needs unblocking. But it also has an intransitive form. With de, it means to emerge or come out from, whereas with sur, the meaning is to lead, to open out into or run into: La rue dé bouche sur une grande vallé e, The road runs into abig valley.

Yet another use of the versatile word tant (first seen in lesson note in the phrase tant que), this time in amore literary context. In aformal register, tant is used at the beginning of adescriptive clause to explain what precedes it. In many cases, it can be translated simply by because: Il é tait impossible de courir, tant il yavait de monde dans la rue, It was impossible to run because there were so many people in the street.

The regular verb emporter, formed from em- ("away,"as in emmener, lesson note 7) and porter, to carry, means to take away, carry off, etc. Une grande pizza s'il vous plaî t - À manger sur place ou à emporter ? Alarge pizza please - To eat here or to take away? By extension, emporter can mean to get the upper hand, to prevail: C'est le systè me le plus simple qui afini par l'emporter, It was the simplest system that prevailed.

title: Les inconvénients du travail à domicile

dialogue.french: Au secours ! Qu'est-ce que j'ai fichu ?
dialogue.english: Help! What have I done?

dialogue.french: Je faisais des tableaux tranquillement avec mon tableur quand je me suis arrêté pour chercher à manger à la cuisine.
dialogue.english: I was quietly making spreadsheets when I stopped to look for something to eat in the kitchen.

dialogue.french: Au retour, je me suis remis devant l'écran, et patatras ! Panne totale.
dialogue.english: When I came back, I sat down in front of the screen, and crash! Total breakdown.

dialogue.french: Maintenant, rien ne marche : ni l'ordinateur, ni le wifi, ni le clavier, ni la prise, rien de rien.
dialogue.english: Now, nothing works: not the computer, not the wifi, not the keyboard, not the plug, nothing at all.

dialogue.french: Aïe ! C'est embêtant. Mais tu aurais dû faire plus attention —
dialogue.english: Ouch! That's annoying. But you should have paid more attention —

dialogue.french: ou plus de ménage : t'as vu le fouillis dans ton bureau ?

dialogue.french: Mais par où commencer le rangement quand tout est sens dessus dessous ?
