dialogue.english: That's not true! There's just a little bit of disorder, that's all, two or three things out of place.

dialogue.french: Je l'aurais rangé hier si j'avais eu le temps mais je travaillais contre la montre.

dialogue.french: À ta place, j'aurais fait le ménage tous les jours. Comme ça tu n'aurais pas eu ce problème.
dialogue.english: In your place, I would have cleaned every day. That way you wouldn't have had this problem.

dialogue.french: Comment tu vas faire pour t'en sortir ? Tu n'es ni électricien, ni réparateur informatique.

dialogue.french: Tu aurais pu demander à Driss, c'est un as de l'ordinateur. Il aurait remis tout en ordre en moins de deux.
dialogue.english: You could have asked Driss, he's a computer whizz. He would have put everything back in order in no time.

dialogue.french: Mais il est parti ce matin à Toulouse pour assister à un atelier.

dialogue.french: Zut ! Si j'avais su, je l'aurais appelé sur le champ mais je pensais qu'il était toujours dans le coin.
dialogue.english: Damn! If I'd known, I would have called him right away but I thought he was still around.

dialogue.french: Je suis certain qu'il serait venu tout de suite si je lui avais demandé. Il est très serviable.
dialogue.english: I'm sure he would have come right away if I'd asked him. He's very helpful.

dialogue.french: Quand même, il aurait pu me dire qu'il partait et qu'il n'était pas disponible !
dialogue.english: Still, he could have told me he was leaving and that he wasn't available!

dialogue.french: Là, tu te livres à ton passe-temps favori : te plaindre après coup. Sniff !
dialogue.english: Now you're indulging in your favourite pastime: complaining afterwards. Sniff!

dialogue.french: Et toi, tu me critiques toujours : « T'aurais dû faire ci, tu n'aurais pas dû faire ça ». Et patati et patata.
dialogue.english: And you, you always criticise me: 'You should have done this, you shouldn't have done that.' And blah blah blah.

dialogue.french: Peut-être bien, mais j'aurais été contente si tu m'avais appelée. J'aurais pu t'aider.
dialogue.english: Maybe so, but I would have been pleased if you'd called me. I could have helped you.

dialogue.french: Comment cela ? Toi non plus, tu n'es pas un crack de l'informatique, que je sache.
dialogue.english: How so? You're not exactly a computer whizz either, as far as I know.

dialogue.french: Peut-être pas, et je n'aurais pas su réparer l'équipement. Mais j'ai de bons yeux et je sais regarder.
dialogue.english: Maybe not, and I wouldn't have known how to fix the equipment. But I have good eyes and I know how to look.

dialogue.french: Ta machine est débranchée : tu as dû te prendre les pieds bêtement dans le cordon d'alimentation.
dialogue.english: Your machine is unplugged: you must have stupidly caught your feet in the power cord.

notes.content: We know that les secours means the emergency services (Culture Note, lesson 60). The exclamation Au secours ! is the equivalent of Help! (The imperative of aider, to help, can be added: Au secours ! Aidez-moi !) The corresponding verb is secourir, to help, assist or, in some contexts, to rescue (lesson line 21). S'il n'avait pas é té secouru par les pompiers, il serait mort, If he hadn'tbeen rescued by the fire brigade, he would have died.
See lesson note 6.

French has an arsenal of onomatopoeia and exclamations. Patatras ! is the equivalent of Boom! (also used in French, though spelled Boum !). Et patati et patata (line 19) means and so on and so forth, while the loan word Sniff ! (line 18), imitating asnuffling sound, is the equivalent of boo-hoo.

aurais dû; here is the past conditional, first seen in lesson line 13. It is formed with the present conditional of avoir or ê tre and the past participle, which, as usual, agrees in number and gender.

The regular verb fouiller to search, rummage for, etc. can be both transitive - La police ne nous apas fouillé s à l'entré e du bâ timent, The police didn'tsearch us at the building entrance - and intransitive, J'ai fouillé dans mes poches, Irummaged in my pockets. The derived noun is une fouille, a search, but the related (singular) noun un fouillis means a jumble, a mess, etc.
See lesson note 8.

Of course, the grammatically correct form is ce n'est pas vrai, but, in this and other exclamations, the ne is often dropped in colloquial spoken French. Since the text of this lesson is atranscription of a dialogue, we have imitated the natural speech pattern to reproduce what you would hear. For example, in line 6, we see t'as vu le fouillis instead of tu as vu, and in line 19, t'aurais instead of tu aurais.

The pronominal verb se sortir means to extricate oneself, to get out of. Le pays s'est sorti difficilement de la crise é conomique, The country emerged with difficulty from the economic crisis. The direct object is replaced by en if it is clear or understood, particularly where the meaning is to manage, cope, get by: Comment t'en sors-tu sans moi, ché rie ? - Je m'en sors trè s bien, merci ! How are you managing without me, darling? - I'mgetting by very nicely, thank you!

Two words in this lesson will be familiar to English speakers and have more or less the same meaning. Un as, an ace, can be used literally (l'as de pique -note the singular-the ace of spades) or figuratively (C'est un as du bricolage, He'san ace DIY-er). Un crack, imported from English, means the same thing: C'est un crack de l'ordinateur, He's acomputer whizzkid. (Another borrowing is le crack, crack cocaine.)

sache, the first and third person singular subjunctive of savoir (see lesson note 1), is found in the expression... que je sache (an ellipsis of pour autant que je sache, insofar as I know), placed at the end of anegative phrase, just like... as far as I know,... that I'maware of, etc. The negative is pas que je sache: Est-ce qu'il est arrivé ? - Pas que je sache, Has he arrived? - Not that I'maware of.

notes.content: In contrast to English, the initial pin Greek-origin French words such as psychiatre is pronounced, hence [pseekee-ahtr].

l'actualité, current affairs, also means news, while les actualité s is anews broadcast/bulletin. On the TV and online, the latter is called le journal té lé visé, or"televised newspaper,"often abbreviated simply to le JT. Each item in the bulletin is called un titre, atitle or, here, a headline.

The regular verb dé rober has more or less the same meaning as voler, to steal (lesson note 1) but includes the notion of stealth, like to purloin. It always refers to the theft of objects (i.e. not personal robbery). The adjective dé robé also means concealed or hidden: un escalier dé robé, aconcealed staircase, often found in châ teaux.

In journalism, une chronique is aregular column or section in anews medium (un chroniqueur, a columnist). News-writers use an array of set phrases, including dé frayer (literally to pay or settle) la chronique, the equivalent of to make headlines. (Chronique is also an adjective, meaning chronic, une maladie chronique, achronic illness.)

Derived from the verb casser, to break, la casse means breakage, damage: Il y a toujours un peu de casse pendant un dé mé nagement, There'salways abit of breakage during a removal. By extension, la casse means damage in the broad sense: S'il n'y apas d'aide gouvernementale, il yaura de la casse dans ce secteur, Without government assistance, the industry will be hard-hit. In familiar or journalistic French, however, the noun is masculine and means a robbery, a heist, etc.

un parquet is awooden -or parquet-floor. In mediaeval times, it was the courtroom floor where magistrates would stand during a trial. Today le parquet is the rough equivalent of the public prosecutor's department, organised regionally around major cities, e.g. le parquet de Lyon. (Unlike magistrates, the justices in medieval courts were seated, assis, whence la Cour d'Assises and the English word assizes.)

une lè vre, a lip, is used in physical descriptions: J'ai les lè vres gercé es, My lips are cracked, but also in expressions, notably du bout des lè vres ("from the tip of the lips"), reluctantly, without conviction. Look alittle further, though, and we recognise asimilar expression to pay lip service to: Il n'adonné son accord que du bout des lè vres, He only paid lip-service to an agreement.

un agriculteur, a farmer, is now the accepted term for this profession, rather than un fermier. However, the latter is widely used as an adjective: les produits fermiers, fresh farm produce. (In the age of industrial agriculture, the noun un paysan, from le pays, the country, literally a peasant, and the identical adjective have returned to the language to signify small-scale, sustainable farming, l'agriculture paysanne.)

The"correct"French word for astar (movies, sports, etc.) is une vedette (lesson line 8), from the Latin verb for to see. However, many French speakers use the loan word une star (always feminine, even if the celebrity is masculine). The word can also be used as an adjective: Jean Gabin et Michè le Morgan formaient le couple star du ciné ma franç ais dans les anné es trente: Jean Gabin et Michè le Morgan were French cinema'sstar couple in the 1930s. (The word for astar as acelestial body, arestaurant accolade and other contexts is une é toile, see lesson line 5.)

brouiller means to mix, muddle, etc. Je dé teste les œufs brouillé s, Ihate scrambled eggs. So, logically, dé brouiller means to untangle. But the pronominal verb se dé brouiller means to manage, get by, etc. (i.e."unscramble"adifficult situation): Il faudra que tu te dé brouilles tout seul, You'll have to get by on your own. Yet again, context is all-important because the possible translations are very numerous. (The adjective dé brouillard means resourceful, smart, street-wise, etc.)

The conditional mood (lesson note 1) can be used if the information conveyed by the verb is unconfirmed or conjectural. This is common in media reports about events yet to be verified. To translate, we use the indicative along with an adverb of supposition, like reportedly or apparently: Selon un porte-parole, l'accident serait dû à une erreur humaine, According to a spokesperson, the accident is apparently due to human error.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Like their English and American counterparts, many French-language journalists rely on tried-and-tested turns of phrase when reporting the news. In addition to défrayer la chronique and disparaître dans la nature, these stock expressions include être àla Une (to be front-page news), tirer la sonnette d'alarme (ring alarm bells), caracoler en tête des sondages (to ride high in the polls), revoir sa copie (to go back to the drawing board), renverser la vapeur ("to reverse the steam,"i.e. change direction) and, most puzzlingly, aux quatre coins de l'Hexagone ("the four corners of the hexagon,"i.e. all over France, see lesson 90). notes.content: In the plural noun les mœurs, the final -scan be voiced ([muhrss]) or silent ([muhr]).

The regular verb rigoler is asynonym of rire, to laugh. Though colloquial, it is widely used in many situations: Il n'y apas de quoi rigoler. C'est triste! There'snothing to laugh about. It's sad! The derivative adjective is rigolo(te) - Ton article é tait trè s rigolo, Your article was very funny -which can also be used as a noun: Malgré son air timide, c'est un vrai rigolo, Although he seems shy, he's areally funny guy. The noun la rigolade means abit of fun / agood laugh (see line 16).

These three adjectives are synonyms for ways of provoking laughter: une histoire drô le, afunny story, une plaisanterie, ajoke (from plaisant, pleasing), and une boutade, a witticism. In amore familiar register, the standard noun for ajoke is une blague (see lesson line 11).

This lesson gives more examples of how verbs are modified by prefixes. Thus fermer, to close, becomes enfermer, to shut in, lock in: Ma fille s'est enfermé e dans sa chambre, My daughter has locked herself in her bedroom. Another, similar prefix is em-, often used to transform nouns into verbs: une poche → empocher, a pocket, to put in one's pocket. Il aempoché une commission, He pocketed a commission. And mé-has the same function as mal, indicating negativity, badness etc., like mis-in English: se fier → se mé fier, to trust, to mistrust / be wary of (line 18).

This word is a faux-ami. Une prime means abonus or subsidy (it'salso the origin of a premium). The translation is context-dependent: une prime de fin d'anné e is a year-end bonus, whereas une prime de mobilité is amobility allowance. But whatever the context, the underlying meaning is the same. However, the verb primer means to award aprize to: Le film aé té primé à Cannes, The movie was awarded aprize at the Cannes film festival.

As you should know by now, the suffix -esse is added to feminine adjectives in order to form nouns. For example: riche → la richesse, wealth; tendre → la tendresse, gentleness; vieille → vieillesse, old age. However, la grossesse means pregnancy. (Added to amasculine noun, of course, -esse creates the feminine: maî tre → maî tresse.)

The prefix a-is added to nouns, adjectives and verbs to convey movement towards aparticular state or being. Thus, folle (from fou, mad) gives us s'affoler (to lose one's head, panic), douce (from doux, gentle) → adoucir, to soften (un adoucissant, a softener). Likewise, lé gè re (from lé ger) → allé ger, to lighten. (In some cases, the initial letter of the adjective is doubled, see lesson 98).

The rules governing adjectives and nouns denoting a person'scountry of origin or their residence are quite complex. The usual endings are -ain(e): (amé ricain-e), -ais(e): (franç ais-e), -ien(ne): (parisien-ne), -ois(e): (strasbourgeois-e) and -on(ne): (breton-ne).
We know that re-is the"repeat"prefix. But since the initial hin habiller is a half-vowel, the eis omitted: Rhabillez-vous, Put your clothes back on, Get dressed again.

la peste, the plague, is used in idiomatic expressions with two verbs: é viter quelqu'un comme la peste, to avoid someone like the plague, and se mé fier de quelqu'un comme de la peste, to be wary of / to mistrust someone. Less dramatically, la peste can also be applied to aperson who is anuisance or... a pest: Arrê te de la taquiner, tu es une vraie petite peste, Stop teasing her, you really are alittle pest.

The feminine noun les mœurs, always plural, means morals. Cette action est contraire aux bonnes mœurs, That act is contrary to good morals. (La police des mœurs is roughly the equivalent of the vice squad). More broadly, the noun means customs, manners or mores: Le gouvernement est attentif aux cultures et aux mœurs des nouveaux citoyens, The government is attentive to the cultures and mores of new citizens.

dialogue.french: Au début, nous avons travaillé sans filet car le projet était innovant et nous n'avions qu'une vision partielle du produit.
dialogue.english: At the start, we worked without a safety net because the project was innovative and we only had a partial vision of the product.

dialogue.french: Jusqu'en juin dernier, ayant fait un vrai parcours sans faute, nous avions le vent en poupe.
dialogue.english: Until last June, having had a truly faultless run, we had the wind in our sails.

dialogue.french: N'avez-vous pas placé la barre trop haut, en cherchant à remplacer quelque chose d'aussi rudimentaire qu'un pneumatique ?
dialogue.english: Haven't you set the bar too high by trying to replace something as rudimentary as a tyre?

dialogue.french: Au départ nous avons voulu brûler les étapes pour coiffer nos concurrents au poteau.
dialogue.english: At the outset we wanted to cut corners to pip our competitors at the post.

dialogue.french: Nous avions le nez dans le guidon, si bien que nous avons failli déclarer forfait au bout de six mois,
dialogue.english: We had our noses to the grindstone, so much so that we nearly threw in the towel after six months,

dialogue.french: car les choses se sont compliquées. Je pensais alors que nous avions fait un faux départ.
dialogue.english: because things got complicated. I thought then that we'd made a false start.

dialogue.french: J'étais même prêt à jeter l'éponge car le projet devenait de plus en plus coûteux.
dialogue.english: I was even ready to throw in the towel because the project was getting more and more expensive.

dialogue.french: Mais mes équipes ont refusé de changer de cap :
dialogue.english: But my teams refused to change course:

dialogue.french: chaque fois que je leur disais qu'il fallait tout arrêter, ils m'ont renvoyé dans les cordes.
dialogue.english: every time I told them we had to stop everything, they sent me back into the ropes.

dialogue.french: Je me rends compte maintenant qu'ils ont reculé pour mieux sauter.
dialogue.english: I realise now that they stepped back to jump better.

dialogue.french: Vous avez soumis un prototype au Fonds régional de capital-investissement, n'est-ce pas ?
dialogue.english: You submitted a prototype to the Regional Venture Capital Fund, didn't you?

dialogue.french: Oui. Mais il a botté en touche, sous prétexte que les fonds nécessaires n'étaient plus disponibles
dialogue.english: Yes. But it dodged the issue, on the pretext that the necessary funds were no longer available

dialogue.french: car un autre projet similaire était plus avancé que le nôtre.
dialogue.english: because another similar project was more advanced than ours.

dialogue.french: Ça alors ! Qu'avez-vous fait ?
dialogue.english: Well, well! What did you do?

dialogue.french: Rebelote. Nous avons modifié légèrement le dossier et l'avons présenté à nouveau,
dialogue.english: Same again. We slightly modified the file and submitted it again,

dialogue.french: mais cette fois-ci au Ministère de l'innovation.
dialogue.english: but this time to the Ministry of Innovation.

dialogue.french: Là, nous avons visé en plein dans le mille ! Le ministre ne pouvait pas rester sur le banc sans rien faire.
dialogue.english: There, we hit the bull's eye! The minister couldn't stay on the bench doing nothing.

dialogue.french: Maintenant que nos résultats initiaux sont convaincants, la balle est dans leur camp.
dialogue.english: Now that our initial results are convincing, the ball is in their court.

dialogue.french: Et je suis sûr que nous allons tirer notre épingle du jeu. C'est la dernière ligne droite !
dialogue.english: And I'm sure we'll pull our pin out of the game (come out on top). It's the final straight!

dialogue.french: Alors ça, c'est formidable !
dialogue.english: Well, that's fantastic!

dialogue.french: On a failli vous mettre KO, mais vous avez encaissé les coups. Chapeau !
dialogue.english: We nearly knocked you out, but you took the punches. Hats off!

notes.content: Like psychiatre and its derivatives (lesson 96), the initial pin words beginning with pn-is voiced. For example, to pronounce pneu, start by saying [puh-nuh], then gradually shorten the first vowel sound and run it into the p: [p-nuh]. The same applies, of course, for pneumatique.
une pousse is ashoot or sprout (des pousses de bambou, bean sprouts). But the term une jeune pousse was coined to describe anewly formed company, in order to avoid the loan word une start-up.

mettre au point has the same notion of precision as in faire le point (lesson note 3). In photography, it means to focus. But in everyday French, the meaning is much broader: to develop, finalise, perfect, etc. and the translation changes with the context: Nous allons mettre au point de nouvelles formes d'é nergie respectueuses de l'environnement, We are going to develop new, environmentally friendly forms of energy. Don'tconfuse the past tense (mis au point) with the feminine noun la mise au point, development, finalisation, etc.

un dispositif (from disposer, to arrange) literally means an arrangement or layout. By construction, it refers to amechanism or device (un dispositif de pointage, apointing device,"mouse"). But the word is widely used in the media and advertising as ablanket term for all kinds of plans, systems, arrangements, etc. Un dispositif d'assurance can be an insurance system, scheme, measure (or set of measures), etc.

The adjective pneumatique has the same meaning as its English cognate, but also means inflatable (un matelas pneumatique, an air bed). As a noun, it means atyre and is almost always contracted to un pneu: Ma voiture n'est pas é quipé e de pneus neige, My car isn'tfitted with snow tyres.

The intensifier si bien que indicates an outcome (so that, with the result that) described in asubordinate clause: Elle est arrivé e en retard, si bien qu'elle amanqué le dé but du film, She arrived and, as a result, missed the beginning of the movie. (In an elevated register, tant et si bien que is used, with no change in meaning.)

failli, the past participle of faillir (the origin of to fail), is used with an infinitive to express the idea of very nearly: Nous avons failli partir avant la fin, We very nearly left before the end. If you hear failli, always listen out for the following verb to find out what was almost done!

Ç a alors ! ("that then") is an exclamation of surprise or disbelief, like Goodness! or How about that! Used disapprovingly, it means Well, really! Finalement, il n'est pas venu à la fê te, malgré ses promesses.- Ç a, alors ! - In the end, he never came to the party, despite his promises. - Well really! Here, it'sthe tone rather than the context that determines the meaning. Don'tconfuse this exclamation with Alors ç a... generally followed by c'est and a qualifier, which means simply Now that... Alors ç a, c'est formidable ! Now that'sreally good.

la belote is avery popular French card game. Belote and Rebelote are the announcements made by aplayer taking two consecutive tricks. In colloquial speech, rebelote means something like here we go again, the same thing, etc. Deux heures pour aller au boulot le matin, et rebelote le soir pour rentrer, Two hours to get to work in the morning and the same in the evening to get home. (In"standard"French... et la mê me chose le soir, etc.)

KO or K-O, pronounced [ka-oh], is a direct, untranslated import from the world of boxing. Le poids lourd tunisien agagné par KO, The Tunisian heavyweight won by a knockout. Outside the ring, ê tre KO means to be worn out, shattered: Aprè s une journé e entiè re avec les gamins, je suis KO, After awhole day with the kids, I'm exhausted.

The expression tirer un coup de chapeau à means to take one'shat off to, i.e. congratulate, acknowledge, etc. The expression is usually shortened simply to Chapeau ! or, in some cases, Chapeau bas ! (as if bowing deeply with hat in hand). While sometimes translatable by hats-off or hat-tip to, the actual choice of word or term will be context-driven (Well done!, Nice one!, etc.).

dialogue.french: Qu'est-ce qu'il y a, Driss ? Tu as l'air complètement KO. Ça ne va pas ?
dialogue.english: What's up, Driss? You look completely KO. Are you okay?

dialogue.french: Si si, mais tout est sens dessus dessous en ce moment. J'ai le nez dans le guidon depuis cinq jours parce que j'écris un article sur les Dauphins.
dialogue.english: Yes, but everything is topsy-turvy at the moment. I've had my nose to the grindstone for five days because I'm writing an article about the Dolphins.

dialogue.french: Cette équipe de foot dont le capitaine, Dulong, a disparu dans la nature en 1980 ?
dialogue.english: That football team whose captain, Dulong, disappeared into the wild in 1980?

dialogue.french: Je m'en souviens bien. C'est une histoire qui a défrayé la chronique à l'époque.
dialogue.english: I remember it well. It's a story that made the headlines at the time.

dialogue.french: C'est vrai, elle a fait couler beaucoup d'encre mais, d'après moi, on n'a jamais su toute la vérité.
dialogue.english: It's true, it generated a lot of ink, but in my opinion, we never knew the whole truth.

dialogue.french: Je n'ai pas réussi à parler avec Dulong, ou, plutôt, il a exigé une somme faramineuse pour une interview.
dialogue.english: I didn't manage to speak with Dulong, or rather, he demanded a fabulous sum for an interview.

dialogue.french: Mais son ancien agent, Jacques Cartier, lui, a donné son accord tout de suite. Bingo !
dialogue.english: But his former agent, Jacques Cartier, gave his agreement right away. Bingo!

dialogue.french: Je pensais qu'il allait accepter du bout des lèvres, mais pas du tout ! Il en avait très envie. J'aurais dû m'en méfier, tant il était enthousiaste.
dialogue.english: I thought he'd accept half-heartedly, but not at all! He really wanted to. I should have been wary, he was so enthusiastic.

dialogue.french: Je lui posais des questions vachement précises mais, à chaque fois, il bottait en touche. Il me racontait la vérité, soit. Mais sa vérité à lui !
dialogue.english: I asked him really precise questions but each time he dodged the issue. He told me the truth, sure. But his version of the truth!

dialogue.french: Tu aurais dû me demander de t'accompagner. « Au secours ! J'ai besoin d'aide ! »
dialogue.english: You should have asked me to come with you. 'Help! I need help!'

dialogue.french: Je serais venue tout de suite. Avec des mecs comme ça, c'est toujours le plus fort qui l'emporte.
dialogue.english: I would have come right away. With guys like that, it's always the strongest who wins.

notes.content: Le passé simple: Le passé simple, or passé historique, is almost never used in everyday conversation or communication but is worth learning in order to be able to read novels, non-fiction and, in some cases, the media. Known in English as the past historic or the preterite, the tense has exactly the same function as le passé composé. 1.1 Formation: To form the past historic, remove the infinitive markers from the verb (-er, -ir, -re) and add the following endings: fermer: je fermai, tu fermas, il/elle ferma, nous fermâ mes, vous fermâ tes, ils/elles fermè rent. finir: je finis, tu finis, il/elle finit, nous finî mes, vous finî tes, ils/elles finirent. descendre: je descendis, tu descendis, il/elle descendit, nous descendî mes, vous descendî tes, ils/elles descendirent. Note that -ir and -re verbs share the same endings. Of course, there are several irregular forms. Here are the main verbs: ê tre: je fus, tu fus, il/elle fut, nous fû mes, vous fû tes, ils/elles furent. avoir: j'eus, tu eus, il/elle eut, nous eû mes, vous eû tes, ils/elles eurent. faire: je fis, tu fis, il/elle fit, nous fî mes, vous fî tes, ils/elles firent. In all three cases, the initial vowel of the first and second persons plural takes a circumflex. However, don'tconfuse fut with fû t, the (increasingly rare) imperfect subjunctive, or with the noun un fû t, meaning, among other things, a barrel: Vin é levé en fû t de chê ne, Wine aged in oak barrels, used much more frequently. 1.2 Use: The passé simple is used to describe a completed, discrete action in the past that has no link to or is unimportant in the present: Elle fut choisie par le roi, qui l'é pousa. She was chosen by the king, who married her. Toute la Cour fit un grand banquet. The entire court held ahuge banquet. Le roi et sa reine eurent quatre enfants ensemble. The king and his queen had four children together. But despite the"historic"tag, the tense is not confined to history books. Nowadays, most young French speakers learn only the third person singular and plural; and most contemporary authors narrate using le passé composé and le pré sent historique (lesson note 2), prompting some grammarians to predict the imminent demise of le passé simple. Even so, abasic knowledge of how to conjugate the main verbs in this tense is important. 1.3 Differences with English: All the actions described with le passé simple are completed, whereas repeated actions in the past require the imperfect. In English, though, we can use the past simple in both cases. Although the actions described with le passé simple are completed, they are not necessarily short.

Use of affixes: Throughout this course, we have seen how prefixes and suffixes modify the meanings of many verbs. Some of these are obvious because they are also used in English (for example, visiter → revisiter, to visit → to revisit). But English also uses phrasal verbs to the same effect. So chausser, dé chausser is translated as to put on / take off shoes. This type of construction is not possible in French, which has no equivalent of these verb-preposition/adverb constructions. In addition, whereas English has a diglossic, or dual-context, vocabulary, consisting of formal Graeco-Latin and informal Anglo-Saxon words, such as regal and kingly (see lesson section 4) French does not. So, for example, amé liorer can be translated as to improve, to make better or to ameliorate. This is why it is so important to identify the correct register in French: knowing the meaning of aword is not necessarily the same as knowing how and where to use it. Here is an overview of some of the main prefixes and suffixes that we have seen so far. 2.1 Prefixes: a-/an-negation: moral → amoral; a- / an-movement or direction: doux → adoucir; dé / dé s-undo, separate: boucher → dé boucher; é-movement toward/away: loin → é loigner; em-movement into: mé nage → emmé nager; en-change/movement to: dette → s'endetter; com- / con-together: pâ tir → compassion; im-/in-negation: mobile → immobile; mal-bad: heureux → malheureux; mé-negative: se fier → se mé fier; pro-movement toward: jeter → projeter; sous-under: payer → sous-payer; super-above: poser → superposer. 2.2 Suffixes: -aille result of an action: se battre → bataille; -ateur / -atrice person performing an action: pré senter → pré sentateur / pré sentatrice; -â tre approximation, -ish: bleu → bleuâ tre; -er/è re profession: boulange → boulanger / è re; -erie shop: boucher → boucherie; -é e result of an action: rentrer → la rentré e; -esse noun derived from adjective: gentil → gentillesse; -ier / iè re profession: police → policier; -ment result of an action: abonner → abonnement; -ure result of an action: brû ler → brû lure. Some of these suffixes do several jobs, but the context will almost always clarify the function if not provide the precise meaning. Spelling: In many cases, when aprefix is added, the initial consonant of the root word has to be doubled: a + lé ger → allé ger. Likewise, the initial cof most words is doubled: a + calme → accalmie. Six consonants are never doubled (h, j, q, v, w, x), while five others double only rarely (b, d, g, k, z).

The past conditional - Conditionnel passé: The past conditional (Iwould have bought/come) is relatively straightforward. It comprises the conditional of the verb'susual past auxiliary (avoir, ê tre), and its past participle: acheter: j'aurais acheté, tu aurais acheté, il/elle aurait acheté, nous aurions acheté, vous auriez acheté, ils/elles auraient acheté. venir: je serais venu/e, tu serais venu/e, il/elle serait venu/e, nous serions venus/-ues, vous seriez venus/-ues, ils/elles seraient venus/-ues. In afull conditional sentence (Iwould have... if you had..., etc.), the second verb is in the pluperfect (lesson note 4), as in English: Je serais venu si tu m'avais invité. Iwould have come if you had invited me. The negative and interrogative forms follow the usual rules: Si j'avais su, je ne serais pas venu. Iwould never have come if Ihad known. Est-ce que tu serais / Serais-tu venu si tu avais su ? Would you have come if you had known? The past conditional, like the present, can be used to talk about apossible action: Aurais-tu oublié quelque chose ? Might you have forgotten something? More idiomatically, it is frequently used in the media when reporting on events that have not yet been confirmed. The English equivalent in this case is generally the present perfect tense with aconjectural adverb: L'accident aurait fait deux morts, The accident has apparently/reportedly caused two deaths. or, more idiomatically, Two people have apparently/reportedly died in the accident.

Gentilics: The rules on the formation of gentilics are quite complex, especially those governing towns and cities. Country adjectives are more straightforward. Rather than along explanation, here is alist of some of the most common masculine and feminine forms, organised by their endings. Remember that, unlike English, gentilic adjectives do not take an initial capital letter but agree in number and gender with their noun. Suffix -ain/aine: l'Amé rique → Amé ricain(e) (American); la Jamaï que → Jamaï cain(e) (Jamaican); le Mexique → Mexicain(e) (Mexican). Suffix -ais/aise: l'Angleterre → Anglais(e) (English); l'É cosse → É cossais(e) (Scottish); la France → Franç ais(e) (French); le Portugal → Portugais(s) (Portuguese). Suffix -ois/oise: la Chine → Chinois(e) (Chinese); le Danemark → Danois(e) (Danish); la Suè de → Sué dois(e) (Swedish). Suffix -ien/ienne: l'Australie → Australien(ne) (Australian); le Canada → Canadien(ne) (Canadian); l'Inde → Indien(ne) (Indian); l'Italie → Italien(ne) (Italian). The"official"gentilic for Les É tats-Unis is É tatsunien but this is rarely used. The most common gentilic for le Royaume-Uni is Britannique (British), although many French-speakers persist in using Anglais for all four UK countries.

Idioms (3): Sports: All the idioms in lesson are related to sports. Some have direct (or almost direct) English equivalents, while others are not immediately obvious. avoir le nez dans le guidon (Cycling):"to have one'snose in the handlebars": to be totally immersed in what one is doing. avoir le vent en poupe (Sailing):"to have the wind on the stern": to have the wind in one'ssails i.e. to be on a roll. botter en touche (Rugby):"to boot in touch": to kick into touch, to sidestep an issue. brû ler les é tapes (Cycling):"to burn steps/stages": to race ahead or to cut corners. changer de cap (Sailing):"to change cape": to change course or direction. coiffer au poteau (Horse racing):"to do hair at the post": to pip at the post. encaisser les coups (Boxing):"to encash blows": to roll with the punches. faire un parcours sans faute (Horse racing):"to do acourse without fault": to do/get everything right. jeter l'é ponge (Boxing):"to throw the sponge": to throw in the towel. placer la barre haut (Athletics):"to place the bar high": to set ahigh standard. reculer pour mieux sauter (Athletics):"to move back in order to jump better": to make astrategic withdrawal or to put off the inevitable. renvoyer dans les cordes (Boxing):"to send back in the ropes": to be thrown on the ropes, to put someone (back) in their place. tirer son é pingle du jeu (Game):"to pull one'spin from the game": to emerge unscathed or to get out of atight spot. viser plein dans le mille (Archery):"to aim fully in the thousand": to score a bull's-eye. Now look back at lesson to review these expressions in context.

dialogue.french: Tu aurais pu me faire signe ou me texter : c'est la moindre des choses, entre amis.
dialogue.english: You could have given me a sign or texted me: it's the least you can do, between friends.

dialogue.french: Ça fait des semaines que tu devais m'appeler mais tu n'as pas fait le moindre effort.
dialogue.english: It's been weeks since you were supposed to call me but you haven't made the slightest effort.

dialogue.french: Bon, passons. Quoi de neuf ? Qu'est-ce que tu deviens ?
dialogue.english: Right, let's move on. What's new? What have you been up to?

dialogue.french: Moi et mes associés travaillons depuis des mois sur quelque chose d'hyper-sensible.
dialogue.english: Me and my partners have been working for months on something hyper-sensitive.

dialogue.french: Quel genre de chose ? Pas le projet dont tu m'as parlé dernièrement ?
dialogue.english: What kind of thing? Not the project you told me about recently?

dialogue.french: Non, pas celui-là. Un autre, qui n'a rien à voir avec ça.
dialogue.english: No, not that one. Another one, which has nothing to do with that.

dialogue.french: Dès que nous aurons finalisé les derniers détails, et quand j'aurai complété le dossier,
dialogue.english: As soon as we've finalised the last details, and when I've completed the file,

dialogue.french: je pourrai t'en parler plus longuement. Pour l'instant, je ne peux te donner que les grandes lignes.
dialogue.english: I'll be able to tell you more about it. For now, I can only give you the broad outlines.

dialogue.french: Vas-y ! Je suis tout ouïe.
dialogue.english: Go ahead! I'm all ears.

dialogue.french: Te souviens-tu du concours Concevons la ville de demain dont tout le monde parle depuis un an ?
dialogue.english: Do you remember the Design Tomorrow's City competition that everyone's been talking about for a year?

dialogue.french: Bien sûr que je m'en souviens ! Et alors ?
dialogue.english: Of course I remember! And so?

dialogue.french: Disons que nous avons un certain avantage par rapport à nos concurrents.
dialogue.english: Let's say we have a certain advantage over our competitors.

dialogue.french: Nous avons tout pensé dans les moindres détails, contrairement à eux.
dialogue.english: We've thought of everything down to the smallest details, unlike them.

dialogue.french: Certains ont misé sur l'informatique — les logiciels et les technologies numériques — ainsi que les solutions haut débit.
dialogue.english: Some have bet on IT — software and digital technologies — as well as broadband solutions.

dialogue.french: Ils envisagent l'avenir sans billets ni pièces de monnaie : que de l'argent virtuel.
dialogue.english: They envision the future without notes or coins: only virtual money.

dialogue.french: D'autres portent leur attention sur une question et une seule : la circulation automobile.
dialogue.english: Others focus their attention on one question and one only: car traffic.

dialogue.french: Ils pensent que la solution miracle serait d'interdire tous les véhicules, qu'ils soient particuliers ou professionnels,
dialogue.english: They think the miracle solution would be to ban all vehicles, whether private or professional,

dialogue.french: et d'obliger tout le monde de se déplacer autrement, ou à pied, ou par les transports collectifs.
dialogue.english: and to oblige everyone to get around differently, either on foot or by public transport.

dialogue.french: Un des grands avantages, disent-ils, est qu'il n'y aura plus d'accidents de la route.
dialogue.english: One of the great advantages, they say, is that there will be no more road accidents.

dialogue.french: Et aussi, il n'y aura plus de PV !
dialogue.english: And also, there will be no more traffic tickets!

dialogue.french: J'ai le sentiment que tu ne prends pas la chose au sérieux.
dialogue.english: I get the feeling you're not taking this seriously.

dialogue.french: Mais si, je te taquinais. Que propose ton équipe ?
dialogue.english: But I am, I was teasing you. What does your team propose?

dialogue.french: Nous avons une solution radicale pour s'attaquer aussi bien à la circulation qu'à la pollution :
dialogue.english: We have a radical solution to tackle both traffic and pollution:

dialogue.french: nous allons construire les villes à la campagne, où l'air est plus pur.
dialogue.english: we're going to build cities in the countryside, where the air is purer.

notes.content: The adjective moindre, meaning less, lesser, least, is used as acomparative or asuperlative and also in set expressions: Merci pour votre aide ! - C'est la moindre des choses, Thanks for your help! - That'sthe least Icould do. Being an adjective, it agrees with the noun: les moindres dé tails (line 13).

The first person plural of passer (lesson note 10) is used as astandalone imperative expression meaning Let'smove onto something else, Let'ssay no more. Le travail n'est pas trè s bien fait mais, bon, passons ("let's pass"): The job hasn'tbeen done well, but let'ssay no more about it.

Here is another idiomatic expression, with the verb devenir, to become. Qu'est-ce que tu deviens / vous devenez ? ("what are you becoming") How are you doing? / What have you been up to? If anoun is used instead of a pronoun, it comes directly after the verb: Que devient Richard ? What's Richard up to? In the past tense, however, the interrogative Qu'est-ce qu'il est devenu ? has the same meaning as its English equivalent: What became of him? As always, the context (and tense) are vital clues.

French uses voir (instead of faire) in the expression n'avoir rien à voir, have nothing to do with. Mon mari n'arien à voir avec cette affaire, My husband has nothing to do with this business. The expression Ç a n'arien à voir, often shortened to Rien à voir, is a rejoinder, meaning That'sbeside the point / That's irrelevant.

Here is the futur anté rieur, or future perfect, composed of the future auxiliary and the past participle. Similar in construction to its English equivalent, this tense describes afuture event in terms of being completed. J'aurai pris ma dé cision avant ce soir, Iwill have taken my decision before this evening. Like the simple future, it is used after time conjunctions (quand, lorsque, dè s que, etc.), whereas English uses the present perfect: Je viendrai te voir dè s que j'aurai terminé cet exercice, Iwill come to see you as soon as Ihave finished this exercise. See lesson section 2.

The feminine noun l'ouï e means hearing (it is related to l'oreille, ear, lesson line 3). The word is often used in the expression ê tre tout ouï e, to be all ears. The other four senses are la vue (sight), l'odorat (smell, masc.), le toucher (touch) and le goû t (taste).

Like many French abstract nouns, l'informatique (fem.) covers abroad spectrum of meanings, in this case relating to information technology. We have seen it translated as computer, but it also refers to IT, computer science, data processing, etc. For example, France'sdata protection statute is called la loi Informatique et Liberté. (The word is also the origin of the technical English term informatics.)

Another way of saying either... or is ou... ou: Ou tu m'aimes ou tu ne m'aimes pas, Either you love me or you don't. While in English either can come before or after the noun / pronoun, in French it must come first. An alternative construction with exactly the same meaning is soit... soit (lesson line 7).

un PV is short for un procè s-verbal. In amotoring context, the initialism means aparking ticket (PV de stationnement) or speeding ticket (PV pour vitesse excessive). The full term has abroader meaning, usually astatement or a report, and, in abusiness context, the minutes of ameeting (un procè s-verbal de ré union). Despite the literal translation ("verbal trial"), the offender goes to court only if they don'tpay l'amende (fem.), the fine.

We know aussi... que as acomparative of equality or inequality: Il joue aussi bien/mal que moi, He plays as well/badly as me. However, the phrase aussi bien... que... is yet another way of saying both (lesson note 2). À cause de la panne, nous avons tout perdu, aussi bien les donné es que les logiciels, Because of the breakdown, we lost everything, both the data and the software. Emphatic pronouns can be used instead of nouns: aussi bien lui que moi, both he and I.

extras.title: Culture note
extras.content: Much of the vocabulary connected with advanced technology is imported directly from English. In information technology, however, French has succeeded in coining native words, such as un ordinateur and haut débit ("high flow,"broadband), that have taken root. But some of these terms do not always have a one-on-one equivalent. For example, un logiciel is asoftware program or package, whereas the uncountable English noun"software"would usually be rendered by a plural. She designs software, Elle conçoit des logiciels. Another example is l'informatique (see note 7). As always, it is the context that will dictate not just the term but its grammatical form. Productive phase: 50th lesson

notes.content: The suffix -phone can be used to form nouns and adjectives relating to speakers of particular languages. Thus the noun un francophone is a French-speaker, and the adjective means French-speaking: un pays francophone, acountry where French is spoken. La Francophonie is the usual title of an organisation promoting the French language internationally. For more information, visit www.francophonie.org.

bienvenu ("well come") is an adjective: un accord bienvenu, awelcome agreement. As such, when used in greetings, it agrees in number and gender: Vous ê tes le bienvenu and Soyez la bienvenue. But in the expression souhaiter la bienvenue, it is anoun and always takes a final"e": Je vais leur souhaiter la bienvenue, I'mgoing to welcome them. At the beginning of a sentence, spoken as a greeting, we always use bienvenue alone: Bienvenue dans notre nouvel appartement, Welcome to our new flat (see lesson 6).

Canadian French has adistinctive accent and vocabulary. For example, un dé panneur, meaning arepairman or mechanic in France, is aconvenience store. Some words come from old French (un char, a car, derives from the word for a cart), while others are imported from America and then -importantly-translated: un chien-chaud, ahot dog!

French is an official language in nearly countries on the African continent. Many words and expressions from these regions find their way into"official"French via mainstream dictionaries. Thus un alphabè te, aliterate person, is alogical back-formation from analphabè te, illiterate; un taxieur is alocal equivalent to un chauffeur de taxi while une essencerie (from l'essence, lesson 66) is apetrol station (rather than une station-service). Though not used in aformal register, these idioms nevertheless show that French is aliving language.

Derived from an Arabic word, une arobase is the official term for the At symbol, used in email addresses. When spelling out an address, however, some French speakers say at rather than arobase. We insist on the latter (listen to the first sentence of the first exercise).

un vasistas is afanlight or small window. The word comes from the German interrogative Was ist das?, What is it?, the gruff greeting supposedly shouted at thirsty French visitors knocking at the spy window of local taverns. Another"gallicised"loan word, this time from English, is un paquebot, an ocean liner, derived from the old term apacket boat. These, and dozens of other borrowings, show how the French vocabulary has been enriched through interactions with other languages and cultures over the centuries.

The adjectival phrase fort(e) de is widely used -usually at the beginning of a sentence-in descriptive writing to emphasise a strength, quality or advantage. Fort de son expé rience, il atout organisé, Drawing on awealth of experience, he organised everything. The actual translation will depend as always on the context because, as with many idiomatic constructions, there is no single translation.

extras.content: We hope you have enjoyed the course - but it isn'tover yet! You still have to complete the Productive Phase, from lesson 51 through to lesson 100. And, of course, you should take every opportunity to read, listen to and practise French. As we said before, Bonne continuation!
